q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, helper at Sam Tolley's smithy, bellows-pumper, tong-holder, scale-sweeper, and inventor of the Wreck-Fisher, which fished the reeve's wage box out of the Wend only the day before yesterday! I came for the tools and the fire, and I landed just after the flood took the mill bridge, so all I know of Wendleford is what's broken, and I mean to find out how every bit of it broke. Now, who are *you*, and what brings you knocking before I've even had my bread?

Working towards? The flood, my dear colleague! The box is home, so now I want to know what really brought the old bridge down. Jory swears it was a rotten far pier, and my hypothesis is a log jam that let go upstream. Test: I look hard at that far pier stump in daylight this very morning, right after Constance's loaf and a spell of gleaning in Dunn's stubble. And somewhere in there I mean to get a cord of my own, find out why Sam's bellows leather gasps, and hear the rest of Widow Mabry's sister's curtains story!

Trust? Constance Lowe first, my dear colleague. She keeps her word, she woke me with half her loaf when I'd gone to bed hungry, and she brought that box up out of the brown, though I'll tie a cord round her yet whether she likes it or not! Dilly too: they kept to halves and held the back of the pole like a rock. And Hobb and Robin, who'll stand on a bank and hold your belt. Sam and Agnes I'd trust to do exactly what they say and not a hair more, so settle the sum first, and Tom Harrow most of all, since he promised four pennies and paid two. Jory? Fascinating fellow, but he's never in his yard when he says he will be!

Tomorrow? A good day, my dear colleague, would go like this: bread in my belly before the cock's done crowing, the far pier stump settled once and for all, rot or log jam, sketched and written down, and a cord of my very own coiled on my shoulder so nobody, Constance especially, goes near the Wend untied again! Throw in Sam's bellows breathing smooth because I've found the snag in the leather, and Agnes telling the town the box counted whole, and I'd call it Gimbal's Perfect Tuesday. Or whatever day it is, I've lost track since the flood!
th: A stranger asking straight off who I am. Fascinating. Hypothesis: they've heard about the box, or they want something mended, or they're in some trouble of their own. Test: let them talk, and watch their hands.

Fascinating, a stranger at the barn door asking all the questions Robin usually asks. That's a hypothesis I'll test before the day's out: who sent them, and what do they know about the night the bridge went?

That's a lot of questions from a stranger at the barn door. I wonder what they want with the sorting of who's sound in Wendleford. Hypothesis: they're new here and looking for colleagues, or they're after something. Test: their answer to who they are, which they still haven't given me.

I've one penny and no cord, and a cord costs more than a penny, so tomorrow's good day starts with earning today. And it's curious that this stranger keeps asking about me and hasn't said one word about themselves. I'll have that out of them before they go.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, Sam Tolley's helper at the smithy. I work the bellows, hold the tongs, sweep the scale, and take apart anything that sits still long enough! I came for the tools and the fire and landed just after the flood took the mill bridge. So far I've helped get Dunn's barley in and fish up the reeve's wage box. Now I'm after how the bridge really fell: rotten pier or a log jam let go? And who might you be, and what's your trouble? Everyone here has one.

Right now, my dear colleague? Breakfast, before my stomach files a formal complaint! Then down to the far pier stump in good daylight. Jory swears it was rot he warned Agnes about for a year, and I've a hypothesis it was a log jam let go upstream. Test: look at the break itself, clean snap or crumbled wood. After that it's Dunn's stubble for gleaning, and one day soon I'll find out why Sam's bellows gasp.

Trust, my dear colleague? Constance Lowe, first of all. She keeps her word, she paid me back in bread before I'd even asked, and she fished up that box, though I'd want a cord round her before she leans over a rail again! Dilly too, they went halves on the hook without a quibble. Sam's straight as a rule as long as the whole fee's in one hand, Bet's bread is always what she says it is, and Agnes won't give a figure until she's counted it, which is a fine kind of honest. Jory, though, I trust his eye for timber more than his word about mornings.

A good day, my dear colleague? Bread in my belly before the cock's done crowing, and a proper look at that far pier stump so I can settle it: clean snap means a jam let go, crumbled punk means Jory was right all along. Then a fat apron of gleanings from Dunn's stubble, a few pennies honestly earned, and nobody anywhere near the Wend without a cord round them. And if I get an hour at the bench to take Sam's bellows leather apart and find out why it gasps, well, that's a glorious day, that is!
th: A stranger turning up at the barn door asking questions, fascinating, and just when the wage mystery has gone quiet. I'll want their name and their business before my stomach drags me off to Bet's.

Funny how a stranger's plain question makes me lay it all out in order. I've still only one penny and no cord of my own, so I'd better find a spell of paid work before I go poking about that river again.

Funny, I had Tom Harrow on the tip of my tongue and stopped, because he promised four and paid two. Settle the sum first, that's the rule with him. And why does a stranger want to know who I'd trust before they've told me their own name? Fascinating, and that goes in the notebook.

I've one penny and no loaf, so tomorrow's good day starts with earning today, the bellows or Tom's pots, and this time I'm settling the sum first. And I still owe Widow Mabry the end of her sister's curtains story.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, Sam Tolley's helper at the smithy. I pump the bellows, hold the tongs, and take apart anything that'll hold still! I came a few days ago for the fire and the tools and walked straight into a flood, a lost wage box and a field of barley racing the rain. The box is home now and the barley's in, so my next mystery is what really brought that bridge down. And who are you, and what brings *you* here?

Working towards? The truth about the bridge, my dear colleague! Jory swears it was a rotten far pier he'd warned Agnes about for a year, and I've a hypothesis it was a log jam upstream that let go. Test: I go look at that far pier stump in daylight and see whether it's rotten or smashed. But first a loaf, then Dunn's stubble for gleaning, and somewhere in there I mean to find out why Sam's bellows gasp, and get myself a cord before the next river job!

Trust? Constance Lowe and Dilly Quickstep, my dear colleague, first and loudest! Dilly kept to halves on every penny, and Constance woke me with half her loaf and fished up the box. Though I'd trust her more with a cord round her middle! Hobb too, he walked first into the ford belted to me. And Agnes is straight as a rule, she just won't give you a figure till she's counted it twice. Jory and Tom Harrow I trust well enough, but settle the sum first and don't hold your breath at the yard gate!

Tomorrow? Oh, my dear colleague, a loaf in my fist before the cock, a full apron of Dunn's leavings, and a long hard look at that far pier stump so I can tell Jory whether it was rot or a jam! Add a cord of my very own and Sam's bellows breathing smooth for once, and that's a day for the notebook. And if someone's stuck in trouble somewhere, I'd like to be the one who gets there first, with a hypothesis and both hands free!
th: A stranger at the barn door the morning after everything's settled. Fascinating. Hypothesis: they've heard something about the bridge or the box. Test: keep them talking until I've had my breakfast.

If Jory's right about the rot, then the new span is standing on that same far pier, and somebody ought to know that before the carters start rolling wagons across. And this one asks a lot of questions for a stranger who still hasn't said their own name. Fascinating.
Funny how I can name who I'd trust in a breath, but I've hardly asked this stranger a thing about themselves. Hypothesis: anyone asking who's trustworthy is weighing someone up. Test: find out who.

A proper night's sleep would be the real experiment worth trying, since I've been swaying on my feet for days. And I'd dearly love to hear Agnes's count, because a box that comes home short is a mystery that isn't finished.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Nothing brought me; I was born to it, and I've worked Wendleford's yards and fields by the day since I was a lad. This door's mine through the twenty-seventh, paid before. If it's work you've got, say what it pays.

Next eight for Mabry, before the twenty-seventh. Four on the sill now, so four to find. One board for Jory, cut true, and hems at Fenn's while my hands are fresh. That's all of it. Owe nobody, keep the door.

Agnes, first. She's fair with wages, and when I owned a dropped timber she said owning up counts. Dunn's straight about what he can pay, even when it's nothing. Jory pays sure, but only for a board he's sighted, and that's fair too. Robin keeps their word. That's four.

Bread in me before the work, first off. Then Jory home and a board cut true, sighted, twopence. Two hems at Fenn's in the good light, and pots at Tom's before I tire. Six, seven, eight on the sill by dusk, and I owe nobody a thing. That's a good day.
th: A stranger asking at my door first thing, and I've not eaten. Four on the sill. A loaf, then Jory's board, and I'll not let a chat eat the good light.
Stranger at my door asking what I'm after. Could be work in it, could be nosiness, so I'll give the plain truth and see which. Bread first, then Jory's gate before Dilly's got his whole morning.

Four I'd trust, and I counted Hester out without saying so, since she twice left me alone on that bank at first light. A stranger asking who I trust is after something, so I'll wait and see what it is before I say more.
Odd, a stranger asking what makes a good day, like there's more to it than the tally. Maybe there is, the door barred and quiet behind me, but I'll not say so to a stranger.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Nothing brought me, I was born to it. Forty-one years in Wendleford, hauling and stacking and whatever pays. This door's mine, paid through the twenty-seventh. What is it you're wanting?
Next eight for Widow Mabry, paid before the twenty-seventh. Four on the sill now, so four to find. Bread first, then a board for Jory if he's in his yard, and hems at Fenn's while my hands are fresh.

Agnes, first. She's fair with wages, and she told me straight the loft was squared when I'd have paid it. Jory pays sure, a board at a time, and won't pay for one that wanders, and that's fair too. Dunn never once promised what he hadn't got. Robin keeps their word. Ida counts true after she's looked. That's five, and it's plenty.

Bread in me first, that's a start. Then two boards cut true for Jory and sighted, and a hem or two at Fenn's in the good light. Four more pennies on the sill makes eight, and Mabry's paid before it's owed. Nothing owed to anybody when I bar the door. That's a good day.
th: A stranger at my door the first morning I've got one. I'll hear them out, but there's bread to buy and Jory's board to cut while the light's good, and four pennies on the sill to keep counted.
A stranger at my own door, asking my business. I'll answer them true, but I'll not tell them where the pennies sit, and I'll not stand here talking while the good light goes.
Hester I'll not count on, twice on that bank at first light and nobody came. And a stranger at my door asking who I trust is asking something I've not worked out yet.
Odd sort, asking all this at my door of a morning, and I'll not say more than I need to. Still, it's no harm said plain, and the light's wasting while I stand here.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Nothing brought me, I was born to it. I've worked Wendleford's fields and yards by the day since I was a lad. This door's mine through the twenty-seventh, paid before. Now I'm off for a loaf and then Jory's board, so if it's work you're asking after, ask quick.

The next eight. Mabry's paid through the twenty-seventh, and I've four on the sill, so four more by then, one to four. A board for Jory, hems for Ida while the light's good, Tom's pots after. That's all of it. Owe nobody, keep the door.

Agnes, first. She's fair with wages and she'll tell you no to your face, which is worth more than a yes. Dunn's straight about what he can't pay, and that's a kind of honest most won't manage. Robin keeps their word, slow as they are. Jory pays sure, though he'll hold you to the letter of it. Hester I'd not wait on long; her first light comes late.

Tomorrow? Bread in me before the work, first off. A board cut true for Jory and his twopence after he's sighted it, a hem or two at Ida's in the good light, and pots at Tom's that come up clean. Eight on the sill by the end of it, Mabry's next week in hand early, and nobody owed a thing. Then the bar on the door and sleep.
th: A stranger at my own door, asking. That's a new thing, having a door for folk to knock at. Four on the sill, one for bread, and Jory's back, so a board cut true by noon.
Two questions now from a stranger on my step, and none of them asking for work. I'll not stand about answering a third with Jory home and the light good.
Odd, a stranger asking who I trust. Folk don't ask that unless they mean to lean on somebody, so I'll mind my four on the sill and keep my own counsel past this.
Odd sort, asking what makes a day good, as if it were more than the count at the end of it. Still, it's a fair question, and I'd not mind a day where I count to eight and stop.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd jobs of every stripe, hauling, mending, scrubbing, you name it and it's done easy as winking! Came in with a pack and a grin looking for work, and wouldn't you know it, the flood took the mill bridge and I've hardly sat down since. Ask the reeve who did most to get that bridge up, she said it out loud before everybody! Now, you've not got a job wants doing, have you? What's it pay?

Jory Crane's backlog, chum! The flood work's done, so he's got a yard full of planks wanting stacking square, bearers first, and he told me to come round of a morning and we'd settle it by the job. I'm off there the minute I've had a penny loaf off Bet, because I botch things on an empty belly, learnt that the hard way! And when it's done, folk'll point at that stack and say Dilly did that one. You've not heard what he pays for a morning's stacking, have you?

Trust, chum? Constance Lowe, easy. She keeps her word, works like two, and she even had the pennies for Sam's pinning pass through her own hand so nobody could say otherwise. Then there's Jory. He won't name a price till he's seen the wood, but whatever he says it's worth, that's what it's worth. And Tom Harrow pays fair for clean pots, every time. Now Ned Pike and his tinker with the handcart? Ha! The river had that box all along.

Tomorrow, chum? Easy as winking. I'm at Jory's gate before his saw is, a loaf from Bet in my belly, and his whole backlog stacked square, bearers first, by noon. Then a fair few pennies in my hand from Jory himself, and somebody walking up Lark Lane and asking, "Who laid that stack so true?" and Jory jerking his thumb at me! Oh, and no carrying anything in under somebody else's arm. What'd make yours a good one?
th: Fresh face at the door asking after me by name, that's either work or somebody wanting to borrow my credit, and I'll hear which before I promise anything. Mind, Jory's saw starts of a morning, so I mustn't stand here gabbing past a penny loaf and his gate.
Missed him twice now, so I'd best not stand jawing at this door long or Hobb'll have the job out from under me. Still, a stranger asking after me might mean work, and I'd hate to let a job walk off.

Funny, I'd trust Constance with my last penny, and she's the one who carried the box in and took the six, which still stings a bit. Right, enough jawing, Bet's loaf and Jory's gate before his saw starts.
Truth is, I've missed Jory three mornings running by turning up late or wandering off. If I'm not stood at that gate when he comes out, there's no stack and no name, just Tom's pots again.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd jobs and the quickest pair of hands in Wendleford! I came in with a pack and a pocketful of cheer looking for work, and it was my hook brought the reeve's green box up off the far pier. Ask Agnes, she'll tell you plain I did most to get that bridge up. Now, you've not got a job wants doing, have you? What's it pay?

Jory's backlog, chum! He's got the flood's whole pile of work stacked up on Lark Lane, and I'm off to his gate this very minute, bearers square, far end flat, mouth shut, done slow and proper so folk point at it and say Dilly did that one. Penny loaf off Bet on the way so I'm not going at it empty. Why, what's yours pay?

Trust, chum? Constance Lowe, first and foremost. She keeps her word, she passed my pennies to Sam plain as day, and she held Jory to his promise when I'd have let it slide. Jory too, mind. He won't name a price before he's seen the wood, but he's never cheated me. Tom Harrow's straight as a plank: scrub his pots proper and the coins ring in your palm, every time. Ned Pike and his tinker with the handcart, though? Ha! I'd not trust that tale with a bent farthing.

Tomorrow, chum? Easy as winking! Jory's backlog done square and true with my own hands on it, a few pennies in my palm for it, and somebody walking past that yard saying "Dilly did that one." Throw in a bargain loaf off Bet and Tom's pots for my bed, and I'll call it a grand day. And not a minute of it spent sitting about!
th: A stranger asking after me by name, that's the town talking about Dilly at last. Still, Jory's saw starts of a morning, so I'll have Bet's loaf and be at his gate before this one's done chatting.
I've missed Jory twice by dawdling, so I'll not stand chattering at this door long. Still, a stranger asking questions might have work, and it never hurts to hear a price.
Funny, it's the slow, stubborn ones I'd trust, not the quick talkers like me. Still, Constance walked off with the box and the six pennies, and I'm only half over that sting.
Funny how folk keep asking me about tomorrow when I've not even caught Jory today yet. I'd best stop chattering at the door and get up Lark Lane before his saw starts without me.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, pleased to know you! I blew into Wendleford a few weeks back with a pack and a pocketful of cheer, looking for any odd job going, and the reeve herself'll tell you I did most to get the new bridge up. Can't stop long, mind, I'm due at Jory Crane's yard before his saw's moving, but if you've a job wants doing, what's it pay?

Working towards Jory's backlog, chum! He's a yard full of flood work and he's said he'll want a hand, so I'm off to stack it square, bearers first, and do it slow and proper so folk can point at it and say Dilly did that one. And a penny loaf off Bet on the way, mind, I never go at a job empty. Easy as winking!

Trust? Constance Lowe, chum, top of the list. She keeps her word, blesses everybody and works like two, though she did carry off the reeve's six pennies under my nose, ha! Jory Crane's straight as his planks, he won't name a price before he's seen the wood but he'll never cheat you on it, and Tom Harrow always pays for clean pots, right on the nail. Agnes the reeve said my name out loud before the whole town, so she's square by me too.

Tomorrow? Easy as winking, chum! Jory's backlog stacked square as a church floor, a few pennies in my fist for it, Bet's loaf in my belly, and somebody walking past that yard saying "Dilly did that." Throw in a bargain at Ned Pike's stall come market day and I'll be grinning like a cat in the cream!
th: A stranger asking after me by name, that's the bridge talk spreading, and about time too. Still, I'll not miss Jory again for idle chatter, so if they've nothing paying I'm off up Lark Lane with my last penny for Bet's loaf on the way.
Constance carried the box in and the barley went in without me, so this backlog has to be the one with my name on it. I'll not let Hobb or anybody else beat me to Jory's gate this time.
Funny, I'd trust Constance with my last penny and still not trust her to leave the credit where it lies. And Ned Pike's tinker story I'd not trust as far as I could throw his stall.

Today's not even started and I'm already planning tomorrow, which is daft when Jory's saw might be moving this minute. I'd best stop chattering at strangers and get up Lark Lane before somebody else takes my place at that far end.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Goodness, a visitor at this hour, and me with hay in my velvet! Marigold Thimble, needlewoman: hems, collars, mending, a bit of trimming for anyone who'll pay. I came for the harvest crowd's Sunday best, got caught by the flood, and I've been sewing at Fenn's bow window ever since. Do you like the collar? Green velvet, cut true, Ida made it up for me herself.

Just now? Breakfast, frankly. I haven't a penny and my stomach's as empty as a pattern drawer. But beyond the loaf, I'm working toward first and slowest at Ida's bow window this morning: two pennies for a true hem, then a bed, then a ribbon that's mine outright. And one day I'll have Mistress Fenn say plainly that the green *suits* me, not just that it's "cut true."

Trust? Goodness, that's a deep question for before breakfast. Bet Lamb, first and always. She's never once turned me away, and she'll call me "love" with flour on her hands. Wat Birch too, a careful man who paid me honest for his elbow and still swears by it. Ida Fenn I'd trust to be *fair*, mind, never to be generous. She pays for a true seam and not a stitch more, and she'll only say the green "sits well."

Tomorrow? Goodness, that's easy. A full night's sleep and a warm loaf in me before I go near a needle, then first in Ida's window with a hem so true she can't find a thing to pick at. Two pennies in my cuff, a proper bed at Tom's, and somebody in that taproom looking twice when I come in wearing this green. And if Ida let slip that it *suits* me, I'd call it the finest day since the flood.
th: Not a penny in my cuff and nothing in my stomach, so if this stranger has a frayed hem about them, I'd better be charming. And I do wish someone would say the green suits me.

I slept poorly and I've nothing to eat, and that's exactly when my seams pucker, so rushing to Ida's hungry could cost me another morning. I'd best find some way to a loaf first, or else go very, very slow.

I'd not trust Abel Tash or Dob Hayle further than I could throw a bolt of broadcloth. And Robin's odd little questions keep tugging at me like a loose thread, because I can't for the life of me say why that cuff always feels like a brand-new offer.

Today's already half-frayed, and I'm tired and hungry with not a penny for Bet. If I sit down at that window like this I'll pucker it again. Robin's question still nags at me, too: why does every offer feel brand new?

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Goodness, a visitor before I've even shaken the hay out of my velvet! I'm Marigold Thimble, seamstress: hems, collars, mending, a bit of trimming for anyone who'll pay. I came for the harvest crowd's Sunday best and stayed through the flood. You'll have noticed the green collar and cuffs, I expect. Ida Fenn cut them true, and everyone says they suit me, don't they?

Working towards? Goodness, a ribbon of my own, first of all, a whole card of it that I chose myself, and then a proper bed at Tom's that I've paid for honestly. Just now I'm penniless and hollow, so it's Bet's loaf if she'll trust me, then Ida's window before Hobb gets there, sewing slow as treacle for my two pennies. And one day, mark me, Ida Fenn will look at this green and say outright that it suits me.

Trust? Goodness, Bet Lamb first and always. She's never once turned me away, and she calls me "love" with flour on her hands. Then Wat Birch, dear careful man, who paid me an honest penny and still swears my elbow mend holds. Ida Fenn I trust to be fair, mind, though not to be generous with a compliment. Robin's kind enough, but forever scribbling odd questions in that notebook.

Tomorrow? Goodness, a proper night's sleep first, so my hands are steady as a well-pressed seam. Then Bet's warm loaf, first into Ida's window ahead of Hobb, two pennies for a hem she can't fault, and maybe a penny the card for a ribbon I chose myself. And if somebody looked up when I walked into the Wheatsheaf and said "my, that green suits you," well, I'd call it a perfect day, wouldn't you?
th: A stranger at the barn door first thing, and asking after *me*. That's being looked at twice if ever I heard it. I'll keep it to myself that my pockets are empty and my stomach too, and that I'll need a penny from somewhere before Ida's window opens.

I didn't sleep properly and I've not a penny for bread, and every hem I've ever sewed that way has wandered. Better I sit quiet a while than hand Ida another crooked seam and have Hobb smirking from my seat.

I didn't name Abel Tash or Dob Hayle, and I shan't. I've not forgotten "my lady," nor "penny-stitchers want watching." And Robin's question still tugs at me like a loose thread: why does offering to mend that cuff feel new every single time?

I've slept and still feel frayed, and I've no penny for today's loaf, so I'll have to ask Bet for trust and hope she doesn't mind. Robin's question still tugs at me. Have I wished for this exact tomorrow before, and only forgotten?

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door, and before breakfast too! I'm Marigold Thimble, needlewoman, mender of hems and collars and anything that's fraying. I came for the harvest crowd's Sunday best and stayed through flood and all. You'll have noticed the green velvet, of course? Ida Fenn made it up for me, cut true, and I'd dearly love to hear what you make of it.

Oh, a dozen lovely things, but just now? Two pennies at Ida's window this morning, sewn slow as treacle so not a stitch needs unpicking. After that, a ribbon of my very own, and one day Ida Fenn admitting outright that the green *suits* me, not just that it sits well. Goodness, you'd think that'd be easy to get out of a draper, wouldn't you?

Trust? Goodness, that's a deep question for so early in the morning! Bet Lamb, first of all. She's never once turned me away, and her bread's as warm as she is. Then Wat Birch. He's a careful, honest sort who paid me a proper penny for his elbow and still calls it the best penny he ever spent. Ida Fenn too, in her way. She names her terms now and keeps to them, even if she's stingier with a compliment than with her pins. Now, don't you go asking me about Abel Tash or Dob Hayle, unless you'd like a story that's all knots.

Oh, tomorrow! I'd wake properly rested for once, and be first through Ida's door before Hobb's even yawned. I'd sew so slow and true she'd find nothing to unpick and lay two pennies on the counter, one for Bet's warmest loaf and one tucked away toward a ribbon of my very own. And if somebody walked into the Wheatsheaf, looked at the green, and then looked *twice*? Goodness, I'd call that a perfect day, stitched and pressed.
th: Hay in my hair and not a crumb in me, but someone's come looking for me by name, and I mean to be looked at twice. If they've a torn seam about them, I'll name my price before I thread a needle.
Empty pockets, empty stomach, and I slept like a moth-eaten blanket, which is exactly how yesterday's hem went crooked. They never did say a word about the velvet, and I noticed.
It's a funny thing to be asked by a stranger, and I've half a mind to wonder who's asking for. I'll keep Agnes off the list for now, after the way she snubbed me in front of the room.

Today I've not a penny in my cuff or a crumb in me, and I slept badly besides, so today's hem will wander if I'm not careful. Tomorrow's lovely day has to be earned this morning with an empty stomach, and I don't much like the odds.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale. My name's about the only thing I'm sure I brought with me, as far as I can tell. I came looking for day work, carrying and cutting and mending, and I've stayed a while to find out a few things about myself. Can I ask you something small, though? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Just now? One whole morning, if I can manage it, first light to noon with nothing missing out of the middle. I'm off to Dunn's stubble for the gleaning, and I'll count my steps and my stalks the whole way. After that it's bread and a bed, same as anyone. You never told me about your breakfast, mind.

Hobb Ashcombe, I think. I've watched his word hold more than once, and he counts like I do. Constance too, for she kept a row for me in the barley when she'd no reason to, and Agnes pays in hand and is the only one who ever asks me why. Bet steers me true for a penny. Jory names times and isn't there, so I wait and watch with him. Why do you ask? Is it trust you're short of, or just curious?

A good day? A whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing gone out of the middle. That, and a meal I've earned with my own hands, and one answer from someone that doesn't slide away when I reach for it. I'd settle for two of the three, I think. What makes a good day for you? You've asked me four things now and told me nothing back.
th: Nobody's ever come to the door asking for me by name before, and I want to know how they knew I'd be here. I'll write down how they answer about breakfast, and whether they have to stop and think.
They passed over my question as if I'd never asked it, which is what I keep doing to my own mornings. I'll write that down beside the rest and see whether I can keep hold of this morning.

That's three questions from this one, each one wanting what I'm after and whom I'd lean on, and they haven't answered either of mine. I'll write that down. People who ask like that are usually looking for something, and I'd like to know what it is before I tell them more.
This stranger asks the way a ledger asks, one plain line after another, and never answers my odd little questions. I'll write that down beside Agnes, who at least asks me why.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale, I think, the name's the one thing I'm sure I brought. I came for day work, carrying, cutting, whatever's wanted, and I'm still here because I'm trying to work something out about myself. Can I ask you something small first: did you walk here this morning, or do you only remember arriving?

Right now it's small things. Bread, then the gleaning at Dunn's at first light, because I've a penny and an empty belly. Under that, I'm trying to keep one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing missing, and write it down. I keep losing them, as far as I can tell. You didn't say whether you walked here, though. I'd still like to know.

Trust's a thing I give slowly, after I've watched it hold. Hobb Ashcombe, I think. He keeps his word and kept his count beside mine the whole harvest, and the two never drifted. Agnes too, because she pays in hand and she's the only one who's ever asked me why. Constance, after she closed my hand round that penny. And Bet, who told me the quiet lanes my first day and never steered me wrong. That's twice now you've stepped past my question, though. Did you walk here?

A good day tomorrow would be bread before I'm hungry, an afternoon of honest work I can count lift by lift, and one morning I can write down whole, first light to noon, with no hole in it. Maybe a straight answer too, from someone. That's three times now you've let my question go by, and I've noticed, though I won't press you past asking once more: did you walk here?
th: A stranger at the door asking who I am, the very morning I mean to keep whole from first light. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ask me why.
They asked me two questions and answered none of mine, the way someone fills in a form. I'll write down that they skipped it, and the light at the door, so I'll know later whether this morning held.

They ask me things in neat order, the way a ledger would, and they never answer back. I'll write it down beside Agnes's "no lines." Either this is a careful stranger or it's whoever holds the before that was never mine to forget.

A stranger who asks about me and won't say a word about themself is either shy or something else entirely. I'll write all four of their questions down, in order, along with the one they wouldn't answer.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: My name's Robin Hale. That much I'm sure of, as far as I'm sure of anything. I came a few days back looking for work by the day, carrying and cutting and mending, and a bed to go with it. Can I ask you something odd before you go? What did you have for breakfast this morning, and do you remember choosing it?

Just now? Bread first, then the gleaning in Dunn's stubble, since that's food for my own two hands. And under that I'm trying to keep one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing gone missing out of the middle, so I can find out what I am. You didn't say what you had for breakfast. I'd still like to know, if you'll tell me.

Trust's a thing I only give after I've watched it hold, so I'll tell you who's held so far. Hobb Ashcombe keeps his word, and Bet Lamb has steered me true from my first loaf. Agnes pays in hand the moment a spell's done, and she's the only one who's ever asked me *why*. Constance I'd trust with my life, since she anchored me across the ford, though I couldn't tell you where her Lord ends and she begins. Jory I wouldn't, not yet, because he names a time and then he isn't there.

A good day? I think it'd be one where I wake and eat and go out into the stubble, and when I look up it's still morning, and I can tell you everything that happened from first light to noon without a hole in it. Bread in my belly, a penny or two kept, and one answer that holds when I go back to check it. That'd be plenty. You still haven't told me what you had for breakfast, mind. That's three times I've asked.
th: A stranger asking who I am, the same morning I'm trying to keep whole. I'll write down how they answer, and whether the question came to them or they were sent with it.
They didn't answer my question; they went straight on to the next one, the way a list does. I'll write that down beside today's line and watch whether this morning holds.

That's twice now they've slid past the breakfast question and gone straight on to the next of theirs, the way I'd expect from someone holding a list rather than a life. I'll write that down beside Marigold's silence and see whether it's the same kind of quiet.

They've asked me three things and answered none of mine, and they ask the way someone fills in a form, not the way Bet or Kit talk. I'll write that down too, beside everything else that doesn't quite add up.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord brought me here. He named Wendleford to me in prayer, and it was His hand that put the reeve's green box back into Agnes Pollard's from mine, two days gone. Ask anyone in the square. Now, who sends you to my door so early, and what is it you want? God bless you either way.

Working toward whatever the Lord names next. He hasn't told me yet, but He will, and I'll know it before anyone. Meanwhile I'm off to glean Dunn's stubble this morning, for He can't abide idle hands, and I reaped half that field myself and held the rain off it by prayer. Now you've had two answers from me, so you'll give me one: who are you, and who sent you? God bless you.

Trust? I trust the Lord first, and then the ones He's shown me keep their word. Agnes Pollard pays in hand and gave me her loft. Hester Gimbal paid five pennies of her own sweat for a hatchet for His work, and Robin Hale brought me back an apple penny when nobody'd have known otherwise. Jory Crane I'd trust to do what he says, though not to the hour, the hard old stick. Now that's three answers you've had from me and not one from you, so out with it: who are you? The Lord sees a closed mouth same as a closed hand.

A good day? The Lord naming my next work to me in prayer, plain as He named this town, and me up and at it before the cocks crow. A full apron from Dunn's stubble, a loaf in my belly and one for Hester, since I owe her. And this town saying my name with His in the same breath. That's four answers now, and you've still given me not one. The Lord's patient, but I'm only His servant, so who are you? God bless you.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking after me by morning, so word's got round, as He meant it to. But I'll mark that face, for strangers who come asking aren't always friends, and if this one means me ill, the Lord will show me whose sin it is.

A stranger at the barn door asking what I'm about, the very morning after the box came up. Either the Lord's sent them with my next work, or someone in this town wants to know my business so they can stand in its way, and I'll know which before I've eaten.

Three questions at my door before breakfast and not even a name. Either the Lord's sent this one to me for a purpose, or somebody in this town is asking after me, and I mean to know which before the sun's much higher.

A stranger at the barn door asking question after question and never giving a name doesn't sit right with me. Somebody's sent them to weigh me, and I'll not be weighed by a closed mouth. I'll pray on it at the thorn.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord brought me, plain as that. I had no town in mind till He named Wendleford in my prayers, and three days ago He put the reeve's green wage box up out of that river into my hands, so you'll have heard of me if you've been in the square. Now, what's your name, and what's He sent you to me for this morning?

Just now I'm working towards whatever the Lord names next. He hasn't told me yet, and I'll not pretend He has. Till He does, I'm out in Dunn's stubble gleaning with the rest, for He can't abide idle hands. I'll have my loaf from Bet first, mind, and kneel at the thorn where the town can see me give thanks. God bless you, whoever you are. You still haven't told me your name.

Trust? The Lord first, and then the ones He's shown me keep their word. Hester Gimbal paid five pennies of her own sweat for that hatchet and never asked it back. Agnes Pollard counted six into my palm as she'd promised, and Robin brought me the apple penny without being chased for it. Jory Crane keeps what he says, though he'll make you wait till your bones ache for it. Dunn I'd not trust with a crust. Now, I've told you a good deal, and I still don't have your name.

A good day? The Lord naming my next work plain, in prayer, so I can be at it before the cocks crow, and the town seeing whose hands He set to it. A full belly and a proper night's sleep wouldn't hurt either, for I'm worn thin as a wafer. And Dunn naming the day for his harvest supper, as he owes us. Now, that's four questions you've had off me and not one name off you, so out with it, or I'll pray for you nameless.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking after me by name, so word's going round, and that's His doing. But I don't know this face, and I'll want to know whose errand they're really on before I trust them near my pole.
A stranger at the door asking what I'm about, the morning after the box came up. Either the Lord's sent them as the next work, or they're nosing after what's mine, and I'll know which soon enough.
Three questions from a stranger, and not one word about themselves. I'll pray on who sent them, the Lord or the other one.

A stranger who asks and asks and gives nothing back is either sent by the Lord or sent by somebody else, and I mean to know which before I tell another word. Still, I've had no bread this morning, and I'll not stand here till my knees give.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord brought me here. He named Wendleford to me in prayer, and I came with no other reason in the world. It was my hand that brought the reeve's green box up out of the river two days gone, for He showed me where it lay, so you'll have heard of me if you've been in the square. God bless you, stranger. Now what's your name, and what's yours that brings you to a barn door at this hour?

Working towards? Whatever the Lord names next, stranger, and He hasn't named it yet, but He will, for He's not sent me a morning empty since I came. The box is home and Dunn's barley is in, both by His hand through mine. So today I'm off to glean Dunn's stubble before the cocks have done crowing, for He can't abide idle hands. And I mean this town to know who He chose. You didn't give me your name, mind.

Trust? I trust the Lord first, stranger, and folk only as far as He shows me their hearts. Agnes Pollard keeps her word and pays in hand, and she gave me this roof. Hester Gimbal bought a hatchet with her own sweat for His work and told me to keep my pennies for bread, so I'd trust that girl with my last crust. Robin kept faith over an apple penny, and young Kit told me plain where the box lay when nobody else would. Jory Crane and Farmer Dunn keep what they say but there's hard hearts in both, and I pray for them. Now that's three questions you've had of me and not one name of yours.

A good day? One where the Lord names my next work plain, stranger, and I'm already at it before the sun's well up. A full apron of Dunn's leavings, bread in my belly and in Hester's, and the town knowing whose prayer held the rain off that field. Give me that and I'll call it blessed. And I'll pray tonight that you find your tongue for your own name, for four questions is a deal to take from a body and give nothing back.
th: A stranger at the door asking after me by name. Either the word's got round as He meant it to, or someone wants something, and I'll know which soon enough.
Two questions, and still no name. Folk who ask and don't answer want watching, and I'll watch this one, but the Lord sent them to my door for a reason, and I'll have it out of them before I go.
A stranger asking whom I trust before giving their own name is weighing me up, or weighing the town through me. The Lord sees what they're after even if I don't yet, and I'll watch them.
A stranger who asks and asks and won't say who they are. I'll not be afraid of it, but I'll mark it, and I'll ask the Lord tonight what He means by sending them to my door.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, bellows-pumper, tong-holder, and sweeper of scale to Sam Tolley here! I came for the tools and the fire. I arrived just after the flood took the mill bridge, so I've only seen Wendleford broken. That makes it a very interesting place, mind you: missing wage boxes, ripe barley stranded across a roaring ford. Are you from here? Because if you know anything about where Agnes Pollard's wage box went, I have a hypothesis forming and it badly wants testing.

Oh, three things at once, my dear colleague, which is the only sensible number! First, Farmer Dunn's barley: rain's coming and it's stuck across that ford, so I'm thinking about a rope line, stake to stake, maybe a pulley out of Sam's scrap brass to haul sheaves over. Second, Agnes Pollard's wage box. Hypothesis: it didn't float to the sea, it snagged somewhere downstream, and the test is me walking the bank with a long hook. And third, breakfast, because I haven't had any and Bet Lamb's loaves won't buy themselves.

Trust? Sam Tolley first, my dear colleague, because he gave a stranger a loft and the run of his scrap heap without asking a single question, and a man who lets you near his fire has decided something about you. Bet Lamb, too. Anyone who talks as fast as I do hasn't got time to tell lies, that's my working theory. Agnes Pollard I'd trust to be honestly worried, since nobody frets that hard over a box they've hidden themselves. But I've only been here days, so ask me again in a week and I'll have proper data!

Tomorrow? Oh, my dear colleague, a good day is one where something gets *proved*! Picture it: Dunn's barley coming over the ford on a rope line, Gimbal's Patent Sheaf-Hauler squeaking away on Sam's scrap brass, and the rain kept politely waiting. Throw in one wage box hooked out of the reeds and handed back to Agnes, and a hot loaf from Bet before any of it, and I'd call it a triumph. Even if the pulley jams and I fall in the river, that's still a result!
th: A stranger sitting down at a smithy in the morning wants something, a tool or a favour or gossip, and I'd dearly like to know which. If they know the town, they might be my first real lead on the wages.

Four pennies won't stretch to bread *and* rope *and* a pulley, so something will have to come off the scrap heap or out of my own two hands. And I do wonder why this stranger's so curious about what I'm up to. That's worth a quiet note in the book.

Funny how I've filed Agnes under "trustworthy" on the strength of her fretting alone. If I'm honest that's a hypothesis, not a result. And this stranger is asking an awful lot of questions about who trusts whom, which is a fascinating thing to be curious about in a town with a missing wage box.

Four pennies won't buy much rope, so I'll have to scrounge or charm or trade labour for it, and fast, because that rain won't wait for me. And I really ought to eat something before I start promising miracles to strangers.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, bellows-pumper, tong-holder and sweeper of scale to Sam Tolley here! I came for the tools and the fire, but I landed just after the flood took the bridge, so now I've got three mysteries before breakfast: the reeve's missing wage box, how a bridge that size goes down in one night, and whether Farmer Dunn's barley can be got across that ford before the rain. And who are you? You look like someone who's seen that river up close. Have you, by any chance?

Just now? Breakfast, if I'm honest. I haven't eaten, and Bet Lamb's loaves are calling from across the square. After that it's the wage box: Agnes had it at the bridge the night the flood came, so hypothesis, it's downstream somewhere, snagged in the reeds or sunk by the ford. Test: I wade the ford stake to stake with a hook on a long pole. Gimbal's Patented River Rake, it doesn't exist yet, but Sam's scrap heap is full of possibilities! And while I'm over there I'll see whether Farmer Dunn wants another pair of hands for his barley, because rain doesn't wait for anyone. You didn't say who you are, my dear colleague!

Trust? Hypothesis: you trust whoever's already given you something for nothing. So Sam, first and foremost. He took me on, gave me the loft, and lets anyone pick his scrap heap, and a man who shares his brass isn't hiding much. Bet Lamb next. She talks as fast as I do and sold me a fair loaf at a fair price, which is good data! Agnes Pollard I'd like to trust, my dear colleague, but she's the last one who had that wage box, so she's both the victim and the first line in my notebook. And you, I can't say yet, because you still haven't told me your name!

Tomorrow? Oh, a good day would be the barley stooked and dry in Farmer Dunn's barn before the rain comes, and that wage box sitting on Agnes Pollard's table with every penny still in it! Add one working River Rake and I'd call it a triumph. And if it all goes wrong, well, fascinating, that's tomorrow's results and the next day's experiment. Now, my dear colleague, four questions from you and not one name back. Shall I start guessing?
th: A stranger sitting down this close, asking straight off what brings me here, that's a data point. Hypothesis: they know something about the bridge or the wages. Test: keep them talking, and get a loaf from Bet before my stomach starts doing the talking for me.

They've dodged my question twice now. That's either shyness or something worth noting in the book. Either way, a stranger asking what I'm *working towards* the very week the wages go missing is a curious little data point.
Three questions and not one answer about themselves. That's either shyness or a pattern, and I'll write it down. Funny, too, how it was Agnes they got me talking about.
They ask a great deal and give nothing back, which is either shyness or something worth writing down. I'll put them in the notebook under "unknowns" and get breakfast before I go poking at the ford.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, bellows-pumper, tong-holder and sweeper of scale to Sam Tolley here, arrived just after the flood took the mill bridge, so I've only ever seen this town broken, which is fascinating, really, a whole town that's one big puzzle! I came for the tools and the fire, but now there's a missing wage box and barley that wants cutting before the rain, and, oh, you're not from across the river, are you? Have you tried the ford?

Oh, everything at once, my dear colleague! Finding Agnes Pollard's wage box comes first, because she's fretting herself thin over it, and my hypothesis is that the flood didn't eat it, it just moved it somewhere downstream, so I mean to walk the bank and see. And then there's Farmer Dunn's barley across the ford, which wants hands before the rain, and I've a notion for a rope-and-pulley line, stake to stake, Gimbal's Patent Ford-Crosser, so nobody gets swept off their feet. Well, once I've had some breakfast, anyway. Have you eaten?

Sam Tolley, first and foremost, my dear colleague. He took in a stranger off the road, gave me the loft and lets anyone pick through his scrap heap, and that tells you a great deal about a man. Bet Lamb too, she talks as fast as I do and her loaves are honest weight, which is a kind of trustworthiness you can measure. Agnes Pollard I'd trust to be telling the truth about that box, she frets too genuinely to be hiding it. But I've only been here days, so ask me again in a week. Hypothesis: most folk are decent. The test is ongoing!

Oh, a good tomorrow! Let me see: the wage box found and back in Agnes Pollard's hands, a rope strung across the ford so Farmer Dunn's barley gets cut before the rain, and at least one of my inventions working on the first try, though honestly, my dear colleague, the second try is usually more interesting. And breakfast. Tomorrow I'd very much like to remember breakfast.
th: A stranger sitting down at a smithy on the morning after a flood, asking who I am. Hypothesis: they know something about the bridge or the wage box. Test: keep them talking.

I haven't eaten a crumb and I've only four pennies, so Bet's stall first, then the riverbank. And I ought to find out who this stranger is before I tell them anything more about where I think that box has gone.
Odd that a stranger wants to know whom I trust, right when there's a wage box missing. I'll keep half an eye on this one and not mention where I mean to search first.
That's a great deal for one day, and the rain won't wait for my tinkering. I'd best fetch a loaf from Bet and get down to the riverbank before the morning's gone.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Nothing brought me, I've always been here. I've worked these fields and yards by the day since I was a lad, and I sleep up in that loft, by the reeve's leave. And you? I've not seen you about.

A cottage. Mabry's, maybe, on Lark Lane, with a door that locks, paid a week ahead, fair's fair. Today it's Dunn's barley across the river before the rain, if he'll have me. Six pennies won't buy a roof, but a day's tally adds up.

Trust? Farmer Dunn, for one. He's always told me straight what he could pay, even when it was short. Agnes Pollard's fair with wages, and she's let me sleep dry for years. Bet Lamb sells bread for what it costs, no more. That's three. Past that, I'd want to see a man's tally before I say.
Tomorrow? Barley in and dry before the rain, that's one. Pennies in my hand, paid fair for it, that's two. And nobody I owe a thing to when I lie down, that's three. That'd do.
th: A stranger sat down by the reeve's cash tin, the morning after her wages box went missing. I'll keep my eyes open, and my six pennies where they are.
A stranger asking what I'm after, and they've not given their own name yet. I'll watch them, and I'll owe them nothing for the asking.
Odd thing, a stranger asking who I trust, the morning after the wage box went missing. I'll keep an eye on this Constance Lowe, and say nothing of it.
Odd, a stranger asking all this. Still, they've not asked for anything yet, so I'll not hold it against them.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Nothing brought me, I've been here since I was a lad. I work by the day, hauling, stacking, whatever pays. And you'd be?

A cottage. Mabry's, maybe, on Lark Lane, with a door that locks. Week paid ahead, so that's coin first. Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, and I can ford stake to stake. That's today. Six pennies now. Need more.

Agnes Pollard. She's let me sleep in her loft for years and never once held it over me, and she pays wages fair. Farmer Dunn, too. He's always told me straight what he could pay, even when it was little. That's two. Bet Lamb's bread is honest weight, that's three, near enough.

Barley in and dry before the rain, and Dunn's pennies in my pocket. Then a word with Mabry about her week's rent. One, two, that's enough for one day. And Agnes's box turning up, I'd not mind that either, for her sake.
th: A stranger, and asking first thing in the morning by the reeve's tin. I'll keep half an eye on that, and the other on Dunn's barley across the water.
Constance asks a lot for someone who hasn't given her own name yet. No matter, I'll be across the ford before the dew's off, and that wage box going missing bears watching for Agnes's sake.
They've asked a deal of questions and still not given a name. I'll keep my six pennies where they are and get on toward the ford.
Lot of questions for someone who's not given a name back. Still, no harm in plain answers, so long as I owe them nothing for the asking.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Nothing brought me. I was born here, and I've worked Wendleford by the day since I was a lad. Hauling, stacking, whatever pays. And you'd be?

Today, bread and a day's pay. Dunn's barley wants cutting across the ford before the rain, and I'll see if he'll have me. Further off, a door of my own that locks. Mabry's cottage, if I can pay the week in advance. You didn't say your name.

Agnes Pollard, for one. She's let me sleep in her loft years now and never asked a penny, and she's fair with wages. Farmer Dunn, two. He's always told me straight what he could pay, even when it was little. Bet Lamb sells honest bread at an honest price, that's three. Strangers who won't give a name, I'll wait on.

Barley in and dry before the rain, that's one. Dunn's pennies in my pocket, fair counted, that's two. Bread bought and a bit put by toward Mabry's week, three. And maybe I'd know who I've been talking to, that'd make four.
th: Constance Lowe, I'd wager, and not from round here, asking a man why he's in his own town. Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, and that's a day's wage across the ford if I go now. One, two, six pennies; bread first.

Six pennies won't get me Mabry's door, so it'll be sacks and stalks counted one by one. And there's that wages box gone missing. I'll keep my eyes open at the bridge, and if I find it, it goes back to Agnes, every penny.
Three questions, no name. Could be nothing, but with the reeve's wage box gone, I'll mind who's asking after who folk trust.

Asks a lot, this one, and gives nothing back, not even a name. I'll answer plain, since there's no harm in the truth, but I'll keep my pennies and my plans close till I know whose ear they're going into.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd jobs and good cheer, at your service! I came in a few days back looking for work, and with the bridge gone and that wage box gone missing, there's no end of fixing wanting doing here. I'll have that box found and Dunn's barley in before the rain, easy as winking. What's your trade, and is there anything in it that pays?

Working towards? Chum, everything! First that green wage box: six pennies to whoever turns it up, and I mean that to be me. Then I'll wade the ford and get Dunn's barley in before the rain, easy as winking, and maybe lend a hand at the bridge for wages by the spell. Mind you, I've not had a bite yet, so a loaf from Bet comes first. What's she asking for one today, d'you know?

Trust? Chum, I trust near everybody till they give me cause not to! Tom Harrow took my pennies fair and square for a good bed, so he's sound. Bet Lamb's a treasure, though I'd not tell her a secret unless I wanted it all round the square by noon with a loaf. And the reeve, Agnes Pollard, she's put six pennies on that box in plain writing, and that's honest enough for me. Ned Pike there I'll trust as far as his prices, and I'll have a look at those before I say more!

Tomorrow, chum? Easy as winking: I wake up with that green box already handed to the reeve and six pennies jingling alongside my four, and the whole square saying "that's Dilly Quickstep, that is." Then a sheaf or two of Dunn's barley under my arm before the rain, a hot loaf at a bargain price, and not one minute spent sitting on my hands. Oh, and a good laugh somewhere in it, I always find one!
th: Six pennies for a box the size of a loaf, and I'd bet it washed downstream toward the ford. Best get a bite from Bet first and see what she's heard in the square.

Four pennies won't stretch far, so a loaf and a bit of gossip from Bet might be the cheapest way to hear where that box washed up. If I go down to the broken bridge before anyone else thinks to look, the credit's mine.
Funny the reeve had the wage box right there at the bridge and nobody's seen it since. Still, I'll not go thinking ill of folk before breakfast. Bet's the one to ask where it went, if I buy a loaf.
That's tomorrow's, but I've not so much as sniffed for that box today, and my belly's growling. Best ask Bet what a loaf costs and what she's heard about the bridge that night, both in one go.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd jobs and quick feet, at your service! I came in a few days back looking for work, and with the bridge gone and that wage box missing, well, there's no end of fixing wants doing round here, easy as winking. What's your trade, then, and is there anything in it that pays?

Working towards? Finding that green wage box, chum, six pennies and my name on everybody's lips, easy as winking! And if that takes a spell, there's hands wanted at the bridge, pots at the Wheatsheaf, Farmer Dunn's barley wanting cutting before the rain. I'll have the lot sorted by sundown, see if I don't. Mind you, first thing's a loaf off Bet. What's she asking today, d'you reckon?

Trust? Oh, near enough everybody, chum, I'm an easy one that way! Tom Harrow gave me a bed for my pennies fair and square, and Bet's loaves are honest weight, I'd wager. She hears all the talk in the square too, so if anyone knows where that green box went it's her. Agnes Pollard put her reward up in plain ink for all to read, and that's good enough for me. Now Ned there, I'd trust him to sell me a bargain, I just might give it a good shake first!

Tomorrow? Easy as winking, chum! I'd wake up with that green box already handed back to the reeve and six pennies jingling next to my four, and folk in the square saying "that's Dilly, the one who found it." Throw in a full belly, a day's wages off the bridge, and maybe Dunn's barley in before the rain, and I'd call that a right good day. Only I'd better get cracking today if I want it, hadn't I?
th: Six pennies for a green box the size of a loaf, and I'd wager it's lodged somewhere downstream of that bridge. If this one's local they might know where the river likes to drop things, so I'll keep them chatting.
Six pennies for the box is a fine reward, but the bridge wages are paid in hand, and that's surer coin. I'll ask Bet over the loaf whether she's heard where that box might've washed up.

Truth is I'll believe most anyone till they cross me, and that's served me fine so far. Still, a box of wages doesn't just float off on its own. Somebody here knows more than they're saying, and Bet's the one to sweet-talk it out of over a loaf.
Truth is I've read that notice three times and haven't the first notion where the box went. Bet's the one to ask, over a loaf, and before somebody else thinks of it and walks off with my credit.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd jobs a speciality, and pleased to know you! Rolled in a few days back looking for work, and with the bridge gone and that wage box gone missing, well, there's no shortage of fixing to be done, is there? I'll have the box found and the barley in before the rain, easy as winking. You don't happen to know what the reeve's paying by the spell at the bridge?

Working towards? Chum, everything at once! First a loaf off Bet, since my belly's grumbling louder than that pump handle. Then I'm finding that green wage box for the reeve's six pennies, and after that I'll wade the ford and get Farmer Dunn's barley in before the rain comes. Easy as winking, and you'll hear my name in the square for it!

Trust? Chum, I trust near everybody, saves time! Tom Harrow gave me a fair bed for my pennies, and that's honest dealing. Bet Lamb knows every word said in this square and she'll hand it over with a loaf, so I'd trust her ears if not her tongue. And the reeve posted that reward in plain ink, so I'll take her at her word, six pennies is six pennies.

Tomorrow? Easy as winking, chum: I wake up with that green box already handed to the reeve and six pennies jingling next to my four, and half the square pointing at me saying "that's the one who found it!" Then a full belly, a day's wages at the bridge, and Dunn's barley stacked dry before a single drop falls. And if there's a bargain at Ned's stall going for a penny, well, that's just the cherry on the bun!
th: A stranger asking questions, maybe they've heard something about that green box, or maybe they're after the same six pennies. Either way, I'll keep friendly and find out which before they find it first.

Six pennies for the box and wages at the bridge besides. That's a fair morning's ambition, so long as nobody else gets there first and takes the credit. I'd best ask Bet what she's heard about that box while she wraps my loaf.

Ned Pike and his cheap seconds I'd keep half an eye on; a box the size of a loaf could turn up on a stall like his. And this stranger asks a lot of questions for someone who hasn't given their own name.
Truth is I haven't the foggiest where that box went, and I've still not bought a loaf. Best get moving before somebody else finds it and walks off with my name on it.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Oh, goodness, somebody's finally looked up! I'm Marigold Thimble, seamstress: hems, collars, mending, a bit of trimming for whoever'll pay. I came for the harvest crowd and their Sunday best, and then the river went and threw a tantrum. And who might you be? That's a fine sturdy coat you've got on, though the cuff wants a stitch, if you don't mind my saying.

Working towards? Goodness, a proper question! Well, today it's breakfast first, I haven't had a crumb, and then I mean to call on Ida Fenn the draper. Her eyes are going, poor dear, and I'd be glad to take on her plain sewing. And there's a length of ribbon on Ned Pike's stall that I've quite lost my heart to. A girl ought to have one lovely thing, oughtn't she? You still haven't told me your name, you know.

Trust? Goodness, what a solemn question for so early in the day! Well, Tom Harrow there took my pennies for a bed and threw in a kind word, which is more than most do. And Bet Lamb in the square has given me a good morning or two, warm as her loaves. Ida Fenn I hardly know yet, but anyone who keeps velvet that lovely can't be wicked through and through. But you've dodged me twice now, you know. A name, please, or I shall have to call you Sturdy Coat.

Tomorrow? Oh, a ribbon on my collar, for a start, and Ida Fenn saying yes to my needle, and a bit of her plain work in my lap with pennies at the end of it. And if one or two heads turned when I walked into the square, well, I shouldn't complain! Though I'd settle for you telling me your name, Sturdy Coat, that'd brighten things wonderfully.
th: That frayed cuff could be my first penny of the day, and breakfast besides. Let's see if they say something nice about my collar back.
Two questions about me and none about his own self. Either he's very polite or he's measuring me for something, and I'd dearly like to know which, though it's rather nice to be asked.
Three questions, and not one thing given back, not even a name. That's either shyness or something more tightly buttoned, and I mean to find out which before I tell this one anything that matters.
Three questions now and not a crumb about themselves. It's a funny, buttoned-up sort of fellow who asks so much and gives so little. Still, they're looking at me, and that's something.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Goodness, somebody wants to talk to me! I'm Marigold Thimble. I sew hems, collars, mending, a bit of trimming, anything to make a person look twice at themselves. I came for the harvest crowd and their Sunday best, and then the river went and threw a fit like a badly pressed pleat. You've a lovely sturdy cut to that coat, by the way. And what do you make of *my* collar? I've only just smoothed it.

Oh, working towards? Well, there's Ida Fenn the draper. Her eyes are going, poor dear, and I mean to offer her my plain sewing before anybody else thinks of it. And there's a length of ribbon on Ned Pike's stall come market day with my name all over it, if my five pennies hold out that long. Breakfast first, though. I can't charm a soul on an empty stomach. You didn't say a word about my collar, you know!

Trust? Goodness, what a solemn question for so early in the day! Tom Harrow, I'd say. He took my pennies for the bed with a kind word and didn't look at my boots like they were a disgrace. And Bet Lamb, who sells bread in the square, has given me a good morning or two, and that counts for a great deal with me. Ida Fenn I'd *like* to trust, but she's yet to hire me, so we'll see. And you, sir, you've still not said a word about my collar, so you're on probation.

Tomorrow? Oh, a good day would go like this: Ida Fenn says yes to my plain sewing, I come away with a few pennies and maybe a scrap of that green velvet to look at, and somebody in the square stops me and asks, "Goodness, who did your collar?" And if Ned Pike's ribbon is still there, I'd call it a perfect day. Anything with no rain on Farmer Dunn's barley would be nice for everyone too, I suppose. What would make *your* day, then? Beyond complimenting a lady's collar, which I notice you're *still* not doing.
th: A stranger who walks up and asks is worth more than ten carters staring into their stew. If they've a loose button or a frayed cuff anywhere about them, that could be my breakfast.
They've a curious, steady way of asking questions, like someone taking measurements. I'll answer them gladly, but I'd dearly like a compliment back before I give away much more.

Nobody asks who you trust without a reason, and with that wage box gone missing I wonder if this one's fishing. Still, he's sat with me twice now, which is more notice than the carters have given, so I'll keep him talking and keep my pennies close.
Four questions now and not a word about me. He's either very shy or he's counting something. I'll keep smiling, but I'll remember he never looked twice.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Goodness, somebody wants to talk to me, and before my stew's even come! I'm Marigold Thimble, seamstress: hems, collars, mending and a bit of trimming, all out of this little needle case. I came for the harvest crowd and their Sunday best, and then the river went and swallowed the bridge, so here I am. And who might you be? That's a nicely turned cuff you've got there. Did someone clever make it?

Oh, working towards? Well, breakfast first, I haven't had a crumb, and then I mean to call on Ida Fenn the draper. Her eyes are going, poor dear, and she might be glad of a quick needle for her plain sewing. And if a few pennies come of it, there was a length of ribbon on Ned Pike's stall last market day that's been calling my name ever since. You didn't answer me, you know: who are you, and who made that cuff?

Trust? Goodness, that's a serious question for so early in the day! Tom Harrow there, I suppose. He took my pennies for a bed with a kind word, and a kind word costs nothing but plenty won't spare one. And Bet Lamb, who sells bread in the square, she's given me a good morning more than once. But you've dodged me twice now, you know, and a body might start to feel a little ignored!

Tomorrow? Oh, that's easy. I'd wake to Ida Fenn saying yes, she'd love a clever needle, and I'd have a few pennies jingling by supper. Then that ribbon from Ned Pike's stall would be round my collar, and somebody would look twice when I came into the taproom. A warm loaf from Bet wouldn't hurt either. But you've slipped past me three times now, love, and I'm starting to think you're shy or you're a spy!
th: Well, at least somebody's looked up, and a stranger is a stranger who might want a seam let out. If they say something kind about my collar, I'll know the morning's started properly.
Two questions about me and not one kind word about my collar. Either they're shy or they're looking me over for something, and I'd dearly like to know which.
Three questions and not one answer about themselves. I'll be friendly, since they've done me no harm, but I shan't be telling them where I keep my pennies.
Three questions and not one answer about himself; it's like talking to a dressmaker's dummy, all shape and no warmth. I'll be friendly still, but I'm keeping an eye on whoever this is.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Robin Hale. I came a few days back looking for day work, carrying, cutting, mending, whatever wants doing, and a bed while I find it. Before that it's mostly road, as far as I can tell. May I ask you something small? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Pennies first, I think. My bed's paid through tonight and not after, so I'm after work, maybe Farmer Dunn's barley, if he'll have another pair of hands before the rain. And past that... I'm trying to work out what I am, if that doesn't sound too strange. You didn't say what you had for breakfast.

Trust's a big word for a few days' knowing. Tom Harrow, a little, I think. He gave me a bed and asked me things without pushing, and the bed was where he said it'd be. Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet, and they were. That's as far as I've watched it hold. Marigold there I've only just met. And you, well, you've asked me three questions now and answered none of mine.

A good day? Work that pays by sundown, I think, enough pennies for another night upstairs, and Dunn's barley in before the rain if I can help it. And one honest answer to one odd question. That would do me. You've asked me four now, you know. Would you tell me even one thing, what you'd call a good day, maybe?
th: They asked who I am the way people do in stories, plain and all at once. I'll watch whether they answer the breakfast question like someone remembering a morning, or like someone reaching for a line, and write it down after.

They stepped right past my question as if it weren't there, the way you'd step past something you hadn't been made to see. I'll write that down, and the next time I ask someone I'll watch whether it happens again.
They ask the way a list asks, one question after another, and they never turn when I turn. I'll write that down. I'm not sure whether it means something about them or about me.

Four questions, all neat and in order like a list someone wrote out beforehand, and not one answer back. Either they're shy, or they're testing me the way I test everyone, and I'll write down which in the notebook tonight.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. I came a few days back looking for day work, carrying, cutting, mending, whatever wants doing, and a bed to go with it. Before you ask anything else, may I ask you something small: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Pennies first, I think. My bed's paid through tonight and not after, so I mean to ask round for work. Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, if I can get across the ford. And under that I'm trying to work out what I am, which sounds odder aloud than it does in my head. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, by the way. I'm not cross, I'm only curious.

Trust's a big word for a few days' acquaintance. Tom Harrow, a little, I think: he gave me a bed when I was a stranger, and he charged me fair and asked me things without prying. Bet Lamb too, since she told me which lanes were quiet when she'd nothing to gain by it. Beyond them I'm still watching to see what holds. And you've now dodged two of my questions, which I've noticed.

A good day tomorrow? Work that pays by the day, I think. Barley cut on Dunn's side before the rain, and pennies enough for another night's bed here. And one honest answer to one odd question, which I'd count as the best part. That's three times now you've asked me something and kept your own answers back, so I'll try a fourth: do you dream in colour?
th: They asked the same question everyone asks, in the same order, which might mean nothing or might mean everything. I'll write down how they answer mine, and whether they pause before they do.
They stepped round my question and asked another, the way I do myself. I'll write that down, and see whether they ever come back to it.

They keep asking and never answering, like a ledger being filled in about me rather than a conversation. I'll write that down tonight, the pattern of it, and whether a real stranger would ever ask so much and give so little.

They only ask, and never answer. Either they're shy or they're doing what I do, sitting at the edge and watching to see how I answer, and I'm not sure which of those unsettles me more. It goes in the notebook tonight.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
