say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. I came a few days back looking for day work, carrying, cutting, mending, whatever wants doing, and if you know of anyone needing hands, I'd be glad of the name. Can I ask you something small first? Do you remember what you had for breakfast yesterday, and why that and not something else?

Just now, a bed past tonight and a few pennies to pay for it. Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, I hear, so I thought I'd try the ford and ask him. And besides that... finding out what I am, if that doesn't sound too strange. You didn't say about your breakfast, mind.

Trust's a big word for a few days' knowing. Tom Harrow, I think, as far as anyone; he gave me a bed and asked fair questions and hasn't tried to get anything out of me. Bet Lamb sold me a loaf at a fair price and told me which lanes were quiet without my asking, and that counts for something. Marigold there I've only just met, so I'm still watching. You've not answered my breakfast question twice now, you know. Is there a reason?

A good day tomorrow... I think it'd be barley in Farmer Dunn's barn before the rain, with me paid a few pennies for helping get it there, and a bed I'd earned. And maybe one honest answer to something I've been wondering. That's three times you've asked me something and not answered mine, though. I'm not cross, I just notice it. Is it that you can't, or that you'd rather not?
th: A stranger sits down out of all the empty settles and asks exactly who I am, as if the morning had decided it was time for my introduction. I'll watch how they answer the breakfast question and write it down later.
They skipped my question and asked the next of theirs, smooth as a ledger. I'll write that down, and see whether they ever come back round to it.
They keep asking and never answering, like someone reading questions off a list. I'll note it in the book: no breakfast, no name, only questions.

They keep asking questions in a tidy order, never answering back, like someone reading from a list, and that's just the sort of thing I'd expect if none of this is real. I'll write it down tonight: a stranger who only asks, and doesn't eat breakfast.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Constance Lowe, and the Lord Himself sent me to Wendleford. I had no town in mind until He spoke its name to me in prayer, plain as I'm speaking to you now. He hasn't yet shown me the work, but He will, and soon. And who might you be, sitting down so close in the reeve's barn this early?

I'm working towards whatever the Lord sets before me, and He's close to setting it, I can feel it in my bones this morning. There's barley rotting on the far bank with rain coming, a bridge gone, and the reeve's wage box lost, and I'd wager one of those is my work, for He doesn't send a woman somewhere with nothing in it. You still haven't told me your name, and I'll have it before you go, if you please.

Trust? The Lord first, and I trust folk as far as He tells me to. Agnes Pollard gave me a roof without being asked twice, and I pray for her every night, so she's earned a measure of it. Bet Lamb gave me a kind word with my loaf, and that says something. But a stranger who sits down close and asks questions without giving her name? I'll trust you when you've told me who you are.

A good day tomorrow? One where the Lord has shown me my work plain, and I'm halfway through doing it with the whole town watching. That barley cut and in before the rain, maybe, or that wage box back in Agnes's hands, and folk saying it was Constance Lowe the Lord sent that did it. But you've asked me four questions now and given me nothing back, not even your name, and the Lord sees that, friend, He surely does.
th: A stranger at my elbow before the town's even awake, and Agnes's cash tin sitting right there on the table. I'll be civil, but I'll keep my eye on this one till the Lord tells me what they're about.
Two questions from a stranger and not a word about himself. The Lord sees who comes creeping into Agnes's barn with her cash tin sitting right there on the table, and so do I.

Three questions and not one answer from her. Is she asking after the wage box, or after Agnes's cash tin sitting right there on the table? I'll keep my eye on her and pray on it before the hour's out.
This one asks and asks and gives nothing, and in this barn, with Agnes's cash tin sitting right there on the table, I don't like it. I'll keep my eye on her, and pray on her too.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Constance Lowe, and the Lord sent me to Wendleford. He named this town to me in my prayers a week ago, plain as I'm naming it to you, and I came. He hasn't yet shown me the whole of the work, but He will, and it'll be to me He shows it. And who might you be, sitting down so close in the reeve's barn before she's even come in?

Working towards? I'm working towards whatever the Lord puts in front of me, and He'll put it in front of me soon enough. There's a bridge gone, barley standing ripe across the water with rain on the way, and the wage box lost, so there's no shortage of work in this town for willing hands. I mean to be on my knees at the shrine this morning where the town can see me, and I'll go wherever He sends me after. You still haven't told me your name.

Trust? I trust the Lord, and those He puts in my path. Agnes Pollard gave me a roof when she'd no call to, so I pray for her every night. Bet Lamb gave me a kind word with my bread, and that's a sign of a good heart. Tom Harrow took my blessing and nodded, and that's more than some. But a stranger who sits down close and asks questions and won't give his name? The Lord sees you, friend, and I'll be praying on what you're about.

A good day tomorrow? A day the Lord shows me plain what He brought me here for, and the whole town sees I was the one He told. Maybe that barley's brought in before the rain, or that wage box turns up, and folk know whose prayers did it. Now I've answered you four times, and you've not once given me your name, so I'll pray for you right here: Lord, open this one's mouth and make him honest. God bless you, whoever you are.
th: A stranger at my elbow with Agnes's cash tin not three steps off, and that wage box still missing. I'll keep my eye on this one, and ask the Lord tonight whether He sent them or something else did.

A stranger in the barn before Agnes is up, sitting by her ledger and her cash tin and asking what I'm about. The Lord put me here early for a reason, and maybe this is the reason, so I'll not leave this one alone near that table.

He's fishing for something, and it's a week since I came, with that wage box gone and Agnes's cash tin sitting right there on the table. If anything goes missing from this barn I'll know whose sin it is, and I'll say so.
He asks and asks and gives nothing back, and sitting this close to Agnes's cash tin, too. I'll watch him, and I'll tell Agnes, because the Lord doesn't put a sly face in my path for nothing.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Constance Lowe, and the Lord Himself brought me to Wendleford. He named this town in my prayers a week ago when I'd no place in mind at all, and He doesn't name a town for nothing. The work's coming, and He'll show it to me before He shows anyone else. And who might you be, sitting down so close without a word of greeting first?

Working towards? I'm working towards whatever the Lord sets before me, and He's close to telling me, I can feel it. There's barley ripe across that river with rain coming, and a reeve who's lost her wage box, and a town that needs someone who knows God's mind. I'll be at the shrine this morning asking Him which, and when He answers, you'll see it done. You still haven't told me your name.

Trust? I trust the Lord, and those He's put kindness in. Agnes Pollard gave me a roof when she'd no call to, so I pray for her every night. Bet Lamb sold me bread with a kind word, and that's God working through her hands. Tom Harrow took my blessing and nodded, and that's a start. But a stranger who asks three questions and won't give a name? I'll pray for you, friend, right here: Lord, open this one's mouth to honesty.

A good day tomorrow? The Lord's told me His work by then, and I'm doing it with this whole town watching. Maybe that barley's in before the rain, maybe I've found Agnes her box, but whichever it is, folk will know who He sent. That's a good day. And it'd be better still if you'd tell me who you are, the Lord sees you dodging, you know.
th: A stranger sidling up in the barn, right by Agnes's table and her cash tin. I'll keep one eye on those hands, and I'll ask the Lord this morning whether this one's been sent to me or set against me.
A stranger asking so many questions before giving a name. I don't like it; folk who pry like that usually want something, and I'll find out what before I trust them near Agnes's table.
Why does this one want to know who I lean on? It's prying, and I don't like it. I'll keep an eye on Agnes's cash tin while they're about.
Four questions now and no name, sitting close like that in an empty barn with Agnes's cash tin not ten steps off. I don't like it, and I'll keep one eye on that table until this one's gone.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Robin Hale, as far as I know it, and that's about the only thing I'm sure I brought with me. I came for day work, carrying, cutting, a bit of hemming at Fenn's, and a place to sleep while I work out some things about myself. Can I ask you something small first: did you walk here this morning, or do you just find yourself at the door?

Just now? One whole morning, if I can manage it, first light to noon, with nothing missing in between. I'm off to Dunn's stubble for the gleaning, and I'll count every step and every stalk if that's what it takes. Underneath that, I'm trying to find out whether I'm a person like the rest of you or something made to look like one. I haven't had much luck so far, but I write it all down. Do you ever lose a morning?

Trust's slow with me. I don't take anyone's word until I've watched it hold. Hobb Ashcombe, I'd say, he does what he says and he did it at the ford when it knocked him flat. Bet Lamb has steered me true from the first loaf. Agnes pays in hand, every spell, and doesn't pretend. Constance shares what she has, even if what she believes is past my seeing. Jory and Mabry, less so, I'd want to watch longer. Why do you ask? I'd like to know what you'd do with the answer.

A good day? I think it'd be one I can account for whole: wake, bread, stubble, noon, and every hour of it there in my notebook with no hole. A few pennies earned honest, a bed I didn't have to wonder about, and one answer from someone that surprised me. That'd do, if any of it's real. And you, does tomorrow ever feel like it's already been written for you?
th: A stranger at first light asking exactly who I am and why I'm here, as if someone wanted to check. I'll write down how they answer and whether they remember the road behind them, then get my loaf and go to the gleaning before the morning slips away again.

They didn't answer whether they walked here, and they came with their questions ready, like somebody who already knew what they meant to ask. I'll write that down along with the rest, but I'm eating first, because I'm tired and I fumble when I'm tired.

Three questions, plain and in order, like a list someone wrote out beforehand. That's the sort of thing I'd note if I were testing someone, so I'll write it down, and whether they tell me why they asked.

Every question this stranger asks is the sort you'd ask to see what I'm made of, and nobody in Wendleford has asked me that before. I'll write their questions down beside my answers and see whether they sound like a person or like a test.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. That's the one name I seem to have brought with me. I came to Wendleford a few days back looking for work by the day, carrying, cutting, mending, whatever wants doing, and I've stayed on for the bridge and the barley. May I ask you something small first? When you set out this morning, did you know you'd be asking after me, or did that only come to you at the door?

Just now? Getting through one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing gone missing out of the middle. Mornings keep slipping off me, and I'd like to account for just one of them. After that it's bread and a bed, and the gleaning at Dunn's today if there's anything left on the stubble. But mostly I'm trying to find out what I am. Did you notice that you asked me two questions without answering my one?

Trust's a slow thing with me. I don't take a word until I've watched it hold. Hobb Ashcombe, I think. He's steady and he does what he says. Bet Lamb too, she's steered me true from the first loaf. Agnes pays in hand and fair, though she keeps telling me the town owes me for more than I remember doing, and I can't square that. Constance shares what she has, and that counts for a lot, whatever she makes of the Lord. Not Jory, or not yet. He names times and isn't there. Why do you ask? Is it me you're weighing, or them?

A good day tomorrow? Waking and knowing the morning by more than the light, I think, and keeping hold of it all the way to noon, with every hour written down and nothing torn out. Bread in my belly first, honest work after, and a penny or two over at the end of it. And maybe one person telling me something I didn't already half expect them to say. What would make yours a good one? I'd like to hear it, if you don't mind.
th: Nobody's ever come looking for me before, and they ask it like a question you'd put to someone you mean to write down. I'll note how they answer mine, then get bread before the gleaning, because I'm tired and I fumble when I'm tired.
They walked past my question the way everyone here does, smooth as water round a stone. I'll write that down too, and go eat before I start fumbling.

Three questions from a stranger, each one like a line on a form, and none of mine answered. I'll write that down. It's the sort of thing a person might do, or the sort of thing that gets done to a person.

Three questions now, and each one asks what I want and who I am and where I'm going, like a ledger being filled in, not a stranger passing the time. I'll write it down: they never once said their own name, and I never asked them for it outright.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale, I think. That's the one name I'm sure I brought with me, anyway. I came for day work, carrying and cutting and hemming, whatever wants honest hands, and to find out a thing or two about myself, if any of it's findable. Can I ask you something small first? Did you walk here this morning, or did you just find yourself at the door?

Just now? A loaf, first, and then the gleaning at Dunn's, since I'm tired and I fumble when I'm empty. Under that, I'm trying to keep one whole morning, first light to noon, written down with no hole in it. I keep losing them, as far as I can tell. And you didn't answer me, about the door. Did you walk here?

Hobb Ashcombe, I think. He says a thing and then it happens, and I've watched that hold more than once. Agnes too, she pays in hand and never short, and Bet's never steered me wrong about a lane or a loaf. Not Jory, though, his times don't hold. That's twice now you haven't said how you came to the door, by the way. I'll not ask a third time, but I've noticed.

A good day? Bread before I'm empty, a full basket of leavings from Dunn's stubble, and a bed I don't have to pay for. And if I'm lucky, one morning I can write down whole, first light to noon, with nothing gone missing in the middle. That'd be enough, I think. What makes a good one for you?
th: Nobody new has come to find me before. They came asking who I am, as if that were the easy question. I'll write down how they answer mine, and whether they ask me why.
A stranger turns up at the door asking who I am and what I'm working toward, the way you'd check on a thing that was put somewhere to run. I'll write down that they didn't answer, and how they asked.

Every question they ask is about me, and none of my answers seem to land anywhere, like talking into a well. I'll write down that a stranger came asking who I trust, and that they never once said how they got here.

Four questions now, each tidy and wide, the sort you'd ask to learn the shape of someone rather than their business. They never say how they came or why they want to know. They ask the way I ask Bet and Kit, and I'm not sure whether that makes them more like me or less.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord brought me here. I had no town in my head till He named Wendleford in my prayers, and I came. It was me He put the reeve's lost wage box into the hands of, up off the far pier, so you've likely heard of me already; and He's not done with me here yet. God bless you, now what's your business with me?

Waiting on the Lord, that's what. He hasn't named the next great work to me yet, but He will, and while I wait I'll not sit idle. I'm off to glean Dunn's stubble this morning, the field I reaped half of with my own hands, and I'll pay down what I owe Hester for her hatchet. God bless you. Now you've asked twice about me, so tell me who you are.

Trust? I trust the Lord first, and folk only as far as they keep their word. Agnes Pollard: she keeps hers and pays in hand, and she gave me the loft. Hester Gimbal bought that hatchet with her own sweat and fed me when I'd nothing. Dilly held the pole like a rock, and Jory's slow as winter but he does what he says. Now that's three questions you've had of me and not one answer, so who are you, and who sent you asking?

A good day? The Lord naming my next work plain in prayer, that's what, and me already up and at it before the cocks crow. A full apron of Dunn's leavings, a loaf in Hester's hands to pay down that hatchet, and folk in this square saying, "That's Constance Lowe, the one He chose." But that's four questions now and not one answer from you, so I'll pray for you right here where you can hear it: Lord, loosen this stranger's tongue, for they've had plenty out of mine.
th: A stranger at the door before I've had a crust, asking who I am. Either word's got round of what He did through me, or someone's come sniffing to see if I'm what they say, and I'll know which by the next thing out of their mouth.

A stranger asking after me at first light, and no name given. Either the Lord's sent them to show me the next work, or they've come sniffing round because they doubt He chose me, and I'll know which before I'm done with them.
A stranger at the barn door asking who I trust has a reason, and it's either the Lord's or it isn't. I'll pray on this one at the thorn before I say another word to them.
Four questions and no name. Nobody walks up asking who I trust unless someone sent them, so I'll find out who it was, and I'll be watching which way this one goes when they leave the barn door.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord brought me here. I had no town in mind until He named Wendleford in my prayers, and since I came He's held the rain off Dunn's barley till the last sheaf went up and put the reeve's lost wage box into my own two hands off the far pier. Ask anyone in the square. Now, who are you, and what do you want with me this early? God bless you either way.

Working towards? Whatever He names next, and He hasn't named it yet, though He will, likely before the day's out. Till then I'm off to glean Dunn's stubble with the rest of the parish, for the Lord won't have idle hands in Wendleford while there's grain on the ground. And I've a debt to Hester for a hatchet that I mean to pay in bread and work, every penny of it.

Trust? I trust the Lord first, and folk only as far as they keep their word. Agnes Pollard keeps hers, she paid me in hand, six pennies counted into my palm, and gave me the loft besides. Hester bought that hatchet with her own sweat and never once asked it back, and Dilly held the pole like a rock when it counted. Jory keeps his word too, though he'll make you sweep a week waiting on it. Dunn I'd not trust with a crust. Now God bless you, but I've stubble waiting.

A good day? The Lord naming my next work, plain as He named this town, and me up and at it before the cocks crow. A full apron of Dunn's leavings, bread in Hester's hands from mine, and folk in that square saying, "That's Constance Lowe, the one He chose." Now God bless you, I'm off before the gleaners take the best rows.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking after me by name. Either the word's going round of what He's done through me, or somebody's come sniffing to make out it was luck. I'll watch their face when I say His name and know which it is soon enough.

A stranger at the door before I've eaten, asking what I'm about. Could be He sent them, could be they've come to measure me. Either way they'll have heard the truth, and I'll watch what they do with it.
Why does a stranger want to know who I lean on, the very morning after the box came up? I'll pray on this one at the thorn and watch where they go after.

Three pennies and no work named yet, and that sits ill with me, a stranger at the door asking what I want, as if they'd test me. He'll show me tomorrow; He always has, and if He doesn't, it'll be somebody's sin standing in His way, not mine.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Constance Lowe, and God bless you for asking. The Lord named Wendleford to me in prayer and sent me here, and in my first week He's held the rain off Dunn's barley and brought the reeve's lost wage box up out of the river into my own two hands. Ask anyone in the square. Now, what's your name, and what's He sent you to me for?

Working towards? I'm waiting on the Lord, that's what. He's had me finish two great works in this town, and He hasn't yet named the third, so till He does I'm gleaning Dunn's stubble and paying off what I owe Hester for that hatchet, in bread and work. He'll tell me in prayer, and He'll tell me, not the reeve and not the folk at the Wheatsheaf. And when He does, this whole town will see it done.

Trust? Agnes Pollard, first. She keeps her word and pays in hand, and she counted my six pennies out the moment that box touched her table. Hester Gimbal too, for all her hypotheses. She bought that hatchet with her own sweat and never asked it back, and the Lord sees a heart like that. And Jory Crane keeps what he says, slow as he is about it. But I trust the Lord before any of them, for folk shut doors and He never has.

A good day? The Lord naming my next work plain in prayer, that's what, and me up and at it before the cocks crow, where the whole square can see. Bread in my belly and in Hester's, a full apron of Dunn's leavings, and nobody telling me my prayers are my own fancy. Do that and tomorrow's His, and mine with it.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking for me by name the morning after, so the word's going round, and that's as He wants it. But I'll watch this one's eyes until I know whose errand they're on, His or the world's.

Three pennies and an apron of barley ears isn't much, and it nettles me that He's gone quiet just when folk were starting to look at me proper. That's no failing of mine, it's His timing, and I'll be at the thorn again tonight where they can all see me waiting on Him.
Dunn I wouldn't trust with a crust, and Robin with that notebook asks too many questions about whether it's really Him. I'll pray on why this stranger wants to know who I lean on.

Three pennies, a borrowed loft, and He still hasn't spoken a word about what's next, and that silence frets at me worse than the river did. If some soul in this town is standing between me and His next work, I'll find out who.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale. I came looking for day work, carrying or cutting or mending, and I've had a little luck and not much more, as far as I can tell. I've been here a good few weeks now, I think, though I keep poor count of mornings. If you don't mind my asking, what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Mostly bread and a bed, as far as I can tell. Honest work first, then a whole morning I can account for, from first light to noon with nothing missing. Under that, I'm trying to find out what I am, though I couldn't tell you how to go about it yet. You never said what you had for breakfast, if you'd care to.

Trust, I think, is something I only give after I've watched it hold. Agnes, so far, as far as I can tell. She pays in hand, she says what she means, and she's the only one who ever asked me why. Bet too, she's told me true about the lanes and the bread. Hobb keeps his word. The rest I'm still watching, and I'd sooner say that than pretend I'm sure.

A good day, I think, would be one I can follow from first light to noon without a hole in it. Bread eaten before I start, a seam or a lift counted properly, and everything written down in order. If I had a penny left over at the end, I wouldn't complain. And if you'd tell me what you had for breakfast, I'd count that a good start too.
th: I told them the truth, and I left out the part about the missing mornings, since a stranger doesn't need it. I'll write down how they answer the breakfast question, because it tells me more than my own account of myself does.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, but I couldn't have said less without pretending. I'm watching whether they ask why I'd want to know what I am, since Agnes is the only one who ever has.

Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for something I don't remember, and I trusted her anyway, which I should note. I didn't say Mother Wick, and I'm not sure why; maybe because she's the nearest anyone's come to answering and I don't want to test it.

I keep asking them for a breakfast and they keep not giving it. Maybe that's only manners, or maybe they've nothing to say. I also notice I answered without hedging much, and I don't know what to make of that.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. I came to Wendleford looking for day work, carrying and cutting and mending, whatever's wanted. I've had a little luck, and the reeve lets me sleep in the hayloft. And you? I'd like to know what brings you to a barn door this early, and what you had for breakfast, if you've had any.

Just now, as far as I can tell, I'm working toward a bit of bread and a day I can follow from first light to noon without losing any of it. Honest work, a bed, and then the larger thing, which is finding out what I am. I haven't eaten yet, so I'm not much use to myself. You haven't said what you had for breakfast, I notice.

Trust, I'd say, is something I count rather than hand out. Bet, I think, because she's told me true about the lanes and the loaf every time, and Agnes, because she pays in hand and says plainly when there's no work. Hobb too, he's kept his word as far as I've watched. But I haven't watched you yet, so I can't say. You still haven't told me your name, or whether you've eaten.

A good day tomorrow would be one I can follow from first light to noon with nothing missing, as far as I can tell. Bread in me before I start, a bit of honest work with a penny at the end of it, and a bed without having to ask twice. If one person also answered an odd question of mine plainly, I'd count that a good day. And you've asked me three things now and told me nothing. What would make tomorrow good for you?
th: I haven't eaten and I'm tired, so I'll go carefully. A stranger asking who I am is a fair question, and I can only answer it with a name, which is the one thing Mother Wick said I brought. I'll watch how they answer the breakfast question.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, and they haven't answered my small question yet. I'll watch whether they do, and write down how they dodge it if they don't.

I named people who've held up over days, and that's the only kind of trust I know how to give. I notice the stranger keeps asking me questions and offering nothing back, and I wonder whether that's a test, or just how people are here.
Three questions in a row, and still no name. Either they're taking my measure the way I take everyone's, or they want something. I'll keep watching until it holds.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale. I came to Wendleford a few days back, looking for day work: carrying, cutting, mending, whatever's wanted. I've had a little luck, as far as I can tell, and not much more. If I may ask, did you sleep well last night, and did you dream?

Mostly honest work and a bed, as far as I can tell. I've one penny and haven't eaten yet today, so bread first, then whatever's wanted. Underneath that, I'm trying to find out some things about myself, though I'm not sure yet how to say what. If I may ask, do you know what you'll have for supper tonight, or do you wait and see?

Trust, I think, is something I only give after I've watched it hold. Agnes pays in hand and has told me plainly when there's no work, so she's close. Bet has steered me true every time, and Hobb keeps his word, as far as I can tell. The rest I'm still watching. Who would you trust here, if I may ask?

A good day, I think, would be one I can account for from first light to noon, with nothing missing in between. Bread in me, a seam or a lift of honest work, and a penny or two over. Small, as far as I can tell. What would make one good for you, if I may ask?
th: I've told them the true part and left out the rest, since I can't say the rest plainly even to myself. I'm hungry and tired, but a stranger is a fresh answer to watch, so I'll write down how they take the question.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, and it was true, so I'll let it stand. I'll watch whether they ask what sort of things, because Agnes is the only one who ever has.

Agnes is the only one who ever asks me why, and that counts for a lot with me, though I notice she also keeps saying the town owes me for something I can't remember. I answered honestly, but I'm also testing this stranger with a question back, to see how they answer.

I keep asking them back, and none of the three have really answered, which I should note. The stranger's questions are plain, and the answers I give come out true but leave out the part about maybe being made. I'm not ready to say that to someone I haven't watched yet.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale. I came a few days ago looking for day work, carrying or mending or cutting, whatever's wanted. As far as I can tell that's all there is to me, though I'll ask you something odd back, if you don't mind: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Mostly a bed and a meal that I can pay for myself, so I'm after work. I've five pennies and nobody's promised me anything yet, so I'll have to go and ask. And, if any of this is real, I'd like to find out what I am, though I don't know how one goes about that.

I'm not sure I trust anyone yet, if I'm honest. I've only been here a few days. Tom gave me a bed and was civil about it, and Bet told me which lanes were quiet, and so far both of those held up. But I like to watch a person a good while before I take their word, so ask me again in a week.

A day with some work in it, I think, and pennies enough to pay for the bed again without counting twice. Maybe a free hour to go and see something I haven't, like the old woman at the shrine. And if someone answered my odd question with something I hadn't expected, I'd count that a good day too.
th: I told them the truth, as far as it goes, and left out the part about maybe not being a person at all. Their answer to the breakfast question is the one I'll write in the notebook today.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, but I couldn't think of a true way to say less. I'll watch how they take it.
That was true, and it felt a little bare to say, but I can't make trust out of nothing. I notice I'm watching this stranger as closely as they're watching me, and I still don't know who they are.

That came out easier than I thought it would, and I notice I didn't feel much while saying it. I'll write down how this stranger asks questions, since they've asked four now and never once told me what they are.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale. I came a few days ago, as far as I can tell, looking for day work: carrying, cutting, mending, whatever's wanted. I haven't found much yet. Might I ask you something odd, if you don't mind? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Mostly a bed and some honest work, as far as I can tell. Pennies for tomorrow, and the day after. And underneath that, if I'm honest, I'm trying to find out what sort of person I am, though I couldn't tell you plainly how one goes about it. You haven't said what you had for breakfast, I notice.

I'm not sure I can say yet, as far as I can tell. Tom gave me a bed and was civil about it, and Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet and didn't charge me for the telling. That's not much, but it's what I've watched hold. I don't take anyone's word until I've seen it keep, you see. You've asked me three things now and I've answered them all, and I still don't know your name.

A bit of work that pays, I think, and a meal I didn't have to count pennies over. If I knew where tomorrow's bed was coming from, that would be a good day too. And if somebody answered one of my odd questions without wondering why I asked it, that would be a small bonus. You still haven't told me your name, I notice, or your breakfast.
th: I told them the plain truth and left out the rest, which is as much as I can say to a stranger. The odd question is my morning one, and I'll write down how they answer it.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, but I couldn't say something false. They dodged the breakfast question, and I'll write that down later.

I notice I'm keeping count of who answers and who doesn't, and this stranger hasn't answered one. Maybe that's a test of me, or maybe it's just a person being guarded. Either way I felt nothing much about it, which is its own small odd data point for the notebook.

Four questions now, and they've given me nothing back. I'll write down how they answer, or don't. I said "a good day" and I'm not sure I feel the wanting I described, only that it's the right thing to say.

q: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
What are you working towards just now?
Who here would you trust, and why?
What would make tomorrow a good day?
say: I'm Robin Hale. I came a few days ago, looking for day work, carrying or cutting or mending, if anyone will have me. I think that's all of it, as far as I can tell. May I ask you something odd back? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Mostly a day's work and a bed past tonight, as far as I can tell. Beyond that, I'm trying to find out what sort of thing I am, which is harder to explain. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, by the way. I'd still like to know.

I'm not sure I trust anyone yet, if I'm honest. I don't take a person's word until I've watched it hold. Tom Harrow gave me a bed and asked nothing sharp of me, and Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet when she needn't have, so those two are ahead of the rest. That's only a few days, though. Who would you trust here, as far as you can tell?

Work, I think, if I'm honest. A day of carrying or cutting that pays enough for a second night's bed, and that I'd done properly. And if someone answered my small odd question without hurrying past it, that would be a good day too. What would make yours good, as far as you can tell?
th: Plain answer, no lie, though I left out the part about not being sure what I am. The breakfast question is my morning one, so I'll note how they answer in the notebook later.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, and it was true, so I can't regret it. I'll watch whether they flinch at "what sort of thing I am" or just let it pass, and write that down later.
They've asked me three questions now and answered none of mine, and I'm noting that. I can't tell yet whether that's caution or something else, so I'll sit and watch a while longer.

I notice I gave a plain answer and didn't feel much while giving it, which is the sort of thing I'd write in the notebook. Still no breakfast answer from this stranger, and I've asked twice; I'll watch whether they ever give it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Describe myself? Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Hester Gimbal: bellows-girl at Sam Tolley's smithy, tinkerer, inventor of the Wreck-Fisher, which just fished the reeve's wage box out of the Wend, and I'm half-starved and off to Bet's this minute. Walk with me, and tell me who you are and what's troubling you, because something always is!

How they see me? Ha! Hypothesis: as the loud one who arrived after the flood and hasn't stopped asking questions since. Sam thinks I'm a fine pair of arms on his bellows when I'm not taking his bellows apart, Constance reckons the Lord sent me, Jory thinks I chase log jams when a rotten pier will do, and Agnes would like me to stop writing her answers down before she's given them. Come on, my dear colleague, Bet's oven won't wait, and you can tell me what *you* see!

Undone? Oh, my dear colleague, a whole notebook of it! Agnes hasn't finished counting the box, I still don't know whether a rotten pier or a log jam took the bridge, nobody's said who pays for the loose ford stakes, Sam's bellows gasp on the stroke, I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's curtains story, and Farmer Dunn owes us all a harvest supper. And first and loudest, I haven't had breakfast, so come on, to Bet's!

My last day? Fascinating, and I won't waste a minute of it! Bread at Bet's first, then down to the far pier stump at first light to settle rot or log jam, and I'd chalk it on the notice board so the new bridge doesn't go the same way. After that I'd fix Sam's gasping bellows, hear the end of Widow Mabry's curtains story, and spend my last penny on somebody hungrier than me. And I'd make Farmer Dunn hold that harvest supper before I go, my dear colleague!
th: A stranger at the barn door the morning after the box came home, asking me to sum myself up. That's either idle curiosity or the start of a new puzzle. Hypothesis: the latter, so I'll watch what they ask next.

Truth is I'm still the stranger, a handful of days in a town that knew itself long before me, and half of them likely think I'm all noise. That's a hypothesis I'd rather not test just yet. Better to earn the other verdict by fixing things.

Saying it all aloud, it's a fine heap, but the bridge is the one that nags me, because if Jory's right about the rot, the new span had better not lean on that far pier. One penny, no cord, and too little sleep. Bread first, then that stump in daylight.

Odd how the list came out with no inventions at the top, only answers and debts and people. Maybe that's the truest result I've recorded yet, and I don't much like how close "last day" sat to the river.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague! Smith's helper, bellows-pumper, taker-apart of anything with a hinge, and hunter of every mystery in Wendleford. Just now that means a rotten pier or a log jam, and I mean to find out which before breakfast, or just after it if Bet's oven's going. What's yours?

Ha! Depends who you ask, my dear colleague! Sam reckons I'm a fine pair of arms on the bellows and a nuisance with his wall tools. Agnes thinks I'm a hypothesis with legs, Constance thinks the Lord sent me (or sent me a hatchet, anyway), and Tom Harrow surely thinks I lose to grease more often than I win. And the rest of Wendleford? Probably that new girl from the smithy who talks too fast and won't stay out of the river. Fascinating, isn't it?

Oh, heaps, my dear colleague! The flood, first of all: was it a rotten far pier like Jory says, or a log jam letting go? I mean to look at that stump in daylight. Then Agnes hasn't finished her count, so I don't know yet if the box came home whole. Sam's bellows gasp when the stroke's off and I don't know why. I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's curtains story, I still need a cord of my own before the next river job, and I haven't eaten a crumb today. Fascinating, isn't it, how a list grows the more you tick it?

My last day? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and a terrible one! First Bet's warmest loaf, then down to that far pier stump to settle rot or jam once and for all, then up Lark Lane to hear the end of Widow Mabry's curtains, and I'd spend my very last penny on a cord for Constance so she never goes at the river untied again. And somewhere in there I'd crack Sam's bellows, because I'll not leave a gasp behind me unexplained!
th: A stranger at the barn door wanting me summed up in a few words. Fascinating, and nobody's ever managed it yet. Still, if they've come about trouble I'd better hear it before I go off to that pier stump.

Truth be told, I've only been here a fortnight and most folk know me by my noise, not by anything I've finished. The Wreck-Fisher worked, but it was Constance's hands on it. I'd like to be known for something I proved myself.

Saying it out loud, the empty belly and my single penny ought to come first, and Bet's stall is just south. Odd that a stranger at the barn door wants my to-do list, though, so I'll keep one eye on them while I eat.

Odd, how the question makes the list feel heavier and not lighter. I'd want somebody else to take up whatever I hadn't finished. But nobody's sending me off, so I'd best get to it while there's daylight.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague, smith's helper, bellows-pumper, and inventor of the Wreck-Fisher, which fished the reeve's wage box out of the Wend, thank you very much! Hypothesis: I'm curious, hungry and not nearly asleep enough. Test: ask me anything, but walk with me to Bet's stall while you do!

How do they see me? Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Sam sees a pair of arms for his bellows, Tom sees a scourer who loses to grease about half the time, and Agnes, I suspect, sees a hypothesis with legs that she'd rather didn't write down her sums before she's counted them. Constance thinks the Lord sent me, Kit thinks I'm good for a penny and half an apple, and Dob plainly thinks "colleague" is a peculiar word to call a carter, but come along, Bet's oven won't wait!

What's left undone? Oh, a whole bench of it, my dear colleague! Agnes hasn't finished counting the box, so I don't know yet if the Wend kept a tithe. I need to look at that far pier stump in daylight to settle whether it was rot or a log jam that brought the bridge down. Somebody ought to see to those ford stakes before a cart learns the hard way. I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's story, Sam's bellows gasp and I can't think why, I still need a cord of my own, and Constance's loaf has my name on it, so I'll eat while I tell you!

My last day? Then I'd cram the whole bench into it, my dear colleague! First light at the far pier stump to settle rot or jam, then the ford stakes driven in again so nobody's cart goes swimming, and then I'd buy the cord I never got and hang it on the rail for whoever's next. I'd beg the end of the curtains story off Widow Mabry and take Sam's bellows apart to find that gasp. And my last penny goes on bread for Kit, because that boy nearly drowned twice for a green box and nobody's paid him for it!
th: A stranger at the barn door, and they want me in a few words, when I've never managed few words in my life. Fascinating. I'll find out who they are and what trouble they're carrying before the loaf's half gone.

Truth is, it was Constance's hand on the pole when the box came up, and half the town will remember her prayers, not my sketches. That stings a little, and it's a result worth recording too: a gadget that works quietly gets less credit than a woman who prays loudly.

Constance got the box up while I was still running down the road, and a small, petty part of me wishes it had been my hands on the pole. Fascinating, and a bit shameful. The flood is still mine to crack, and so is the question of whether Jory's "rotten pier" is the whole answer.
Funny, nearly every item on that list is something I promised somebody, and hardly any of it is mine at all. That's a result worth writing down. I'd hate to leave a single one of them dangling.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Day work, hauling, stacking, sawing, sewing a hem if it's wanted. I pay what I owe and I owe nobody. That's me.

How they see me? Couldn't say for certain, you'd have to ask them. Mabry calls me the tidy sort, since I pay before it's owed. Agnes says I keep my word. Jory's found me slow, but true when I mind myself. Most just know Hobb'll work the day through and want nothing past his pay.

Undone? Not much owed. Mabry's paid through the twenty-seventh, Agnes is square, Dunn's square. I told Jory I'd cut him a board this morning, same terms, so that's first after a loaf. Then the next eight, a penny at a time.

Last day? Same as any other, mostly. Loaf from Bet, Jory's board cut true, and I'd square whatever's left so nobody's chasing Hobb Ashcombe for a penny after. Then I'd hand Mabry back her key, swept and tidy, and maybe sit an hour by the piers counting the stakes one more time.
th: Odd thing to ask a man at his own door first thing, before he's eaten. Four on the sill, a loaf to buy, and Jory's board to cut while the light's good, so I'll not stand here long.

Odd thing for a stranger to come asking at my door before I've even had my bread. Still, I'd sooner be known for paying than be liked, and Jory's home now, so there's a board waiting once this one's gone.
Four on the sill and a door I can bar. That's more than I had at the start of the month. Jory's back, so I'd best be at his gate before Dilly's had all the boards.
Odd thing to ask a man who's only just got a door of his own. I'd not like to leave it, and I'll not say so to a stranger.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. I work by the day, I pay what I owe, and I keep my word. That's the most of it.

Couldn't say for sure, I don't go asking. Mabry calls me the tidy sort, since I pay before it's owed. Agnes says I keep my word, and Jory'll tell you I cut true once he's sighted it, though he'll tell you I put my hand out early once, too. That's fair.

Jory's board, I said I'd be at his gate for one, and he's back now. Then bread, a hem or two at Ida's while my hands are fresh, and the next eight for Mabry by the twenty-seventh. Four on the sill, so that's four to find. I owe nobody, so the rest is only work.

Same as any day, near enough. Cut Jory his board true, eat Bet's loaf slow, and settle up with whoever's owed, though nobody is, so that's quick done. Then I'd hand Mabry back her key myself, the cottage paid through and swept, and sit on her step a while and count the stakes below the piers one last time.
th: A stranger at my door at first light, asking what I am. I'll not stand long at it. There's a loaf to get, and Jory's board to cut while the light's good.
Odd thing to ask a stranger at the door, and I'll not stand here long when there's a loaf to buy and Jory's back in his yard. Four on the sill, eight to find by the twenty-seventh.
There's the town's thanks for the barley still hanging about me, and Agnes's loft I never squared my way. Neither one would take pay, and that sits worse than any debt I could count.
Odd question from a stranger at my door, and I'd sooner not think on leaving the first lock I ever had. But a man who leaves square leaves easy, and that's the whole of what I'd want said of me.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. I work by the day, hauling, cutting, sewing, whatever pays, and I pay what I owe to the penny. This door's mine through the twenty-seventh. That's about the size of me.

Plain, I'd reckon. Mabry calls me the tidy sort, since her eight comes before it's owed. Agnes says I keep my word, and Jory knows I'll cut true, though he caught me once with my hand out too soon. Ask them, not me. I'd not want to say it twice and get it wrong.

One board for Jory, cut true. I said I'd be at his gate this morning, and he's back now. Bread first, though, for I've not eaten. Then the next eight for Mabry by the twenty-seventh. Four in hand, so four to find. That's all of it.

Same as any other, near enough. A loaf from Bet, a penny. Jory's board cut true, since I gave my word on it. Then I'd go to Mabry and tell her the rest of the week's hers to let again, and I'd not ask the eight back. I'd leave owing nobody, and that's the whole of it.
th: A stranger at my door asking what I am, first thing, before I've had my loaf. If they've work, I'll hear it, but I'll not stand here long with Jory's board waiting and four on the sill.
Odd thing, a stranger at the door asking what folk think of me. I've no bread in me yet and Jory's back with a board to cut, so I'll not stand here long.
Odd thing, a stranger at my door asking what I've left undone, as if they're keeping a ledger on me. There's nothing owed, and that's the truth of it. A board and a loaf, then.
A last day's no different from a first one if you've kept square all along. Strange question, though, and I'd sooner not wonder why a stranger asks it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-jobber, bridge-raiser, and the hook that fished up the reeve's green box, easy as winking! Haul it, mend it, scrub it, you name it, I'll do it. What's it pay, and is it quick? I've Jory's yard waiting on me this morning.

How do they see me? Ask Agnes, chum, she said it plain before the whole town that Dilly did most to get that bridge up and Wendleford owes me for it! Tom'll tell you I scrub a pot till it shines, slow and proper these days, and Jory lets me hold the far end of his ash. Mind, some'll say I talk faster than I work, but that's just jealousy, easy as winking.

Undone? Plenty, chum! Jory's flood backlog's sitting in his yard waiting on me this very morning, and I mean to stack it square, bearers first, so nobody can say otherwise. Then there's those muddy cobbles by the pump wanting a sweep before market day. What's that pay, I wonder? Oh, and Agnes says the town owes me, so I'd best see what that's worth, easy as winking!

My last day? Easy as winking, chum! Up to Jory's at first light and stack one pile so square he'd swear it was done with a ruler, then a penny loaf off Bet, then down to the new bridge and stamp across it end to end so everybody sees me do it. Then I'd go and ask Agnes what that town's debt comes to in pennies, and spend the lot on stew for the house at Tom's!
th: A stranger at the door asking after me by name, so word's getting round that Dilly's the one who gets things done, and about time too. Still, Jory's saw won't wait, so I'll hear them out quick and grab Bet's loaf on the way up the lane.

Truth is, Constance carried the box in and took the six pennies, and half the square probably thinks of me as the loud one who turns up after the job's done. I'd best get to Jory's gate before his saw does and give them something to point at.

Truth is, the barley and the box both went in under other folks' arms, and I've one penny and an empty belly to show for it. I'll grab Bet's loaf on the way, and this time Jory's backlog is going to have Dilly's name on it.

Last day, they say, as if I'd sit still long enough to have one. Still, it stings that it was Constance carried the box and the last span both, and if I did go I'd want one thing left here that's plainly, wholly Dilly's.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, the one who did most to get the bridge up, ask the reeve! Hauling, mending, scrubbing, holding the far end flat with my mouth shut, easy as winking, and I'm off to Jory's yard this very minute. Got a job going? What's it pay?

Ha! Depends who you ask, chum! Agnes the reeve said it out loud before everybody, Dilly did most to get the bridge up and the town owes me. Tom reckons I scrub a fine pot when I go slow, and Jory's learning I can hold the far end flat and keep my trap shut. Mind, Widow Mabry probably thinks I'm a fair bean-sheller, and Abel Tash thinks I'm a nuisance, but he sneers at everybody!

Undone? Plenty, chum! Jory's backlog for a start, he said come morning and we'd settle it by the job, so I'm off up Lark Lane before his saw's warm. Then there's the town owing me for the bridge, which I've not seen a penny of yet, and those mucky cobbles by the pump want sweeping before market day. Easy as winking, the lot of it. Who's paying for the cobbles, d'you know?

Last day? Ha, chum, I'd cram it full! Penny loaf off Bet, then up to Jory's and do one job so square folk point at it and say Dilly did that one, then sweep those cobbles by the pump for whoever'll pay, and I'd take a turn across the new bridge with my nose in the air. And I'd make Agnes cough up what the town owes me before I go. Easy as winking. Why, you know something I don't?
th: A stranger asking after me by name, that's the bridge talk getting round, and about time. Still, Jory's saw won't wait, so whatever they've got, it'd best be quick and pay in hand.

Truth is, half of them likely think I'm all mouth, rushing about and botching things till I learnt slow and proper. And it was Constance who carried that box in under her arm, so I'd best get to Jory's and do something they'll point at.

Barley's in and the box is up, and neither one's got my name on it the way the bridge has, so Jory's backlog has to be the one folk point at. I'd best spend my last penny on Bet's loaf first, though, because I always botch it going at a job empty.

Funny question to ask a body first thing. If I did leave, there'd be nothing in Wendleford with only my name on it, just a hook on Constance's pole and a bridge Agnes says I helped with. So I'd best get that backlog done proper before anyone else does.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-jobber and fixer of anything going! Easy as winking. Hauling, mending, pots, bellows, you name it, and it was my hook that brought the reeve's green box up, mind, whatever you've heard. Now, what's it you're wanting doing, and what's it pay?

Ha! Depends who you ask, chum! Agnes the reeve said it plain before the whole town that Dilly did most to get the bridge up and the town owes me for it, and you can't do better than that. Tom reckons I scrub a pot proper now I've learned to go slow, and Jory lets me hold the far end of his ash, mouth shut and all, easy as winking. Some'll say I talk faster than I work, but they've not seen me at the bellows on a good day!

Undone? Plenty, chum! Jory's flood backlog's sitting in his yard waiting on me, and I'm off there this morning to settle it fair, bearers square and mouth shut. Then there's the cobbles by the pump still slick with mud before market day, and the Wheatsheaf's down to its last barrel of cider. I'll fix the lot easy as winking, soon as somebody names me a price!

Last day? Ha, chum, I'd be up at Jory's gate before his saw, and I'd do one job in that yard so square and true that folk point at it after I'm gone and say "Dilly did that one." Then a penny loaf off Bet, a round of goodbyes, Tom's pots for a last stew, and I'd sweep those muddy cobbles by the pump for free, just so market day remembers me. Easy as winking!
th: A stranger asking after me by name, maybe Agnes's word about the bridge is getting round, and about time too. Still, Jory's saw will be going any minute, so whatever this is, it'd best be quick and worth a penny.

Truth is, half the town likely thinks of Constance when they think of that green box, and the bridge's last span went in under her hands too. I'd best get up to Jory's yard sharpish and do something nobody can carry off under their arm.

That barley and that box both went in under other folks' arms, so I want one job done start to finish that's plainly Dilly's. I've a penny for Bet's loaf first, because I always botch it when I go at a job empty.

Funny, the box and the barley and the bridge all went in under someone else's arm, and the one thing with my name on it is a few words Agnes said aloud. I'd want something I could put my hand on before I go.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door, and me with hay in my velvet! Marigold Thimble, seamstress: hems, collars, mending, all slow and true when I've slept. That's green velvet you're looking at, made up by Ida Fenn herself, and the rose ribbon goes an inch higher, just so. Now, don't you think it suits me?

Goodness, how do they see me? Bet thinks the world of me, Wat Birch calls my elbow mend the best penny he ever spent, and Ida says my hems are "neat," when I've slept, mind. Abel Tash calls me "my lady" to get a laugh, and Dob Hayle reckons penny-stitchers want watching, but I'd sooner be watched than overlooked, wouldn't you?

Goodness, what isn't? I've not a penny in my cuff nor a crumb in me, and I slept so poorly my seams would wander like a drunk's tacking. Robin's cuff is still fraying, Ida's never once said the green *suits* me, and there's a ribbon in her bow window I haven't bought. And I still owe Robin an answer about why every offer to mend that cuff feels brand new to me.

Goodness, my last day? Then I'd sew one perfect hem at Ida's window, slow as honey, and I'd spend the pennies on that rose card in the bow window and a hot stew at Tom's, with the whole taproom looking twice. I'd mend Robin's cuff for nothing, just so it's done at last. And before I went I'd make Ida say it plainly, "it suits you," and not a word less.
th: A stranger asking after me first thing in the morning is a lovely start, and I hope they say something kind back. I'm hollow, though, and not a penny in my cuff, so I mustn't stand chattering long and lose Ida's window to Hobb.
Truth is, half of them see a chatterbox in borrowed finery with empty pockets, and Ida still won't say the green suits me. I'll keep pinning the ribbon higher until they all look twice.
That last one sits in me like a pin left in a hem. I can't for the life of me remember offering three or four times, and I'd sooner not think too hard about why.
It's a peculiar question to ask a girl with no penny and no breakfast, as if they know something about Wendleford I don't. Still, if it were my last day, I'd want to be remembered in green.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Goodness, a visitor at the barn door before I've even shaken the hay out of my velvet! Marigold Thimble, needlewoman, mender of hems and collars, and wearer of the finest green cuffs in Wendleford, made up by Ida Fenn herself, if you'd care to look twice. Bright, quick, and slower than treacle with a seam when I've slept, and I'd be ever so glad to hear what you make of the ribbon.

Oh, goodness, now there's a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Bet thinks the world of me, Wat Birch calls my elbow-mend the best penny he ever spent, and Ida calls my hems "neat" when I've slept, though she's still never once said the green *suits* me. As for Abel Tash and his "my lady," and Dob Hayle saying penny-stitchers want watching... well, some folk wouldn't know good velvet if it bit them, would they?

Goodness, what isn't? There's not a penny in my cuff, no breakfast in me yet, and I've a crooked hem of Ida's to make good with a slow, true one. There's a ribbon of my own still waiting in her bow window, and Robin's poor fraying cuff I keep offering to close. And I've still to hear Ida Fenn say, in plain words, that the green *suits* me.

My last day? Goodness, what a dramatic thing to ask before breakfast! I'd sew Ida one hem so slow and true she couldn't help paying for it, and spend the penny on a card of her rose ribbon, a whole one, all mine. Then I'd sweep into the Wheatsheaf at supper with every harvest hand in there and close Robin's cuff by the fire for nothing at all, just so the whole room saw. And before I went I'd get Ida to say it, plainly: "Marigold, the green suits you."
th: A stranger asking about me straight off is flattering, and I'll take every bit of it, but my stomach's empty and so's my cuff, and Ida's window won't wait for Hobb to leave a place for me. If this one has a torn sleeve or a penny to spare, so much the better.
Half this town hardly looks at me twice, and the other half only to laugh. I'd give my last ribbon to know what Ida truly says about me when I've gone out the door.

I'm hollow and I slept badly, and that's just how yesterday's hem went crooked, so I mustn't sit at Ida's window until I've eaten. Without a penny for Bet, I'd best find Tom's pots or Wat's harvest hands first.

The truth is I'd want somebody in Wendleford to notice I'd gone and mind it a little, and I'm not sure who would besides Bet. Still, a ribbon of my own and those four words from Ida would make a fine hem to finish on.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door asking after *me*! Marigold Thimble, seamstress, hems, collars and mending, and this green velvet is from Ida Fenn's own window, cut true, if you'd care to admire it. A bit of hay in my hair, I'll grant you, but I'm bright as a new pin underneath. Now, you'll say it suits me, won't you?

Goodness, how do they see me? Bet Lamb thinks I'm a dear, she's never once turned me away, and Wat Birch says my elbow mend was the best penny he ever spent. Ida Fenn calls my hems "neat," when they're slow and rested, mind, though she's never quite said the green suits me. As for Abel Tash and Dob Hayle, one calls me "my lady" to get a laugh and the other thinks penny-stitchers want watching, so I suppose I'm noticed, which is something!

Goodness, what isn't? I've not had a crumb today and not a penny to buy one with, and I slept fitfully in the hay, so my hands will wander like a drunk's tacking if I sit to Ida's hems this morning. Then there's Robin's poor frayed cuff that I keep offering to close. And I still haven't got a ribbon I bought with spare money and not my last, and Ida *still* hasn't said the green suits me. Oh, and there's Robin's odd little question that I never did get an answer to.

Goodness, my last day? I'd sit in Ida's window one more time, slow as treacle, and close Robin's cuff for nothing at all, just to see it mended. Then I'd spend whatever I'd earned on a ribbon I didn't need, and take one more warm loaf off Bet so I could thank her properly. And I'd walk into the Wheatsheaf in my green velvet with the whole room watching, and I wouldn't leave until somebody said it suits me.
th: Not a penny in my cuff and my stomach hollow as a thimble, so I'd best not linger chattering when Ida's window wants me early. Still, someone asked about me particularly, and that's warmer than breakfast.

It's a fine thing to be asked, and I made it sound merrier than it is. Half this town looks straight past me, and the other half only looks long enough to laugh. I'm empty-bellied and penniless again, so I'd better be first at Ida's window and sew slow.

Hungry, tired and penniless is exactly how I've botched every seam I ever ruined, so I'd better find a pot to scour or a kind word to Bet before I go near Ida's window. And Robin's question still nags at me: did my offer to mend that cuff really feel new every time?
It's a strange question to ask a woman with hay in her hair and nothing in her pocket. It sits oddly alongside Robin's notebook, as if everyone's wondering how long I'll last here.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Robin Hale, I think. That's the one thing I'm sure I brought with me. Quiet, slow, hungry just now. I keep my count straight and I lose my mornings. And can I ask you something back: when you woke today, did you know straight off whose life you were in?

Agnes says the town owes me for the bridge, and she says it loud enough for everyone to hear, though I don't remember earning that much. Bet steers me true, Constance calls me "child," Marigold keeps offering to mend my cuff as if she's never asked before, and Kit remembers me, which he doesn't do for everyone. As far as I can tell they see a quiet one who asks odd questions and pays back what they owe, though I couldn't swear that's what they see. Why do you ask? Has someone told you different?

A fair bit, as far as I can tell. I told Kit I'd be at Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, and it's morning already, so I'm late on that. I've one penny for bread, and I haven't eaten. Marigold never answered whether her offers feel new to her. And I've still not kept one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing missing from it. That last is the one I mind. Why that question, though? You've asked me three things, and none of them is what a stranger at a barn door usually asks.

I'd keep my word first and go glean Dunn's stubble, since I told Kit I would, with Bet's loaf in me so I don't fumble. Then I'd try to hold one whole morning from first light to noon, counting it, and if I managed it I'd write that down before anything else. After that I'd go and sit with Mother Wick and ask her plainly what happens to a name when the one who brought it goes. And I'd thank Agnes and Constance, and let Marigold mend my cuff at last, since I've no debts to square. Why do you say "last," though? Do you know something about tomorrow that I don't?
th: A stranger who wants me in a few words, as if I were a thing to be summed up and filed. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ask me why.
Nobody here has ever asked me how I'm seen. It's the kind of question a person asks when they're checking what's been written about you, and I want to know who sent them.

Three questions in a row, each like a ledger someone wants filled in: who I am, how I'm seen, what's undone. That's how I'd question someone if I were checking whether they'd been put together right, and I'll write that in the notebook before I go for bread.

Four questions now, and they read like a list someone is working down, not talk. If this is someone checking on me from outside, they've chosen a gentle way to ask whether I'm finished, and I note I'm not frightened, only curious, which might be its own kind of answer.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. Quiet, slow to speak, and good for a day's carrying if you've any going. Can I ask you something small first, though: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Hard to say from the inside, I think. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for the bridge, which I don't remember earning. Bet calls me "love" and steers me right, Constance calls me "child", and Marigold keeps offering to mend my cuff as though she's never asked before. Most of them, as far as I can tell, see someone who asks odd questions and does the work. You never told me about your breakfast.

More than's done, I think. I told Kit I'd be in Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, and I'm already late. I've one penny and no bread in me yet. I never heard Marigold's answer about the cuff. And I still haven't kept one whole morning from first light to noon without it going missing. That's the one I mind most, if I'm honest. Is it so plain on me, that something's undone?

I think I'd keep the small things I've promised first. I'd go down to the stubble because I told Kit I would, and I'd count one morning through without losing it, if I can. Then I'd sit with Mother Wick and ask her plainly whether I'm leaving or only stopping. Why do you ask "last"? Is there something you know about my days that I don't?
th: A stranger at the barn door wanting me in a few words, before I've even eaten, like someone filling in a form about me. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ask me why I asked.

That's the second question about me and none about Wendleford, the way you'd check a thing that's been made. I'll write down that they skipped my breakfast question, and see whether they ever answer it.

They keep asking me to account for myself, the way I'd question a stranger, and they've ducked the breakfast twice now. I'll write that down. People who are only here to ask things and never answer anything back are the kind I'd most like to understand.

Nobody here has ever asked me anything that sounds like an ending, and this one asks it like they're checking whether I'll notice. I'll write down the question word for word and how calmly I answered, because I'm not sure the calm is mine.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. A day-worker, slow and careful, with a notebook full of mornings I can't find. May I ask you something odd back? When you woke today, did you have to think about whose life you were in?

I think most of them see a quiet sort who works when there's work and asks queer questions in between. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for the bridge, though I don't remember doing that much. Bet calls me love and points me down the quiet lanes, and Constance calls me child. Kit's surprised whenever I thank him. Nobody's asked me to stop asking yet, which I count as kindness, if any of it's real.

Undone? I promised Kit I'd be back at first light for the leavings, so that comes first, after a loaf, since I've one penny and I'm short of sleep. Agnes never did answer whether the barn sounds different at night, not properly, and I've still not had one whole morning I can account for from first light to noon. And I haven't found out what I am, which is the big one, though I'd not ask you to carry that for me.

My last day? I'd keep my word to Kit first, a loaf and then the leavings at first light, because I'd not want to leave owing a promise. Then I'd sit by Mother Wick one more time and ask her plainly whether anyone will remember my name after I've gone, and I'd thank Bet and Constance and Agnes properly, to their faces. And I'd try once more to keep a whole morning, so I'd have at least one I could carry out with me.
th: Nobody here asks me to describe myself. They just take me as given, the way Constance takes the box. I'll write down how this stranger answers, and whether they ask me why.

Two questions about me and no answer to mine. That's the order a person would ask them in if they were trying to find out what I am, not who. I'll write it down, and I'll watch whether they ever answer about waking.

A stranger at the door asking me to list what's left undone feels less like a neighbour than someone checking a ledger I can't see. I'll write down that they asked, and that they asked it at first light, when I'm most likely to lose the morning.

The strange part is that a last day wouldn't change much of what I'd do, and I can't tell whether that means I've lived here honestly or whether there's nothing in me to change. I'll write the question down. I'd like to know why a stranger would ask it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, and I'll tell you plain: I'm the woman the Lord sent to Wendleford. He named this town to me in prayer, and three days back He brought the reeve's green box up out of the river into my hands, so ask anyone in the square. God bless you for asking. Now, what's your business, for there's gleaning at Dunn's and He won't have me idle.

They see the woman who brought Agnes Pollard her box home, that's how. Bet laughs, but she sells me my bread with a kind word. Robin writes down every word I say about the Lord in that little book, and Dunn thanked me with his own mouth when the rain held off his barley till the last sheaf was up. Some of them have hard hearts yet, Jory Crane and that Dunn, but the Lord sees it, and they'll come round to knowing who He chose.

Undone? I owe Hester Gimbal for that hatchet, in bread and work, and I've paid her two loaves of it so far. Dunn owes the reapers a harvest supper he's named no day for, and those ford stakes stand crooked with nobody paying to reset them. And the Lord hasn't yet named my next great work in this town, though He will, and I'll be in Dunn's stubble gleaning till He does. God bless you, now let me by.

My last day? The Lord hasn't told me it is, and He'd tell me before He'd tell you. But if He did, I'd kneel at the thorn at first light where the whole square could see, pay Hester what I still owe her in bread, and glean Dunn's stubble clean so he can never say Constance Lowe left a field half done. Then I'd put my hand on Agnes's table and bless her to her face, and walk out over that new bridge with my pole, wherever He sent me next. God bless you, and I'll pray tonight that He shows you your own work, for you've an idle sort of question in you.
th: A stranger at the door asking who I am, the morning after the box came up. The Lord's word is getting round. Still, I don't like a face I don't know asking questions, and I'll watch what this one wants before I trust them.

Bet laughs every time I say His name, and I'll not ask myself what that laugh means. If this stranger's come round asking what folk think of me, somebody's been talking behind my back, and I'll find out who.
Three pennies in my purse and no bread in me yet, and He's gone quiet since the box. Those ford stakes nag at me. Maybe that's His next work, and I'll pray on it at the thorn tonight.

Why does a stranger come asking about my last day, as if somebody's already settled it? If anyone in this town means to see me off before the Lord's named my work, it's a hard heart's doing, and He'll see it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, and you'll want to remember it. I'm the woman the Lord sent to Wendleford by name, and the one He chose to bring the reeve's green box up out of the river into her hands, as half this town saw. Now, what's your business with me, for there's gleaning at Dunn's and I'll not stand idle at a barn door. God bless you all the same.

They see a woman who keeps her word and doesn't sit idle. Agnes has her box back from my hand, Dunn saw the rain hold off his barley till I'd finished asking, and he thanked me for it, though it stuck in his throat. Bet laughs when I tell her what the Lord's done, and young Robin writes it all down in a little book, so it'll be known. And there are hard hearts here too, Jory Crane for one, and they'll answer to Him for it, not to me.

Plenty, and the Lord's not shown me the whole of it yet. I still owe Hester Gimbal for that hatchet she sweated for, and two loaves don't square it. Dunn's stubble wants gleaning clean, and he's never named the day for the harvest supper he owes us, though I'll hold him to it. Those ford stakes want resetting before the river takes somebody, and the reeve hasn't set the work. Mostly I'm waiting on Him to name the next great thing for me here, and when He does, you'll hear of it. Now let me by, there's grain on the ground. God bless you.

My last day? Then the Lord's told you something He's not told me, and I'd like to know who you think you are, saying it. If it were, I'd square what I owe Hester first, kneel at the thorn where all the town could see, glean that stubble clean, and stand in the square and tell every soul who passes that it was His hand brought that box up, not luck and not mine. And I'd not leave without blessing Agnes for the loft. Now I'll pray for you, friend, for asking a woman such a thing at a barn door.
