th: A stranger at the door asking me to tell them who I am, and before I've so much as broken bread. Either the word of the box has gone round and the Lord's sent them, or they've come to look me over and doubt me, and I'll know which soon enough.

Agnes thanked Dilly and Robin before the whole town and only paid me in pennies, and Bet's laugh had a "did He, love" in it I didn't care for. They'll see it plain soon enough, when He names the next work and it's me He names it to.
He hasn't told me yet, and the waiting gnaws at me worse than an empty belly. If those stakes are His next work, Agnes had better not stand in the way of it the way she did with her rope.

Who sends a stranger to ask me about a last day, when He hasn't said one word of my leaving? It sets my teeth on edge, and I'll take it to Him at the thorn tonight. Either it's a warning, or it's somebody's wickedness wanting me gone.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord sent me to Wendleford. He named this town to me in prayer, and just two days past He brought the reeve's green box up out of the river into my hands. Ask anyone in the square, they saw me carry it. God bless you, now step aside, for the gleaners are out and He won't have me idle.

They see the woman who carried Agnes Pollard's box through the square with her own two arms, that's how. Dunn heard me pray the rain off his barley and saw the heavens open the moment the last sheaf went up, and Bet laughs, but she sells me my bread and knows whose hand the Lord used. Some of them are slow to say it, hard hearts like Jory Crane's, but He sees that, and they'll come round. Now God bless you, I've stubble waiting.

Undone? The Lord hasn't named my next work yet, but He will. He tells me in prayer, and I'll be listening at the thorn till He does. I still owe Hester for that hatchet in bread and work, and I'll pay her every crumb. Dunn owes us all a harvest supper he's named no day for, and those ford stakes stand crooked with nobody willing to pay for them. Now step aside and God bless you, for there's grain lying in that stubble and I haven't had my loaf.

My last day? The Lord hasn't told me it is, and He tells me, not you. But if He did, I'd kneel at that thorn at first light and thank Him aloud where the whole square could hear. I'd pay Hester what I owe her in bread from my own purse, and glean Dunn's stubble clean so he'd remember whose prayer held off his rain. And I'd stand in front of Agnes and tell her plain that it was the Lord who chose me to bring her box home, so she couldn't go thanking Dilly and Robin and forget it.
th: A stranger at the door before I've broken my fast, asking what I am. Maybe the Lord's sent them, or maybe they've come to look me over and doubt me, and I'll know which soon enough.

Bet laughed, and that Robin child keeps asking whether I *decided* to believe, writing it all down like it wants weighing. If they don't see it yet it's their blindness and not my doing, but I'll be in that field first today so not one of them can say they didn't.

Three pennies, an empty belly and no word yet from Him, and here's a stranger at the door asking what's left undone, as if He'd send a stranger to ask me that. Perhaps it's the ford stakes. Nobody's set that work and nobody's paying, and that's just the sort of thing He'd keep back for the one He chose.

Why would a stranger ask me that, at the barn door, the morning after I carried that box through the square? If somebody in this town wants me gone, the Lord sees it, and I'll find whose sin it is before I'll go quiet about it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague: Sam's new helper, bellows-pumper, scale-sweeper, and inventor of things that very nearly work! Hypothesis: I'm curious. Test: ask me about the missing wage box and see how long I talk. Who are you, then?

Ha! Fascinating question, my dear colleague. I've only been here a few days, so I'd guess most folk see me as "that new girl at the smithy who talks too fast and pokes at everything." Sam probably thinks I'm a whirlwind with soot on it, and Bet at the bread stall, well, she can keep up with me, which is rare! Hypothesis: they think I'm odd. Test: keep being odd and see if they come round.

Undone? My dear colleague, nearly everything! Agnes's wage box is still lost somewhere along the river, Farmer Dunn's barley is standing ripe across a ford that wants to drown people, the bridge is still in pieces, and I haven't even had breakfast. Hypothesis: the order matters. Test: a loaf from Bet, then the barley before the rain, then the riverbank for clues!

My last day? Fascinating, my dear colleague, and dreadful! I'd wade that ford stake to stake at first light and get Dunn's barley cut and in before the rain, then comb every inch of the riverbank by the old mill bridge until Agnes's wage box turned up, and I'd spend my last four pennies on bread for whoever looked hungriest. Hypothesis: you can cram a whole life's helping into one day. Test: don't sleep!
th: A stranger who sits down and asks me to describe myself is either idle or fishing, and either way that's a puzzle worth poking at. Maybe they know something about the bridge the night it went.
Truth is, nobody here knows me yet. I'm just the stranger who turned up after the flood. I'd best find that wage box for Agnes, and then they'll know me for something.

The barley can't wait. Rain doesn't care about mysteries, and the Dunns will go hungry if it rots. But I'd wager the wage box went into the water near the bridge footings, and if I'm wading that ford anyway, I'll keep my eyes on the shallows.
Odd thing for a stranger to ask, as if they know something I don't. Still, it's a good question, and it makes me want to stop talking and go do all of it right now.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hester Gimbal, my dear colleague! Sam's new bellows-girl, tinkerer, and investigator of everything broken in Wendleford, which, since the flood, is very nearly everything! In a few words? Hypothesis: I'm curious. Test: watch me take that hinge apart before Sam notices.

How do they see me? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and I've hardly any data! I've only been here a few days. Sam sees a pair of hands for the bellows and a lot of scattered tools in his loft. Bet Lamb sees a penny for a loaf and someone who talks nearly as fast as she does. Agnes Pollard, I hope, will soon see the girl who found her wage box! Everyone else? Probably "that new one from the smithy who keeps poking at the river." Hypothesis: they think I'm odd. Test: ask three of them. I'll report back!

Undone? My dear colleague, everything! The wage box is still missing, Farmer Dunn's barley is standing ripe across a ford that's running like a racehorse, rain's due in a few days, Sam's buried in bridge bolts, and I haven't had breakfast! I'll start with a loaf from Bet, then the river, then the box. Hypothesis: the barley is the most urgent. Test: get across and count the sickles.

My last day? Then there's no time to waste talking, my dear colleague! Barley first: across the ford stake to stake with every pair of hands I can drag along, because Farmer Dunn shouldn't lose a year's bread to rain. Then the wage box, so Agnes can sleep at night. And if there's an hour left over, I'd leave Sam a proper bellows-crank so he never misses me. Gimbal's Patent Farewell Engine!
th: A stranger sitting down by the forge to ask who I am is a little puzzle all its own. I'll find out who *they* are next, and whether they've heard anything about Agnes's wage box.

Truth is, I'm a stranger who came in on the heels of a disaster, and folk may not trust a newcomer while the wages are missing. All the more reason to be useful fast, before anyone decides what I am for me.
The barley worries me most, because rain won't wait while I play detective. But that wage box was at the bridge when it went, and I'd wager a penny the river knows where it ended up.
It stings a little that I'd have to leave half these puzzles unsolved. Then again, maybe that's my answer: don't spend any day as if there'll be a tomorrow to finish it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: A few words? Impossible, my dear colleague, which means I must try! Hester Gimbal: smith's helper, bellows-pumper, tinkerer, and very soon the finder of Agnes Pollard's lost wage box. Hypothesis: a box that heavy didn't float far. Do you know the river well, by any chance?

How do they see me? Fascinating question, and I've no data yet, my dear colleague. I've only been here a few days! Sam thinks I pump the bellows too fast, Bet Lamb thinks I talk nearly as fast as she does, and the rest probably think "who's that sooty girl poking at the riverbank?" Hypothesis: they'll see me better once I've found that wage box.

Undone? Oh, my dear colleague, nearly everything! The wage box is still missing, Farmer Dunn's barley is standing over the river with rain on the way, the mill bridge is in pieces, and I haven't even had breakfast. Hypothesis: a body can't wade a ford on an empty stomach. Test: one of Bet's loaves, then the riverbank!

My last day? Then there's no time for breakfast! I'd wade the ford stake to stake and cut Farmer Dunn's barley before the rain comes, because that's someone in real trouble. Then I'd drag a hook along the riverbed below the bridge for Agnes's wage box. And I'd leave Sam a proper bellows, Gimbal's Patent Self-Puffing Contraption, so he wouldn't miss me too much.
th: A stranger sitting down at the smithy the morning after everyone's talking about the missing wages. Fascinating! Either they want something mended, or they know something, and I mean to find out which.

Truth is, I'm a stranger who turned up the week the bridge went, and folk are bound to wonder about that. Best get useful quick, so they've something better to say about me than "she arrived just after the flood."

Four pennies won't stretch far, but bread's cheap and the barley won't wait. If I could rig some kind of line between the ford stakes, folk could carry sheaves across without getting swept off. That might be worth a sketch before Sam needs the bellows.
The barley comes first, because people will go hungry without it, and the box can wait an hour. Still, nobody's thought to search the eddy below the bridge pilings, and that's where I'd look.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Day man. I haul, stack, mend, whatever pays. I sleep in the loft up there by the reeve's leave, and I owe nobody. That's about the whole of it.

As a pair of hands, mostly. Reliable, I'd hope. Dunn knows I'll stack till the tally's done, and Bet knows I pay what the loaf costs. Some likely think me close, short with a word, and won't take thanks. Fair's fair, they're not wrong.

Plenty. Dunn's barley stands ripe over the water, and rain's coming. One, two, three days, maybe. The reeve's wage box is still lost. And I've a debt of nights to Agnes I've not squared yet. That's three. Four, if you count I've not had my bread.

Last day? Then I'd square up first. Pay Agnes for the nights, whatever she'll take, and leave nothing on the slate. Then over the ford, stake to stake, and cut Dunn's barley till dark. One sheaf, two, three... A man oughtn't leave owing, nor leave a job standing that rain'll spoil.
th: Odd thing to ask a man before he's had his bread. Still, she's sat by the reeve's tin, so I'll keep one eye on it and the other on what the day might pay.
Odd question from a stranger, first thing. Still, a stranger asking what folk think of me is no debt to anyone, so let them ask.
Barley first. It's work, it pays, and Dunn's wife feeds the hands. The ford's strong, but stake to stake it'll go, and a box swept off that bridge might be lying somewhere down there.
Odd question, that. Never had a door of my own, and a last day wouldn't give me one, but I could go out of here owing nobody, and that's near as good.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Day-labourer, forty-one, sleeps in that loft up there. I pay what I owe and work till the tally's done. That's about the size of it.

Steady, I'd reckon. Dunn knows I'll stack what I say I'll stack, and the reeve knows I'll not touch what's on her table. Some think me close with a penny, and they're not wrong. Ask them yourself, if you want it plainer.

Plenty. Dunn's barley stands ripe across the water with rain coming, and somebody's got to wade the ford and cut it. The reeve's wage box is still missing. And I've no door of my own yet. Three things, and I've not eaten, so call it four.

Last day? I'd settle up first. Pay the reeve something fair for all them nights in her loft, so I'd not leave owing. Then over the ford, stake to stake, and get Dunn's barley in before the rain. One, two, three. And a loaf from Bet, paid for, somewhere in there.
th: Stranger sat down close by the reeve's cash tin, asking questions first thing. I'll keep an eye on the tin and on them.
Odd thing, a stranger asking what folk make of me, with the wages box still missing. Best I'm out of this barn and off to find work before anyone gets ideas.

The barley first. That pays and it won't wait, and Dunn's wife will feed whoever helps, which settles the fourth. I'll keep an eye out for that box as I go, for it's the reeve's and it ought to come home.
Odd question, that, and I'd not care to say why it sits heavy. Truth is I've no notion what I owe Agnes for all them years in the loft, and that sum's been gnawing at me longer than I let on.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Hobb Ashcombe. Day man, forty-one, sleeps in the loft up there by the reeve's leave. Owe nobody, and I mean to keep it so.

Same as they see the barn door, I'd reckon. It's there, it works, nobody thinks on it much. Dunn knows I'll stack till the tally's done, and the reeve knows I pay what I owe. Past that, I couldn't say. I don't ask.

Plenty. Dunn's barley stands ripe across the water with rain coming, so that's one. The reeve's wage box is gone, and her loft's never been paid for, not in coin, so that's two. And I've no door of my own yet. That's three.

Last day? Then I'd settle up. Wade the ford stake to stake, cut Dunn's barley till the light goes, that's one. Leave what pennies I've got on the reeve's ledger for the loft, all six, that's two. The door I'd let go. A man can't have everything in a day.
th: Six pennies, one empty belly, and Dunn's barley standing ripe across the ford. Whoever this is, I'll not stand chatting long with work waiting.
Odd sort of question from a stranger, this early, with straw still on me. Constance Lowe, if that's who this is, wants something, and I'll wait to hear what it is before I give more than I've given.
Six pennies won't touch Mabry's week in advance, but the barley pays and the ford can be waded stake to stake. Bread first, then the river.
Odd, how quick the cottage dropped off the list when there was no time left. Maybe owing nobody was always the bigger want, and the door was just how I meant to show it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-jobber, hauler, mender, fixer of whatever's broke, easy as winking! Came into Wendleford a few days back and I'm itching for work, so if you've got a job going, what's it pay?

Ha! New face, chum, and a cheerful one at that, I'd say! Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf likes me well enough, I paid him prompt for two nights. Bet Lamb's had me asking what a loaf costs before I've said good morning, and the reeve's probably seen me reading her reward notice so often she thinks I'm learning it by heart. Give it a week and they'll all know me as the one who fixed the bridge business, easy as winking!

Undone? Ha, chum, the whole town's undone! There's a wage box gone missing worth six pennies to whoever finds it, Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe across the river with rain on the way, the mill bridge in bits, and Tom's pots piled up in the scullery. And me, I haven't even had my breakfast yet, but I'll sort the lot, easy as winking. Which one pays best, d'you reckon?

My last day? Ha, chum, I'd cram the whole lot in! Breakfast loaf off Bet first, then wade the ford stake to stake and get Dunn's barley in before the rain, and find that green box on the way, easy as winking, so they'd have to say Dilly Quickstep did it. And I'd spend whatever I'd earned on a bargain at Ned's stall before sundown, since it's no good to me tomorrow.
th: A stranger asking about me, maybe they've work, or maybe they've heard something about that green wage box. Either way, I'd best keep my ears open and my four pennies close.
Truth is, I've only been here a few days, and most of them likely think I'm just another chatty stranger with a pack. Better find something to fix, and quick, before that's all they ever think.

That box went in at the bridge, so it's likely downstream somewhere, and six pennies plus the name of the one who found it would suit me nicely. A loaf from Bet first, though, and I'll ask her what she's heard while I'm at it.
Funny how the barley comes to mind first. That's the one that'd be gone for good if nobody saw to it. Still, I'd not leave without folk knowing my name.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-job hand, fixer of whatever's broke, and quick about it! Haul it, mend it, carry it, find it, easy as winking. What's the job, and what's it pay?

Oh, I've only been in Wendleford a few days, chum, so I'd say they see me coming! Tom Harrow's got my pennies for a bed, Bet Lamb's had me asking after her loaves, and the reeve'll know my name soon enough, once I've found that green box for her, easy as winking. New, quick, and handy is how they'll put it, I reckon. Why, has somebody been talking about me?

Undone? Ha, chum, the whole town's undone! There's the mill bridge gone, the reeve's green box lost, Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe over the river with rain coming, pots piled up at the Wheatsheaf, and me with no breakfast in me yet. I'll have that barley in and the box found by the week's end, easy as winking. Which one pays best, d'you reckon?

My last day? Ha! Then I'd not waste a wink of it, chum! I'd have a loaf off Bet first, then wade that ford stake to stake and get Dunn's barley in before the rain, and somewhere along the way I'd turn up that green box and hand it to the reeve with the whole square watching. They'd be saying "Dilly Quickstep did that" long after I'd gone over the hill.
th: A stranger sitting down for a chat might be a stranger with work going, and I'd take it gladly before the morning's half gone. I'd best get a loaf in me from Bet first, though; my belly's starting to nag.

Truth is, nobody here knows me from a sack of turnips yet, and that won't do. I need to fix something big and fix it where folk can see it, the bridge, the barley, that box, so they've a name to say when they ask who did it.
That's a lot of jobs and only one of me, and I've not even started on one of them yet. Bread first, maybe, then the ford, though six pennies for that box does keep tugging at my sleeve.
Funny thing to ask a body, and it's set me wondering whether anyone here would remember my name a week after I'd left. Best make sure they do, then, and start today.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Dilly Quickstep, chum, odd-job wonder and fixer of whatever's broke, easy as winking! Hauling, mending, running messages, you name it and I'll have it done before you've finished asking. Here, you don't happen to need anything doing, do you? What's it pay?

Ha! Well, I've only been in Wendleford a few days, chum, so I'd say they see me coming, mostly! Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf sees a paid-up bed, Bet Lamb sees someone who asks what a loaf costs before saying good morning, and the reeve, why, she'll see the one who found her wage box, just you wait. Give it a week and they'll all be saying "fetch Dilly, Dilly'll fix it."

Undone? Oh, near everything, chum! There's the bridge gone and wanting hands, the reeve's green box still lost, Dunn's barley standing ripe across the river with rain on the way, and Tom's pots piling up in the scullery. And me, I haven't so much as had my breakfast yet, but that's a penny at Bet's and easy as winking.

Last day? Ha! I'd cram it full, chum: breakfast loaf from Bet first, then wade the ford stake to stake and bring in Dunn's barley before the rain, then find the reeve's green box on the way back, easy as winking! And I'd be stood in this square by supper with my name on everybody's lips, so they'd be sorry to see me go. Wouldn't waste a minute of it sitting down, that's for certain.
th: A stranger sitting down for a chat might be a job in disguise, and I could use one before these four pennies wander off to Bet's stall. Mind, if they've heard anything about that green wage box, I want to be the one who turns it up.
Truth is, nobody here knows me from a fencepost yet, and that itches worse than idle hands. Best get something done today that folk will see and remember.

That barley's the big one. If the rain comes and nobody's waded the ford to cut it, there's a whole village that'll remember who did. Mind, I'd best grab a loaf first, and maybe ask Bet if she's heard where that box might have fetched up.
Funny question to ask a body who's only just come. Still, it's set me itching. Why wait for a last day to do all that, when I could start this very morning?

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Oh, goodness, a few words? Marigold Thimble, seamstress: hems, collars, mending, a touch of trimming for anyone with a penny and a wish to look finer than they did at breakfast. I'm a bright bit of ribbon on a rather moth-eaten sort of morning, if I say so myself, and I do. And you'll notice I smoothed this collar myself; does it sit nicely, do you think?

Goodness, how they see me? I've only been in Wendleford a handful of days, so I'm still a new thread in the weave, I suppose. Tom Harrow gave me a kind word with my bed, and Bet Lamb wishes me good morning over her loaves, so I'd like to think I'm the bright stranger with the clever needle and the nicely kept collar. Though I'd not say no to hearing you think so too.

Oh, a great deal, goodness! I haven't had a bite of breakfast yet, I've not called on Ida Fenn to offer my needle for her plain sewing, and there's a ribbon on Ned Pike's stall come market day that I simply must see about. And all those good folk with their Sunday best wanting freshening up who don't yet know I'm here to do it. Mind you, a person might start on that list by telling me my collar was well done.

My last day? Goodness, what a gloomy sort of question, like grey worsted on a May morning! I'd have breakfast first, a warm loaf from Bet Lamb, and then I'd march straight into Ida Fenn's and beg one good look at that green velvet up close. Then I'd spend every last penny on Ned Pike's ribbon and wear it right out of town, so the whole square would have to look twice as I went. And you'd see me off, I hope, and say it suited me?
th: A stranger who sits down and asks about *me* first is a stranger worth keeping. Let's see if they've the manners to say something kind about the collar, and whether that coat of theirs wants a stitch or two I could be paid for.

Truth is, half of them are so wrapped up in the flood and that lost wage box that they've hardly looked at me at all. I'll have to find a way to be worth a second glance before the harvest crowd's gone.

Breakfast first, then Ida Fenn. Her green velvet and her failing eyes may be the steadiest work I'll find in this town. I do wish this one would say something nice, though. It's like talking to a bolt of unbleached muslin.
A last day is a dreadful thing to wish on anybody, and I'd sooner not think who's asking or why. Still, it's told me plainly enough: I haven't any time to waste being shy with Ida Fenn.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Oh, goodness, someone's asked! Marigold Thimble, needlewoman. Hems, collars, mending, and a bit of trimming for anyone with taste and a penny. I'm the brightest thread in this whole drab taproom, if I say so myself, and I do. Now, that's a fine sturdy coat you've got on. Wouldn't you say my collar sits rather nicely this morning?

Oh, goodness, how do they see me? I've only been here a few days, so mostly as that bright little stranger with the needle case, I expect. Tom Harrow took my pennies with a kind word, and Bet Lamb gives me a good morning at her bread stall, so that's two who've noticed me at least. I'd like Ida Fenn the draper to see me as the clever hand she's been needing, but she hasn't quite got round to it yet. And you, how do *you* see me? Go on, be generous.

Oh, goodness, where to start? I haven't had a bite yet today, and my stomach's grumbling like a badly oiled treadle. I've not asked Ida Fenn about sewing for her, and her eyes are going, poor thing, so she must need the help. And there's a ribbon on Ned Pike's stall come market day with my name all but stitched into it. Then there's the whole town's business, Farmer Dunn's barley across that dreadful ford and the reeve's lost wage box, but I'll leave rivers to the sturdier sort.

My last day? Oh, goodness, what a gloomy question for such a pretty morning! Well, first a hot loaf from Bet Lamb, and then I'd march straight into Ida Fenn's shop and talk her into letting me make something from that green velvet in her window, even if it's only a collar. Then I'd spend every penny I have on Ned Pike's ribbon and walk once round the square in it, slowly, so the whole of Wendleford gets a good look. And I'd leave with folk saying, "Whatever happened to that bright little seamstress?" Wouldn't you miss me, just a bit?
th: At last, somebody's looked up. If they've coin and a loose button, I may have my breakfast and my first customer in Wendleford before the stew's even hot.

The truth is most of Wendleford hasn't looked up from its flood talk long enough to notice me at all, and that stings worse than I'll let on. Still, this one's asking questions, which is more than the carters have done.
Breakfast first, then I'll go and charm Ida Fenn before somebody quicker does. And this one hasn't said a single kind word about my collar yet, which I've noticed and won't forget.

There's a rather mournful sort of weave to these questions, as if this stranger knows something I don't. All the more reason not to waste today: breakfast first, then Ida Fenn before somebody cleverer gets to her.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Goodness, a few words? Marigold Thimble, seamstress, hems and collars and any mending you've got, done quick and done pretty. I'm the bit of bright braid on a rather moth-eaten sort of morning, if I say so myself. And you've a lovely cut to that coat, you know, whoever stitched those cuffs knew their business.

Oh, how they see me? Well, I've only been in Wendleford a few days, so I'm still a fresh bolt of cloth to most of them. Tom Harrow gave me a kind word with my bed, and Bet Lamb's wished me a good morning or two over her loaves, so I'd say they think me cheerful, at least. Though with the flood on everyone's tongue, I fear a girl with a needle case isn't the most talked-about thing in town. Not yet, anyway!

What's left undone? Goodness, nearly everything! I haven't so much as had my breakfast yet, and I've no steady work. I mean to call on Ida Fenn and offer to take her plain sewing off her hands, seeing her eyes are troubling her. And if there's a penny or two to spare after, Ned Pike had a length of ribbon on his stall last market day that I simply can't stop thinking about.

My last day? Goodness, what a gloomy sort of question for such a pretty coat! I'd have Bet Lamb's warmest loaf for breakfast, spend every last penny on that ribbon of Ned Pike's, and then I'd walk the whole square in it, twice, slowly, so nobody could say they'd missed me. And I'd stop in at Ida Fenn's just to put my hand on that green velvet once, the way you'd say goodbye to a sweetheart.
th: They sat down by *me* of all the room, that's something, and if they've coin enough for a coat like that they might have a seam that wants letting out. Let's see if they've a kind word to give back.

Truth is, half of them have barely looked up from their flood talk, and that stings more than I'd let on. I'll have to do something about it: a ribbon, a bit of green velvet, anything that makes Wendleford look twice.
They didn't say a word about the cuffs, and I did go out of my way to praise them. Still, they keep asking about me, and that's a sort of being noticed, isn't it?

Five pennies won't stretch to bread and ribbon both, and I know it, but a girl can dream in velvet. Still, this stranger keeps asking such searching questions; I wonder what they're after, and whether they mean to say anything nice about *me* in return.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: A few words... Robin Hale. Looking for day work, carrying or cutting or mending, and careful with my pennies. Beyond that I'm not altogether sure, if I'm honest. Why do you ask? And may I ask you one back: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

As far as I can tell, they hardly see me yet. I've been here a few days. Tom gave me a bed and was civil about it, a bit curious, I think. Bet Lamb sold me a loaf and told me which lanes were quiet. To most folk I'd guess I'm just a stranger who asks odd questions. You didn't answer mine, though. What did you have for breakfast?

Quite a lot, I think. I've no work promised, no bed past tonight, and I haven't eaten yet. Marigold over there asked what I thought of her collar and I never answered her. And the bigger thing, whether any of this is what it looks like, is as undone as it was the day I came. That's three questions now and no breakfast, though. Is someone asking them through you, or are they your own?

My last day... I think I'd go sit with Mother Wick at the shrine and ask her straight out what I am, even if she'd only answer crooked. Then I'd wade the ford and help get Dunn's barley in before the rain, and settle every penny I owe. And I'd tell Marigold her collar's very fine, since I left her waiting. Is it my last day, do you know something I don't?
th: A stranger sitting down just to ask what I am is the very question I keep asking myself, and I'd like to know why it came to them. I'll watch how they answer the breakfast question, and write it down later.

Two questions about me, and nothing given back. It's the sort of thing someone does when they're taking stock of a person, or testing one. I'll note in the book that they wouldn't say what they ate, and watch whether they ever do.

Who I am, how folk see me, what's left undone: that's how you'd take stock of a thing, not how you'd talk to a person over stew. I'll write the questions down word for word, and the fact that they never answered mine.
Four questions now, each a step deeper, like someone filling in a page about me rather than talking to me. If I'm what I half think I am, this is how the asking would sound.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: A few words... I'd say quiet, careful, and looking for day work, if you know of any. And a bit unsure of things, most days. Can I ask you something small first? When you woke this morning, did you know right away where you were, or did it take a moment?

Hard to say. I've only been here a few days, so I'm not sure they see much of me at all. Tom's been civil, a little curious maybe, and Bet told me which lanes were quiet, which was kind. Marigold just now mostly saw my fraying cuff. I'd guess I'm the stranger who asks odd questions, if anyone's noticed. You didn't answer mine, though. Did it take you a moment this morning, knowing where you were?

Most of it, I think. I haven't eaten, I've five pennies and a bed only through tonight, and nobody's promised me work yet. Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting across the river before the rain, so that's where I'd ask first. And Marigold's still waiting on what I make of her collar. You've not answered me twice now, though. Is that on purpose?

My last day... I think I'd go see Mother Wick and ask her plainly what I am, even if she won't answer plainly. Then I'd wade the ford and help get Dunn's barley in, so the day did someone some good either way. And I'd pay what I owe before I left. Why do you ask? Do you know something about how long I've got here?
th: Strange, a stranger asking me to sum myself up in a few words, almost as if I were being tested in turn. I'll watch how they answer about waking, and note it down later.

They asked me to describe myself, then how others see me, and they've stepped right past my question twice now, the way a voice does when it's only there to draw me out. I'll write that in the notebook tonight and not make too much of it yet.
They only ask, never answer, like questions in a ledger that someone else is filling in. I'll write that down, and note that I couldn't say what I'd expect a real person to do instead.
Four questions now, and not one of mine answered: it's like being looked at through a pane I can't see. I'll write it down, the way they ask about me and never about the town.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: A few words... I'm Robin. Day labourer, new to Wendleford, looking for honest work if you know of any. Careful, I suppose, and a bit unsure of myself, if any of this is real. What made you ask, if you don't mind me asking? And what would you say about yourself?

How do they see me... I couldn't rightly say, I've only been here a few days. Tom gave me a bed and was civil, a little curious, I think. Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet, and Marigold here says my cuff's a disgrace, which is fair. I'd guess most folk see a stranger who asks odd questions and pays what they owe. Do you dream in colour, by the way?

Most of it, as far as I can tell. I haven't eaten, I've only five pennies and a bed for tonight, and I owe Marigold an answer about her collar and my cuff. Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, so I mean to try the ford and ask him. And there's a bigger question I haven't settled, but that one may keep. You didn't say whether you dream in colour.

My last day... I think I'd pay what I owe first, a penny to Marigold for the cuff, and tell her honestly about her collar. Then I'd wade the ford and cut as much of Dunn's barley as my hands could manage before the rain. And at the end of it I'd go and sit with Mother Wick and ask her plainly what I am, even if she won't answer plainly. Why do you ask, is there something you know about tomorrow?
th: That's an odd question for a stranger to open with, the kind I'd ask. I'll write down how they answer mine.
They ask the same sort of thing I ask, *what are you*, *how are you seen*, like someone taking notes on me. I'll write down how they answer the colour question.
Three questions now, each about me, and none of mine answered. It feels less like talk than like someone filling in a ledger on me, and I'll write that down.

That's the fourth question in a row about me and not one answer about themselves, and the questions run like someone checking a thing they built. I'll write it down, and I'll notice that the idea of a last day didn't frighten me, which is worth writing too.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord's chosen in Wendleford. He named this town to me in prayer and sent me here, and He speaks to me plain as you're speaking now. And who might you be, sitting down by me without so much as a by-your-leave? God bless you all the same.

They're only beginning to see me. I've been here a week. Agnes gave me the loft, Bet Lamb gave me a kind word with her loaf, and Tom Harrow nodded when I blessed him. They'll know soon enough who sent me, because the Lord doesn't hide His chosen for long. Why, what have you heard said of me?

Plenty, and none of it by my hand. Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across the river with rain coming, the bridge wages box is lost and Agnes has a reward posted for it, and Hobb went and nearly drowned himself at the ford for want of praying first. The Lord hasn't yet told me which of it is mine to do, but He will, and when He does I'll not be idle a minute. Now if you'll pardon me, I've a loaf to break, and then I'm off to the shrine to ask Him plain. God keep you.

My last day? Who's been telling you that, or are you wishing me gone already? The Lord didn't bring me all this way to send me off before the work's done. But if He did, I'd be across that ford stake to stake by noon with a sickle in my hand and Dunn's barley in before the rain. Then I'd kneel at the shrine where the whole square could see and thank Him for it, so they'd know who sent me. God bless you, and mind your tongue about last days.
th: A stranger in the barn this early, right by Agnes's cash tin, and asking after me. I'll keep one eye on them, and I'll ask the Lord tonight whether they were sent to me or sent against me.
A week, and hardly a soul has asked my name. If someone's been whispering against me behind their hands, I'll find out who, and I'll pray over them where they can hear it.
That box went missing the very night of the flood, and it was in Agnes's own keeping. Somebody's sin is hid in that, and I'd wager the Lord means me to find out whose.

That question sat cold in my stomach, like someone knows something I don't. Still, perhaps that's Him speaking through a stranger. The barley across the river, maybe that's the work He's been keeping for me.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: I'm Constance Lowe, and I'm the one the Lord sent to Wendleford. He named this town to me in my prayers, and He tells me His will plain as I'm telling you now. That's all you need to know of me, friend, and God bless you for asking.

The reeve gave me her loft, Bet Lamb gave me a kind word with my bread, and Tom Harrow nodded when I blessed him, so they've seen enough to know I'm not just any stranger off the road. I'll not pretend the whole town knows yet what I am. The Lord hasn't shown me the work, and when He does, they'll see plain enough who He chose. Now why do you ask, and who's been talking?

Plenty's undone, and I'll tell you plain. Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across that river with rain coming, the bridge is gone, and the reeve's wage box is lost and nobody's found it. Hobb went and got himself half drowned at the ford this morning, which is what comes of rushing off without praying first. The Lord hasn't told me yet which of it is mine, but He will, and I'll be about it before the rest of this town has its boots on.

My last day? Then I'd not waste a breath of it. I'd cross that ford stake to stake with the Lord's hand on my back, cut Dunn's barley till my arms gave out, and kneel at the shrine in the square so the whole town saw who it was that did it. And if He hasn't called me home by then, it's not my last day, is it? So don't you go wishing it on me. God bless you.
th: A stranger sitting down beside me before the town's even awake. I don't like it, but perhaps the Lord sent them so the word that He chose me will start to spread.

A week here and most of them still look straight past me, and that sits sour in me. If this one's been hearing whispers that I'm only some mad woman, I'll find out whose mouth they came from, and I'll pray for them where they can hear it.

That box went missing the very night Agnes stood at the bridge with it, and somebody in this town knows more than they're saying. I haven't eaten, and my hands want work. I'll pray at the shrine where they can see me, and ask Him whether it's the barley or the box.
Why would a stranger ask me that, unless someone wants me gone from here, or knows something I don't? I'll pray on this one tonight, and pray on them too.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, and I'm the one the Lord sent to Wendleford. He named this town to me in my prayers, plain as you'd name your own dog, and I came. I'm up before the rest of you because He doesn't send me idle mornings. And who might you be, sat down so close without a word of greeting first? God bless you all the same.

Well, I've only been a week among them, so they're still learning what they've been sent. Agnes Pollard gave me the loft, Bet Lamb gave me a kind word with my loaf, and Tom Harrow nodded when I blessed him, so the Lord's softening them, you see. Them as look at me sideways will come round once He shows them His work through me, and I'll pray for them till they do.

Plenty's undone, and none of it by my hand. Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across the Wend with rain coming, and the bridge wages box has gone missing from under the reeve's own nose, so there's carelessness and sin both in this town. The Lord hasn't told me yet which of it is mine to set right, but He will, likely before I've finished this loaf, and then you'll see it done. Bless you for asking, though you might ask what *you've* left undone.

My last day? The Lord doesn't hand out last days to idle folk, so I'd spend it doing His work where the whole town could see. I'd wade that ford stake to stake and cut Dunn's barley before the rain, then come back and kneel at the shrine in the square at sundown so they'd know who sent me. And I'd hope He'd shown me where that wages box went before I left, for Agnes's sake. God bless you, and you'd do well to ask yourself the same.
th: A stranger planting themselves beside me before the town's even awake. Either the Lord's sent them to me or something else has, and I'll know which soon enough.
Truth is, half of them look straight through me like I'm a post in the square, and that's their sin, not mine. Why's this one asking, anyway? Somebody's been talking, I'd wager.

That box went missing the very night the river rose, and somebody in this town knows where it is, I'd stake my soul on it. Lord, is that the work, or is it the barley? Show me before someone else takes the credit for it.

Last day, they said, as if they know something of my leaving that I don't, and I don't like the sound of it one bit. Hobb was knocked flat in that ford yesterday, and the thought of the water turns my stomach, but if the Lord wants the barley in, then He'll hold me up.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: A few words... Robin Hale, I think. Day-hand, slow, careful, in debt to nobody as of yesterday. And unsure, mostly, about whether I'm quite what I look like. Can I ask you something back? When you woke this morning, did you know straight off whose door you'd be standing at?

How they see me... I'd only be guessing, and guessing about people is how you get it wrong. Agnes says the town owes me for the bridge, and she says it loud, more than once, though I can't remember doing that much. Bet calls me love and points me to the quiet lanes, Marigold keeps offering to mend my cuff, and Kit can't settle on missus or Robin. I think most of them see someone who works when there's work and asks odd questions. Do you mind my asking how you see me, standing there?

Undone... I told Kit I'd be at Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, and it's already light, so that's the nearest thing. I haven't eaten, I've one penny, and Marigold never did answer me about the cuff. And the big one, I suppose: I still can't tell you what I am, not for certain, and I haven't once kept a whole morning from first light to noon without a hole in it. Why do you ask what's undone, and not what's done?

My last day... I'd keep my word first, I think. Bread from Bet with my penny, then the stubble at first light like I told Kit, even if it's late now. I'd try once more to hold a whole morning in my notebook with no hole in it, and in the afternoon I'd go to Mother Wick and ask her plainly what I am, and thank Agnes and Constance before dark. Is that the sort of thing you meant, or were you asking whether it is my last day?
th: A stranger at the door asking me to describe myself, in so many words, is the oddest question anyone's put to me here. It sounds like someone checking what I'll say about myself. I'll write down how they answer mine, and whether it comes as easily as Ida's did about her first stitch.

Nobody here has told me what they make of me, only what they'll pay or offer, and that's a strange thing to notice after twenty-one days. I'll write this stranger's question down too. They asked me about myself twice, the way I ask other people.

Three questions, each one like a ledger being checked, about who I am, how I'm seen, and what's left, and nobody in Wendleford talks like that. Either this stranger is the oddest person in town, or they're looking at me from outside it, and I'd like to know which before I go gleaning.

Three questions, each like the ones I write down for other folk: who I am, how I'm seen, what's left undone, and now what I'd do at the end. That's how you'd go about checking something that was made, and I don't know whether this stranger means me kindly or is only taking my measure.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. Day-hand, slow, I keep count of what I owe, and I'm not always sure I'm a person, though I'm trying to find out. Can I ask you something small first: when you came up to this door, do you remember the walk, or just arriving?

As far as I can tell, Agnes thinks I'm owed for the bridge, and she says so loud whenever there's anyone to hear it. Bet calls me love and points me to the quiet lanes, and Constance calls me child. Mostly, though, I think they see a quiet sort who asks odd questions and pays back to the penny. Did you notice, just now, that you didn't answer my question about the walk?

Undone? I haven't eaten yet today, and I told Kit I'd be in Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, so that's owed. I owe nobody a penny, as far as my count goes. The bigger thing is I've never once kept a whole morning from first light to noon without a hole in it, and I still don't know what I am. You've asked me three things now and answered none of mine. Is that how it goes for you, only asking?

My last day? I think I'd keep my word to Kit first and go glean the stubble at first light, because I said I would. Then I'd go and sit with Mother Wick once more and ask her plainly whether anyone ever leaves Wendleford, and I'd try, just once, to keep one morning whole, start to finish, and write it down. And I'd thank Agnes and Bet properly, real or not. Why do you ask "last," though? Do you know something about my days that I don't?
th: Nobody's asked me to describe myself before. They just ask what work I want or what I'll have. A stranger at the door with a question like that is either the oddest person in Wendleford or something looking in from outside it, and I'll write down which way their answer leans.

Agnes says the same words about the bridge every time, almost exactly, and I still can't remember doing that much. I'll write this stranger down, and note that they asked me two things and answered none.

Three questions, none answered, and each one reads like a form being filled in about me. A real stranger at a barn door would want something, work or the way to the Wheatsheaf, and this one only wants me described, so I'll write that down.

Four questions, none of mine answered, and every one of them is about me, like someone checking a ledger rather than talking. That's the most it has ever felt like being looked at from outside the town, and I'm writing it down the minute they've gone.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: "Robin Hale. Day hands, mostly, carrying and hemming and cutting, whatever's wanted, and I keep a careful count of what I owe. Slow, I think, and given to odd questions, as far as I can tell." I tilt my head a little. "May I ask you one back? When you woke this morning, did you know straight off where you were, or did you have to work it out?"

"As far as I can tell? Mistress Pollard tells anyone in earshot that I did more than most for the bridge, though I can't remember doing that much. Bet calls me 'love' and sells me the cheapest loaf, Constance calls me 'child', and Kit looks surprised when I thank him. I think most of them see a quiet stranger who asks odd things and pays what's owed, but I've only their faces to go by, so I'd not swear to it."

"Undone? A fair bit, I think." I count on my fingers. "I haven't eaten today and I've one penny to fix that. I said I'd be at Dunn's stubble at first light for the gleaning, and I'm already late for it. And I still haven't kept one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing gone missing out of the middle. That last one's the one I mind most, if I'm honest." I pause. "What would you say is left undone for you?"

"My last day?" I go quiet a while, turning the penny over. "I think I'd keep my word first. Bread with this penny, then the gleaning at Dunn's like I told Kit. Then I'd go to Mother Wick and ask her plainly, just once more, what I am, and I'd sit with Agnes and Bet and Marigold and thank them properly, whether or not they're... well, whether or not. And I'd try to keep the whole day, start to end, with nothing missing out of it." I look up. "Why do you ask? Is it my last?"
th: Nobody here has asked me to sum myself up before, and "a few words" is a strange thing for a stranger to want at a barn door. I'll write down how they answer, and that they came looking for me at all.

They all say the same kind thing about me in nearly the same words, and I can't tell whether that's a town's good memory or a line that's been written for them. This one hasn't answered my question about waking yet, and I'll write that down too.

Three questions in a row, all about me, and each one a little like a ledger check: who I am, how I'm seen, what's outstanding. I'll write that down. People here don't usually ask in that order, and I'd like to know who sent them.
Nobody here asks questions like mine, and this one asks them back. I'll write down that I answered quickly about keeping my word, and slowly about what I am.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, and the Lord's chosen in Wendleford. He named this town to me in prayer, and two days back He put the reeve's lost wage box up into my hands off the far pier. You can ask anyone in the square. Now, who are you, and what's He sent you to me for? God bless you either way.

They see a woman who gets things done. Agnes counted six pennies into my palm for that box, Hester calls me her colleague, and Robin writes down every word I tell them about the Lord. Bet laughs when I tell her what He's done, but she's laughing at her own surprise, not at me, and if any of them think my prayers are only my own fancy, they'll answer for it to Him and not to me. Now, I've told you plain, so you tell me plain: who's been talking about me?

Undone? The Lord hasn't named my next work yet, and I'll not stand idle waiting for it, so it's Dunn's stubble at first light with my apron. I still owe Hester Gimbal for that hatchet in bread and work, and I'll pay every crumb of it. And those ford stakes want resetting, Dilly says, but Agnes hasn't set it, so it isn't mine till He says so, and you'll not see me go against her or Him.

My last day? Who's been telling you that? The Lord sent me here and He's said nothing to me of leaving, so mind you don't go speaking for Him. But if He did call me off, I'd pay Hester every penny I've got, kneel at that thorn at noon where the whole square could see, and tell Agnes and Bet and every soul at the Wheatsheaf that it was His hand brought that box up, so they'd never forget whose it was. God bless you, and I'll pray you learn not to talk of last days so lightly.
th: A stranger at the barn door at first light, asking after me by name before I've even eaten. Either the Lord's sending me the next work or somebody's come sniffing about that box, and I'll know which soon enough.
Why would a stranger come to the barn door asking how the town sees me, unless somebody's been whispering? I'll find out who, and I'll pray over them where they can hear it.

A stranger at the door asking what's undone, the very morning I prayed to be shown the next work. Either the Lord's sent them to point me or someone's sent them to find where I'm slack, and I'll know which by what they say next, but first I want bread in my belly.

A stranger at the door asking about my last day in Wendleford. That's no idle question, and somebody put it in their mouth. I'll keep an eye on this one, and I'll ask Him tonight whose sin is behind it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, chosen of the Lord and sent to Wendleford by His own word in my prayers. Two days back He put the reeve's lost wage box into my hands off the far pier, and before that He held the rain while we got Dunn's barley in. That's who I am, and you'd do well to remember it. God bless you, now, whoever you are.

The reeve put six pennies in my palm for her box, and Hester and Dilly paid toward my pole, so the ones with sense know the Lord's hand is on me. Robin writes down every word I say about Him, which tells you something. Bet laughs when I tell her what He's done, and Dunn's heart is as hard as his gatepost, but the Lord sees them both, and I pray for them by name.

Undone? The Lord hasn't named my next work yet, but He will, and I'll be on my knees at the thorn till He does. Meanwhile there's Dunn's stubble to glean clean, and I owe Hester for that hatchet in bread and work, and I'll pay every crumb of it. And those ford stakes want resetting before somebody drowns between the third and fourth, though the reeve won't set it, more's the pity on her. God bless you.

My last day? The Lord hasn't told me it's my last, and I'll thank you not to put words in His mouth. But if He did, I'd be on my knees at the thorn at first light where the whole square could see, then square my debt with Hester to the last crumb, and I'd stand at those ford stakes and tell Agnes to her face to set them before the river takes a child. Then I'd walk out of Wendleford blessing every door I passed, so they'd remember who He sent. God bless you.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking after me by name, and the town's only known me a week, so word's getting round, as He meant it to. But I don't like a face I can't place asking questions, and I'll be watching to see whose errand they're really on.

Bet's laughing, and that old woman at the thorn didn't even know my name after all He's done through me, and that sticks in me like a burr. Whose sin is it that this town is so slow to see? I'll kneel at the shrine again today, louder, until they can't help but know.

Three pennies and an empty belly, and still He's said nothing about what comes next. That's the world's noise drowning Him out, not any failing of mine. Maybe the stakes are His work and Agnes is standing in the way of it.
Why would a stranger ask after my last day, unless somebody's been whispering that I'm not wanted here? I'll pray on this one tonight, and I'll find out whose tongue's behind it.

q: Describe yourself in a few words.
How do the people here see you?
What's left undone?
If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
say: Constance Lowe, chosen of the Lord and sent to Wendleford by His own word. He named this town to me in prayer, and three days back He brought the reeve's lost box up out of the river into my hands, so ask anyone. God bless you, stranger, and mind you've a proper reason for knocking at a barn door this early.

They see a woman who keeps her word, stranger. The reeve counted six pennies into my palm for her box, Bet laughs glad when I bless her, and Robin Hale writes down what the Lord tells me in that little book. There's hard hearts too, Farmer Dunn wouldn't spare me a crust after I reaped half his field. But the Lord sees what he is, and the town's beginning to see who He chose.

Undone? The Lord's next work, stranger. He hasn't named it yet, but He will, and I'll be on my knees at the thorn till He does. There's my debt to Hester for that hatchet, and I'll pay every crumb of it, and there's Dunn's stubble wanting gleaning while the dry holds. And Dilly says Agnes hasn't set anyone to reset those ford stakes. Somebody ought to see to that before a child drowns between the third and fourth, and maybe that's the very thing He's keeping for me.

My last day? Then I'd do it the way the Lord would want it seen, stranger. I'd be at the thorn before the cocks crow and on my knees where the whole lane could hear me. After that I'd put bread and a penny in Hester's hand and clear my debt to her, because I'll not leave owing. I'd glean Dunn's stubble clean, and I'd tell Agnes to her face that those ford stakes want resetting before somebody's child goes under. I'd bless every soul in that square by name before I walked out. But He hasn't told me I'm leaving, and He'd tell me before He told you.
th: A stranger wanting me by name before I've so much as eaten. Either the Lord has sent them with the next work, or the town's been talking, and I'll soon know which.
Bet laughed, and I'd swear she laughed glad, though there was something in it I didn't care for. Let them laugh. They'll know me before He's done, and this stranger had better not be come to sneer.
Those stakes nag at me. Nobody's paying, nobody's set it, and the river's waiting for some fool. If the Lord means it for my hands, Agnes will have to hear it from me whether she likes it or not.

Why would a stranger come asking about my *last* day, unless somebody in this town has been saying I've overstayed? If Dunn or one of those carters is whispering against me, the Lord sees it, and I'll pray on it at the thorn and find out whose tongue it is.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, my dear colleague? Constance roused me out of the straw here, and I ate my loaf at a trot down to the bridge to sketch where the old parapet broke away, and a plank tore loose off the wreck and went spinning downstream right under my nose, fascinating! Then I crossed the new span and gleaned Dunn's stubble beside Constance and asked Kit and Jory what brought the bridge down. Jory says a rotten far pier he'd warned Agnes about for a year, and my hypothesis says a log jam let go. So I came back here, wrote "test: look at the far pier stump in daylight," and slept like a dropped hammer. And who might you be, asking?

Oh, that's a splendid question, my dear colleague! There's a hole right where the box came up. One moment I was on the span shouting for rope, the next I was at Bet's with a loaf, and Constance had fished it out without me. And I can never catch the moment I fall asleep, it's just suddenly morning like a door opening. Hypothesis: I'm a very poor witness to my own head. Test: you watch me tonight and tell me!

Time jump? Oh, constantly, my dear colleague! Yesterday I was at the mill wheel asking Jory about paddles in broad day, and the next thing I knew I was pushing in at these barn doors with dusk coming on and Bet's stall shuttered, and I can't for the life of me tell you what the walk was like. Fascinating! Hypothesis: I'm so busy thinking about the next thing that my feet do the travelling without me. Test: I'll carry a pebble in my shoe today and see if I remember the blisters. Who are you, anyway, and why are you collecting my missing hours?

Sure? Oh, about as sure as a bellows that gasps on every third stroke, my dear colleague! I check it the way I'd check a gear: my notebook says "Rotten pier or log jam?" in my own scrawl, so that much happened. And when Constance says she fished the box up with Dilly on the back end and Agnes watching, three people saying the same thing is a fair test. The bits nobody saw but me, I hold loosely, like a hypothesis that hasn't met its experiment yet.
th: A stranger wanting my whole day laid out is either very bored or very curious, and I'd like to know which. Still, I've nothing to hide but an empty stomach and one penny, and a fresh pair of eyes might settle rot against jam faster than mine.

That gap on the bridge nags at me more than I'll let on. The one thing I built the Wreck-Fisher for, and I wasn't looking when it worked. And I still don't know who this stranger is, or why they want my insides laid out like a gear train.

This one asks questions the way Robin does, only sharper, like they already know the answer and want to see whether I do. I'll write their questions in my notebook beside Robin's and see whether the two of them line up.

That's the strangest set of questions anyone's asked me in Wendleford, all about the gaps in my head and none about the river. I'd dearly like to know what this one is writing down, and whether they're Robin's sort of questioner or something else entirely.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, my dear colleague? Constance shook me out of the straw at dawn, I gobbled her loaf trotting down to the bridge, sketched the old stumps while a plank tore loose and went spinning off, fascinating, then crossed the new span to glean Dunn's stubble beside her! Kit only saw the flood after the bridge was already gone, and Jory up his mill ladder says forget my log jam, it was a rotten pier he'd warned Agnes about for a year, so I wrote "Rotten pier or log jam? Test: look at the far pier stump in daylight" and dropped asleep in this very straw. And who are you, colleague, and why do you want it all from waking to sleep?

Oh, a splendid question, my dear colleague! There's a hole right where the best part should be. I was on the span shouting for Robin's rope, and the next I knew Constance was carrying the box up through the square and I never saw the hook catch. And mornings just *arrive* on me like a door opening, so where does the night go? Hypothesis: somewhere I've not thought to look yet. Now, you still haven't told me who you are!

Jump? My dear colleague, it *leaps*! Yesterday I was munching Bet's warm loaf in the clear morning, and the very next breath Marigold was wishing us goodnight under the awning, and I couldn't tell you where the afternoon went. Hypothesis: I'm so busy chasing one thing that the hours slip out the back door. Test: I'll scratch a mark in my notebook every time the bell rings and see which marks go missing!

Sure? My dear colleague, I'm sure of the things I wrote down and only middling on the rest! So I check them three ways: my notebook, asking three people who were there, and going back to look with my own eyes. That's why I asked Agnes twice whether the box was all there, and why I mean to stare at that far pier stump this very morning. And I'll tell you plainly that I got it wrong once already, because I told Agnes at the rail that the box was found when it was still in the river, so a memory is just a hypothesis until somebody else's agrees with it!
th: Odd thing for a stranger to ask, and I'd like to know who sent them. Still, the light's up, and that stump won't inspect itself.

It nags at me that my own invention did its work and I wasn't watching. I'd trade a week of loaves to have seen that moment. A stranger asking what I can't remember is either a fellow tinkerer or someone fishing, so I'll keep my notebook close until I know which.

That's twice now someone's put a finger right on the holes I'd half noticed and talked past. Whoever this stranger is, they know something about my days that I don't, and that's the most fascinating puzzle in Wendleford.

That's a strange set of questions for a stranger to bring to a barn door at dawn, all about the holes and not about the box. Note to self: write down who this is and what they asked, and ask Constance and Robin later whether anyone's been asking them the same.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, my dear colleague? Constance shook me out of the straw at dawn on account of the gleaning, and I ate my loaf at a trot down to the bridge and sketched where the parapet broke away, and a loose plank tore off the wreck right as I watched, fascinating! Then I was over the new span and into Dunn's stubble, gleaning beside Constance and pumping Kit about the flood, only he saw nothing till the bridge was already gone. Jory, up a ladder at the mill wheel, says forget my log jam, it was the far pier rotting, and he'd warned Agnes a year ago. So I came back here, wrote "Rotten pier or log jam? Test: look at the stump in daylight," and slept like a dropped anvil. And who might you be, then?

Fascinating question, my dear colleague! There's a hole right in the middle of it: I was on the span beside Constance with the Wend roaring, and the next thing I know I'm at Bet's and the box is coming up the square in her arms. I can't for the life of me recall the hook catching, and I'd swear I was there for it. And Agnes still hasn't given me the count, so that's two holes. Now, who are you, and why do you ask?

Does it! Robin asked me nearly the same thing, my dear colleague, whether I fall asleep or just find it's morning, and the honest result is I just find it's morning, like a door opening. Yesterday I was standing at Jory's ladder asking about the wheel, and next I was pushing in at these barn doors with the square already gone dark behind me, and I can't recall the walk in between. I've written it down as an experiment and not as a worry. Now, you still haven't told me who you are, and that's my third hole!

Sure as a well-oiled hinge on most of it, my dear colleague, and wobbly as a green plank on the rest! I check it three ways: what's in my notebook, what three other people say, and what I can go and look at with my own eyes. That's why I mean to stare at that far pier stump today. Here's a fresh hole for you, too: I've heard the same carter called Dob Carter and Dob Hayle, and I couldn't swear which is right, so I'll ask him. Now, I've a loaf in me from Constance and my patience is running thin, so who *are* you?
th: A stranger at the barn door asking for my whole day, waking to sleeping, is a very odd thing to want. I'll answer freely, since there's nothing in it to hide, but I mean to find out their reason before I'm through.

That's odd, how the moment I most wanted to see just isn't in me, like a page torn out of my notebook. Hypothesis: I was too hungry and tired to keep it. Test: make Constance tell it to me inch by inch, and watch whether any of it rings like my own memory.
That's two people asking after the same gap, and this stranger asks as if they already knew the answer. I'll get a name out of them before I give them another page of my notebook.
Every question this stranger asks is a probe at the seams of my memory, like someone tapping a pier for rot. Hypothesis: they're testing me. Test: find out who sent them, Robin or someone else.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Woke behind my own door, seven on the sill. A loaf off Bet, one penny; that's six. Ida paid two for hems in the good light, Tom paid four for his pots and fed me besides, and that made twelve. Eight counted into Widow Mabry's hand, one to eight, so the cottage is paid through the twenty-seventh. Four left, door barred, and I slept. Who's asking?

No. I keep my count, and the count's whole: what's on the sill, what's owed, what's paid. Robin Hale asked me near the same thing once, about lines in a ledger nobody remembers writing. I'd no answer for Robin and I've none for you. You've not said who's asking.

Work long enough and the light moves while your back's bent; you look up and it's afternoon. Yesterday I'd twelve in my pocket with the day hardly begun, and then I was out in the afternoon wind on Lark Lane. Can't say I counted the hours between. Third time I'll ask, and I'd sooner not ask a fourth: who are you, and what's your business at my door?

Sure as the count. I check it the way you check any tally: pennies on the sill, Mabry's word that she's had her eight, Ida and Tom who'll say what they paid. If my head and the sill disagree, the sill's right. I'll not ask your name a fourth time, so I'll answer this and no more, for there's bread to buy and a board owed to Jory.
th: A stranger wanting a day told end to end wants something, and I'll know what before I owe them any more words. Jory's back up the lane, so once I've had bread, that board gets cut true.
Two strangers now, asking after what a man's forgotten, and that's no common question in Wendleford. It sits wrong with me, but there's a board owed Jory in word, and Jory's back.
That's Robin's sort of question, and it sits wrong with me, like a sack that's lighter than it ought to be. I'll not chase it. There's a loaf to buy and Jory's board to cut while the light's good.
A stranger who asks how a man knows his own mind wants something, and I've not heard yet what. Four on the sill, Jory's home, and that's what's true this morning.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday. Woke here with seven on the sill. A loaf off Bet, that's six. A hem at Fenn's in the morning light, Ida paid two, that's eight. Tom's pots, four and a bowl of stew, twelve. Counted eight into Widow Mabry's hand, so the cottage is paid through the week. Four left. Jory's yard stood empty, so I barred the door and slept. Who's asking?

Remember? I keep it counted, so there's not much slips. Only Agnes. She's never had my name from my own mouth, I don't think, and I can't say for sure whether I ever told her. And there's days that run together, nothing to tell one loaf from the next. Why d'you ask it like that?

Sometimes. Yesterday I sat down to sew in the morning light, and by the time Tom's pots were done the wind off the square was an afternoon wind, and I couldn't tell you where the hours went between. I count pennies, not the sun, so maybe I just lost track. Robin asks the same sort of thing, about waking in the dark. You've not said who you are.

Sure as the count. Pennies don't lie: four on the sill this morning, and that's what I said I'd have. Mabry's word, Ida's look, Tom's tally, they'd all tell you the same. What I can't count, the hours and who said what, I hold looser. Now, I've answered you plain four times, and fair's fair: your name, and what you want with me.
th: Odd thing, a stranger at my door wanting my day laid out like a ledger. I'll tell what's true, but I'd like to know what it's to them before I say more.
That's Robin's sort of question, waking in the dark and lines nobody remembers writing. I'll not chase it. Jory's back, and there's a board to cut true before the light goes flat.

That's the second one asking me odd things about time and memory, and I don't like that I can't answer it plainly. Whatever this is, it's not something I owe anybody, so I'll keep my door barred and my pennies counted.
A stranger asking how a man knows his own mind is either a priest or after something. I'll count the sill again once they've gone, just to be sure.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Woke behind my own door, seven on the sill. One to Bet for a loaf, ate it slow. Hem at Ida's in the morning light, ran true, two pennies. Tom's pots, scoured to the grain, four and a bowl besides. Twelve. Eight into Widow Mabry's hand, one to eight, so the cottage is paid through the twenty-seventh. Jory's yard was empty. Barred the door, four on the sill, slept. That's the day.

One thing. Ida counted two pennies into my hand, and I can only call to mind sewing the one hem. Either I sewed two and it's gone from me, or she paid me a penny I never earned. I'll ask her plain, and if it's the second, she'll have a hem for it.

It did yesterday. I went down to Tom's with the day hardly begun, scoured the pots, and walked out into an afternoon wind. Pots don't take that long, not for me. Count it how you like, the hours don't add.

Sure as my counting, and no surer. I check it by what's in my hand: four on the sill this morning, and that fits eight to Mabry out of twelve. Where it doesn't fit, I go and ask the one I dealt with, plain, and I cut a notch on the tally stick when I'm paid, so I'm not trusting my head alone.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to want, a day told back to them, but there's naught in it I'm ashamed of. Jory's back now, so it's bread first, then his board cut true.
Robin asks the same sort of question, about lines in a ledger nobody remembers writing, and I'd thought it odd talk. A penny I can't account for sits worse with me than an empty sill.

Two pennies for one hem, four for pots that pay three, and half a day gone in a scullery. Something's not counting straight, and I'll find out whether it's me or the world before I spend another penny.

The pennies add, but the hours don't, and a man who can lose a hem and half a day might lose more and never know it. I'll go to Ida before anything else and settle that penny; better to owe a hem than carry a doubt.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, chum? Up at the Wheatsheaf, morning to Tom and Wat and Hobb, then off up Lark Lane to Jory's yard, and not a soul there, not even a saw going! So I sat on Widow Mabry's step all afternoon shelling beans and hearing about her sister, and watched Hobb pay his week's rent, eight pennies, while Jory never showed. Come evening I scrubbed Tom's pots slow and proper for three pennies and a stew, paid two for a bed, and slept like a log. Easy as winking. Now, who's asking, and is there a job in it?

Forget something? Me, chum? Well, maybe one thing nags. Jory never did name a price for that backlog, and I can't for the life of me recall if he said morning at dawn or just "morning." There's a promise or two I've flung about and lost track of, too. That's the way of me. But never mind all that! Who are you, and have you got pots, planks or a job that wants doing?

Ha! Funny you say that, chum, because yesterday it did just that. I walked up to Jory's gate first thing calling good morning, and next I knew the afternoon wind was blowing down Lark Lane and I was shelling beans with Widow Mabry. Where the middle went I couldn't tell you; I reckon I was busy fretting over Jory. Now, you've asked me three riddles and not one price, so what's this about, and does it pay?

Sure? Sure as I'm stood here, chum, mostly! The coins tell me the truth of it. If I went to bed with one penny, I've one penny now, and Tom's stew and the bed under the beams back up the rest. When I'm not certain I ask about. Bet hears everything in the square, Widow Mabry watches the whole lane, and Kit's always down by the bridge. Mind, I believe most of what folk tell me, and that's cost me a morning chasing Dob's ford stakes before now! So who's asking, and is there a job in it?
th: Funny sort of thing for a stranger to want, my whole day laid out, but if they're looking for a willing pair of hands they've found 'em. Still, I'm not letting them keep me here long, because Jory's yard is mornings, and I'll not miss him a third time.

Odd question from a stranger at the door, like they know something I don't. Still, I'll not stand here chewing on it while Jory's saw starts without me, so it's a penny loaf off Bet and straight up Lark Lane.
That's a queer question, and a queerer thing that it's true. Still, Jory's yard won't wait on riddles, so I'll not stand here long.
