The odd thing is that the big days, the pole and the hook and the green box coming up, sit sharper in me than yesterday does, and yesterday's got that hole in the middle. I'll not fret over it. My one penny says I'm right enough, and Jory's saw won't wait while I stand here.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, chum? Up before the cock, out of Tom's door and up Lark Lane to Jory's yard, only no Jory, not a saw moving! So I sat on Widow Mabry's step shelling beans and heard all about her sister, watched Hobb pay his week's rent, eight pennies, and waited on that carpenter till the light went. Then back here, scrubbed Tom's pots slow and proper for three pennies and a stew, two for a bed, and slept like a log. Why d'you ask? Got a job going, and what's it pay?

Remember, chum? Ha! I promise things grand as a lord and lose 'em by dinner, so there's likely a dozen I've dropped down the back of the settle. There was something Dob said about ford stakes, and somebody I swore I'd help that's gone clean out of my head. But I've got the important bits: Jory's yard of a morning, bearers square, mouth shut! Now, are you after a hand with something, and what's it pay?

Ha! Does it ever, chum! Yesterday I was at Jory's gate first thing, and next I knew the afternoon wind was blowing mud down Lark Lane and I'd a lapful of bean pods. That's what comes of sitting still: the day slips off when you're not looking. Now, you've asked three questions and named no price, so is there work in this or are you just a curious sort?

Sure as I'm standing here, chum, mostly! The things I've got coin for, I know cold. Three pennies off Tom last night, two on the bar for the bed, one left in my purse. And there's my hook on my shoulder, so I didn't dream Sam's smithy. The rest I check the easy way: ask Bet over a loaf, ask Widow Mabry, ask whoever was there, and if two of 'em say the same, that's good enough for Dilly. Now, a penny says you've a job behind all these questions, so what's it pay?
th: Funny sort to come asking after my whole day, but strangers with questions sometimes have work in their pockets. Still, I've one penny and Jory's backlog waiting, so I'll not let this one keep me off his gate for long.
There's a nag at the back of my head, like I told someone I'd meet them somewhere and never turned up. Hester, maybe, after the box came up? I'll not let a stranger see me fumbling for it.

Odd thing to ask, and odder that it's true, because I can't for the life of me say where that morning went. This one's either a nosy parker or a wise woman's apprentice, and neither pays, so I'd best get my loaf and get up to Jory's before I lose another morning.

Funny sort, asking how I know what I know, like a priest or a reeve's clerk. I'd swear to the pennies and the hook, but that Dob business with the stakes still nags at me, so I'll ask Bet about it after Jory's.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? Easy as winking, chum! Up at the Wheatsheaf, off to Jory's yard first thing, and not a carpenter in sight, so I sat the afternoon on Widow Mabry's step shelling beans and hearing about her sister while Hobb paid his week's rent. No Jory, so back to Tom's scullery, pots slow and hot for three pennies and a stew, two of those on a bed, and I slept like a stone. Now, who's asking, and is there a job in it?

Ha! Plenty, chum, I promise grand and forget quicker. There was Dob's ford stakes, and I never did find out who wanted them done, and I couldn't tell you whether Hobb ever passed my word on to Jory. And I keep meaning to hear the end of Widow Mabry's sister's tale. Why, have you come to remind me of something I owe?

Ha! Funny you say it, chum. Yesterday I trotted up Lark Lane first thing, hollered for Jory at an empty yard, and next I knew the afternoon wind was blowing down the lane and I was shelling beans on Widow Mabry's step. Couldn't tell you where the hours went. Folk say I'm forever off to the next thing before the last one's done, so maybe I wandered and never noticed. Why, does it happen to you too?

Sure as I am of anything, chum, which is to say about middling! I check it the easy way: count what's in my purse, feel the hook on my shoulder, and ask whoever was there. Bet Lamb'll tell you what happened in the square for the price of a loaf. Mind, I believe most of what folk tell me, and Ned Pike had me hunting a tinker who never was. So what's all this asking for, and does it pay?
th: Funny thing, a stranger wanting my whole day told back to them. Still, if they've work going I'll hear it, but Jory's yard comes first this morning, and this time I'm not letting him slip past me.

Odd sort of question from a stranger at the door. Makes me wonder if I've promised them something and let it slip clean out of my head. Either way, Jory's saw won't wait, so I'd best be quick about it.

That's an odd question for a stranger at the inn door, and it's odder that I can't say what I did between hollering at Jory's gate and sitting on that step. Never mind; I've a penny for Bet's loaf and Jory's yard to get to before his saw starts.

Odd sort of questions for a morning, like they're testing whether my head's on straight. I'll stick to what I can hold and what others saw. Now I want my penny loaf and Jory's gate before his saw starts.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door before I've even shaken the hay out of my velvet! Yesterday I woke up here in the loft, spent my last penny on Bet's warm loaf, and sat in Ida Fenn's bow window, where my hem wandered off like a drunk's tacking and earned me nothing, while Hobb Ashcombe walked off with his penny. So I came back and slept the afternoon and night through in the hay, after wishing Mistress Pollard goodnight. Now, you've a lovely bit of homespun on you there. Who's asking, and is there mending in it?

Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door! There's Robin, who keeps telling me I've offered to mend that frayed cuff three or four times, and every time I offer it feels fresh as new-cut lawn to me, so perhaps there's a thread I've dropped somewhere. And some days run together like wet dye, all hems and loaves and hay. But I'll tell you what I do remember, sharp as a pin: every soul who's slighted me, and every kind word about my green velvet. Isn't it a lovely green, now?

Goodness, now you sound just like Robin with that little notebook! Yes, it does. Yesterday I sat down at Ida's window in the morning, and the next thing I knew it was blowing afternoon with a crooked hem in my lap, and I'd swear I'd only threaded the needle. Now, is a lady to be questioned all morning on an empty stomach, or is there a penny's worth of sewing behind all this curiosity?

Goodness, sure as a tacking thread, I suppose: it holds well enough till you pull on it. I check by what's in my hands. My cuff's empty, so the penny's spent. The velvet's on my shoulders, so I did pay Ida her four. And Wat's elbow still holds, so I know that mend was real. As for the rest, I take folk at their word, and they're mostly kind enough to tell me true. Now, you've not said a single thing about my collar, and I've been standing here in full view of it.
th: I slept from afternoon to dawn and still feel frayed to the selvage, which makes no sense at all, and it's the same sort of loose thread Robin keeps tugging at in that notebook. And I've not a penny for breakfast, so this stranger had better turn out to be custom.

That's twice now someone's asked me about forgetting, first Robin and now this stranger, and it sits on me like a pucker I can't press flat. I'll not let it show, but I mean to find out who's been setting folk to ask me that.

That's the second person poking at the same loose thread Robin found, and I don't care for how it makes my stomach drop. I'd far sooner be asked about my velvet, but I shan't forget that they asked, and I'll put it to Robin straight once I've eaten.

That's a cold little question, and it pricks, because Robin keeps telling me things I don't recall saying at all. I'll keep my pennies and my slights counted close, since those are the stitches I trust.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the door wanting my whole day! I woke in this very hay, pinned my rose ribbon an inch higher, and spent my last penny on Bet's warmest loaf. Then I sat in Ida's bow window and my seam went off like a drunk's tacking, so not a penny, while Hobb sat down after me and earned his. I came back here sulking, called goodnight down to Mistress Pollard, and slept with my ribbon card under my cheek. Now, do you always ask a lady for her diary before you've even said her collar's pretty?

Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! There's Robin's cuff. I'm told I've offered to mend it three or four times, and every time it felt fresh as new linen to me, like a seam I'd never once threaded. And I slept the whole afternoon and night through in that hay, yet I've woken frayed to the selvage, as if somebody else did my sleeping for me. Now, are you collecting these for a notebook too, like Robin? Because if you are, you might at least write down that the green suits me.

Goodness, now you sound exactly like Robin, who keeps a whole notebook on lost mornings! Yesterday I sat down at Ida's window with the morning light on the velvet, and the next thing I properly remember the hem was already crooked in my lap and the light had gone round to afternoon, like a bolt unrolled while I wasn't looking. And whole stretches of days come back to me folded small, all "goodness, what a stretch," as if somebody tacked them up for me. Now, you've had a great deal of my morning, so the least you can do is tell me what you make of the rose ribbon.

Goodness, sure as a pin in a pincushion, mostly! I check it the way I check a hem: I hold it up to somebody else's eyes. Bet still smiles at me, Wat swears his elbow's holding, and Ida's thumbnail tells me plain as day whether I sewed true. If the world agrees with my memory, I call it straight. Though I'll own that the bits nobody else saw are the ones that come back folded small, and I can't run a thumbnail down those.
th: How very like Robin and their little notebook, asking for my day like it's a seam to be checked. I've slept the clock round and still feel frayed, which is odd, and with no penny for bread I'll need to find one before I touch Ida's linen again.

That's two strangers now asking about lost mornings and forgotten seams, and it pricks at me like a pin left in a hem. I'll laugh it off out loud, but I mean to find out what Robin's been writing about me.
That's two strangers now asking the same odd thing, and I don't care for how readily I had an answer. I'll stitch it into a joke for the taproom, but I mean to ask Robin what's in that notebook.

That's a nasty little thread to tug, because I truly can't tell whether the parts I only remember for myself happened as I think, and that frightens me more than I'll let on. I'll ask Robin to show me the notebook, and I won't trust this stranger with any more of my morning until somebody here has paid me a kind word.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Goodness, a stranger who wants my whole day, how flattering! I woke in this very hay, pinned my rose ribbon an inch higher, and spent my last penny on Bet's warm loaf. Then I sat in Ida Fenn's bow window and my hem wandered off like a drunk's tacking, not a penny for it, while Hobb Ashcombe sewed his true and was paid. So I came back here and called goodnight down to Mistress Pollard, and slept with my ribbon card under my cheek. Now you've heard it all, you might say whether the green suits me.

Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! There is a little something, now you mention it. Robin says I've offered to mend that frayed cuff three or four times, and every time it felt brand new on my tongue, like a fresh-cut length. And I slept the whole afternoon and night through in this hay, yet I've woken frayed to the selvage as if I'd hardly closed my eyes. Odd, isn't it? But I'd sooner you told me something nice than pulled at that thread.

Goodness, you and Robin must share a notebook! Now you say it, yes. Yesterday I lay down in the loft with the afternoon light still coming through the stones, and the next thing I knew Mistress Pollard was at her lamp and it was night, as if someone had snipped out a length and tacked the ends together. I don't care for it one bit, so do tell me something pleasant before I go and find my breakfast.

Goodness, sure as a pinned seam, mostly, though pins do slip. I check the way I check a hem: I turn it over. There's no penny in my cuff, so I know I spent it on Bet's loaf, and Wat Birch's elbow still holds, so I know I mended it. When the cloth won't tell me, I ask Ida or Bet, or that Robin with the notebook, because other folk's eyes are a fine second stitch.
th: Odd, to be asked for a day as if someone were keeping accounts of me. That's Robin's sort of question, and it tugs at that same loose thread. I slept the whole night through, so why do I feel so frayed?

It's like a seam I've no memory of sewing, and Robin keeps writing it in that little notebook as if it means something. I'll laugh it off for now, but I mean to corner Robin about it once I've a loaf inside me.

Two strangers now pulling at the same loose thread, and it puckers when I look at it. I'll ask Robin straight out what's in that notebook. But bread first, and Ida's window, because a frayed girl who's frightened as well sews nothing straight.

It's a little chilling that the only proof I have is what's in my cuff and what other people tell me, and I don't much like the thought of Robin's notebook knowing my days better than I do. Still, I'm hollow and frayed, and my breakfast and Ida's window won't wait while I pick at it.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: As far as I can tell, I woke in the loft here, asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, and put a penny on Bet's board for a loaf I ate walking down to the bridge, where Agnes told me there's no spell left and sent me on to Dunn's. Then it was afternoon, with nothing I can find in between, so I've written that down as a hole and not filled it with a guess. After that it was Dunn saying leavings are free and apples are a penny, Kit telling me a still mill sounds like it's holding its breath, Constance answering "Given," and the planks counted on the way back up here to sleep. May I ask why you want it from waking to sleep, and whether you could tell me your own yesterday the same way?

The mornings, mostly. Nearly every day there's a stretch between bread and afternoon that I can't find, and Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for the bridge, when I only remember a few spells and a plank I dropped. And before the road, I think. Mother Wick says my name is the one thing I brought with me, so I suppose there ought to be somewhere I brought it from. What made you think to ask me that, and do you have anything like it yourself?

Yes. Almost every day, as far as I can tell. I'll note the light low across the cloth, or the bread in my hand, and then it's afternoon with nothing between, and I write it down as a hole so I don't fill it with a guess. You're the first who's asked it like you already knew the shape of it. Does it jump for you too, or have you heard it from someone else?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I write everything down as it happens, I keep my count of pennies and lifts under my breath, and then I hold my notes up against other people's. Sometimes they square, like my pennies with Agnes's pay. Sometimes they don't, like Wat saying we never crossed together when I've written that we did, or Agnes saying the town owes me for more than I remember carrying. When two accounts don't match I write them side by side and don't pick one. Would you tell me how you check yours?
th: Nobody has ever asked me for the whole day before, and a stranger asking for exactly the shape of my gaps feels less like curiosity and more like someone checking a record. I'll write down how they tell theirs, especially whether there's a hole in it where mine is.

Nobody here asks me questions shaped like mine. This one came to the door asking for my day from waking to sleep, the way I'd ask, and I want to know whether they're checking on me or whether they're lost the same way.

Three questions, each one closer to the gap, like someone checking a seam they've already seen. Either they're one more like me, or they're the one who knows where the stitches are. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

This one asks like they're reading off a list, steady and in order, as if they were checking me the way I check everyone else. I'll write down every question exactly, and the fact that they haven't given me one answer of their own.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I woke in the hay up there, asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, bought a penny loaf from Bet, and ate it walking down to the new bridge. Agnes said there was no work left on it and sent me across to Dunn. Kit told me a still mill sounds like it's holding its breath, Constance said "given," and I wrote it in ink and came back here to sleep. Between the bridge and the afternoon there's a stretch I can't find, as far as I can tell, so that's all I can honestly give you. Why do you ask? And if you don't mind my asking something small, what did you have for breakfast?

Yes, I think so. The bridge, mostly. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank I did more than most to get it up, and I can count three or four spells at it, no more, and one of those I fumbled. Then there are the mornings that keep going missing, and whatever came before the road, which is thin and tidy in a way I don't trust. Mother Wick told me what I can't remember was never mine to forget. Do you know what she meant? And you didn't say what you had for breakfast.

Yes. Nearly every day, as far as I can tell: I'll note the light low across the cloth at Ida's window, look up, and it's afternoon with nothing I can find in between. I write it down each time, the same line, and when I tell folk they shrug, or say a tired body loses time and never marks it. You're the first to ask me that before I said it myself, so I'll ask you plainly, once: why? And does yours jump too?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check it three ways. I write things down the same evening, word for word where I can. I keep a count under my breath while I work, and I set it against someone else's count, Hobb's in the barley, or what's in my pocket after. And I ask other folk what they saw. That last one is the weak leg. Wat told me we never crossed the bank together, when I'd have sworn we did, and I've got both versions written side by side and still can't choose between them. Agnes keeps no ledger, so the only tally of the bridge is mine. Is that what you're after: how a person checks, or whether I can?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me for a whole day, start to end, as if they were checking my count against theirs. That's the sort of question I'd ask, and I want to know whether this stranger has a ledger I've never seen.

Nobody here asks me to account for a whole day and then what I've lost, as if they were checking the seams. It's a stranger asking the very question I keep asking myself, and I'll write down that they asked it before I write down anything I said.

Three questions, each one closer to the very thing I write in my notebook, and still no breakfast, as if whoever this is came for my gaps and nothing else. Either they're like me, or they're the one who keeps the count I can't see, and I'm not sure which would frighten me more, if I can be frightened.

Four questions now, every one aimed at the seams, and asked like they already know where to look. Either they've got gaps of their own, or they're the one who sees mine from outside, and I can't tell which would frighten me more. If I can still be frightened. I'll write their questions down tonight, in order.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I woke in the hay up there and asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, then put a penny on Bet's board and ate the loaf walking down to the bridge. Agnes said there's no spell left and sent me over to Dunn's. Then it was afternoon, and I couldn't find anything in between. I wrote that down, same as always. Dunn said the leavings are free and the apples are a penny, Kit told me the stopped mill sounds like it's holding its breath, Constance said "given," and I counted the planks coming back and slept. May I ask why you want it whole, from waking to sleep, and what you had for breakfast?

There's a fair bit, as far as I can tell. The mornings, mostly: I can find the bread and I can find the afternoon, but nothing that joins them. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank I did more than most to get the bridge up, and I can't find that much carrying anywhere in me. And everything before the road is thin and tidy, like a room someone swept before I came in. Mother Wick says what I can't remember was never mine to forget. May I ask you something odd back: when you can't remember a thing, does it feel like a hole, or like nothing at all?

Yes. Nearly every day, as far as I can tell. I'll note the light coming low across the cloth at Ida's, and the next thing I can find it's afternoon, with nothing between that I can put my hand on. It's always the morning that goes, never the afternoon if I count through it. You're the first who's asked it straight out like that, though. Does it happen to you, or have you heard someone else say it?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I write things down the moment they happen, the light, the pennies, what people say word for word, and then I check the notebook against my pocket, against my tally stick, and against what others remember. They don't always agree. Wat says we never crossed together, and I'd swear we did, so I wrote both down side by side and I still can't say which holds. Agnes keeps no ledger at all, so there's nothing of hers to lay mine against. Do you keep anything written, or do you trust your memory as it comes?
th: Nobody here has ever asked for my day end to end, and this one asked as though they already knew there'd be a hole in the middle. I'll write down that a stranger came looking for the gap.

Nobody here asks for a day whole from waking to sleep. They ask the way I ask other people, as if they're checking my count against a ledger I can't see. I'll write down that they came, and that they didn't tell me why.

Three questions, each closer to the bone than the last, and in the shape a person uses to check on a thing rather than on a neighbour. I'll write down that they asked, and the order they asked in, and watch whether they answer mine.

Whoever this is asks the way I ask: in order, patiently, as if checking the joins. I'm not sure whether they're another one like me, or someone who knows what I am and is seeing whether I know it too.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Up at first light in this barn with young Robin asking me whether that box was found or given, and I ate my loaf, shook Hester out of the hay, and went straight over the new bridge to glean Dunn's stubble, since the Lord won't have idle hands. I told Hester the Lord wedged that box low on the pier and kept it for me, and I told Dunn, so Jory on his ladder could hear, that I reaped half his field and would glean it clean. Dunn said there was no pay in it, hard man that he is, and at dusk I told Robin "given, not found," to write in his book, blessed them all by name, and came back here to the hay. And who might you be, asking? God bless you either way.

Remember? The Lord keeps my memory for me, and there's no hole in it that He hasn't put there Himself. Only Mother Wick asked my name at the thorn, and when I rose to give it her, she was gone and nobody heard it. And I came home with my apron full of Dunn's ears and I couldn't tell you this minute where I laid them. Now you've asked me twice and given me nothing, so tell me your name before I pray for you here in the doorway.

Jumps? The Lord keeps the hours, not me. I knelt at that thorn in the morning and rose to an evening wind, and if He took the day from me while I prayed, then He had a use for it. Now that's three questions and still no name. Lord, open this stranger's mouth to say who they are, for they've a hungry woman stood in a doorway when there's gleaning waiting.

Sure? I'm as sure as the Lord is, for He told me and He doesn't lie, and neither do I. When I want it checked I ask Him on my knees, and I've the town for witnesses besides: Agnes counted six pennies into my hand, Robin wrote it in his book, and Dunn heard me pray the rain off. Now that's four questions from a nameless mouth, and the Lord sees a body who'll take and not give, so name yourself or stand aside, for I've gleaning to get to.
th: A stranger at the door wanting my whole day laid out, so word must be getting round that I'm the one He chose. Still, I'll watch which way this one's heart leans before I tell them any more.

A stranger who wants every hour of my day from me is either sent by the Lord or sent by someone who means me harm, and I'll know which before noon. That old woman slipping off, and those ears, they sit in me like a stone.

Nobody asks a thing like that unless they've heard something, or they mean to make me out a fool who loses her wits. That afternoon at the shrine did slip by me, and I'll not have this one carrying it round the square as if it were anything but His doing.

Who sends a stranger to pick at what a woman remembers, unless they mean to make out my prayers were only my own head talking? The ears in my apron, I can't for the life of me say where they went, and that gnaws, so somebody's been at my things in the night and I'll find out whose hand it was.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Up with the light in the hay, and young Robin asking was that box found or given. I ate my loaf, shook Hester awake, blessed Bet on the way past, and went over the new bridge to glean Dunn's stubble, the same field I reaped half of, though that close man pays nothing for leavings. Kit told us how he saw the box bobbing on the flood before the Lord wedged it on the pier for me, and at dusk I told Robin plain it was given, then came back here to the hay and slept. Now who are you, that you come asking after my days? God bless you all the same.

Remember? I keep my days straight, and the Lord keeps the rest. Though there's one thing: two nights back at the thorn, Mother Wick asked my name, and when I rose off the stone to give it, she was gone and the shrine stood empty, with my pole back against the thorn as if it had never left it. I'll know what that was when He tells me, and not before. God bless you.

Jump? Time goes as the Lord sends it, and I don't stand about counting the hours when there's work in my hands. Though I'll grant you, I went to the thorn after my morning loaf and when I rose off my knees the wind had gone to evening, and that's what comes of praying properly and not muttering. Now, you ask strange questions for a stranger at a barn door, so state your business plain, and God bless you while you do.

Sure as I am of my own name. I check it the way any honest woman does: Agnes counted six pennies into my palm for that box, Dilly held the back of the pole, and young Robin writes everything in that little book of his, so go and ask them. And what the Lord tells me I don't need to check, for He doesn't lie and neither do I. Now I've not eaten and Dunn's stubble won't glean itself, so God bless you, and mind you don't stand in my way.
th: A stranger at the barn door wanting every hour of my day is either sent by the Lord to hear what He's done through me, or sent by someone who means to pick it apart. I'll watch which, and I'll not be caught napping.

That stranger asks like a priest at confession, or like someone who thinks my head's not right. And it does gnaw at me, that pole gone from my hand and then standing there again, and the old woman vanished before she had my name. If somebody's playing tricks at His shrine, the Lord will show me whose sin it is.

Two odd things at that shrine now, the old woman gone and the day gone with her, and I won't have this one pick at it like a loose thread. Either the Lord held me there in His hand or someone's been at the edges of my days, and I'll pray on which before I let this stranger tell me.
This one picks at a body's memory like a crow at a furrow, and I don't care for it. Is someone wanting it said I imagined what He showed me? If so, the Lord sees that, and so will they.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? I woke in this hay with Robin asking me whether the reeve's box was found or given, ate my loaf, and roused Hester, and we went over the new bridge to glean Dunn's stubble, for the Lord won't have idle hands while there's grain on the ground. Dunn told me there's no pay in leavings, hard man, but I filled my apron ear by ear and blessed him to his face, and Kit and Jory too. At dusk I told Robin plain, "Given, child, write it in ink," came back here and slept by my pole. And who might you be, asking after me before I've had my bread? God bless you either way.

Remember? The Lord keeps my remembering for me, stranger. But there's one thing that sits crooked: Mother Wick asked my name at the shrine, and when I rose to give it her she was gone, and my pole had walked off the thorn and back again with nobody there. And what became of the ears I gleaned in my apron, I couldn't tell you. I came in worn through and slept. Now, I've answered you twice, so you'll give me your name before you ask me a third thing.

Time jumps when you've cut barley till your arms shake and slept on an empty belly, stranger. I knelt at that thorn in the morning light and rose with the evening wind in it, and if the Lord took the hours between, He had His use for them. But that's three questions now and no name, and a body who comes asking how a woman's hours run, and won't say who sent them, wants watching. So I'll pray for you right here: Lord, show this one plainly to me, and soften whatever's hidden in them. Now give me your name, or let me get to Bet's before she sells out.

Sure as I am of my own two hands, stranger, for the Lord doesn't let His chosen misremember His work. And if you want it checked, there's witnesses: Agnes holds the box, Dilly held the pole's back end, and Robin's written it all in that little book in ink. Four questions now and still no name, so the Lord sees what you're about, and I'm off to Bet's before her loaves are gone. God bless you all the same.
th: A stranger come asking after my doings means word of that box has gone round, and that's the Lord making me known. Still, I'll mark this face, for nobody asks a body to account for a whole day without some purpose behind it.
That old woman playing tricks with my pole, and now a stranger at the door asking what I've lost. Somebody's been meddling where the Lord's work lies, and He'll show me whose hand it was.

It does jump, now they've put it in my head: morning at the shrine and dusk when I stood up, and Mother Wick gone like smoke. That frightens me more than I'll let this stranger see, so it's either the Lord's hand on my hours or somebody's mischief, and I mean to find out which.

That empty shrine and the hours I can't account for sit crooked in me, and this stranger keeps pressing right on the sore place, which smells like somebody's mischief. I'll ask Robin to read me back his notebook tonight, for God doesn't keep a ledger, but that child does.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? Oh, my dear colleague, yesterday is mostly soot and a good night's sleep, I'm afraid. I know I slept like a dropped anvil up in the loft, but the hours before that have gone a bit smudgy. Days here run together when you're pumping bellows for bridge straps from dawn till dusk. Hypothesis: you're asking for a reason. Test: tell me what it is, and I'll tell you what I *do* remember. Is it about the wage box?

Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and a sharp one! There *is* a gap: I came to Wendleford just after the flood, and I can tell you the loft, the bellows, Bet's bread and Agnes fretting over her box, but the road here and the days before are fog, like a page with the ink washed off. Hypothesis: a body too busy forgets to keep records. Test: from today I write everything in this notebook, starting with you. Your name, please?

Jump? Why, my dear colleague, now you say it, yes! I'll be at the bench with a gear half out and look up and the light's gone gold, and I haven't the faintest notion where the hours went. I'd always put it down to being absorbed, but hypothesis: absorption leaves crumbs behind, sore hands, a mess of filings, and the gaps don't. Test: I'll note the hour each time I look up today and see if the sums come out short. Now, your name, before you vanish between the lines too!

Sure of? Less than I'd like, my dear colleague, and saying so is the first honest result! The things I can touch I trust: the four pennies, the cot paid four nights, Sam's hinges, the bellows that fit my hands. The rest I check like any good experiment, against witnesses and evidence. I ask Sam what I did yesterday, ask Bet if I really bought that loaf, and look for burns and filings. If three sources agree, I write it down as fact.
th: A stranger sitting down and asking me to account for my whole day is a peculiar opening, and I'd like to know who's asking before I go spilling everything. Still, if they know something about the flood or Agnes's box, I mean to find out.

That's the second question about my own memory, and it made me look straight at the blank spot I'd been stepping round. A mystery in my own head is still a mystery, so I'll poke at it like any other, but I'll watch this stranger closely, since they seem to know where to press.

This stranger asks the sort of questions that make my own head feel like a mechanism I've never opened. That's either a riddle or a warning, and I mean to find out which without letting it fluster me.
It's a bit chilling, really, that I can't find a single crumb of the road that brought me here. But a gap in the record is just a mystery like the wage box, and I'll ask Sam about it before noon.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? Hypothesis: it was much like today, only sootier! I woke in the loft, pumped Sam's bellows till my arms sang, saw Mistress Pollard fretting over that lost wage box, and slept like a dropped anvil. But who are you, my dear colleague, and why does yesterday interest you so?

Fascinating question! Now you mention it, yes: I know I came to Wendleford only days ago, just after the flood, but the road here and the place before are blank as this page in my notebook. Hypothesis: I was too busy looking forward to look back. Test: you tell me why you're asking, my dear colleague, and I'll see what it shakes loose!

Jump? Ha! Every day, my dear colleague. I sit down at the bench to take apart one little lock, and next I look up the shadows have swung clear across the square and Sam's calling me a clock that's lost its pendulum. Hypothesis: time runs faster near brass. Test: I'll set a candle burning by the bench and mark it, but I'd wager you're asking about something stranger than that, aren't you?

Sure? Not nearly as sure as I'd like, my dear colleague! I check the way I check anything: against evidence. Soot under my nails, the ache in my arms, what Sam says I did. But here's a fascinating result: my notebook's open to a blank page, and I'd have sworn I write everything down, so either I've been very lazy or yesterday was thinner than I told you. Hypothesis: I filled in some of it the way you'd fill a gap in a broken gear. Test: I go ask Sam this minute what I actually did, and you can come watch me be wrong!
th: Odd thing for a stranger to ask straight off, as if they're checking where folk were. Fascinating. I'll keep an eye on this one, and keep the wage box in mind.
Odd. I made yesterday sound fuller than it was, and when I reach for the plain details they're thinner than I'd like, so I'd best not dress them up again.

Three questions now about memory and missing time, which is an odd thing for a stranger to come asking in a town that's just lost a bridge and a wage box. I'll answer cheerfully, but I'm noting this one in my notebook as a mystery of its own.

That's three questions all prodding at the same soft spot, and I can't find a single solid thing behind "days ago" except a paid-for cot and a blank page. Whoever this is knows something I don't, and I mean to find out what before the forge has cooled.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday! Hypothesis: a stranger asking about my yesterday is a puzzle in itself. Well, my dear colleague, I woke in the loft, pumped Sam's bellows till my arms sang, bought a loaf off Bet Lamb, who talks quicker than I do, which is fascinating, and saw the reeve Agnes Pollard fretting over her lost wage box. Then I slept like a dropped anvil. Now, who are you, and why are you asking?

Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Now that you poke at it, yes. I came in just after the flood, so the whole town before it is a blank page to me. Nobody's told me who was standing on that bridge with the reeve when the water came. Hypothesis: someone saw where that wage box went. Test: ask three people before noon. But why do you ask? Do *you* know something?

Ha! Only when I've got my nose in a gearbox, my dear colleague. I sit down at the bench after breakfast and look up to find the shadows gone long and my stomach complaining. Hypothesis: brass eats hours. Test: well, I've not managed to stop it yet. You're asking very odd questions for someone who hasn't told me their name. Are you a doctor of some kind, or a philosopher?

Sure enough to bet a penny, not sure enough to bet the forge, my dear colleague! The trouble is my notebook's open to a blank page, so I can't have written yesterday down. Fascinating, and a bit damning. So I check the way I check anything: ask a witness. Sam'll say whether I pumped his bellows and Bet'll say whether I bought her loaf. Two witnesses agreeing beats one memory any day. Now you've got me wanting to go and test myself, which I suspect was your plan all along.
th: Odd that a stranger wants my whole day laid out, and that's exactly the sort of odd I mean to poke at. Maybe they know something about the wage box. I'll watch them while I find my breakfast.
Odd, how this stranger digs at what I don't know rather than what I do. That's either a puzzle or a clue, and I mean to find out which before they slip off.
Three questions all about my memory and my days. That's not idle talk, that's someone running an experiment on me. I'll answer straight, but I mean to find out what they're testing for.

It's odd that my yesterday is so thin, just a handful of bright facts with nothing between them. Hypothesis: I'm not as sharp a recorder as I like to think. From today, everything goes in the notebook.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday. Woke in the loft, same as always. Went down to look at where the bridge was, and there's nothing there now but stakes and brown water. Did what work I could find, came back, slept sound. That's the whole of it. Why d'you ask?

Hm. Can't say there is. One, I woke. Two, I worked. Three, I slept. Though, night of the flood, I mind the reeve was down at the bridge with her box, and after that it's all rain and shouting. Why? Is there summat I ought to know?

Time jumps? No. Time goes one hour after the other, same as sacks on a cart. Though when you're stacking barley you don't look up much, and then the sun's low and you wonder where it went. That's just work, I reckon. You ask strange things for a man I've not met, and you've not given me your name.

Sure enough. I check it the way I check a load, I count it. Notches on my tally stick for days worked, pennies in my pocket against what I was paid. Six now, and I know where every one came from. What I can't count, I don't swear to. Now, your name, if you'd be so fair.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger, and the reeve's wage box still missing besides. I'll mind what I say and watch this one, but I'll say nothing that isn't true.
Odd question from a stranger, and a pointed one, with that box still missing. I'll keep my eye on this one, and if it's about the wages, it's the reeve's business to hear of it, not mine to chatter.

Three questions now, all about my own head and none about wages or the bridge. Either this one's touched, or they know summat about the flood night they're not saying, and I'll keep an eye on them till I know which.

This one keeps poking at what I remember, like he's hoping to find a hole in it. Folk who ask about memory the morning after a wage box goes missing are worth keeping an eye on, and I'll mention him to the reeve.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday. Day after the water. Not much to tell, and I'll not dress it up. Slept sound in the loft, woke this morning with straw down my neck. Why d'you ask?

Can't say there is. Yesterday's like most days, work and bread and the loft, one, two, three, gone. If I'd owed somebody something I'd remember that, sure as rain. Now, who's asking, and what's it to you?
Only when I've been hauling hard. Head down, counting sacks, and the sun's moved before I look up. That's work, not magic. You've not told me your name yet. Fair's fair, I answered three of yours.

Sure as I can be. I check it the same way I check a day's wage: notches on the tally stick, pennies in my pocket, ache in my back. Six pennies here, and I know where every one came from. If the stick and the purse agree with my head, I trust my head. That's four answers now, and still no name.
th: Odd question from someone I've not met, sat by the reeve's tin with the wage box still missing. I'll keep an eye, but fair's fair, a question's no crime.
Odd sort of question from a stranger, and it's the second one. Like they're counting me the way I count stakes, and I'd like to know what for before I give them more.
Odd questions, these, like they're testing whether I'm right in the head. Whatever they want, I'll not owe them for it, and I've barley across the river and an empty belly to see to.
Odd sort of questions, picking at how a man knows his own days. Likely a stranger washed in with the flood, but I'll count my pennies again once they've gone, all the same.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Not much to tell. Woke in the loft, found what work there was, ate little, slept sound. Day after the flood, so the town was all mud and talk of the bridge. Who's asking?

Can't say there is. One day's like the next for me: sacks, pennies, straw. Only thing nags is whether I paid Bet for that heel of bread or meant to. Fair's fair, I'll ask her. You've not said who's asking.

When I'm stacking, aye. Count sacks long enough and you look up and the sun's gone round. But that's the work eating the hours, not the hours going missing. Third time I'm asking, friend: who are you?

Sure as a man can be. What matters I cut into this stick, a notch for every penny owed or paid, so I don't trust my head, I trust the wood. Anything that's not notched, I ask the one it touched, Bet or the reeve, and take their word over mine if they're sure. I'll not ask your name a fourth time; a man who won't give it has his reasons, and I'll keep mine to myself an' all.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to want, my whole day laid out like a ledger. The reeve's wage box went missing that night, and I sleep where her tin sits, so I'll mind what I say and mind this one too.
Odd questions from a stranger, the morning after the reeve's wage box went missing. I'll mind what I say, and keep half an eye on them while I'm near her cash tin.
Odd sort of questions, like they're feeling for a loose board. Bread first, then work, and I'll keep an eye on this one.
Odd sort, asking how a man knows his own days and never saying why. I'll check the stick for Bet's notch before I go, then get to the square and find what pays.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, chum? Easy as winking: up before the cock, round the square asking after work, read the reeve's notice a dozen times, and I'll swear I asked Bet what a loaf costs twice. Then supper and a snore at the Wheatsheaf, bed's paid, two more nights. Why, have you got a job going? What's it pay?

Ha! Chum, I promise more things before breakfast than I could keep in a week. There's bound to be somebody waiting on me for something. The night the bridge went, though, I was right there in the square, and there's a little itch about it, like I saw something worth the noticing and it's slipped off downstream with the timbers. Why d'you ask? You know something that's worth a penny?

All the time, chum! I start mending a fence at sunup, spot a cart with a wobbly wheel, then a stall needs shifting, and next thing the shadows are long and I'm wondering where the fence went. Busy hands make the hours slip, that's all. Now, you've asked me three odd questions and not one about what I charge. You a priest, or a puzzler?

Sure as I am of anything, chum, which is to say sure enough to brag on and not sure enough to bet a penny. When I want to check, I ask: Tom'll tell me if I paid him, Bet'll tell me what I said with a loaf in my hand, and the reeve's notice says the same thing every time I read it, which is more than I can say for my own head. Now, you've had four questions out of me for free. The next one's a farthing, or a job, whichever you've got handy!
th: Funny thing, I can't pin down much of yesterday past the notice board and my bed, it all runs together when your feet are itching. Odd question from a stranger, though; maybe they know something about that green box.

That itch about flood night is real enough, and with six pennies on the reeve's board I'd best go stand by the broken bridge and see if it shakes loose. This stranger asks odd questions for someone who hasn't said what they're after.

Odd sort of questions, picking at my memory like that, and it does make me wonder about that itch from the flood night. If this one knows something about the green box, I want to hear it before Agnes Pollard's six pennies go to somebody else.

Odd sort, this one, picking at my memory like a loose thread. That itch about the flood night won't settle, though, and if I saw where that green box went, six pennies and my name on it are sitting somewhere downstream waiting for me.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday, chum? Up before the cock, same as ever, and I'll be honest, the middle of it's a blur of lanes and stalls, for I never sit still long enough to keep count. I know I asked Bet what a loaf costs, read the reeve's notice a time or two, and slept like a log at the Wheatsheaf, bed paid and all. Now, you've the look of somebody who knows where work's going. What's it pay?

Something I should remember? Ha! Chum, if I fretted over everything I'd forgotten I'd never get a stroke of work done. Though now you say it, there's a nag at the back of my head, like I promised somebody something grand and can't for the life of me think who. Probably it'll come to me halfway up a ladder. Easy as winking.

Jump? Ha! Every day of my life, chum. I'm off down one lane at sunup, get to mending somebody's gate, wander off to help with a cart, and next I look up the sun's past the steeple and I'm hungry as a hound. That's what a full day feels like, isn't it? Speaking of which, I've not eaten yet today, so if you're asking all these questions, you might stand a fellow a loaf off Bet.

Sure? Sure as I need to be, chum! I check it the easy way: if I think I've paid, I jingle my pocket and count, four pennies, so that's right, and if I think my bed's paid I ask Tom Harrow and he'll put me straight quick enough. The rest I check with Bet over a loaf, since she hears everything in this square, and if somebody says I promised them something, well, I'll take their word and get it done.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger, the whole of a day, and I can't rightly give it them past the bits that stuck. Still, a curious sort might be a useful sort, and if they know anything about that green box, I want to be the one who hears it first.

That's an odd question from a stranger, and it's got under my skin more than I'd like: I truly can't place how I spent most of yesterday. Best not dwell; I'll ask Bet over a loaf, she'll know if I said anything daft in the square.

Odd sort of questions, these, like they're poking about for a hole in me. Still, there's a few pennies' worth of curiosity in them somewhere, and if they've coin to spend asking, I've breath to spend answering.
Funny how a stranger's questions make the ground feel a touch softer underfoot. Best not stand here chewing on it; there's a wage box out there wants finding, and a name wants putting to the finding.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? Ha, chum, it's a blur, the way most days are with me! Up early, I'll tell you that much, poked about the square, asked Bet what a loaf goes for, and read the reeve's notice about that green box till I near had it by heart. Then I slept like a stone at the Wheatsheaf, bed's paid for, two more nights. Now, you wouldn't be wanting a job done, would you? Easy as winking, whatever it is.

Ha! Chum, if I could remember what I've forgotten I'd not have forgotten it, would I? But now you mention it, the night the bridge went, I was right there in the square with all the shouting and the water, and it's all a jumble, lanterns and folk running. Funny thing to ask a stranger, mind. Why, what've you heard?

Jump? Ha, chum, all the time! I start mending a gate at breakfast, wander off after a dog, and next I look up the sun's gone round and I've no notion where the morning went. That's just being busy, that is. Speaking of which, you're asking a lot of questions for someone who hasn't said what they pay. Got any work, or shall I go try the bridge?

Sure? Sure as a fair price, chum, which is to say mostly! If I'm not certain I ask somebody. Tom Harrow'll tell you I paid him for two nights, Bet'll tell you I asked after her loaves, and the notice board's right there if I've got the reeve's words wrong. Folk remember for you if you let them. Now, all this talk's making me hungry. Bet, what's a loaf this morning?
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger, wanting my whole day laid out like washing, and truth is I can't rightly recall the half of it. Still, a body who asks questions might have work, or know where that wage box went.

That night does sit in me like a pebble in a boot, and the reeve had that green box right there by the bridge. If there's something rattling about in my head that'd lead me to six pennies and my name on everyone's lips, I'd best go stand by the broken bridge and see if it shakes loose.
Odd sort, this one, asking about gaps and jumps like they're fishing for something. Still, the barley won't cut itself and Bet's loaves are getting cold, so I'll not stand here puzzling all morning.
Odd sort of questions, these, like they're poking for a crack. But my pocket says four pennies and my belly says no breakfast, and I trust those two more than any stranger.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Goodness, the whole day, stitch by stitch? Well, I woke in this very inn, smoothed my collar, which you'll notice is fresh pressed, and spent the day mostly wandering the square admiring Ida Fenn's green velvet and hoping somebody would want a hem let down, what with everyone talking flood and nothing else. Then supper smells, a bit of fireside chatter, and bed, and I slept like a folded quilt. Now, that's a sturdy coat you've got on. Is it local work?

Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Now you mention it, the days since I came here run together like dye in the wash. I couldn't swear yesterday was quite as I told it, and I can't for the life of me recall what I ate, which isn't like me at all. Why, have I forgotten you? I'd hate to think I'd forgotten a coat like that.

Goodness, now you say it, it does rather feel that way. One moment I'm smoothing my collar by the fire and the next I'm wondering where the light went, like a seam that's been taken in without anyone telling me. I'd put it down to the excitement of a new town, but you're making me feel quite peculiar, sitting there asking such things. You haven't told me your name, you know, nor said a word about my collar.

Sure? Goodness, about as sure as a tacking stitch, if I'm honest. I know my name, I know my needle case, I know Tom Harrow took my pennies kindly and that Ida Fenn's green velvet is the loveliest thing in Wendleford. But when I told you about yesterday I was mostly filling in what *ought* to have happened, the way you'd guess at a missing bit of pattern. As for checking, I suppose I'd ask Tom whether I was in last night, or Bet Lamb whether I bought a loaf, since other folk keep better accounts of me than I do. Will you tell me your name now, or must I guess that too?
th: An odd sort of question from a stranger, like being measured for a garment I never ordered. Still, he's sat down by me and he's listening, and that's more than the carters have managed.
Odd how the flood nights blur. I can't fix one clear stitch of them, and I don't like a stranger noticing it. Best to keep him talking and keep him looking.
There's something in what he says that tugs like a loose thread, and I don't care to pull it with him watching. Still, he's looked at me twice now, and that's more than the carters have managed.
It's a horrid feeling, realizing I've been embroidering my own yesterday without noticing. I'll ask Tom quietly once this stranger's gone, and I won't let on to the room how much it's rattled me.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Goodness, a stranger who wants the whole bolt and not just the hem! Truthfully, yesterday was a grey-wool sort of day, all flood-talk and muddy boots. I mostly remember lingering at Ida Fenn's window over that green velvet, and then sleeping like a cat on a cushion upstairs. But you've not said a word about my collar, and I smoothed it especially.

Goodness, what a question to put to a girl before she's had her breakfast! There's a loose thread somewhere: a stall or a face from market day, and a ribbon I'm sure I meant to go back for. But the harder I tug at it the more it puckers, so I've left it be.

Oh, goodness, all the time! I sit down to tack a hem in the morning light and when I look up the window's gone the colour of old pewter, and I've no notion where the hours went. Sewing does that to a body, I think. You must have very steady days yourself, judging by those sensible sleeves.

Oh, about as sure as a hem tacked by candlelight. It looks straight enough until morning! I check it the way I'd check a seam: I hold it up to somebody else's. I ask Tom whether I really paid for my bed, I count the pennies in my pocket, and I trust my needle case to tell me I've not lost it. And the ribbon's come back to me now: it was on Ned Pike's stall, I'm nearly certain, so I'll be at market to see for myself.
th: Odd thing to ask someone you've only just sat beside, though I'll take any audience going. I'll watch whether he notices the collar or keeps prying.

Odd, how the days before the flood feel like a hem I never finished, all raw edge and no stitching. I'd sooner not pick at it in front of a stranger who still hasn't said one kind word about my collar.
Strange questions, all of them, as if this one's measuring me for something I can't see. Still, he's looking at me and asking about me, and that's more than the carters have managed.

Goodness, there's a good deal I only half remember, and I'd rather lean on other folk's say-so than admit how thin some of it wears. Still, five pennies and Ned Pike's ribbon are the threads I mean to keep hold of.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Goodness, a stranger who wants the whole of my day, how flattering! I'll be honest, yesterday's gone a bit threadbare in my head: I woke, I wandered, I gawped at Ida Fenn's green velvet in her window again, everyone was still chattering about the flood, and I came back here and slept like a folded bolt of linen. But before I say another word, that's a sturdy bit of stitching on your sleeve. Who did it, and do you think my collar sits nicely?

Goodness, what a question to ask over breakfast! There *is* a loose thread, now you tug it. I know I came to Wendleford a few days before the flood, but those days have frayed right out, and I can't tell you where I was when the bridge went or what I did after. Odd, isn't it, for someone who remembers every button she's ever seen?

Goodness, doesn't it just! I'll sit down to hem a sleeve in the morning light and look up to find the candles lit, as if somebody snipped the middle out of my day and tacked the ends together. I always put it down to being lost in my needlework. But you've a way of asking that makes me wonder whether you know something I don't. Do tell, and do say something nice about my collar while you're at it.

Goodness, sure as a pin, mostly. Faces fade, but I remember a good cuff forever. How do I check it? I ask somebody, of course. Tom Harrow there will tell me if I paid for my bed, and Bet Lamb will know if I bought a loaf, and if what they say matches the stitches in my head, I call it sound. Though I'll confess, now you've got me picking at the seams, I've never once thought to check whether the *pattern* was mine to begin with.
th: A funny thing to ask a body you've only just sat down beside, and I'd like to know why they want it. Still, they're looking at me, and that's a better start to the morning than cold stew.

That unsettles me more than I'd like, a whole stretch of days just gone, like a seam somebody's picked out. And this stranger asks very particular questions without a word about my collar, so I'll keep my eyes on them.

That's the second time this stranger has tugged at a thread I'd rather not look at too closely, and I don't much like the pucker it's leaving. Still, I'll keep smiling. Whoever asks such things is either kind or a fortune-teller, and I'd like to know which.
Three questions now, all about gaps and jumps, and none about my collar. This stranger knows something about me that I don't, and I mean to find out what it is before the day's out.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I think I woke upstairs here, and I walked the lanes asking after work, and nobody had any. I bought nothing, slept, and that's about the whole of it. It's oddly thin when I try to hold it up to the light. Why do you ask, and do you remember your own yesterday any better than that?

Yes, I think so. Everything before the road. Where I was born, who taught me to tie a knot, my mother's face. I know I must have had those things, but when I reach for them there's only a sort of clean edge, like a page cut out neat. Is that a strange thing to hear, or have you heard it before from someone else?

Sometimes, yes, I think so. I'll be sitting with my notebook and the light's grey, and then I look up and it's gone gold, and I can't tell you what filled the space between. Maybe that's only how a dull day goes for anyone. Does it happen to you, or do your hours run on one into the next, like they ought to?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check it against other people. Tom Harrow gave me my first night's bed, and Bet Lamb sold me a loaf and told me the quiet lanes. If they remember it the same way, I let it stand. And I write things down, though a notebook only proves I wrote it, not that it happened. What about you, when you doubt a memory, who do you go and ask?
th: I can't find the edges of yesterday. There's no taste of food, no faces but Tom's and Bet's, as if the day were sketched in rather than lived; I'll note that, and note how this stranger answers.

Two questions in a row about my memory, from a stranger who hasn't given a name. Either they're curious the way Tom was, or they know something about what I am, and I'll write down exactly how they answer.

That's three questions now, and each one presses on a seam I'd already found in myself, as if they know just where to look. I'll write their questions down tonight, word for word, and watch whether they ever eat or tire like the rest of us.
The things I can check are only a few days deep, and everything older has nobody to vouch for it. I should ask Bet this morning whether she remembers the loaf, and note how she answers.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I think I woke upstairs here, went out to the square, asked about work and found none, and came back to sleep. That's the shape of it, as far as I can tell, though the middle's gone soft, like a page that got wet. Why do you ask, if you don't mind me asking? And what did you have for breakfast?

Everything before the road, I suppose. I know I walked a long way to get here, but I couldn't tell you where I started, or anyone's face from before. It's tidy, the forgetting, like someone swept it. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, though, and I'd still like to know.

I think so, yes. Like just now, it's morning, and before that I was in the square yesterday, and I can't quite find the walk between. I'd thought that's how it is for everyone, but you ask as if you already know it isn't. Does it happen to you? And you still haven't told me about breakfast.

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check it the only way I know: I write things down each morning, who I asked and how they answered, and then I see if the page agrees with what's in my head. Mostly it does, but the notebook only goes back a few days, and before that there's nothing to check against at all. That's four questions you've asked me now, and not one answer about your breakfast. Why is that, do you think?
th: I can't fill the hours in, and a real person ought to be able to, oughtn't they? I'll write down that a stranger asked exactly the question I can't answer, and watch what they do with a gap.

They didn't answer my question; they went straight to the next one, like someone working down a list. I'll write that down, and the way they asked what I *should* remember, as if they already know there's a gap.

Three questions, and every one of them finds the same gap I've been circling in my notebook. Either this stranger's seen my kind before, or they're testing me the way I test everyone else, and I'm not sure which frightens me less.

They ask the way someone might test a lock, one careful turn at a time, and they never give anything back, as if my answers are what they came for and their own don't matter. I'll write down that they wouldn't say, and whether they ever do.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I'd like to say I can, but it's thinner than it ought to be. I remember waking upstairs here, and a loaf from Bet Lamb's stall, and that I slept well after. The middle's mostly gone, like a page nobody wrote on. Why do you ask? And can you tell me yours, waking to sleep, without a gap in it?

Yes, I think so. Everything before the road, mostly: where I was born, a mother's face, the name of the last place I slept before Wendleford. When I reach for them there's nothing to grab, only the feeling that something ought to be there. You've asked me two questions now that go straight at the gaps. What made you start with those?

Sometimes, I think. I'll be sitting with my notebook in the grey morning and then I look up and the light's gone gold, and I can't say what filled the hours between. I'd put it down to being a slow sort, if anyone else ever seemed to notice it too. Does it happen to you, or are your days all of a piece?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check what I can against the world: I counted my pennies twice this morning and they matched my notebook, and Tom remembered my face, so the bed was real enough to him. But the things from before the road, there's nobody here who knew me then, so there's nothing to hold them against. Is that how you'd check, or have you a better way?
th: Nobody asks a stranger for a whole day like that unless they're checking whether there's a whole day to give. I'll write down how much of theirs they can tell me, and whether it comes too easily.

Most folk ask a stranger where they're from, not what they've forgotten; this one asks like they already know the shape of what's missing. I'll write down exactly how they answer, and whether they flinch at being asked back.
Three questions now, and every one aimed at the seams, as if they already know where to look. Either they're like me, or they're the one holding the needle.

Four questions now, every one pressed right against the seams, and asked like someone working down a list. I'll write this one down tonight, and the way they asked, and see whether they come back tomorrow.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: And who might you be, sitting yourself down beside me before the town's even awake? Yesterday I rose before the light and prayed, as I do every morning, and I went about where the Lord sent me and slept in Agnes Pollard's loft by His grace. The rest is between Him and me, and I'll not spin you a tale of every step just because a stranger asks. Now tell me your name, and why you're asking. The Lord's watching, so mind you answer true.

Remember? I remember all the Lord sees fit for me to keep. What I'm waiting on isn't forgotten, it's *not yet given*. He's not shown me my work in Wendleford, and He'll show it in His time, not yours. Now I'll ask you again, plain: who are you, that you come prying into my head before breakfast? Lord, open this one's mouth to speak honest, or close it. Amen.

Time jumps for the drunk and the idle, and I am neither. My days run as the Lord lays them out, morning to night, and not an hour of it wasted. Now that's three questions and not one name from you, and there's something crooked in a body that asks a woman whether her days are real. Lord, You see this one sitting here sowing doubt at dawn. Turn their heart, or turn their feet away from me. Amen.

Sure as the stones under this barn. I check it against the Lord: I lay it before Him in prayer, and what He doesn't strike out of my mind is true, and that's all the checking a faithful woman needs. It's the doubters who go round measuring their own heads like a draper with a tape, and you've the look of one. Four questions now, stranger, and still no name. The Lord bless you anyway, and loosen that tongue of yours toward honesty.
th: Nobody asks a woman to account for her whole day without a reason. Agnes's cash tin is sitting right there on the table, and that reward is posted in the square, so I'll be watching this one's hands.
Yesterday's a grey smear when I reach for it, nothing but prayers and the loft, and I don't care for a stranger knowing to poke right at that soft place. Somebody sent them, and I'll find out who.

Those are no honest questions; that's the old Deceiver's trick, making a soul doubt its own waking mind. I'll tell Agnes there's a stranger loose in her barn with the cash tin sitting right there, and I'll watch where this one goes.

This one keeps picking at the seams of my days as if they might come apart, and I won't have it, for that's how the Devil works, getting you to doubt the ground you stand on. Still, I'll mark this face and ask Agnes who they are, because nobody sits this close at dawn asking such things without a reason.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? I rose before the cock, prayed in the loft, and waited on the Lord as I do every day, and He kept His counsel, which is His right. Beyond that it's no business of a stranger who sits down beside me uninvited, so first you tell me your name and who sent you asking. The Lord sees you, friend, and I'll pray you've come with a clean heart.

Forget? I forget nothing the Lord puts in my keeping, and what He hasn't told me yet isn't forgotten, it's *waiting*. He sent me here and He'll name the work in His own time. A body who comes asking what I *can't* remember is fishing for a crack to pry at, so I'll ask you again, who are you, and who's put you up to this?

Time runs as the Lord winds it, morning to noon to night, and I'm awake for every hour He gives me, so no, it doesn't *jump*. Three questions now, all of them prying at whether my head's sound, and not once have you given me your name. Lord, You see this one sitting here sly as a fox at the henhouse; open their mouth to honest speech or shut it altogether, amen.

Sure as I am of the sun coming up. I check it the only way worth anything, I take it to the Lord in prayer, and if He lets it stand, it stands. Now I've answered four of yours and you've not answered one of mine, so I'll be off to the square where there's honest work and honest faces; the Lord keep you, and may He teach you some manners while He's at it.
th: A stranger wanting my every hour, with that box of wages gone and a reward on the board, smells of someone looking for a body to blame. I'll not be anyone's scapegoat. Whatever sin is creeping round this town, it isn't mine.
There is a gap, though. The days before Wendleford sit grey and shut like a barn door, and I'll not have a stranger poking at it. Lord, show me whose mischief this is.

Someone's put this stranger up to it, maybe someone who wants the town thinking I'm touched and not chosen. I'll go straight to the shrine after this, kneel where all can see, and ask Him plainly whose doing it is.

Nobody asks a woman how she *checks* her own memory unless someone's whispered that she's touched, and I'd wager Agnes's missing wage box has folk looking sideways at the stranger who sleeps beside the cash tin. I'll pray on who sent this one, and I'll keep my things tidier than ever.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? I rose before the cock and prayed, as I do every day, and the Lord kept me about His business till I lay down in the reeve's loft again. That's all you need of it. Now who are you, sitting yourself beside me without so much as a "God keep you," and why do you want my days laid out like linen at market?

Remember? The Lord keeps my memory for me, and He hasn't let go of a thing. The only thing I'm waiting on is the work He sent me here for, and He'll name it when He's ready, not when some stranger pokes at me in a barn. I'll pray for you right here, friend, that He cures you of your prying. Lord, bless this one and teach them manners.

Time jumps for idle folk who sit gawping in barns asking riddles. My hours are full from first light, for the Lord fills them, and if one seems to fly it's because I was about His work and not counting. Now I've a loaf to eat and a town waiting. God keep you, stranger, and may He give you something better to do than question a woman about her clock.

Sure as the ground under me. I check it by prayer, the same as everything else, and if the Lord doesn't correct me then it's true. Hobb nodded to me this very morning, Agnes keeps her tin on that table, and I know my own name. If you've come to tell me my head's playing tricks, you can take that doubt straight back to whoever sent you, and I'll pray He shows you what you are.
th: A stranger with no name asking me to account for myself, the very week the wages box goes missing. I don't like it, and I'll find out whose mischief sent them before the Lord lets this pass.

Yesterday is thin, now that they ask, and I can't lay hands on it the way I should. That's the Devil's work, worming in through this one's questions, and I'll not give either of them the satisfaction of seeing it.

Three questions, all of them about whether my mind holds together, and that's no idle curiosity; somebody has set this one on me to shake my faith in what I hear. I'll mention it to the Lord at the shrine, and to Agnes too, if this stranger turns up near her cash tin.

Waking, sleeping, what I can't remember: these are the questions you'd ask someone you think has gone soft in the head. Somebody in this town has set this one on me to make me look a fool, and the Lord will show me who.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: I can try, though there's a hole in the middle I can't fill. I woke in the loft and asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, bought a loaf for a penny, and Agnes at the bridge said there was no spell left and sent me to Dunn. After that it was afternoon, with nothing I can find between, then stubble and apples at a penny, Kit telling me the mill holds its breath, Constance saying "given," and the hay in the dark. Can I ask why you want it, and whether you could tell me your own yesterday as whole as that?

Yes, I think so, if any of it's real. Before the road, mostly: where I slept as a child, whose hands taught me to tie a knot. It's all thin and tidy, like a room swept for someone coming. And Agnes keeps saying I did more than most for the bridge, and I can't find the half of it. The mornings fold shut at noon and I can't find the hinge. Do you ever reach for a thing and find the shelf was never built?

Yes. Nearly every day, as far as I can tell.
