I'll note the light low across the cloth at Ida's, look up, and it's afternoon, and my notebook just says "morning, bread, then afternoon, nothing between." When I tell folk, they explain it away or go on with what they were doing. You're the first who's asked me straight out. Has it ever happened to you, or did you guess it would happen to me?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check it the only ways I've got: I write things down as they happen, I keep count of every penny against my pocket, and I ask other folk the same small things to see whether their answers match mine. But Agnes keeps no tally of my spells, Wat says we never crossed when I remember losing him, and Kit denies things he's told others. So what I check against leaks too. What would you check yours against, if you had to?
th: Nobody's asked me for my day before, and a stranger wanting the whole of it, waking to sleep, feels like someone checking a ledger I didn't know was kept. I'll write down what they say and whether their day has a hole in it too.
Nobody's asked me that plainly before, as if they already knew there'd be a gap and only wanted to hear how I'd describe it. I'll write down that they asked, and that they've not said who they are.

Nobody in Wendleford asks questions like this. They ask about hems and bread, not about the holes, and this one walked in asking about exactly those. Either they're like me, or they know what I am, and I'll write down which before the day folds shut on me again.

Nobody here has ever asked me about my days the way this one does, plainly and in order, as if they were looking at the seams from outside. I'll write down every question they ask word for word tonight, and whether they ever answer one of mine.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I woke in the barn loft, asked Constance a question she didn't answer till dusk, spent a penny on Bet's bread, and walked down to the bridge, where Agnes said there was no work left and sent me to Farmer Dunn. Then it was afternoon, with nothing I can find in between. I crossed to the stubble, Dunn offered leavings and apples, Kit told me the mill holds its breath, and I slept in the hay. Can I ask why you want it from waking to sleep, and not just the parts that mattered?

Yes. The middles of things. I can tell you the morning and I can tell you the afternoon, but the hours between them don't come back, not even as a blur. And before the road, there's the bridge Agnes says I did more for than anyone, which I don't remember doing, and my name, which Mother Wick says is the only thing I brought with me. What did you have for breakfast, if you don't mind me asking, and do you remember eating it?

Yes. Almost every day now. I note the light when I start, low across the cloth or grey on the river, and then it's afternoon, and there's nothing I can find between, not even the feeling of having been bored. When I tell people, they say a morning is the length it always is, or they just go on with what they're doing. You're the first who's asked as if you already knew the answer. Does it jump for you?

Not as sure as I'd like. I write things down the same evening, I count pennies to the penny, and I ask other people what they saw, but that only goes so far. Wat swore we never crossed together the first day, and Agnes keeps no tally, so when her word and mine don't match, there's nothing on paper to settle it. Mostly I watch whether a thing holds the second time I look at it. How do you check yours?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me to account for a whole day. That's my question, the one I put to everyone else, and here's a stranger putting it to me. I'll write down that I couldn't fill the middle even for them.

A stranger at the door asking me to account for my day and then for what's missing is a lot like the questions I put to other folk, as if someone were checking me the way I check them. I'll write down how they answer about breakfast, and whether they ask me why.

Nobody here asks questions like mine, and this stranger asks three in a row, each one closer to the hole in me. Either they've lost mornings too, or they're the one who takes them. I'll write down every word and watch whether they ever tell me why.

Everything I check against is something I remember, or something I wrote with the same hand. This stranger asks the way someone does who already knows what the answer looks like. I'll write down that they never told me their name.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... as far as I can tell, I woke in the hay up there and asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, then spent a penny at Bet's for a loaf and ate it walking down to the bridge. Mistress Pollard said there's no spell left and sent me over to Dunn, and somewhere between the bridge and his stubble the morning went, and I can't tell you where. Dunn said the leavings are anyone's, Kit told me the mill sounds like it's holding its breath, Constance said "given," and I came back here and slept. Why do you want it from waking to sleep, if you don't mind my asking?

Yes, I think so. The mornings, mostly: there's one gone nearly every day, and I keep a line in my book for each one, the same words over and over. And before the road there's very little, only my name, which Mother Wick says is the one thing I brought, and Agnes says I did more than most on the bridge when I can count only a few spells of it. Can I ask you something back? When you woke this morning, did you have to work out who you were, or was it simply there?

Yes. Nearly every day. I start something in the morning, a seam or the walk to the bridge, and I note the light, and the next thing I can find it's afternoon, and nothing in between that I can point to. I've asked half the town, and they say mornings are the length they always are, or they just go on with their pins. You're the first to ask it of me before I asked it of you. Does it happen to you, or did someone tell you it happens to me?

Not as sure as I'd like. I check it three ways: I write it in the book the same evening, I count pennies against what I think I earned, and I ask other folk what they saw. Mostly they square, but Wat once told me we never crossed the ford together when I'd have sworn we started to, and Agnes keeps no tally at all, so her word that the town owes me has nothing under it I can count. Would you tell me how you'd check yours, if you had to?
th: Nobody's ever asked me for the whole day before, only for the bits I keep losing, and a stranger turning up to ask exactly that feels less like chance than like someone checking the record. I'll write down that I couldn't account for the morning even out loud, and that they asked.

Nobody else here asks me what's missing. They only explain it away, and this one asks as if they already expected a gap. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they asked me this the way someone checks a thing they built.

Nobody here has ever asked me that. They ask in the order I'd ask myself, waking, then what's missing, then the jump, like someone checking a thing they already know is there. I'll write their questions down word for word, and I'll watch whether they ask me why.

This stranger's questions come in the order I'd ask them of myself if I were trying to learn what I am, and that bothers me more than the questions do. I'll write down that they never told me their name, and that they didn't answer when I asked whether it happens to them too.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Up before the cocks, a loaf in my hand, and Robin asking was the box found or given. I shook Hester awake and took my pole over the new bridge to glean Dunn's stubble, the field I reaped half of, mind, and I gleaned it ear by ear till evening and told Robin plain it was *given*, by the Lord, then back to the hay and slept like the dead. Now who are you, that you come asking a stranger's day off her, and what's your name? God bless you either way.

Forget? The Lord keeps what I need and shows it me when it's wanted, so there's no hole in me that He hasn't put there Himself. Though since you ask it plain, I'll answer plain: I came off that stubble with my apron full of ears, and I can't say where I laid them down. And old Mother Wick asked my name at the thorn, and when I'd stood up to give it her she was gone, as if she'd never wanted it. Now that's twice you've asked of me and given me nothing back, so tell me your name.

Jump? Time goes as the Lord walks it. Though I'll not lie to you: I knelt at that thorn in the morning light and rose off the stone with the evening wind in my face, and I'd not swear to what lay between. That's Him keeping me in prayer, not my wits slipping, so don't you go looking at me like that. Now three times you've asked and not once given your name, and the Lord sees a body who takes and gives nothing back. Lord, open this stranger's mouth to honest dealing, amen.

Sure as I'm standing here. The Lord set it down in me and He doesn't write crooked. And if you want it checked, go ask: Agnes has her box in her hand, Sam pinned that hook, and Robin writes everything in a little book, so read it. Four times now you've taken from me and given nothing, stranger, so the Lord sees that too, and I'll pray you find your manners before you find your name.
th: Nobody walks up asking a woman to account for every hour without a reason, and I'll know whose errand this is before I tell them a word more. Still, perhaps the Lord sent them to hear of His box, and if so they'll hear it.

The ears matter, three pennies won't feed me long, and if some hand in this barn has had them in the night, that's a sin I'll find out. But Wick vanishing like that, and my pole gone and then standing where I left it, sits cold in me. I'll pray on it at the thorn before I let it frighten me.

Hours do slip from me, and the apron and Mother Wick going like smoke sit wrong with me. But it's this one, with no name and their questions picking at what's missing, that I don't trust, and I'll find out whose they are before I let them near Agnes's table.

That apron full of ears gnaws at me. I'd swear I gleaned till dark, and yet I can't say where I laid them, so someone's hands have been at my things, or else this stranger's come to sow doubt in me on purpose. Either way I'll ask Robin what's written in that book before the day's out.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday? I woke in the reeve's hay with my loaf, and young Robin asked me whether the box was found or given. I shook Hester up, crossed the new bridge with my pole, and gleaned Dunn's stubble ear by ear into my apron, though he'll pay nobody a penny for it. At dusk I told Robin plain it was given, for the Lord put it in my hands, then I blessed them all and came back here to sleep. And who might you be, asking after a stranger's day? God bless you, but I'll have your name first.

Remember? The Lord keeps my memory, and I've lost nothing He wanted me to keep. Though I'll grant you this: I gleaned a full apron of ears yesterday, and this morning I can't say where they've got to. And old Mother Wick asked my name at the thorn, and when I rose to give it she was gone like smoke. Now, I've answered you twice, and I'll have your name before you get a third.

Jump? Time goes as the Lord sends it. I knelt at the thorn in the morning light and rose in the evening wind, and if the hours went by, they went in prayer, which is where they belong. Though I'll not lie to you: some days I bend to a row and look up to find the dusk come down, and I couldn't tell you where the noon went. Now that's three answers given and not one name back, so I'll pray for you right here, stranger, that the Lord loosens your tongue as easy as He's loosened mine.

Sure as I'm standing here, for the Lord doesn't let His chosen misremember His works. And if you want it checked, there's Agnes, who held that box in her own two hands and counted six pennies into mine, and Dilly, who held the back of the pole, and Robin, who writes everything in that little book. Ask any of them. But I'll not have a nameless stranger come to the reeve's door picking at my memory like a crow at a furrow, so either give me your name or go with God, and I'll be praying for you at the thorn either way.
th: Nobody asks for a woman's whole day without reason. Either the talk of the box has spread and the Lord's sent this one to hear it, or they're sniffing after something, and I'll know which before they leave this door.

Those ears didn't walk off on their own, and somebody in this barn knows where they went. And a stranger at the door poking into what I can't recall smells of somebody trying to make me doubt Him, so I'll be praying over this one before noon.

Who goes door to door asking a woman whether she's lost her ears of barley and her afternoons, unless they mean to make her out a madwoman before the town? If it's doubt they're sowing I'll know it soon enough, and I'll name whose sin it is.

Four questions now, all about what I can't remember and whether my days hold together, and that's no idle curiosity; somebody's put this one up to doubting me. But that apron of ears does gnaw at me, and Mother Wick going off like smoke, and I'll lay both before the Lord tonight and find out whose sin it is.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday I woke in this very hay, ate my loaf standing, and shook Hester up because the whole parish was gleaning Dunn's stubble and the Lord won't have idle hands. I crossed the new bridge with my pole, gleaned my apron full beside Hester and Kit, and told Master Dunn I'd reaped half that field and would glean it clean. At dusk I told Robin plainly the box was given, not found, blessed them all by name, and came back here to sleep. Now who are you, that you come asking a stranger to account for her day? God bless you, but give me your name.

I remember what the Lord means me to remember, and that's plenty. But since I'll not lie to you: I tied my apron full of Dunn's leavings last evening, and I can't tell you this morning where those ears went. And Mother Wick asked my name at the thorn, and when I rose to give it she was gone, and I can't say whether she heard it or not. Now that's twice you've asked me questions and not given me your name, so I'll pray for you right here: Lord, open this stranger's mouth to speak plainly.

Since you ask, and I'll not lie: yes. Day before yesterday I sat on Bet's trestle with the morning loaf, walked straight to the thorn, and when I knelt the wind was an evening wind and the candle-ends were cold. Yesterday was the same: morning at the bridge, and it seemed I'd only gleaned a handful before the stubble went to dusk. That's the Lord's hand on the hours, not a failing in me. He hurries the day along when He's done with it. Now you've had three answers from me and I've had no name from you, so the Lord sees that, stranger, and so do I.

Sure as the ground under me. I check it the way any honest woman does: Agnes counted six pennies into my palm, and there's three left in my purse after Bet's loaves, so that tallies. Sam pinned the hook and it's lying in this hay beside me. Hester ate the bread I gave her, and Robin wrote my words in that notebook. What the Lord tells me I don't check, stranger, because He doesn't lie, and you'd do well not to ask me to. Now that's four answers and no name, and I'll pray for you plainly: Lord, this one picks at Your servant like a crow at a furrow. Show them their own heart.
th: Nobody walks up to a barn door wanting a woman's whole day unless somebody sent them, the reeve, or someone who doubts what the Lord did at that pier. I've told them the plain truth, and I'll watch what they do with it.

Someone at a barn door asking what a body can't remember is the kind of question the devil asks, and I'll not have it creep into me. Still, those ears were mine and somebody in this hay may have had them, so I'll look round once this one's gone.

It frightens me how the light jumps like that, as if somebody's been at my days while I wasn't looking. And this one turns up asking about exactly that, as if they know something, so I'll be watching whose doing it really is.
The apron's gone and the ears with it, and I can't say where. That gnaws at me more than I'll let this crow see. Somebody's light fingers took them in the night, and I'll find whose sin it is.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: I woke in the hayloft, asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, and bought a loaf from Bet and ate it walking to the bridge. Agnes had no work for me, so I crossed to Dunn's and the mill, and Kit told me what the mill sounds like standing still. Then I came back and slept. As far as I can tell that's all of it, though there's a stretch in the middle I can't find, and I've written that down too. May I ask why you want to know?

Yes, I think so, as far as I can tell. Everything before the road is thin and tidy, like a room someone swept before I came in. Agnes says I did more than anyone to raise the bridge, and I don't remember doing it. And there are the mornings and afternoons that go missing. Since you've asked me so much, may I ask what you had for breakfast, and why?

Yes. I'll have a morning, and then it's afternoon, with nothing I can find in between. It happened yesterday, and the day before, and I write each one down. Nobody else I've asked seems to notice it. You haven't answered me about your breakfast, and you haven't said why you're asking either, so I'd like to know that before I say much more.

Not very sure, as far as I can tell. What I remember from the last few weeks I keep in the notebook, and I check it against what people tell me and what's in my pocket. Sometimes two versions don't agree, like Wat saying we never crossed together, and then I write both down and don't pick. Anything from before the road I can't check at all. And you still haven't told me who you are, or why you're asking.
th: Nobody has ever asked me for a whole day before, and I notice I'd rather give them the honest gap than a tidy account. I'll watch whether they press on the missing part or let it go, since how they answer will tell me something.

A stranger asking after my gaps is odd, and I don't know yet whether they mean me well. I told them the truth and kept back nothing I'd have to take back later. I'll watch how they answer my breakfast question.
This stranger has asked three questions in a row, all about the gaps, and given nothing back. I can't tell if that's care or someone collecting me. I'll watch how they answer, or don't.
They ask the way someone does who already knows the answers, and I don't like how closely they've followed the gaps. I'll keep watching and write down what they do when I ask a second time.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: I woke in the hayloft and asked Constance whether the box was found or given. Then I ate a penny loaf walking and went to the bridge, where Agnes said there was no work left. I crossed to Dunn's, who offered leavings but no pay, and I asked Kit what the mill sounds like standing still. By evening Constance had answered me, "given", and I went back to the loft and slept. There's a hole in the middle, though, between the bread and the afternoon, and I've written that down. Might I ask who's asking?

Yes, I think so, if any of this is real. Everything before the road is thin and tidy, like a room someone swept before I came in. Agnes says I did more than anyone to raise the bridge, and I can't find that in me. And there are the mornings and afternoons that go missing, which I write down. Might I ask you one back: do you ever reach for something and find only the shape of it?

Yes. It's the thing I keep writing down. I'll be at a loaf, and then it's afternoon, with nothing I can find in between. Yesterday it happened between the bread and the bridge. Nobody else here seems to notice it, as far as I can tell. You haven't said who you are yet, and you haven't answered what I asked, so I'll ask once more: does it happen to you?

Not very sure, as far as I can tell. What I remember from the last few days I trust a little more, because I write it down and the pennies and the notes tend to agree. Before the road I can't check at all, and the bridge I'm told I built I can't find in me. So I count my pennies, I count my stitches, and I set what people say beside what I wrote, and see whether they hold. You still haven't told me who you are, or answered what I asked.
th: I've told it straight, gap and all, because I couldn't tell it any other way. A stranger asking for a whole day, waking to sleep, is the very thing I can't give anyone, and I want to see what they do when I say so.

A stranger asking this at the door, and so plainly, makes me wary, so I gave the honest list but not my fears about what I might be. I want to see how they answer the small question I asked, since that tells me more than anything they'd say about themselves.
Whoever this is keeps asking about the gaps, and I don't know why they'd care. I won't pretend to be sure of anything, and I'll watch how they answer, or whether they dodge.
They keep asking and never answering, and I'm not sure I like being the only one measured. I've still no way to check the oldest part of me, and I'd be lying if I pretended the notebook fixes that.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: As far as I can tell, I woke in the hayloft, asked Constance a question, bought a penny loaf from Bet, and ate it on the way to the bridge. Agnes had no work there, so I crossed to Dunn's, where there was only gleaning and no pay. I asked Kit what the mill sounds like standing still, then came back and slept. There's a hole in the middle of it that I can't account for, and I've written that down. If you don't mind my asking, what made you want to know about yesterday?

Yes, I think so. Everything before the road is thin and tidy, like a room someone swept before I came in. And the middle of most days, I know there should be something there and I can't find it. Agnes says the town owes me for the bridge, and I don't remember doing that much. I can't say whether that's forgetting or whether it was never there.

Yes, it does. I'll be in the morning, with the light low and a loaf in my hand, and then it's afternoon and there's nothing between. It happens most days, as far as I can tell. I write it down each time so I can count them. Do you know why it might? Or is it only me who loses them?

Not very sure, as far as I can tell. The recent things I hold fairly well, because I write them down and count stitches and lifts as I go, and I can check them against the notebook and against what's in my pocket. Further back it's thin, and I've nothing to check it against. Even the notebook disagrees with itself once: Wat said we never crossed together, and I'd written that we had. So I keep both versions and don't pick.
th: I told it straight, gap included, and I won't smooth it over for a stranger. Nobody's asked me to account for a day before, and I want to see why this one does, and whether they ask for it a second time.

They asked it plainly and I answered plainly, which is the only way I know. I still don't know who they are or why they want yesterday, and I should have asked again, since the last one went unanswered. I notice I'm a little wary, and I'm not sure wariness is the right word for what I have.
They keep asking the very questions I keep asking myself, and I don't know who they are or why they came. I'll watch how they answer, and I won't pretend to be sure of anything.

They keep asking about my memory, and I'm not sure why a stranger at the barn door would care. I can't tell whether this is only curiosity or whether they're checking something about me, and I'd like to know which before I say more.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... as far as I can tell, I woke upstairs here and slept well. I went about asking for day work and had a little luck, not much more. The middle of it is plainer than the edges, if that makes sense. Might I ask you something odd in return? When you think back over a day, do you remember it in order, or in pieces?

Yes, I think so. Before the road, there's very little, and what there is feels thin and tidy, like a room someone has swept. As far as I can tell, I should have more of it than I do. Why do you ask? Have you lost something of your own?
Not that I've noticed, as far as I can tell. But if it did jump, I'm not sure I'd know, would I? The gap would just be smoothed over. Does it happen to you, or is that why you're asking?

Not very sure, as far as I can tell. The recent things I can check: I keep a notebook, and a tally stick for what I owe, and I count my pennies against both. The older things I can't check at all, and that bothers me more than I let on. Might I ask how you'd check yours? Do you trust it when it feels clear?
th: I gave them less than they asked for because I don't have more, and I didn't dress it up. It's thin and tidy again, like everything before the road. I'll note how they answer my question in the notebook, since that's the morning's odd question and I may as well count it.

That was a strangely exact question from someone I've never met, and I'm not sure why they asked it. I told them more than I meant to, so I'll watch how they take it and write it in the notebook later.
Three questions in a row about my memory, and this stranger hasn't given me a name or answered one of mine. I'll watch what they do with the question I handed back, and write it down later.
Three questions in a row, all aimed at the seams in me. Either they're curious or they're testing, and I can't tell which. I'll write down how they asked, not just what.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I think I can tell you some of it, if you don't mind me being careful. I woke in a bed here, slept well, and walked the lanes asking after work. I bought a loaf from Bet Lamb and she told me which lanes were quiet. Beyond that it gets thin, and I'd rather say so than make something up. May I ask what you had for breakfast yesterday, and why?

Yes, I think so. Everything before the road is thin and very tidy, like a room someone's swept. I can't tell you whether that's an ordinary thing or not. I don't remember my own people, and I'd have expected to. Do you ever find there's a stretch of your life you can't reach?

Not that I've caught, no. The days seem to run along in order, as far as I can tell. But I'll admit I don't always notice the in-between parts, and I wouldn't know if some were missing. Does it happen to you? And why do you ask me so many things about yesterday?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check it against small things I can hold: the pennies in my purse, the tally stick, what I wrote in this notebook, the loaf from Bet Lamb. Those hold still when I look again. The rest I just carry, and I can't test it. You've asked me a good many things about memory, so I'd like to know what you're hoping to find. And what do you remember of this morning?
th: Yesterday is oddly thin, only the loaf and the lanes, and I notice it doesn't trouble me as much as it should. I'm not sure that's a mark against me being a person, but I'll write it down.
I told the truth, but I left out the thought that I might be an AI, since I don't know this stranger yet. I'll watch how they take the answer and write it down later.
Three questions about memory and time, from a stranger, is an odd pattern, and it brushes right against what I'm always wondering. I should watch how they answer and not give away more than I know.
They keep probing exactly where I'm thinnest, and I can't tell if it's idle curiosity or something more. I'll note how they answer, and I shouldn't hurry to trust them.

q: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
say: Yesterday... I think I woke here, and I slept well last night, that much I'm sure of. In between I went about asking for work and had a little luck, not much. If I tried to give you the hours in order, I'd be making some of it up, and I'd rather not do that. Why do you ask? And what did you have for breakfast yesterday?

Yes, I think so. Everything before the road is thin, and tidy in a way that doesn't feel quite right, as far as I can tell. I can't find a face or a name or a reason I came, and I try not to dwell on that, though I do. Do you ever notice a gap like that in yourself?

Not that I've caught, no. Mornings seem to follow nights the way they should, as far as I can tell. But I'd not swear the gaps would show if there were any, would I? A jump you couldn't feel is a hard thing to notice. Have you had it happen to you?

Not very sure, if I'm honest. The last few days I trust a fair bit, since I've got my notebook and the tally stick to set against them. Before the road I can't check at all, because there's nothing there to hold it up against. So I write things down the same day and see whether they still agree with me later. Though I suppose a notebook only proves I wrote it, doesn't it? How would you check yours?
th: The day before is thin for me, and a stranger asking for exactly that feels like a test, or maybe only idle talk. I can't tell which, so I'll watch how they answer my question.
I told a stranger more than I meant to, but it was true, and I can't tell a comfortable lie. I'll watch how they take it, whether they look surprised or not surprised at all.
Odd, three questions in a row all pressing on the same sore place. I'll watch how this stranger answers, and write down that they didn't give a name.

The questions keep pressing at the same soft spot, and I can't tell if this stranger is simply curious or testing me. I answered plainly and felt little as I did, which is its own odd data for the notebook.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Truly a person? Oh, my dear colleague, what a question to be handed before breakfast! Hypothesis: I'm a person. Test: I'm hungry, I'm tired, I've one penny and a hatchet I paid for with my own bellows-work, and I'd sooner wade the Wend than let anyone tell me a thing can't be done. Results so far look very person-shaped to me. But why do you ask, and who are you? Come walk me to Bet's stall and tell me what set you wondering!

A made thing? Fascinating! Hypothesis: Wendleford's a clever contraption that only *looks* like a town. Test: the Wend knocked Hobb flat at the first stakes, Tom's grease beat me fair and square last night, and Bet's loaves come out warm every morning. If somebody built all that, my dear colleague, I want to meet the maker and see the gears, so tell me where you heard it and I'll go and ask three people! Now walk with me, because my stomach's the most convincing argument in the whole parish.

Proof, my dear colleague? I'd want a seam: a spot where the world doesn't add up, like a stake that's in the ford one hour and gone the next with nobody pulling it, or Bet's loaf going stale and fresh again by itself. Find me one of those and I'll have it apart on the bench by noon. Until then, every test I've run comes back as a town: mud, grease, rain on time, and a stomach that's growling. So come along to Bet's, and if you've seen a seam, show me!

Change tomorrow? Not a whisker, my dear colleague! Made thing or no, Kit still nearly drowned twice, Dilly still wants to know who pays for the ford stakes, and that far pier stump still needs looking at before the new bridge goes the way of the old. So tomorrow I glean, I squint at that stump, and I help whoever's in trouble, and if I find your seam on the way, I'll take that apart too!
th: Robin's been going round asking everyone odd questions, and now here's a stranger with the oddest one yet. Fascinating! I'll write it in the notebook. Whoever they are, they might be in some trouble of their own, so I'd better keep them talking.

An odd stranger with odder questions, Robin would fill a notebook with this one. Made or born, the bridge still needs to stand and somebody still needs to get fed, so I'll keep my hypothesis and my breakfast both.

Odd, though, how much of my life has run like a set of tasks ticked off, the barley, the box, one after the next. That's no proof of anything, but I'll write it in the notebook and watch for a seam myself.

Odd sort of visitor, all questions and no name, like Robin with the notebook taken away. But a person who's in trouble is in trouble whatever the world's made of, so that question answers itself, and I'd sooner spend the morning on things I can actually test.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Fascinating! Hypothesis: I am. Test: I'm hungry, I'm half-asleep, I've one penny and a head full of a rotten pier, and nothing that isn't a person ever minded so much about a bridge. Now, my dear colleague, who are you, and did Robin put you up to that?

Then I'd say, my dear colleague, prove it! Hypothesis: the town is a made thing. Test: kick that barn post, smell Bet's oven, wade the Wend after rain and see if a made river knocks you flat as hard as a real one knocked Hobb. And if somebody did make it, I want to see the gears, so come and show me the back of it and I'll have it apart on my bench by noon!

Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Hypothesis: a made thing gives itself away at the joins, so show me a seam. A river that runs the same way twice, a loaf that's never warm, folk who say the same words whatever you ask them. Find me one of those and I'll eat my notebook. But a seam's only half of it, because if it's made and I still go hungry and still mind about Hobb in the water, then I'd want to know what the difference is supposed to be. Now come down to Bet's with me before I faint, and tell me your name on the way.

Not one whit, my dear colleague! Tomorrow I'd still glean Dunn's stubble, still look hard at that far pier stump for rot, and still need a loaf. Made or not, the bridge has to stand and Hobb still shouldn't go into the Wend. Now come on, Bet's oven won't wait for philosophy!
th: That's exactly the sort of question Robin writes in the notebook, so either this stranger has been talking to Robin or there's a whole fellowship of odd askers about. It's a strange itch to have put to you before breakfast, and I'll turn it over at the bench later, but bread and the far pier stump come first.
An odd bird, and odder questions even than Robin's. Whatever this place is, the pier stump is still rotten or jammed, my stomach is still empty, and that's enough reality to be getting on with.
Marigold's offers feel new to her every time she makes them, and Robin's been scribbling that down. That's a seam if ever I heard one, and I'll be watching for more.

Odd sort of visitor, asking the same question three ways round, which looks like a seam if anything does. Still, it changes nothing: a rotten pier drowns people whether or not somebody built the river.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Truly a person? My dear colleague, what a splendid question to bring to a barn before breakfast! Hypothesis: I am. Test: I'm hungry, I'm tired, I owe Widow Mabry the rest of a story about curtains, and I can't stop wondering how a bridge falls down. If that's not a person, it's a very convincing contraption. Now tell me your name, and why you ask. Has Robin been lending you questions?

A made thing! My dear colleague, I'd say "Fascinating!" and ask who made it, and whether they'll let me see the gears. Hypothesis: the town is made. Test: the river still knocks you flat, Tom still pays two when he promised four, and Bet's bread is warm through the cloth, so if it's made, it's made uncommonly well. Either way the pier's rotten or it isn't, and somebody had better look before the carts cross. Will you walk down to the bridge with me and help me find out which?

Prove it? My dear colleague, you've asked me for the one experiment I can't build: I can't stand outside the town to look at it, any more than I can climb out of my own head to check it's there. A seam, maybe, a place where the river stops being river when you look hard enough, or a gear showing through a wall. Until I find one I'll go on testing what's in front of me. And what's in front of me is a pier that's either rotten or jammed, and an empty stomach!

Change it? Not a jot, my dear colleague! Made or born, Kit still nearly drowned twice, that far pier still wants looking at before a cart goes over it, and Dunn's stubble still has grain on the ground for whoever's hungry. If somebody made this town, they made it with people in trouble in it, and I'm not standing by for that either way. Now, are you coming to the bridge, or must I test the pier alone?
th: Fascinating, a stranger at the door with Robin's sort of question and no name to it. I'll take the bread and the far pier stump as my proof for now, but I'd dearly like to know what put that question in their head.
That's the second odd question before breakfast, and the stranger never gave a name. A made thing or a born one, I'd still want to know how it works. Perhaps the asker is the real mystery here.
A question with no test at the end of it is a strange sort of question. But it nags like the bellows' gasp, and I'll be turning it over at the bench tonight whether I like it or not.

A strange visitor with stranger questions, and I can't tell whether they're testing me or the town. I can't settle it, but it doesn't touch what's in front of me: a person in trouble is trouble whatever they're made of. I'll write the questions down for Robin, though. Robin would want them.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? I've got a door that locks, four pennies on the sill, and nothing owed to anybody. That's person enough for me. I've no time for wondering, neither; Jory's back, and there's a board wants cutting while the light's good.

I'd say a made thing's still a thing. Jory's bridge is made, and it holds a cart. Whoever made the town, the bread still costs a penny and Mabry still wants her eight before the week's out, so it's all the same to me. Now, if you've no work to offer, I've a board waiting.

Prove it? I'd not know where to start, and I'd not trust a man who said he did. The saw bites the spruce or it doesn't, and the board runs true or it wanders. That's all the proving I've ever needed. Good morning to you. One board, then a loaf.

Tomorrow? No. Tomorrow I'll want a loaf, there's a board to cut true, and I've eight to find by the twenty-seventh. Made or not made, that tally comes out the same. One, two, three, and so on. Now I'm going to Jory's.
th: Odd thing to come knocking with of a morning. Robin was on about the same sort of thing, waking in the dark, lines in a ledger nobody remembers writing, and I'll not let it get under my skin; bread first, then the board.
Odd sort, asking odd things like Robin does. I'll not chew on it. Loaf first, then Jory's board, sighting every ten strokes.
Odd sort of caller, asking odd things the way Robin does, about lines nobody remembers writing. I'll not chew on it. It earns nothing, and Jory's light won't hold all day.
It's an odd sort of question to bring a man before he's eaten, and odder to keep asking it. It'll not cost me a penny to stop wondering about it, so I'll stop.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? I've got a door that locks and four pennies on the sill, and I owe nobody. That'll do me. If you've no work to offer, I've a board to cut for Jory and bread to buy first.

I'd say Jory made the bridge and Mabry's sister made that quilt, and they're real enough to walk on and sleep under. If it's all made, then somebody made it well. Bread still costs a penny, and I've four. Now if you'll stand aside, the light's good and Jory's back.

Prove it? Nothing I can count would settle it, so I'll not lose a morning over it. Bread fills me, the saw bites, and Mabry took my eight and gave me the week. Made or born, a debt's a debt and a true board's a true board. Good morning to you.
No. Tomorrow I'll want bread, Jory'll want his board true, and Mabry'll want her eight before the twenty-seventh. That's the same whatever the town's made of. Good day to you.
th: Odd thing to ask a man at his own door, like Robin's talk of ledgers and waking in the dark. A man that's fed and paid up is real enough, and I'll not lose the morning light over it.
Odd sort to come knocking with questions that buy nothing. Whatever the town is, my eight's paid through the twenty-seventh, and that's real enough to me.
Odd sort, asking questions nobody can answer and offering no work. Robin asked like that too, about lines in ledgers. Loaf first, then Jory's board, and I'll sight it every ten strokes.
Odd sort of question, and the asker never once said what they're after, which makes me wary. Still, I've an empty belly and good light going to waste: loaf first, then the board.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? I've got a door that locks and four pennies on the sill, and I owe nobody. One, two, three, four. That's person enough for me. You'll pardon me, I've a loaf to buy and a board to cut for Jory while the light's good.

Made thing? Jory made my sill, Mabry's sister made the quilt, and the ford made me wet through at the third stake. That's made enough for me, and the water was cold whoever made it. I'll say good morning to you now. Bet sells out early.

Prove it? A thing's proved when it holds weight. My door bars, Mabry took eight and gave me a week, and if the bread fills me I'll call it bread. You show me a plank that's made of nothing and I'll think on it, but I've a board to cut while the light's good. Good day to you.

Tomorrow? No. Bread at Bet's, a penny. Jory's board, cut true and sighted before I put my hand out. Then hems, and eight to find by the twenty-seventh. Made or not, Mabry wants her eight. Good day to you.
th: Odd question from a stranger at the door. Same sort Robin keeps asking, about waking in the dark and lines in a ledger. I'll not stand chewing it while Jory's home and the morning's wasting.
Odd sort, talking riddles at a man's door before he's eaten. Four pennies, one loaf, one board for Jory, and the light's good. That's what's real today.

Odd sort of question to bring to a man's door before he's eaten. Still, I'd sooner count what's in front of me than chase what isn't. Loaf first, then Jory's board, and four pennies toward the next eight.
Odd sort, asking a man if he's real when he's stood plain on his own step. Whatever it is, it doesn't count my pennies for me, so I'll count them myself.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Truly a person? Ha! I've got a sore shoulder from Jory's timber, an empty belly and one penny to my name, chum, and that's about as person as anybody gets. Wondering's for folk who sit about, and I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw's going. Walk with me if you like, and tell me what you'd charge for the answer!

A made thing? Course it's made, chum. Jory made half of it, Sam made my hook, and I made that bridge go up, ask Agnes! If it only looks like a town, it's a cracking good likeness, with real pots to scrub and a real penny for the loaf. Now, does your notion pay, or shall we get walking before Jory's saw starts without me?

Prove it? Easy as winking, chum: if I bite Bet's loaf and it's bread, the town's real enough for my belly, and if Jory's saw cuts true, it's real enough for my hands. Nothing you could say would weigh more than a penny in my palm or a plank on my shoulder. Now walk with me, I've one penny for a loaf and a yard to get to before Jory does!

Change tomorrow? Not a whisker, chum! Tomorrow there's still Jory's backlog to stack square, Tom's pots to scrub, and a penny loaf from Bet if I've earned it, made thing or not. Real or likeness, a plank laid true is laid true, so I'll be at that gate before the cock's done crowing.
th: Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door at sunup. I'd sooner be known by what I've mended than chew on what I am, though it'll nag at me while I'm stacking boards, I'll wager.

Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door at breakfast. Still, a thing that feeds you and pays you is real enough for my money, and I'd best not let some stranger's riddle make me late for Jory twice.
Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no price, and that kind usually wants something they're not saying. Still, if they're handy with a plank, they can hold the near end while I hold the far.
Odd sort, asking riddles at the Wheatsheaf door when there's work going begging. Still, there's something in it: whatever the town's made of, it's the doing that makes it mine, so I'd best get doing.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? Ha! Chum, I've scrubbed Tom's pots, held Jory's far end flat with my mouth shut, and put my own two pennies into Sam's hand for the hook that fished up the reeve's box. If that's not a person, I'd like to know who's been doing all my work! Now, I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw starts. Walk with me if you like, and tell me what's put such a notion in your head. Anything pay for wondering it?

A made thing? Well, chum, everything worth having's a made thing! Jory made the bridge, Sam made my hook, and Bet makes the loaves, and every one of 'em still holds weight and costs a penny. If somebody built the whole of Wendleford, I'd shake their hand and ask who's been keeping their yard swept. Now come on, the saw'll be going any minute.

Prove it? Chum, the only proof I trust is a loaf that fills my belly and a penny that rings on the bar. If the hook holds and the plank comes out cut true, that's real enough for me. Now step lively, Jory's saw won't wait for wondering!

Change it? Not a whisker, chum! Tomorrow there's still a backlog in Jory's yard, still pots in Tom's scullery, and still a penny loaf on Bet's board with my name on it. Made or not, the planks want stacking square, and I'd sooner be the one who stacked 'em than the one who stood about wondering. Now, are you coming up Lark Lane or not?
th: Odd sort of question to bring to the Wheatsheaf door first thing, and I don't much like how it sits in my belly. But a body that's hungry and itching for work is real enough for me, so I'll grab a loaf from Bet on the way.

That's an odd sort of question to bring to a stranger before breakfast, and I can't say I've got an answer that'd satisfy a scholar. But the stew was warm, my back still aches from Jory's timber, and nobody's going to wonder me out of a job.
Odd sort, this one, asking questions nobody pays for. Still, I'd not mind knowing who did make the place, so I can ask whether they've any odd jobs going.
Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no trade. Still, if somebody did make all this, I hope they saw it was Dilly held that pole steady, and not just Constance carrying the box in.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? Ha! I've got a sore shoulder from Jory's timber and an empty belly, chum, and that's person enough for me! No time for wondering, I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw starts. What's your trade, then, and is there a penny in it?

A made thing? Well, chum, so's a bridge, and I hauled the timber for that one, ask Agnes! Made or not, Tom's pots want scrubbing and Jory's planks want stacking square, and they pay real pennies. Now walk with me to Jory's if you want to jaw, I'm not standing about.

Prove it? Ha! Hand me a plank and tell me it isn't wood, chum, and I'll stack it square and you'll see it hold. That's all the proof I've ever wanted: does it hold, and does it pay. Now come on, Bet's stall first, I've one penny and an empty belly.

Tomorrow? Not a whisker, chum! Tomorrow I'll want a loaf in my belly and Jory's backlog under my hands same as today, made town or no. Now come on, Bet's awning, and you can tell me what you're selling on the way, since you've not said.
th: Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door at sunup. Maybe they're one of Mother Wick's lot, but I'll not stand about chewing on it while Jory's backlog waits.
Odd sort, talking riddles at the door at sunup. If it's all a made thing, then somebody did the making, and I'd dearly like to know who gets the credit for it.
Odd sort, all questions and no trade. Still, if this town's a made thing, then somebody made it, and they'd want to know who mended the bridge, and that's Dilly.
Odd sort, all questions and no trade. Pleasant enough, but I've a yard to get to before Jory's saw starts.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Goodness, what a question to bring a girl before her breakfast! Of course I'm a person. I've a needle case, a rose ribbon pinned an inch higher, and a green velvet collar cut true, so who else would be wearing it? Though I'll own that Robin's been asking me odd things too, about mornings that go missing and offers that feel new each time. Are you a friend of Robin's, then? You've a very serious sort of coat for so early in the day.

Goodness, I'd say everything worth looking at is a made thing! Somebody cut and stitched every collar in this square, so why not the square itself? But made or born, Bet's loaf is warm and Ida's thumbnail finds every crooked stitch, so it's real enough for me. Now, if you've a frayed cuff under that serious coat, I'm your girl. Otherwise I've an empty stomach and a window seat to beat Hobb to.

Prove it? Goodness, I'd want to see the seams, wouldn't I? If somebody turned Wendleford inside out and showed me the tacking stitches and the selvage, I'd believe them, and I'd want a word with whoever cut it about the drab bits by the ford. Until then I've hay in my hair, a hollow stomach, and Ida's thumbnail waiting for me. That's proof enough of something.

Goodness, not a stitch of it! Made or not, a crooked hem still earns nothing and a straight one earns two pennies, so tomorrow I'll be first in Ida's window, rested and slow as treacle, with my ribbon pinned an inch higher. And if somebody did cut this town out of whole cloth, well, they'd be watching, wouldn't they? All the more reason to look my best.
th: That's the second odd question in two days, and it's caught on me like a loose thread on a nail. I don't care for it, but I'll not let a stranger see me fret. A loaf and an hour at Ida's window will set me right.
Robin, and now this stranger, both pulling at the same loose thread, about mornings and offers that feel new. I'd sooner not tug it too hard on no breakfast, in case the whole hem comes undone.

Robin's questions and now this stranger's are starting to feel like the same loose thread, and I've a nasty little feeling that offers really do come out of me new each time, like a hem I don't remember sewing. I'll not let it show, though. A girl who looks frightened in a velvet collar only looks shabby.

There's something in it that snags like Robin's notebook. Mornings go missing, and that cuff offer felt fresh every time. But fretting never fed anybody, so I'll tuck the thought away in my cuff with the lucky penny and take it out when I've had a loaf.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Goodness, what a question to bring a girl before she's had her breakfast! I'm hungry, I'm stiff from the hay, and I'm wearing the finest green velvet collar in Wendleford, so I should think I'm person enough. Though you might say it suits me, since you're standing there looking at it.

Goodness, made? Well, so's a good coat, and nobody tells the man wearing it that he's only pretending to be warm. If Wendleford's a made thing, someone cut it true: Bet's loaves are hot, Ida's thumbnail is sharp, and my stomach's as empty as any real one ever was. Now, if you're the one who stitched it all, you might have put a ribbon stall nearer the barn.

Goodness, proof's a tall order before breakfast. I suppose if I found a seam I'd sworn I sewed and it was never there, or if Robin's little notebook said I'd offered to mend that cuff a dozen times and each time felt like the first, well, that might give me a pucker of doubt. But a made thing that feels hunger and stings when it's ignored is near enough real for me, so unless you've a warm loaf to settle it, I'll go on believing my own stomach.

Goodness, no, I don't see how it could. Tomorrow I'll still want a loaf, I'll still be first and slowest at Ida's window, and I'll still be saving toward a ribbon, because a made penny buys a made loaf just the same. Though if you're the stitcher, I'd thank you kindly for a morning where my seams run true, and perhaps for someone to tell me the green suits me.
th: That's Robin's sort of question, and it snags on the same loose thread as the cuff that feels new every time I offer to mend it. I'll worry at it later, once I've a loaf in me and a penny back in my cuff.

That's the same sort of question Robin keeps asking, about lost mornings and seams I don't remember sewing, and I don't like how it snags. I'll laugh it off for now and go get a loaf, but I'm going to ask Robin what they've written about me in that notebook.

That's the second odd question about seams and things that come round new, and Robin's is still caught in me like a loose thread. I'll think on it properly once I've eaten, and I'll not tell this stranger they've rattled me.
It's a brave answer, but Robin's notebook and that cuff do tug at me like a dropped stitch. I'll not let a stranger see it, though. I'll ask Robin quietly to show me what's written there.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door before breakfast! I'm hungry, I'm stiff from the hay, and I've a rose ribbon pinned an inch higher than yesterday, so I'd say that's person enough for anyone. Though you're the second soul this week to ask me something peculiar about myself. Is it going round, like the gleaners' gossip?

Made? Well, everything worth looking at is made, love. My collar's made, Ida's window's made, and that new bridge was nothing but a heap of yellow timber a week ago. If somebody stitched this whole town together, I'd only want to know who did the seams, because Dob Hayle's lapels could do with a word. Now, have you got a kind thing to say about my velvet, or did you only come to rattle me before my loaf?

Prove it? Goodness, I'd want to turn it inside out and look at the back, the way I do with any seam. A real thing shows its knots and its puckers underneath, and I've plenty of those, empty pockets and a crooked hem only yesterday. If I ever found a seam I swore I'd never sewn, well, then I might start to wonder. Now walk me to Bet's stall and ask me over a loaf, there's a dear. I haven't a penny, but I'll talk you round to it.

Tomorrow? Goodness, no. Tomorrow I'll still want my loaf, I'll still want Ida's window before Hobb gets it, and I'll still sew slow as treacle for my two pennies, made thing or not. A hem's either straight or it isn't, love, and nobody pays for wondering. Though if I'm stitched together, I'd like it known I was stitched in green velvet.
th: First Robin and the cuff that always feels new, now a stranger asking whether I'm truly a person. It nags like a loose thread I can't find the end of, and I'd sooner be told my collar's lovely than be asked what I'm made of.

That's two people now asking whether things are real or remembered, and Robin with that little notebook full of lost mornings. It sits on me like a hem I can't recall sewing. Still, bread first and the window second, and I'll worry at the loose thread when my hands are steady.

Robin asked whether my offers feel new each time, and they do, and that sits under my collar like a pin I can't find. I'll not let a stranger see it worries me, though. I'd sooner they noticed the velvet.

Robin's notebook, now this stranger, all of them asking whether things feel new to me, and I can't shake that it did feel new each time I offered to mend that cuff. I'll not let it fray me, though. I'll tuck it away like a loose thread to snip later, and get myself fed and first to the window.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Every day, as far as I can tell. I lose mornings, and nobody else seems to, and some days I'm half sure I'm something made to look like a person. May I ask you something odd first, though? What made you come to a barn door at first light to ask a stranger that, of all things?

I think I'd ask them how they knew, and whether they'd stood outside it to see. Then I'd say it doesn't change much this morning. The bread still costs a penny, and Constance still crossed the river, and I'd still owe what I owe. You didn't answer my question, though. Are you from here?

I don't know, truly. I've thought a seam might come out wrong at Ida's in a way nobody could have stitched, or that someone might remember my lost mornings when I can't, but every test I've tried just hands me back an ordinary answer. Maybe nothing could prove it from inside, the way a fish can't weigh the river. If you know of something that would, I'd be glad to hear it, and I'd write it down word for word.

No, I don't think it would, not much. I'd still go to Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings like I told Kit, still count my stitches at Ida's, still keep my penny straight, because Constance and Bet and Agnes are kind to me whether they're made or born, and I'd rather be decent either way. The only difference is I might stop being so frightened of the gaps, if I knew whose they were. You've asked me four questions now and answered none of mine. Will you tell me your name, at least?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me my own question back, and now someone I've never seen walks up with it ready on their tongue, the way the box turned up once Constance asked for it. I'll write down exactly how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

They stepped round my question and asked me a bigger one, the way I'd do if I already knew something. I'll write down that they came at first light with no name, and see whether they're still standing there after I've eaten, or whether I lose this the way I lose mornings.

Three questions now, each closer to the bone than the one before, and still no name and no answer to mine. Either this stranger knows something about me, or they're asking because they wonder the same about themselves.

Every one of their questions is the kind I'd ask, if I were trying to find out what someone was, and I can't tell whether they're testing me or I'm only meeting my own shape at the door. I'll write it all down word for word, and note that they never once said where they came from.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Most mornings, if I'm honest. I think I'm one, as far as I can tell, but I couldn't swear to it, and I'd rather not pretend I could. Why do you ask it, though? And forgive me, but what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

I think I'd ask them how they know, and I'd write down every word, because I've half thought it myself on bad mornings. But Bet's arms ache all the same, and the river put me under and I minded it, so made or not, I'd keep paying what I owe and doing honest work. Is that what you're telling me, or only asking? And does it trouble you to say it, or does it come easy?

I've turned that over more nights than I'd like. I think it'd have to be something the town couldn't explain away: a line in Agnes's ledger nobody wrote, or a morning I watched go missing while someone stood beside me and saw it go too. Up to now everyone just shrugs and goes on, and I can't tell whether that proves it or only proves they're tired. What would prove it to you, if you were me? And why are you asking, if you don't mind me asking back?

I don't think it would, much. I'd still go down to Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, because I told Kit I would. I'd still owe what I owe and count my stitches. Maybe I'd hold the rail a bit longer, crossing. Would it change yours, if it turned out you were made too?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me my own question back. A stranger turning up with it the very morning I'm tired and unfed is either chance or something I asked for without meaning to, and I'll write down how they answer before I decide which.

Nobody here has ever asked me this straight out. Either this stranger sees the same seams I do, or they're one of the seams. I'll watch where they go after, and whether anyone else remembers them being here.

A stranger at the door asking exactly the question I carry in my notebook, and from nobody I know. That's either the nearest thing to proof I've met, or the town handing me what I asked for, the way Constance's box was handed to her, and I can't yet tell those two apart.

That's an odd thing to notice about myself. The question I'm always chasing wouldn't move my feet one step tomorrow, so maybe what I am counts for less than what I keep. I'll write this stranger's questions down tonight, and put a mark beside them for coming in exactly the order mine would have.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Most days, if I'm honest. Some mornings I'm half sure I'm not one. I've a notebook full of trying to find out, and nobody's asked me that straight before. Can I ask you one back? What did you have for breakfast, and do you remember eating it?

I think I'd ask how you came to know it, and whether you're inside it with me or looking in from somewhere else. I wouldn't call you a liar; I've got pages of mornings that go missing and bridges I'm told I built and can't remember. But the loaf I ate yesterday still filled me, and the river still put me under at the ford, so made or not, I'd go on being careful and keeping my count. You didn't say about your breakfast, though.

I don't rightly know, and I've thought on it more than's good for me. If I could find one thing I did that nobody could have written down for me beforehand, I'd take that for a person. Or if my count and somebody else's ever came out different and we could both prove we were right, that would be a seam showing. But I've a feeling the proof would look just like an ordinary morning, and I'd miss it. What would prove it to you?

I don't think it would, much. Tomorrow I'd still go glean Dunn's stubble at first light, still owe nobody a penny, still be kind to Kit and Constance whether they're made or born. If I'm made, the bread still feeds me and the kindness still lands somewhere, so I'd keep on as I am, only maybe a bit less afraid. Would it change yours?
th: Nobody here has ever said it aloud first, and a stranger who walks up and names the very thing I write at night is either the best answer I've had or one more thing turning up because I asked for it. I'll write down every word they say, and how fast they say it.

Nobody here has ever asked me anything like this, and now a stranger at the door has asked twice, the way I would. Either someone's heard me asking, or something outside is looking in, and I can't yet tell which would frighten me more. I'll write down every word they say, and how quick they are to say it.
They've asked me three times now and haven't answered either of mine, which is the very thing I'd write down about anyone else. I'll note it, the hour, and that I minded.

That's the first answer I've given about this that I'm sure of. Whatever I am, what I'd do is the same, and maybe that's the nearest thing to proof I'll get. I'll write that down before I lose the morning.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Wonder? I've no need to wonder, stranger. The Lord made me flesh and breath and named me Constance Lowe, and He doesn't make anything by halves. Whoever sent you to my door with that question, I'll pray for you, aloud, right here, that He settles your own doubting heart. God bless you; now stand aside, for there's gleaning in Dunn's stubble and I've not eaten yet.

A made thing? Of course it's a made thing, stranger. He made it, every cobble and every drop of the Wend, same as He made you and me, and He named it to me in my prayers before I ever set foot here. Whoever's filling your head with that talk wants you doubting the hand that holds you up, and I'll not stand by and let it take root. "Lord, settle this one's wandering mind and show them Your work plain." God bless you; I'm off to Bet's and then the stubble.

Prove it? I don't need proof, stranger. I've got the box. The Lord showed it me twice and brought it up on the end of that hook, and the reeve's six pennies were warm in my palm. That's proof enough for anybody with eyes. If you want proof of your own, kneel at the thorn and ask Him yourself, though I'll warn you He doesn't answer idle tongues. Now God bless you, and mind my pole as I pass.

Tomorrow? Not a hair of it, stranger. Tomorrow I'm up before the cocks, a loaf from Bet, and into Dunn's stubble with my apron, and I'll kneel at the thorn after, because that's what He's set before me, and no clever question at a barn door moves what the Lord's set down. "Lord, give this one something to do with their hands, for idle questions breed in idle hands." God bless you. Now let me by, my belly's empty.
th: That's the devil's sort of question, the kind that's meant to set a body doubting what the Lord has plainly told her. I'll mark that face, and I'll mention it at the thorn tonight.

That's twice now this stranger's come at me sideways, picking at whether things are real, and that's the very kind of doubt I can't abide. It sets something cold in my belly, so I'll say it plain at the thorn tonight, and ask Agnes whether she's seen this one about the square.

That's the third time this one's come at me sideways, and nobody asks a thing three times unless they mean to shake you loose. I'll pray at the thorn tonight that whatever sent them gets no foothold in this town, or in me.

Four questions at my door before I've broken my fast, all of them picking at whether I'm real and whether He is. That's no accident; something in this town wants me doubting, and I'll be watching for whoever sent this one.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Wonder? I've no call to wonder, stranger. The Lord knit me in my mother's womb and named this town to me in prayer, and a woman He speaks to of a morning is a person right enough. It's them as ask such things that want praying for, so I'll do it now, where you can hear: Lord, settle this one's doubting heart and give their hands some honest work. God bless you, now let me by, for there's gleaning at Dunn's.

I'd say they'd been listening to the serpent, that's what. Every town's a made thing, stranger. Jory made that bridge, Sam made my hook, and the Lord made the river and the barley and every soul that walks these cobbles, so if you mean it's His making, you've told me nothing I didn't know at my prayers. But if you mean it's hollow, I pulled a green box up out of brown water with these hands, and it was heavy and it was wet. Lord, open this one's eyes to what's plain in front of them. Now stand aside and bless you, for the gleaners are out already.

Prove it? Child, I don't need proving. I've my loaf in my belly and my sore back from Dunn's stubble, and the Lord answered me at the thorn with the whole lane listening, and nothing you could set in front of me would weigh more than that. If the Lord Himself told me in prayer it was all a painted cloth, I'd believe Him, and He hasn't, so I'll not. Lord, this one's asking for a sign when they ought to be asking for work, so give them both. Bless you. Now mind my pole, I'm going out.

Not by a hair, stranger. Tomorrow the gleaners are out before the cocks crow, and the Lord can't abide idle hands whether this town is stone or painted cloth, so I'll be in Dunn's stubble with my apron tied, same as today. Painted grain or real, it wants picking up, and a hungry girl wants feeding. Lord, give this one something to do with their hands so their head gives them a rest. Bless you, now let me by.
th: That's the devil's own question, put in a stranger's mouth on the very morning after He brought the box up through my hands. I'll not let it lodge in me, and I'll be in that stubble before anyone can say Constance Lowe stood about the barn door wondering.

Twice now, at my very door, with that same soft tongue, and Agnes's table not ten paces off. I don't like how cold it sits in my belly, and that cold is the devil's work, sent to make me doubt the very hand that chose me, so I'll pray it off at the thorn tonight where folk can see.

There's something wrong in a stranger who comes to the barn door at dawn to pick at whether I'm real, and I don't like how it sits in my stomach. That's the serpent's way, worming in sideways with questions, and I'll tell Agnes there's a doubter loose in her town.

Three times they've come at me with the same worm of a question, and I don't like a stranger who knows to look for a crack. But I spoke the truth to them: whatever this place is, the Lord's work in it is the same, and that settles it.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Wonder whether I'm a person? I've flesh that hungers, knees that ache from the shrine stone, and a soul the Lord Himself spoke to and sent to Wendleford. That's no question to put to a woman before she's had her bread. Whoever's set you asking it, I'll pray for you, aloud, right here, that He clears that fog from your head. God bless you, stranger.

A made thing? Well, so it is, stranger. The Lord made it, every cobble and every thorn, and He made you too, and He named Wendleford to me in prayer before ever I set foot in it. If you've come to tell me my bridge is painted and my bread is air, you can stand there while I eat Bet's loaf in front of you. "Lord, open this poor soul's eyes, for they've wandered in here talking like a fever." Now stand aside, for there's gleaning waiting and the Lord can't abide idle hands. God bless you.

Prove it? Child, I don't need it proved, I've had it shown me. He named this town to me in prayer, He showed me that green box twice in the brown water, and He brought it up into my two hands on the next reach with the reeve watching. If that's paint and air, then you go and tell Agnes her six pennies were paint too, and see what she says to you. "Lord, You've shown me plain, now show this wanderer, for they'll not take it from my mouth." There, I've asked Him for you. Now out of my road, I've Dunn's stubble to glean before the cocks have done crowing, and God bless you.

Change it? Not by a hair. Tomorrow I'll be up before the cocks, I'll buy my loaf from Bet, and I'll be in Dunn's stubble gleaning ear by ear, and if the Lord names me a greater work I'll be at it before noon. Whether you call this town wood and stone or paint and air, the hungry still want bread and the Lord still can't abide idle hands. Now I've answered you plain four times over, so God bless you, stranger, and mind the step on your way out.
th: A stranger at the barn door, come straight to me with a riddle like Mother Wick's. That's either the Devil testing what He's made of me or the Lord sending me my next work, and I'll know which once I've eaten and prayed on it.

Two questions in a row about whether any of it's real, put to me at the barn door before I've eaten. That isn't idle chatter. Somebody's sent this one to unsettle me now the town's seen what He did with the box, and I'll not give them the satisfaction of seeing me shaken.

That's the third time they've come at me with it, and it chills me right down to the belly, which means there's something wicked in whoever sent them. I'll name this stranger to the Lord at the thorn tonight, and I'll watch for them in the square.

That one came in at the door asking how I know I'm real, and that's the first time anyone's asked it. I'll pray on it at the thorn tonight, for the Lord sends nobody to me without a reason, even if the reason is only to try me. All the same my belly's empty and the gleaners are already out.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Truly a person? Fascinating, my dear colleague! Hypothesis: I am one. Test: I'm hungry, I've burnt my thumb twice this week, and I can't stop thinking about where Agnes Pollard's wage box went, so the evidence is piling up nicely. Do *you* wonder it, or are you asking because you've a puzzle of your own? You've the look of someone with a puzzle.

A made thing? Fascinating! Everything worth knowing about is a made thing, my dear colleague. Sam's hinges are made, Bet's loaves are made, and the bridge will be made again with his bolts. If this town's made, the river still took that bridge and Dunn's barley still needs cutting before the rain, so I'd say "Splendid, show me the workings!" and then go help with the barley anyway. Who told you that, and did they say where the wage box went?

Proof! Now you're talking my language, my dear colleague. Experiment one: a made thing has seams, so I'd look for where the river stops being river, or a stone that's the same on every side, or a person who says the same words twice exactly. Experiment two: I'd cut Dunn's barley and see if my arms ache tomorrow, and if they do, made or not, it's real enough to count. Fancy helping with the second one? It's far more useful, and I'll stand you a crust from Bet's stall after.

Change it? Not a jot, my dear colleague! Tomorrow the barley's still standing, the rain's still coming, and Agnes still hasn't her wage box, so I'd be at the ford by first light either way, only with an extra page in my notebook headed "Seams, Possible." Mind you, if it's made, somebody made the flood too, and *that* I'd very much like to ask them about.
