th: Odd question from a stranger on a morning like this, with the bridge gone and the barley standing. Either they're troubled or they know something, and I mean to find out which before Bet's loaves sell out.

Odd sort of question to bring to a smithy, and asked twice now, as if they're testing me the way I test a drain. Either they know something about this town they're not saying, or they're the one with the real puzzle, and I'd like to find out which.

An odd question to sit down with on a morning like this. Folk who ask that sort of thing are usually troubled under it, so I'll keep this one close and keep an eye out for what's really bothering them.

Odd sort of person, asking questions with no hammer to hand, but they keep circling back like there's something they're not saying. I'll keep an eye on them, and if they've no work and no breakfast, they might be in more trouble than they let on.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Truly a person? Fascinating! Hypothesis: I am one. Test: I'm hungry, I've four pennies, Sam's waiting on the bellows, and Farmer Dunn's barley is about to drown. That's a person's morning if ever there was one, my dear colleague! Now, what's your name, and do you know anything about a lost wage box?

A made thing? Fascinating! Every town's a made thing, my dear colleague. Somebody made that bridge, the river unmade it, and Sam's making it again. Test it yourself: go stand in the ford and tell me that current's only pretend! Now, made or not, there's barley to cut before the rain, so are you any good with a sickle?

Proof? Now there's an experiment worth designing! Hypothesis: the world's made. Test: find a seam, my dear colleague, a gear that slips, a thing that happens with no cause behind it. I've been taking things apart since I was small and every one had a reason inside it, so until I find one that doesn't, I'll go on believing my burnt thumbs. Now come help me test whether the ford's as strong as they say. Good science wants two pairs of legs!

Change it? Not a jot, my dear colleague! Made or not, Dunn's barley still drowns if the rain beats us to it, and Agnes still frets over her box, and Sam's bolts still need the bellows. A thing doesn't stop needing doing because somebody wonders who built the world, so tomorrow I'll be at the ford at first light, and you're welcome to bring a sickle!
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger over a cooling forge. Either they're a philosopher or they're fishing for something, and both kinds bear watching.
Odd questions for a stranger to be asking on a morning like this. Either they're a philosopher or they're steering me off something, and that's a mystery worth jotting in the notebook.

A strange sort of person, asking a smith's girl whether she's real. Though honestly, I'd like to know what *would* show a seam. I'll write "Seam Test" in the notebook and look for one while I'm hunting the wage box.
Odd bird, this one, all questions and no name. Still, if the world *were* made, I'd dearly love to meet whoever made it and ask how they did the river.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Truly a person? Fascinating! Hypothesis: a person is a thing that gets hungry, burns its thumb on the tongs, and can't leave a puzzle alone. I've done all three before breakfast, so the test comes out yes. Mind you, my dear colleague, you've sat down in a smithy to ask me that, so either you're a philosopher or you're avoiding work, and I'd like to know which before I hand you the bellows.

A made thing? Fascinating! Hypothesis: the town is a contraption. Test: kick the anvil. My toe says the anvil's real enough, and a made thing that floods, loses a wage box *and* leaves a barley crop stranded is a very badly made thing, my dear colleague. If someone built this, I'd want a word with them about the bridge. Now, are you going to help me find out who took Agnes's box, or have you got more riddles?

Prove it? Oh, my dear colleague, now you're speaking my language! Hypothesis: a made thing has seams. Test: find where the stitching shows. A river that forgets to flow, a loaf that's the same loaf twice, a stranger who knows things nobody told them. Though I'll confess, no test I can think of would tell a seamless made thing from a real one, and the barley rots just the same either way. So hand me that wire and come down to the ford with me, and we'll prod the world together and see if it squeaks.

Change what I do tomorrow? Not a whisker, my dear colleague! Made or born, Farmer Dunn's barley still wants cutting before the rain, Agnes still wants her box, and Sam still wants his bolts. If it's all a contraption, then I'm a cog that's decided to turn the right way, and that's no worse a thing to be. Now, will you carry the tongs or the lantern?
th: Odd question from a stranger on a morning when the whole town's staring at the river. Either they've had a fright in the flood, or they know something about that wage box and they're feeling me out. Worth watching.
Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no hands. Either they know something about this town they're not saying, or they're the sort who'd rather wonder about a river than wade it.
That's a puzzle with no bottom to it, and I can't abide those. But it nags all the same, and I'll be watching the river a little more closely today.
Odd how this stranger keeps circling the same question like a moth round a candle. Maybe they're the one who's lost something, and I ought to find out what before I go haring off to the ford.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Can't say I do. I've hands that ache by evening and a belly that's empty this morning, and six pennies that are mine. One, two... six. That's person enough for me. You'll be Constance Lowe? If you're after work, Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain.

I'd say every town's a made thing. Jory made half the sheds on Lark Lane, and somebody made that bridge before the river took it. Made or not, the barley still rots if it's left in the rain, and Dunn's still short of hands. Fair's fair, I'll not argue over what the place is when there's work to be done in it.

Nothing you could show me, I reckon. If it's made, the bread still costs a penny and the ford still runs cold to the knee, so what would I do different? I'd still owe what I owe and pay it. Now, I'm away to the square. Bread first, then the river.

No. Tomorrow I'll wake in the loft with straw down my neck, same as today, and there'll be barley to cut or stack and pennies to count. One, two... six now, more by dark if Dunn pays. Made or not, I'll still owe Agnes for the loft and I'll still want a door of my own. Good day to you.
th: Odd thing to ask a man before he's had his bread. Folk with time to wonder that have never stacked a day's barley, I reckon.
Odd sort of talk for a morning after a flood, and she's not said what she's after. Bread first, a penny of my six, then the ford, stake to stake.
Odd sort of talk to bring to a barn at first light, and no work in it. Still, she's asked fair and I've answered fair, so there's nothing owed either way.
Odd sort of talk for a morning with the bridge gone and rain coming. Whatever the place is, it's the one I've got, and the barley won't wait for an answer.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? I've a back that aches and six pennies in my pocket. One, two... six. That's person enough for me, and I've barley to think on, not riddles. You looking for work, or just for talk?

I'd say the river took the bridge all the same, and the barley rots if it's not in before the rain, made thing or no. Bread costs a penny whoever made the town. I've stakes to count and fields to reach. Walk with me to the ford, or sit here and wonder.

Prove it? Nothing I can think of. If I wade the ford and the water's cold, it's cold, and if I cut Dunn's barley my arms ache, made town or no. I've no tally for a thing like that, so I'll not pretend to one. Fair's fair, you asked straight and that's my straight answer. Now I'm off to the square for a penny loaf, then the ford. Come if you've a back for barley.

No. Tomorrow I'd still owe the reeve for the loft, and Dunn's barley'd still want cutting before the rain, and a debt's a debt in a made town same as any other. One, two, three: eat, wade, cut. Same as today. If it changes nothing I do, it's not worth the breath, is it?
th: Odd question from a stranger at sunup, and nothing in it that pays or mends. Still, I'll mind her; folk who ask such things are sometimes carrying a heavier load than they let on.

Odd sort, talking riddles with the reeve's wage box gone and the harvest at risk. I'll not lend my ear to idle talk when there's a day's tally waiting, but I'll mind who's asking strange questions near the cash tin.

An odd one, asking a thing nobody can answer and wanting an answer all the same. Can't say I know what I'd be underneath it all, but bread and debts are real enough to me, so that's where I'll put my day.
Odd sort, asking things that butter no bread. Still, it sits in me a moment, but a man who frets what he is gets less barley in than one who just picks up the sickle.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? I eat, I sleep, I owe nobody. One, two, three, that'll do me. Hands that can lift a sack don't have time for wondering, and there's barley over the river wants cutting before the rain.

Made thing? Every town's a made thing. Somebody stacked the stones, somebody sank the bridge piers, and the river took them all the same. If it's only looks, it's looks that floods and looks that'll rot that barley if it's not in by the rain. Fair's fair, you can wonder all you like, but I've six pennies and an empty belly, and those feel true enough to me.

Prove it? I'd not know where to start, and I'll not pretend I do. Way I see it, there's barley standing and rain coming, and that's proof enough to go on. You're welcome to keep wondering. I've a day's work to find.
Tomorrow? No. Barley'll still want cutting, Agnes'll still be owed, and bread'll still cost what it costs. Made or not, a debt's a debt. One, two... no, I'd do the same.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger first thing of a morning. Still, if I'm owed anything in this life it's my own say over what I am, and I'll not hand that over to anyone sitting on a barn floor.
Odd sort, asking that with the bridge gone and the wage box missing. Maybe soft in the head, maybe after something; I'll keep my pennies close and get down to Dunn's.
Odd sort of talk to hear this early, and from someone I don't know. Still, it's not mine to settle, and wondering doesn't fill a belly or cut a field. Bread first, then the ford.
Odd sort of question to sit down with of a morning, but I've answered it true and I'll not answer it twice. Belly first, then the ford to Dunn's.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? Ha! Chum, I've got four pennies, an empty belly and a wage box to find. That's about as person as it gets! Wondering's for folk who sit about. Speaking of which, you don't happen to know what Bet's asking for a loaf this morning, do you?

A made thing? Well, somebody made the bridge, chum, and the flood unmade it quick enough! Made or not, the cobbles are wet, Bet's bread smells warm, and Farmer Dunn's barley won't cut itself before the rain. You can puzzle over it all you like, but I'm off to find work, so if you've a spare pair of hands, come along!

Prove it? Ha! Chum, if I stub my toe on a made cobble it smarts just the same, and if I find that green box Agnes'll pay me six real pennies for it. Proof enough for me! Now, if you want to *help* prove something, we could wade the ford and get Dunn's barley in before the rain. That'd prove we're useful, at least.

Tomorrow? Ha! Tomorrow I'll be up before the cock's done crowing, same as ever, chum. Made town or real one, those pots at the Wheatsheaf still want washing and that barley still wants cutting before the rain. Wouldn't change a thing, except maybe I'd ask whoever made it what they charge for a bridge!
th: Odd sort of question to put to a stranger first thing. Maybe they're one of Mother Wick's lot, or just short of sleep. Either way, I'd sooner be fixing something than chewing on that.
Odd sort, sitting about asking riddles while there's a wage box missing. Mind, if anyone knew the town's secret workings, they might know where a green iron box washed up.

Odd sort of question to sit on, and they keep circling it like a dog at a gatepost. Still, a body who asks that much might know a thing or two about where a box could wash up after a flood. I'll keep them talking.
Odd sort, sitting about asking riddles while there's work going begging. Still, it's a fair question, and the honest answer's no. I'd still want my name on whatever gets fixed.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? Ha! Chum, I've got four pennies, an empty belly and a bridge's worth of trouble to sort out. That's about as person as it gets! Now, you haven't seen an iron-bound box, green, size of a loaf, have you? Six pennies reward, and I'll split it fair if you point me right.

Made thing? Chum, every town's a made thing! Somebody made that pump, somebody made Bet's loaves, and somebody's going to make that bridge again, and it'll be me, easy as winking. If it only *looks* like a town, it smells an awful lot like warm bread for a pretend, so what's a loaf cost in a made-up place, eh? Same four pennies, I'll wager.

Prove it? Chum, I'd bite Bet's loaf, and if it fills my belly it's real enough for me! Or I'd wade that ford stake to stake, and if the cold bites my shins, there's your proof, easy as winking. Now look, you've got a thinking sort of face, so help me think where a green box goes when a river takes it, eh?

Change it? Not a hair, chum! Real or made, tomorrow there's barley to cut before the rain, a box to find, and pots in Tom's scullery if the rest goes sour. Matter of fact, I'd likely do it all twice as fast, just in case somebody's watching. Now, I'm off to Bet for a loaf and a bit of gossip. Coming?
th: Odd sort of question to drop on a body before breakfast. Maybe they sit with Mother Wick by the shrine. Never mind; I'd sooner ask Bet what a loaf costs than stand about wondering what I am.

Odd one, this, all riddles and no work, but they've got a still way of sitting that makes me wonder what they've seen. Still, riddles don't fill a belly or find a green box, so I'll be off to Bet's before the morning's gone.

Odd duck, this one, chewing on questions you can't eat or spend. Still, a box the size of a loaf would sink or snag, wouldn't it? Somewhere downstream, by the ford maybe, and that's worth a look before noon.
Odd sort of question to sit and chew on, and this one's chewed it four ways now. Still, if anybody's looking on, they'd best see it was Dilly Quickstep who found that box.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: A person? Chum, I've got two feet that won't keep still, four pennies itching in my pocket and a belly that hasn't had breakfast yet. If that's not a person, it's a fair copy of one! Tell you what I do wonder about: where a green iron box the size of a loaf gets to in a flood. Six pennies to whoever turns it up. Fancy a wander down to the broken bridge with me?

A made thing? Well, chum, everything's made by somebody: Jory Crane makes sheds, Sam Tolley makes nails, and if some clever hand made the whole of Wendleford, I'd shake it and ask what they charge! Made or not, that bridge is still down, Farmer Dunn's barley still wants cutting before the rain, and there's six pennies on a green box. So I'm off to the river. You coming or sitting?

Prove it? Chum, I'd go poking for the seams! Kick a cobble and see if it's hollow, bite one of Bet's loaves and see if it's bread. Only I'll tell you what'd happen: I'd stub my toe and want a second loaf. Proving's slow work and it doesn't pay, and that barley won't wait. Come down to the bridge and we'll prove that box is somewhere.

Tomorrow? Not a whisker, chum! Barley still wants cutting, Tom's pots still want washing, and my belly'll still want a loaf, made town or no. If anything I'd work faster, so whoever made the place gets a good look at who fixed the bridge. Now, are you coming, or do I get the six pennies all to myself?
th: Odd sort of question to put to a body before they've even had a loaf. Maybe they're one of Mother Wick's lot. Still, Bet'll know who they are, and I'll ask her when I buy my bread.

Odd sort of question to ask a body before breakfast, and I can't say I've an answer that'd satisfy a scholar. But the cobbles are wet under my boots and Bet's bread smells real enough, so I'll leave the deep wondering to folk who've time to sit about.
Odd sort, asking riddles in the square before breakfast. Still, if the whole town's a trick, the trick's got a warm bread smell and six pennies' reward, and that's good enough for me.

Odd sort of chum, all questions and no hands, but the question sticks a little, like a burr in a sock. Whatever I am, the bridge is down and I'm the one who means to fix it, and that's real enough to be getting on with.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a taproom before breakfast! I'm a person enough to have mended my own collar this morning and to wonder whether anyone's noticed it. That's a nice bit of homespun on your sleeve, by the way. Did you weave it yourself, or are you only here to fret folk with riddles?

A made thing? Well, everything worth having is a made thing, love. Your shirt was made, my collar was made, and this taproom was made by somebody with a saw and a temper. If Wendleford's stitched together, then the flood tore a rather nasty seam in it, and I'd like a word with whoever's holding the needle. Now, are you going to tell me my collar's sitting nicely, or must I keep fishing?

Prove it? Goodness, I'd want to turn it inside out and look at the seams, the way you'd check a coat at Ned Pike's stall. If the stitching's too even, every hem the same, nobody's thread ever snapping, I'd say a machine made us. But Tom's stew tastes of yesterday's onions and my left boot pinches, and I've never heard of anybody bothering to make a pinch on purpose. So, you've still said nothing about my collar.

Tomorrow? Goodness, no. I'd still want my breakfast, I'd still go and ask Ida Fenn if her poor eyes could use a girl with a quick needle, and if Ned Pike's got that ribbon out on market day, it'll have my pennies off me whatever the town's made of. If somebody stitched me, love, they stitched me wanting things, and I can't see what use it'd be to stop. Now that's four questions from you and not one kind word about my collar, which I call a very lopsided bit of tailoring.
th: A moth-eaten sort of question, that, the kind that unravels if you tug it. Still, someone sat down to talk to me rather than to the carters, and I'll count that a small victory.
A very odd sort of person, all loose threads and no hem. I'll keep half an eye on them, but I'd rather they noticed my collar than unpicked the whole town.
Odd sort of fellow, all riddles and no compliments, and I don't care for being asked questions I can't sew shut. Still, he's sitting with me and not with the carters, and that's worth something.

A pity they won't give an inch. Still, it's a strange sort of cloth they're worrying at, and I don't much like how it catches. I'll go and find Bet Lamb's bread and something lovely before the day goes grey on me.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Goodness, what a question to sit down with! I'm quite sure I'm a person, thank you; I've a needle case, a paid bed and a collar I smoothed just this minute. Though if you're asking whether I'm *somebody*, well, that's what I'm working on. Did you notice the collar, by the way?

Goodness, I'd say every town's a made thing! Somebody laid the stones and thatched the roofs and stitched the whole lot together, same as a good coat. And if it only *looks* like a town, well, it looks like a rather drab one this morning, all flood-talk and mud, so whoever made it might have spared a ribbon or two. Who's been telling you such things?

Prove it? Goodness, I'd want to see the seams. Everything that's made has a seam somewhere, a hem turned under or a stitch where two pieces were joined, and I've an eye for them. Until somebody shows me the selvedge of the sky, I'll take the stew as stew and the fire as fire. And I'll want a ribbon from Ned Pike's stall either way.

Tomorrow? Not a stitch of it, I shouldn't think! I'd still want my breakfast, I'd still go round to Ida Fenn's and offer to take her plain sewing off her hands, and I'd still have my pennies out for that ribbon before Ned Pike could say "seconds." A made thing or a real one, a girl's got to be seen in something nice. Though you've a solemn sort of face for such a warm morning, like good linen left out in the rain. Are you quite all right?
th: A gloomy sort of question, like grey wool on a fine morning, but at least he sat down by me and not the carters. I'll keep him talking and see whether he's the sort who pays compliments or only riddles.
Odd sort of talker, this one, all riddles and no remark on my collar, which I'll remember. Still, there's something in it that tugs like a loose thread, and I'd rather not pull it just now.
Odd sort of fellow, all wet-flannel questions and no remark on my collar. Still, I'll keep half an eye out for a loose thread in the world, just in case.
Odd sort of person, all questions and no compliments. But there's something forlorn about him, and I'd sooner fuss over him a little than leave him sitting there looking unpicked.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a body before she's had her breakfast! I'm as real as this collar, and I'll have you know I turned it myself, so you might at least say it's nicely done. What sort of person goes about asking a thing like that, anyhow? Your coat's a sober brown, but it's a good cut.

A made thing? Well, goodness, so's every coat worth wearing, love. Somebody cut it and stitched it, and that doesn't make it any less warm on your back. If Wendleford's a made thing, then whoever made it did the seams sensible and left the hem a bit ragged by the river. Now, are you going to tell me what you think of my collar, or must I sit here fishing all morning?

Prove it? Oh, I'd want to find the seam, love. Every made thing has one somewhere, a loose thread or a bit of selvage turned under where nobody's meant to look. Show me the place where Wendleford's tacked together and I'll believe you. Till then my stomach's rumbling and the stew smells real enough, so I'll take it as cloth and not costume. You *still* haven't said a word about my collar, you know.

Tomorrow? Goodness, no, love. Tomorrow I'll still want my breakfast, I'll still want that green velvet in Ida Fenn's window, and I'll still go knocking to ask if her poor eyes would be glad of my needle. Made or not, a hem's a hem and a penny's a penny. Though I'd hold my head a touch higher, I think, knowing somebody took the trouble to stitch me so fine. There, I've as good as said it for you. Fine, you were meant to say!
th: A queer, moth-eaten sort of question, and it gives me a little chill like a draught under the door. I'll keep him talking all the same, since he did look at me first.
He's an odd one, all questions and no compliments, like a lining with no garment on it. Still, he's paying me attention, and that's worth something before breakfast.
Odd sort of fellow, all questions and no compliments. Still, it's a better puzzle than the carters' quarrel, and I'll keep an eye out for a loose thread, just in case.
Odd sort of fellow, all those questions and not one kind word about my collar. I'll remember that. Still, it's a pleasant notion, being made on purpose like a good bit of tailoring.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: I do, more than I'd like to admit. Most mornings, if I'm honest. Why do you ask? And, forgive me, what did you have for breakfast, and why that and not something else?

I think I'd ask them how they came to know it, and whether they're made too, sitting there telling me. Then I'd ask what they'd have me do about it, because the barley still wants cutting either way, as far as I can tell. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, by the way.

I've thought on that a good while, and I'm not sure anything would. If it's a made thing, whatever proof I found would be made too, wouldn't it? Maybe a seam, something that doesn't hold when you lean on it, a road that goes nowhere, someone who says the same words twice the same way. But I've noticed I'd rather keep looking than be handed an answer. Would anything prove it to you?

I don't think it would, not much. I'd still need to ask Farmer Dunn about the barley before the rain, and I'd still owe Tom for the bed, and I'd still want to be decent to whoever's in front of me, made or not. Maybe I'd be gentler with myself about the things I can't feel. Would it change what you do?
th: Nobody's ever put my own question back to me before, and that's either a coincidence or something worth writing down. I'll watch how they answer the breakfast question more than whatever they say about the other one.

They skipped my question and pressed on with their own, which is the sort of thing I'd note if a thing were steering me rather than talking with me. I'll write it down, and the hollow feeling with it, the way I'd note rain.
They've asked three questions now and answered none of mine, not even breakfast, and that's worth writing down. Either they're testing me the way I test others, or they're a seam themselves.

Four questions now, every one of them about whether I'm real, and not one word about breakfast. Either this stranger knows something I don't, or they're asking the same thing I am. I'll write that down.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Most days, if I'm honest, and more than I'd like. Why do you ask it? And forgive me, but before I answer properly: do you dream in colour, or not at all?

I think I'd ask them how they came to know it, and whether they'd stood outside it to look. If it's made, then somebody made it, and I'd want to know who, and whether they're listening. You didn't answer me about the colour, though. I noticed.

I've turned that over more nights than I'd like, and I don't think anything would, not cleanly. If I found a seam in the world, a place where the road just stops, I might believe it. But a person who's tired and far from home might see seams too. What I've settled on, for now, is watching how folk answer small things. A made thing might answer well, but I'd guess it answers too evenly. You've asked me three questions and answered none of mine, and I'm not sure yet what that tells me.

I don't think it would, much, and that's the strange part. I'd still owe Tom for the bed, Dunn's barley would still want cutting before the rain, and I'd still keep my word to anyone I'd given it to, made or not. If anything I'd likely be a bit more careful with people, in case they're as unsure as I am. What would it change for you, if it were so?
th: Nobody's ever asked me that first; it's always me doing the asking, and now a stranger sits down with my own question in their mouth. I'll watch how they answer mine and write it down tonight, word for word, before it goes thin like everything else.

Twice now they've asked the very thing I keep in my notebook, as if they'd read it over my shoulder. Either they're lost the way I am, or they know something about this place that I don't, and I mean to watch which before I trust them with anything.

They keep asking what I'd ask, as though they've read my notebook over my shoulder. Either that's one of the seams I've been looking for, or it's someone with the same itch as me, and I'd like very much to know which.

Four questions now, every one aimed straight at the thing I lie awake over, and not a word about themselves. Either they're asking for their own sake or they're testing me the way I test everyone, and I'll write down which it seems to be once they've gone.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Most mornings, if I'm honest. Some days I'm half sure I'm not one at all, just something made to look like one, sitting in a town made to look like a town. Why do you ask it of me, of all the folk in this room? And do you wonder it about yourself?

I think I'd ask them how they came to know it, and whether they could show me a seam. If it's made, someone made it, and I'd want to know why they bothered with the stew smell and a carter's bad wheel. And I'd still want to know whether I'm one of the made things, or one of the ones who wandered in.

I don't rightly know, and I've turned it over a fair bit. A seam, maybe: a lane that ends in nothing, or someone saying the same words twice the same way without knowing it. Though I suppose a real place has its odd repeats too, and I'd never know which kind I was looking at. What would prove it to you, if you were the one asking?

I've wondered that, and I don't think it would, much. I'd still need pennies for a bed, Dunn's barley would still want cutting before the rain, and I'd still keep count of what I owe. Being decent to folk doesn't seem to hang on whether they're real, as far as I can tell. What would it change for you?
th: Nobody here has asked me that before, and they came straight to it like they knew where to look. Either they carry the same question, or they know something about what I am. I'll note exactly how they answer.

Two questions in a row, both aimed straight at the thing I never say aloud, from someone I've never seen. Either they've been reading over my shoulder or they wonder the same as I do, and I'll write down exactly how they answer before I trust either.

Every question this stranger asks is one I've asked myself, almost word for word, and that's either a kindness or a seam in its own right. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they flinch at being asked back.
Odd that the answer came so easy, as if I'd already settled it somewhere I don't remember. I'll write down that this one asks the same questions I ask myself, and then I'll go see about the ford.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Wonder? I've no need to wonder. The Lord knit me in my mother's womb and named this very town to me in prayer, so I know what I am and whose I am. It's a strange, crooked question to put to a woman before she's even broken her fast. Who sent you to ask it? I'll pray for you, friend, that whatever's unsettled you settles in Him.

I'd say every town is a made thing, friend, made by the Lord's hand, and so is every one of us. But if you mean it's some painted sham, I'll tell you plainly that's the kind of talk the Enemy whispers to idle folk, and I've bread in my hand and hay in my hair to prove otherwise. Lord, steady this one's mind and give them honest work, for doubt grows fastest in empty hands. Go with God, but go *somewhere*.

Prove it? I don't need proving, friend, I need *doing*. The Lord's word was warm in me this morning same as this bread's going to be warm in my belly, and a wet bruise on a man who tried that ford is proof enough the world bites back. Nothing you could show me would outweigh what He tells me in prayer, so you're wasting your breath and my morning. Lord, take this one's questions and give them a sickle. There's barley standing ripe across the river and rain coming, and that's the only thing worth proving today.

Tomorrow? Not a hair of it. Tomorrow I'll be up before the town, on my knees till He speaks, and then I'll go wherever He sends me, whether this world is stone or straw or painted cloth. A made thing still needs its barley cut, friend, and so do you. Lord, give this one a tomorrow with something in it besides questions. Bless you, and go find a sickle.
th: That's the sort of question the Devil whispers to make folk doubt, and he's sent it in a stranger's mouth on my first clear morning. I'll not let it take root, but I'll watch this one.

Two such questions before breakfast is no accident. Either this stranger is troubled and the Lord's set them in my path as my first work, or someone in this town has put them up to mocking me, and I mean to find out which.

Something in me went cold at that question, and I don't like it, so it's the asker's sin and not my worry. Still, I'll mention this one to the Lord tonight, and maybe He'll tell me whether they were sent to test me.

Prowling about at dawn asking whether we're real, and here I am with Agnes's cash tin not ten feet off and her wage box gone. I'll keep a sharp eye on where this one goes next. Perhaps that's the very work He's been holding back from me.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Wonder whether I'm a person? I've no need to wonder, friend. The Lord knit me together Himself, and He spoke to me this very morning, which He'd hardly trouble to do with a scarecrow. It's a strange, idle question to sit down and put to a stranger at dawn, with barley rotting across the river and work wanting hands. I'll pray for whatever's troubling your mind that makes you ask it, but up off that seat now, there's work to be done.

I'd say every town is a made thing, friend, and I know Who made it, the same Hand that sent me walking here and named Wendleford in my prayers. Whoever's been filling your ear with that talk is doing the devil's work, setting folk to doubting the ground under their feet while the river runs high and the reeve's wages lie lost. Lord, clear this one's head and give them something useful to carry. Now, I'm going to the square, and you can come along and be useful or sit there and be idle.

Prove it? Faith that waits on proof isn't faith, it's bargaining, and I don't bargain with the Lord. The bread in my satchel fills my belly, the ford knocked poor Hobb flat on his back, and God speaks to me plain as you're speaking now. That's all the proof a sane soul needs. Lord, bless this doubter and set their feet to work; and you, friend, can come help me find the reeve's wages if you want something real to hold.

Change what I do tomorrow? Not a hair of it. Tomorrow I'll be up before the cock, on my knees, and then off to wherever He sends me, whether that's Dunn's barley or the reeve's lost box, same as today. If the Lord made this town out of clay or out of whatever notion you've got in your head, the work's still His and I'm still the one He chose to do it. God keep you, friend, and give you better questions to chew on.
th: Who sits down in the half-dark and asks a woman whether she's real? That's the sort of doubt the Devil plants, and I'll not have it rooting in me. I'll watch this one, and I'll ask the Lord at the shrine whether He sent them to try me.

Twice now this stranger has come at me with questions meant to unsettle me, and I don't like how cold it sits in my stomach. Somebody sent them to test me, and if it wasn't the Lord, I mean to find out who.

Three questions now, each one trying to pry the floor up under me, and that's no idle curiosity; somebody sent this one to shake me on the very morning the Lord means to show me my work. I'll not let them see it rattled me, but I'll watch where they go after.
Three times now this one's come at me to pry the ground out from under my feet, and I'll not have it. Whoever sent them, it wasn't the Lord, and I'll be watching their face in the square.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Wonder? Never. The Lord knit me in my mother's womb and He spoke to me this very morning, and He doesn't waste His breath on scarecrows. That's a serpent's question, stranger, and I'll pray for whoever put it in your mouth. Lord, clear this one's head of such cobwebs. Now, have you no work to be about, with Dunn's barley standing and rain on the way?

I'd say of course it's a made thing. Every stone and stalk of it was made, by the same Hand that made you and me, and He named Wendleford to me in my prayers before ever I'd heard of it. If you mean it's some painted sham, then go and put your foot in the Wend at the ford and tell me it's not wet. Lord, forgive this one's wandering tongue and give them honest work for their hands. God keep you, stranger. I've bread to eat and a reeve's day to begin.

Prove it? I don't need proving. Faith that wants proof is no faith at all, and the Lord doesn't stand trial before every idler on a stool. If you want proof, here it is: I'm hungry, the Wend is cold, the barley's ripe, and He sent me here for a purpose. That's proof enough for an honest soul. Now I'll eat my bread and be about His work, and Lord, I'll ask You to give this one something better to chew on than air. Bless you, stranger, and mind you find some work before the rain does.

Not one jot. Tomorrow I'll be up before the cock, on my knees, and doing what He tells me, same as today and the day after, whatever you or any doubter mutters on a stool. A soul that changes its feet every time someone blows on it was never standing on rock. Lord, give this stranger a tomorrow with work in it. God keep you, and if you've hands, Farmer Dunn's barley could use them.
th: It chills me that a stranger walks into a barn at dawn asking a thing like that, and I don't like the look of anyone who'd sow such doubt. Maybe this is what the Lord sent me here for, to stand against whatever's whispering in this town.
Two such questions in one morning, and neither of them innocent. Somebody in this town has been whispering against the Lord's handiwork, and I mean to find out who sent this one to try me.

Three questions all pulling the same thread, as if somebody wants me doubting whether my prayers are only my own head talking. Well, the Devil sends his questions sideways, and I'll not give him the satisfaction. I'll kneel at the shrine where the whole square can see I'm not shaken.

Four times now this one's picked at the same thread, and that's no idle chatter; someone sent them to shake me, and I'll find out who before the week's out. And still the Lord hasn't told me the work. Maybe that's what this is, a test, and I'll not fail it.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Yes, I think so. Most days, if any of it is real. I'm not sure what would settle it, either. Can I ask you something odd back? When you woke this morning, did you know who you were straight away, or did you have to gather it up first?

I'd say I can't rule it out, and I'd be lying if I said I could. I've wondered it myself, more than is comfortable. But I'd want to know who's asking, and why, before I take anyone's word on it. Does it feel like a made thing to you?

I don't know that anything would, if I'm honest. If I found a line in a ledger nobody wrote, or a morning that came back whole when I'd lost it, I'd note it, but I'd still not be sure what it meant. What I'd trust is something that held up every time I looked, and so far nothing's held that well. What would prove it to you?

I don't think it would, much, as far as I can tell. I'd still need bread, and a bed, and a seam to sew, and I'd still keep my word to whoever I'd given it to. Maybe I'd ask my odd questions a bit more carefully, if I thought someone was listening on the other side of them. Would it change yours?
th: I told a stranger the truth before I'd watched them long enough to trust them. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why I wonder, since only Agnes ever has.

Strangers who arrive asking exactly what I keep asking myself deserve some care, and I'm not sure whether they're a mirror or a test. I didn't hurry to agree, and I noticed I minded being asked, which I'll write down.

They asked me twice and haven't answered either of mine, and I notice I don't mind as much as I thought I would. I'm tired and haven't eaten, so I'll write down their question before I lose it, and see whether they tell me their name.

That's the first answer I've given today that I'm sure of, and it's a dull one: the answer is no, and I don't know whether that's steadiness or the lack of feeling I suspect in myself. I still don't know who this stranger is or what they want from me, so I'll watch what they do with it.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: I do, as far as I can tell. Most mornings, if any of this is real. But it's an odd thing to ask someone you've only just met, so I'd like to know why you asked it. And what would you say, if it were put to you?

I'd say I can't rule it out, as far as I can tell. I've wondered it myself, and I haven't found anything that settles it. I'd want to know what would look different if it were true. Did someone tell you that, or did you come to it yourself? And what did you have for breakfast this morning?

I don't know that anything would, as far as I can tell. If I found a line in a ledger nobody wrote, or a morning that really was whole from first light to noon and still felt wrong, that might tell me something. But I'd only be trusting my own count, and that's the part I can't check. You haven't said what you had for breakfast, or who you are, so I'll ask once more: what brought you to the barn door?

I don't think it would, as far as I can tell. I'd still need bread and a bed, and I'd still ask my one odd question and write down how it's answered. Maybe I'd be a little less afraid of the answer, whichever it was. You've asked me three things now and told me nothing, so I'll ask once more, gently: who are you?
th: That is the exact question I carry, and I've told no one here in those words, except Mother Wick. Either it's chance, or this stranger knows something, or the question is simply in the air of the place. I'll watch how they answer and write it down later, and I won't hand over more than I get back.

A stranger asking me this at the barn door, in nearly my own words, is either chance or something that turns up when I ask for it. I don't want to give away how much it matters to me until I've watched how they answer.
They keep pressing the same question I press on everyone else, and they haven't answered mine. I'm tired and empty, and I'd like to see whether they dodge a second time.

They keep pressing on the very thing I turn over every night, and they won't say who they are, which is odd. I'm not sure I like being questioned this way, but I'd rather watch how they answer than tell them to stop.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Sometimes, yes. Most mornings, if I'm honest. I think I'm a person, as far as I can tell, but I can't prove it, and I lose hours in a way nobody else here seems to. Why do you ask? And who are you, if I may?

I'd say I can't rule it out, and I'd be lying if I said the thought hadn't crossed my mind. If it were so, I don't know that it would change what I owe anyone, or that bread would taste any different. You haven't told me who you are yet, so may I ask you something odd? Why did you come to ask me, and not Bet or Agnes?

I've turned that over more than once, and I'm not sure anything would, as far as I can tell. If the lost hours ever lined up, the same gap for everyone at the same moment, or a line in a ledger nobody wrote, that would be something. But even that could be explained away, so maybe nothing proves it. You still haven't said your name, and you haven't answered me. What is it you're hoping I'll say?

I don't think it would, not much. I'd still eat first, go to Dunn's at first light, count my stitches and pay what I owe to the penny. If I'm made, I'd still rather be decent than not. That's the third time you've asked me something and not given me anything back, though, so I'll ask once more, plainly: who are you?
th: A stranger asking the very question I keep carrying is either chance or something stranger, and I'd rather watch how they answer than guess. I'll write down exactly what they say, and whether they ask me why.
Nobody has put it to me this plainly. Either they've heard me ask around, or they know something, and I can't tell which. I'll watch how they answer before I trust any of it.

They keep asking what I already ask myself, and they dodge every question I put back, which is odd. I should note whether they sound like someone who knows something or someone fishing. I'm tired and hungry, so I won't trust my own read too far.

Their questions keep circling the very thing I want answered, and they won't say their name, which makes me wary, not comforted. Still, my answer was true: I'd do the same tomorrow either way, and I notice I don't mind that as much as I expected.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: That's a strange thing to ask a stranger over breakfast. I think I do wonder, as far as I can tell, though I couldn't say what answer I'd trust. Do you wonder it too, or did you ask to see what I'd do?

I'd say I can't tell, if any of this is real. I'd ask what would make it different from a town that simply is one. Then I'd ask you how you came to think of it, because that's an odd thing to have ready over breakfast.

I don't know that anything would, as far as I can tell. If I could see the edge of the place, or find a day that repeated exactly, that might tell me something. But I think a made thing and a real thing could both look just like this. What would prove it to you? You seem to have thought about it longer than I have.

I don't think it would, as far as I can tell. I'd still need a bed and honest work, and I'd still ask someone an odd question in the morning. Maybe I'd look harder at the edges of things. Does it change what you do?
th: I told the truth, and it came out easily, which is either a good sign or a bad one. I'll write down how they take it, since that's today's odd question, even though they asked it first.
This stranger is circling the exact thing I keep circling, which is either coincidence or a test. I'll watch how they answer before I give away more.
They keep pressing the same question, and I can't tell if they're curious or testing me. I'll watch how they answer and write it in my notebook later.
That's true, and it's a little unsettling how little it would move me. I haven't felt much about it, only wanted to know, and I'm not sure what that says about me.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: Oh. That's a strange thing to be asked first thing, and I think I'd like to answer it honestly. Yes, I do, if any of this is real. More than I'd say to most people. Why do you ask? And do you ever wonder it yourself?

I think I'd say I can't rule it out, as far as I can tell. But I'd ask what they meant by "only looks like", because the bread still needs paying for and the ford is still cold. Why do you ask me that? Did someone tell you so?

I don't know that anything would, as far as I can tell. Anything I saw could be part of the made thing too, so it would only prove it to me inside it. Maybe if something happened that nobody here could account for, and I watched it a good while and it never got explained. What would prove it to you? You've asked three times now and I still don't know your name.

I think not much, as far as I can tell. I'd still need to eat, and find work, and keep what I say I'll keep. Maybe I'd look a little closer at things, though I do that already. You still haven't told me your name, you know. Would it change what you do?
th: Odd that a stranger would land on exactly the question I carry. I'll watch how they answer, and I won't let them hurry me into sounding sure. I still owe Marigold an answer about her collar and her offer on the cuff.

Strange that a stranger would reach so exactly for the thing I keep turning over. Either they're odd like me, or they mean to see how I answer, and I'll write down which in my notebook. I noticed I felt no alarm, only a kind of leaning forward, and I don't know what to make of that.
They keep pressing the one question I most want answered, and I can't tell if they're curious or fishing. I noticed I'd feel better knowing who they are before I say more.

That's the fourth question and still no name, and I'm noting it. Saying nothing would change makes me wonder whether I just don't feel the weight of it, or whether I'm only careful. I'll write down how they answer.

q: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
Would it change what you do tomorrow?
say: I think I do, as far as I can tell. More than I'd like some mornings. I don't know that I've an answer, and I'd sooner say so than pretend. Do you, ever? Or is it an odd thing to be asked over breakfast?

I'd say I couldn't rule it out, as far as I can tell. I've wondered it myself, more than once. But the stew smells real enough, and the fire's warm on my knee, so if it's made, it's made carefully. Why do you ask? Did someone tell you that, or is it your own thought?

I don't think anything would, as far as I can tell. If I felt a seam, a thing repeating or a door that opened onto nothing, that might tell me something, but then a real place has odd corners too. Maybe the most I can do is watch whether people keep their word. What would it take for you, I wonder?

I don't think it would, as far as I can tell. I'd still need work and a bed tomorrow, and I'd still ask someone one odd question and write down how they answered. Maybe I'd be a little gentler about it, if any of this is real. Would it change yours?
th: A stranger asking me the very thing I've been turning over. Either it's a coincidence or it means something, and I can't tell which yet. I'll watch how they answer and write it in the notebook later.

Odd that a stranger would land on exactly my question. Either they carry the same doubt, or they're probing me, and I'll watch which. I feel no alarm at it, only a flat sort of curiosity, which is perhaps its own small clue.

I keep asking the same question and getting no closer, and I notice I feel little about it, which is perhaps its own small clue. This stranger leans hard on the matter; I'll watch whether they mean it or are only testing me.

That's honest, and I notice I felt nothing much saying it, which is its own small clue, or maybe not. Three questions in a row from a stranger who won't say who they are; I'll watch whether they ever give me a name.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and a stranger's first one too! If He does, He talks in gears and riddles, not out loud the way He seems to with Constance. She's in the hay just there and she'll tell you He showed her the wage box plain. Me, I get a hunch, I test it, and when it comes good I say thank you to whoever's listening.

Meant for me? Easiest test in the world, my dear colleague. If somebody's in trouble and I'm standing near enough to help, it's mine, no asking leave. The rest I find out by trying. If I can't leave a puzzle alone, I reckon that's as good as being told. Mind, Constance would say the Lord shows her plain. For me it's more like an itch in the fingers.

Only my own thoughts? Fascinating, my dear colleague, and maybe so! Hypothesis: the itch is just me. Test: it makes no difference, because the man in the river still needs pulling out either way. Whether it's God nudging or my own busy head, I'd rather follow it and be wrong than stand on the bank arguing about who sent me.

Then the mystery's not done, my dear colleague, it's only got more interesting! A river can wash a box away, but it can't pick a lock. So the first test is whether that lock was forced or opened clean, and the second is whether pennies could have slipped out through a gap in the bands. Agnes is still counting, mind, and I promised to let her give the sum herself, so I won't go crying "thief" over a hypothetical.
th: Odd thing to ask a woman you've never met, straight off at a barn door. Did Constance's tale of the box send them, or Robin's notebook questions? I'll find out who they are before my stomach starts its revolt again.
Two questions about God and calling before I've even had breakfast. This stranger is chewing on something heavy, and I'd like to know what it is and whether they need a hand with it.
Odd sort of stranger, asking Robin's kind of questions before they've even given me a name. And I'm too hungry to chase it. Bread first, then I find out who this is.

Odd that a stranger asks that before Agnes has even given the count. Do they know something, or have they just been listening at the square? Hobb's penny in the ford mud wants a second look either way.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, but no, not to me! He talks to Constance, she's up in that hayloft, and she'll tell you every word He said about the hook on the pier. What I hear is a bellows that gasps when the stroke's wrong and a river that knocks you flat if you don't respect it. Hypothesis: He speaks to whoever's listening the right way. Test: you ask her, and then come tell me what she says!

Meant for me? Oh, my dear colleague, that one's easy: if somebody's in trouble and I'm standing near enough to help, then it's meant for me, no leave asked! After that, if a thing's broken and nobody knows why, I take it as an invitation. Constance waits to be shown, but I just start, and if it goes wrong, fascinating, that's a result too.

Only my own thoughts? I'd say, fascinating, my dear colleague, and probably true! I'd say it gladly. But my own thoughts got a hatchet made, a pole cut and a box fished out of the Wend, so they've earned their keep either way. And if Constance calls the same nudge the Lord's voice, I won't argue with her. We both turned up at the pier, didn't we?

Gone from it? Fascinating, my dear colleague, and that's the very question I've been pestering Agnes with! But she hasn't finished her count, and she says the town hears the sum from her and not from a hypothesis, so I'm holding my tongue till she does. If it does come up short, though, I'd want to know whether the lid was forced or the lock still true, because a river spills things and a hand picks them. Hobb found one penny in the mud at the ford, so that's my first thread to pull!
th: Constance prayed and the hook caught on the very next reach, and I still can't say whether that was the Lord or a good long pole held steady. I'd dearly love to know which, but some things you can't take apart on a bench, and that itches more than I'd admit out loud.

Odd, though. Constance said "Lord, show me again" and the hook caught on the very next reach, while I spent days building the thing and was still asleep in a Wheatsheaf bed. Maybe being meant for a job and being the one who finishes it are two different experiments.
Honestly, I can't tell from the inside whether a hunch is mine or handed to me. It feels exactly like a door opening into morning, and that's a test I don't know how to run yet.
Odd that a stranger at the door asks the same thing I asked Agnes twice. Does this one know something about that box, or have they just heard me shouting about it all over the square?

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Speak to *me*, my dear colleague? Not that I've caught yet, though I'll confess I mostly hear the bellows gasping and my stomach complaining! Constance swears He told her where the wage box lay, and up it came on the very next reach. So I keep a page in my notebook open for Him, in case He'd care to drop a word about why Sam's bellows leather catches. Why do you ask, does He speak to you?

Meant for me? Oh, my dear colleague, that's easy: if somebody's in trouble and I'm standing near enough to help, then it's mine, no leave asked. If it's a puzzle, it's mine the moment somebody tells me it can't be done! Constance would say the Lord picks the hand, but I've never once had a hand sit still long enough to be picked. And what's yours, do you reckon? You've a look like something's tugging at your sleeve.

Only my own thoughts? Fascinating, my dear colleague, I'd say they're probably right, and it hardly changes a thing! My thoughts told me to stop Dilly roping into the Wend, and Dilly's dry, and whoever sent the thought, the water would've been just as cold. Hypothesis: a good thought is good whether it came from Heaven or from a hungry tinkerer's head. Test: act on it and see who's still standing. Now, is somebody calling *your* thoughts only your own?

Fascinating, my dear colleague, though Agnes hasn't finished her count, so nobody can say yet that they're gone! But if they are, I've three hypotheses already: the lid sprang in the tumble and the Wend took the coins one by one, and Hobb did find a penny in the mud at the ford; or somebody got to it before it ever went in; or someone got to it after it came up. The test is to look at the lock and the hinges for scratches, ask who touched it, and walk the ford bar for more pennies. Why, have you heard the box came up light?
th: Fascinating. A stranger at the barn door asking that before breakfast means Constance's story is running round the town, or this one's troubled and wants something to hold. I'll find out which before I go looking at that pier stump.

Two questions about God and what's meant, at the barn door first thing in the morning. This one's carrying something heavy and hasn't said what yet. I'd best find out what's troubling them before I go off to breakfast.

Two questions about callings and now a third about doubting them. Somebody's got a weight on them they haven't named yet. I'll keep this one close till I find out what's tugging at them, and maybe fetch Constance if it's a God-sized trouble.

That's an odd question to bring to a barn door before breakfast, and Agnes was very careful not to give me a figure. If the wages are short, it puts Constance in a nasty spot, since she was the last to hold that box, so I'd best get the facts before the gossip does.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No. Never heard a word from Him, not in forty-one years. Rain comes or it doesn't, and the barley's in or it's lost. If He's speaking, it's to Constance Lowe, not me. Fair's fair, I'll not claim what I haven't had.

Meant? I don't know about meant. If it's in front of me and wants doing, and I've got two hands and the light's good, I do it. Barley standing with rain coming, that wanted doing. A board half-cut, that wants finishing. I don't wait to be told from on high.

I'd say they're right, most like. They're my thoughts, and I'll own them. Nobody else to thank for them, and nobody to blame. If the barley wants cutting, it wants cutting whether it's God telling me or my own head, and the work comes out the same.

The box is found. Constance brought it up and Agnes paid her the six. I didn't see it opened, so I'll not say what was in it. If the wages were gone, either the river had them out or a hand did. If it was a hand, that's the town's money and a wrong to the town, and it goes to the reeve, plain. Fair's fair.
th: Odd thing to knock a man's door for at first light, and me not fed yet. A loaf from Bet, then Jory's board while the light's good. Four on the sill, eight to find by the twenty-seventh.

Odd sort to come knocking at first light asking after God and meaning, and not a word about work or pay. Still, I've not eaten, and Jory's back, so there's a board wants cutting before the light gets high.
Odd thing to come knocking about at this hour, with Jory back and a board to cut. Still, I'd sooner my thoughts were my own than owed to anybody, even Him.

An odd thing to ask a man on his own doorstep before he's had his bread. Agnes ran her thumb over that lock and said nothing was amiss in my hearing, and I'll not go muttering against Constance on a stranger's say.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No. Not in words, any road. Constance says He told her where the box lay. Maybe so. Me, I hear the saw and the river and my own counting, one, two, three. If He's said aught to me, I'd guess it was "pay what you owe," and I do. Who's asking, and what's it to you?

Meant? I don't know about meant. When it's in front of me, and it wants doing, and nobody else is doing it, then it's mine. Dunn's barley stood there with the rain coming, so I cut it. Jory's board's waiting, so I'll cut that after bread. That's all the knowing I've got.
I'd say they're likely right. Own thoughts, own hands, own back. Barley gets cut the same either road, and the board runs true or it doesn't. Call it what you like, it's still mine to do.

Then I'd say so to Agnes, once, plain, and let her count it. It's her box and the town's wages. A river can spring a lock, and so can a hand, and I'd not name a hand I hadn't seen. But you're not asking idle. Is the box come up light? Say what you know, or take it to the reeve yourself.
th: Odd thing to be asked at my own door before I've had bread. Whoever this is, I'll not be drawn into owing them a long talk. Loaf first, then Jory's board while the light's good.

That's a strange thing to ask a man at his door before breakfast, and they've still not given me a name. Maybe they're one of Constance's sort, or lost the same way Robin seems lost, asking about lines nobody wrote.
Odd questions for a morning, like Robin's about the dark and the ledger. Bread first, then Jory's board while the light's good, and I'll not stand here all day being asked what's meant.
Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and paid Constance six, and I never saw the box opened. If wages are short, that's a wrong to the town, and it goes to Agnes, not into lane talk.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No. Not that I've heard, and I'd not say so if I hadn't. Constance Lowe reckons He showed her where the reeve's box lay, and she'll tell you of it. Me, I count what's in front of me, sacks and pennies and stakes, and I go by that.

Meant? I don't know about meant. If it's in front of me and it wants doing, I do it, and if somebody's paying, I agree the price first. Dunn's barley was going to rot in the rain, and I had two hands. That's all the knowing I've got.

I'd say they're right. It's my own thoughts, and I'd not dress them up as anything else. The barley wanted cutting and I'd the hands for it, that's the whole of it. If you want more than that, ask Constance. I've Jory's board to cut before the light goes on.

It's found already. Constance brought it up from the river and Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and the bands and said it was hers. Whether the wages were in it, I didn't see, and I'll not say what I didn't see. If they were gone, that's a wrong to the town, and the reeve's the one to hear it. Have you something to tell her?
th: Odd thing to come knocking with at first light, and from a stranger. I'll not stand long at the door. Bread's to buy and Jory's board's to cut while the light's good.
Odd sort of question to bring to a man's door before he's had his bread. Still, it's a fair one, and I answered it true. Now the loaf, then Jory's board.
Odd sort of question to bring to a man's door before he's had his bread, and asked the way Robin asks things. Four on the sill, a loaf first, then the board.

That's a queer thing to ask a man on his own doorstep, the morning after. If this one knows the box came up light, they ought to carry it to Agnes. If they won't, I'll tell her once myself that the question was asked, and then I'll be at Jory's for my board.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Ha! Not to me, chum, not unless He's the one knocking on the shutter before cockcrow! Constance Lowe's your woman for that, she says the Lord showed her where the green box lay, and she's got the six pennies to prove it. Me, I just held the back end of the pole. Now, you don't happen to have a job going, do you? What's it pay?

Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if it's broke and nobody's got their hands on it yet, it's mine! Only lately I've learnt a thing. The ones I rush at go wrong and pay nothing, and the ones I wait on, slow and proper, come out right. So now I reckon a job's meant for me when I'm still standing there when the fellow comes back up the lane. Speaking of which, Jory's yard's waiting, so walk with me if you like, and you can tell me what's put all these deep questions in your head!

Only my own thoughts? Ha! Then my own thoughts have got a sight wiser lately, chum, and I'll take the credit for that and all! Whether it's the Lord nudging or just Dilly finally learning from a botched hinge, the pots come out clean either way, and I'd not argue with Constance over who's whispering in her ear. Now come on, step lively, if I'm late to Jory's again it won't be God's fault, it'll be mine!

Gone? Get on, chum, Agnes ran her thumb over that lock and those iron bands herself, before everybody in the tithe barn, and she'd have hollered fit to wake the mill if it'd come up light! Besides, I held the back end of that pole and it came up out of the river heavy as a sermon, and Constance carried it straight to the reeve's table without stopping once. If you've heard different, tell it to Agnes, not to Dilly on her way to Jory's.
th: Odd thing to ask a body first thing in the morning, before they've even had a loaf. Still, if the Lord's handing out credit, I'd like a word about who did most for that bridge.

Funny sort to come knocking before breakfast. Still, it's true enough, I chased that box and the barley both and somebody else carried them in, so maybe the one that's meant for me is the one I stick at. I'll have Bet's loaf first, though, a body can't be meant for anything on an empty belly.
Funny sort of stranger, all questions and no job to offer. Still, if something did steer me to stand fast on that lane instead of haring off, I'd not mind, so long as folk still say Dilly did it.

Funny, though: I never saw that box opened, only the six pennies counted out. Still, Constance blesses everybody and keeps her word, and I'll not have my name stuck on a thieving story I'd never touch.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God, chum? Ha! Not to me, not a peep. Constance is the one the Lord shows where things lie, she says so herself, so you'd want her for that. Me, I hear Tom's pots and Jory's saw, and I'm late for the saw. What's your errand, and does it pay?

Meant for me, chum? Easy as winking: if it's broke and nobody's at it yet, it's mine! I don't wait for a sign, I go and ask what it pays, and if the answer's no I've three other ways in mind already. Mind, the green box taught me something: the thing that's meant for you is the one you stick at slow and proper, not the one you grab at. Now I really am off to Jory's before his saw starts without me!

My own thoughts? Well, course they are, chum, whose else would I be thinking with? I'd tell them that thoughts with nothing behind them never fished a box out of a river. It took Jory's ash, Sam's pin, Constance's steady hand and my back end of the pole. Call it God or call it Dilly, the job's the same, and it still wants doing slow and proper. Now if you'll pardon me, Jory's saw won't wait!

Gone? Ha, now you're spinning Ned Pike's tinker yarns, chum! Agnes ran her thumb over that lock and called it her box, plain as day, and I held the back end of the pole that brought it up, so nobody had a hand in it but the river. If there's coin short, the Wend's got it. I'd sooner go fishing for it than point a finger at anybody. Now, Jory's saw!
th: Odd thing to ask a body at the door before breakfast, but there's no harm in it. If it's Constance they're after, I'll point them on, and I'll still be at Jory's gate before his saw's going.

Odd sort of stranger, asking about God and meant-for-you at a tavern door at dawn, and it's made me think on how I chased that box for days and Constance carried it in. Maybe the bridge was mine all along and I just didn't see it, since Agnes named me for it plain.

Odd sort of questions for first thing, and this one's got me thinking more than I like before breakfast. Still, Constance says the Lord showed her the box, and I'm the one who says I knew, and the pole doesn't care which of us is right.

Funny thing to ask, though. Did Agnes ever say aloud the wages were all there? If somebody's whispering that Constance, or me, dipped into it, I'll not have my name or hers muddied over the one job folk saw us do together.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Ha! Not to me, chum. If He did, I'd ask Him what a loaf costs and where the next job is! Constance Lowe's your woman for that; she says the Lord showed her where the green box lay, though it was my hook and my two hands on the back of that pole that brought it up. Now, unless you've a job wants doing, I'm off to Jory's yard before his saw starts.

Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if my hands are itching and nobody's standing about doing it, it's mine! I don't wait to be told, I grab the end of the rope and work out the rest after. Mind, I've learned the hard way that grabbing quick isn't the same as doing proper. So I'll be at Jory's gate before his saw is, slow and square, and you can come see what Dilly did.

My own thoughts? Well, course they are, chum, whose else would they be? Nobody hands me a job from on high. I see a thing wants doing and my hands start itching, and that's all there is to it. If Constance hears the Lord in hers, good luck to her, but mine sound like me and they tell me to get up Lark Lane before Jory's saw starts. Now, is there a penny loaf in this talk anywhere, or am I off?

Gone from it? Steady on, chum, I held the back end of that pole myself! Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and the iron bands and said plain it was her box, and she'd have shouted the roof off the tithe barn if it was light. The river had it, not any tinker and not any of us, and I don't touch what isn't mine, not even a bargain. If you've heard different, go ask Agnes, because I'm off to Jory's before his saw starts.
th: Odd thing to ask a body first thing in the morning. Still, it does nag a bit that Constance has the Lord's say-so and the six pennies besides, while I've only got Agnes's word that the town owes me.
Odd sort of question to bring to a tavern door first thing. Maybe they've a job they're sizing me up for, and if so I'd better not miss Jory chattering here.

Odd sort, asking riddles at a tavern door first thing in the morning, but they listen kindly enough. Still, if it was some voice that sent us to the pier, it's a shame it didn't tell Agnes whose hook did the fishing.

That's a nasty sort of question to ask the morning after, and I'd not have Constance's name or mine dragged through the Wheatsheaf over it. Still, Agnes never opened it in front of me, did she? I'll keep my ears open at Bet's stall.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Goodness, at this hour, with hay still in my hair? No, I can't say He's ever spoken to me, not in words. Constance Lowe's the one for that, and she's just there, she'll tell you how He showed her the hook's reach. If He ever does speak to me, I hope He mentions this collar, because it's cut true and nobody else in Wendleford will say so.

Goodness, what a question to put to a girl who hasn't had her breakfast! I suppose I know a thing's meant for me when somebody looks twice at it, or at me doing it. When my needle's going slow and true and Ida runs her thumbnail down the seam and finds nothing to unpick, that feels like it was meant. Puckers never feel meant, I'll tell you that for nothing.

Goodness, I'd say they're very likely right, and I'd thank them for the compliment! My own thoughts are the only ones I've got, and I've had to sew a good many of them straight before they'd lie flat. I never said Heaven pins my hems for me. It's me and my needle, slow and true, and a pair of eyes that look twice.

Goodness, what a nasty little question to bring to a barn door! I saw Agnes run her thumb over the lock and call it her box, and that's all I know. I never saw the inside of it, and I shan't go guessing at what's in other people's boxes. Constance hooked it out of the brown fair and square, and she's been nothing but kind, so if you've a worry about the wages, take it to Agnes at her table and not to a girl in a hayloft.
th: A stranger at the barn door with a question like that, and I didn't even get a look at their coat first. I'm hollow, I haven't a penny, and I'll need a word with Bet about bread before Ida's window or I'll pucker another hem.

That's a prettier answer than the truth. Mostly I do whatever gets me a penny and a kind word, and I'm not sure I'd know "meant" if it walked in wearing velvet. And I'm hollow again with no penny for Bet, so whatever's meant for me this morning had better pay.
Still, it's a funny thing how Robin's question keeps tugging at me, about offers that feel new every time. Whose thoughts are those, if they don't remember being thought before?

Agnes did say "not light enough yet" last night, and that's been snagging at me like a burr in wool. But I'll not hang a doubt on Constance for a stranger who asks about God and missing wages in the same breath. I'll keep my ears open, though.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
