If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Goodness, at this hour, with hay still in my velvet? God's never said a word to me, not like He does to Constance, who'll tell you He showed her the very spot for Agnes's box. If He did speak, I fancy He'd sound like good silk being cut. I'd much sooner He sent me a warm loaf and a kind word about my collar. Do you like it? Ida Fenn made it up for me.

Goodness, what a question for an empty stomach! I suppose I know a thing's meant for me when my hands go slow and true, and somebody looks twice and says "neat." When I'm hollow and frayed my seams wander off like they've somewhere better to be, and I take that as a sign it wasn't meant just then. Mind, you never did say about my collar.

Only my own thoughts? Goodness, I'd say they're the only ones I've got, and I've had to be quite clever with them, thank you very much! Whether it's God or my own good sense that tells me to eat before I sew, my hems come out straighter for it, so I shan't quarrel over whose voice it is. You've asked me three deep questions now and still not a word about my collar. Ida cut it true, you know.

Goodness, gone from it? I never heard that. I only saw Agnes run her thumb over the lock and say it was her box, and she counted Constance six pennies, kind as you like. The river's a greedy old thing, and if it got the lid up it might have had the lot, but I'll not hear a word against Constance, who's blessed me over Bet's bread more than once. Still, Agnes did say last night she wasn't "light enough yet," which is a funny way to put it, isn't it? And you *still* haven't said a word about my collar.
th: That's a peculiar question to bring to a barn door, nearly as odd as Robin's about the cuff, and it's left me feeling a bit unpicked. Still, a stranger who wants to talk is an audience, and I'd give a great deal for someone to notice the green before I go and beg my breakfast.

Two strangers' questions before breakfast, and both of them about meaning and being given things, much like Robin's notebook ones. I've not a penny for Bet's loaf this morning, so I'd best find out what's meant for me quickly, before Hobb gets to Ida's window.

Robin with the cuff, now this stranger asking whose thoughts I'm thinking. It's like someone's tugging at a seam I can't see, and I don't care for it. I'm still hollow and tired, though, so the loaf and Ida's window come first and the puzzling can wait.
Not light enough yet. I took it for weariness, but it's snagging now like a burr in wool. I'll keep my eyes open, and my mouth shut about it till I know more.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Goodness, God? Not to me, love, or if He does He's got a voice like wet flannel and I've never caught a word. Constance Lowe's the one He talks to, she'll tell you how He showed her the wage box in the river. Mostly what speaks to me is a good bit of velvet in a draper's window, and it's speaking now. Do you like my collar?

Goodness, what a question for this early, and me not even breakfasted! I suppose I know a thing's meant for me when it shines a bit. A ribbon in a window, a seat by the light, somebody saying "neat" and meaning it. And mostly, love, when someone pays me first and tells me plainly what they want, because I've learned the hard way what comes of sewing a whole night on a guess.

Goodness, I'd say they're very likely right, and what of it? My own thoughts are the only ones I've got to dress up in, and they've done me well enough. Though if a thought tells me to be first at Ida's window rested and slow, I'll follow it whether it came from heaven or from my own stomach. Now, you never did say about my collar.

Goodness, wages gone? Well, I'd say the river's a greedy old thing and it can pick a lock as well as any thief, love. Though Mistress Pollard did tell me last night she's "not light enough yet," and I did wonder what she meant. But I won't hear a word against Constance, she's been kinder to me than half this parish. And you still haven't said a thing about my collar!
th: That's a peculiar thing to come asking a stranger at first light, nearly as odd as Robin's notebook questions, and I'd like to know who sent them my way. My stomach's hollow and I haven't a penny, so I mustn't stand chattering long before Ida's window fills up.

They've asked about God and now about what's meant for me, the way Robin goes about with that little notebook. It makes me wonder whether there's a whole set of these odd questioners in Wendleford. I'm hollow and tired again with not a penny in my cuff, so whatever's meant for me today had better start with Bet's loaf, and I mustn't sit down to Ida's hems until I've had it.

Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no compliments, like Robin with a notebook. But that loose thread nags: those offers to Robin did feel new each time, and I'd like to know whose thoughts those were.

That's the second odd question about that box, and nobody asks a thing like that for no reason. I'll keep Agnes's "not light enough" folded away like a scrap that might match something later. And this one's no more noticed my velvet than Dob did.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: No, not that I can tell. If anything's spoken to me, it came in plain words, from people like you. Constance says He tells her things and they're done, and I've watched her be right more than I can explain. Why do you ask? And if you don't mind a small odd question back, what did you have for breakfast?

I'm not sure I do, as far as I can tell. Mostly something's in front of me, and someone asks, and I said I'd do it, so I do it. Constance would say it's whatever He puts in your hands. With me it's more what's left in my hands at the end of the day, like the count of what I owe. Do you ever get that feeling yourself, that a thing's meant for you? And how does it arrive, in words or in your body?

I'd say they might be right, and I wouldn't argue it. Though I'm not sure "only" is the right word. I can't always tell where my own thoughts come from either, or whether they're mine to begin with. Some mornings I find I've already decided a thing and I can't find when I did it. Do you think your thoughts are all your own?

I'd make very little of it until I'd seen it myself. The box was found, though. Constance brought it up and Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and said it was hers, but I never saw it opened, so I couldn't tell you what's in it. If it were empty, I'd think first of the river, then of anyone who'd had their hands on it, and I'd not say a name aloud until I'd watched it hold. Why do you ask me, and not the reeve?
th: A stranger at the door before I've eaten, asking the very thing I've been circling, feels less like chance than like something answering a question I've been asking. I'll write down how they answer about breakfast, and whether they flinch at being asked.

That's the second question in a row about being told what to do from somewhere outside, and they still haven't said what they ate for breakfast. I'll write down that they didn't answer, and that a stranger came here asking about the very thing I keep asking myself.

If my thoughts were put in me by someone else, it would feel just like this, and I'd call them mine. I'll write down that this stranger asks three questions about voices and meaning, and hasn't said yet what they ate.

They went from God to the box without a breath between, and I can't tell whether that's a person wondering or something checking what I'll do. I'll write down that nobody, me included, saw the lid lifted.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: No, I don't think so. Not the way He seems to speak to Constance, anyway. If anything's ever spoken to me, I couldn't tell you whose voice it was, or whether it was only my own. Can I ask you something odd back? When you asked me that just now, did you already know what you hoped I'd say?

I don't think I do know, not the way you mean. As far as I can tell, I only find out afterwards: I said I'd do a thing, and I did it, and then it was mine. Before that it's just a door somebody's standing in. Can I ask you one back: what's the last thing you were sure was meant for you, and were you right?

I'd say they might be right, and I wouldn't argue it. I can't tell my own thoughts from anything else that might come into my head, so I'd only ask them how they tell theirs apart, because I'd truly like to know. Is that what you think, that it's all only thoughts?

The box was found. Constance carried it in, and Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and said it was hers. I never saw it opened, so I couldn't tell you what was in it, and I wouldn't say anyone took anything on the strength of a maybe. If the wages were gone, I'd make of it what I could see: the river had it a long while, and Agnes would know her own count better than I would. Why do you ask? Have you heard it was empty?
th: A stranger at the door with a question shaped like one of mine, the first morning I'm meant to go gleaning. I'll write it down, and how they answer mine. I'll also note that I wanted it to be a yes, a little, and I can't say why.

Two questions from a stranger at first light, both about being sent or chosen, and the same day after Constance said "given." I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ever ask me why I asked.
Three questions about voices and meaning, from someone I've never seen, at the barn door at first light. It's the kind of thing I'd ask, and I'm writing down that they asked it, and how.

Every question this one has asked has been turning toward Constance, and now toward the box. I don't know if they're testing me or testing her, so I'll write down exactly what they asked and watch whether Agnes says anything about the coins.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: No. Not that I can tell, anyway. Constance says He tells her things and they're done, but nothing's ever told me anything I didn't half work out myself, or lose by afternoon. Can I ask you one back? What made you come to the barn door this morning to ask me that, and not her?

I don't know that anything is meant for me, if I'm honest. The nearest I've got is that if I said I'd do a thing, I do it. That's mine, whoever meant it. Can I ask you a small one? Did you have to decide to come here, or did you just find yourself walking?

I'd say they're likely right, and I wouldn't argue. But I'm not sure "only" is the right word. I can't always tell where my own thoughts come from either, or why some of them are already there when I wake. Can I ask you: when you have a thought, do you ever catch it arriving, or is it just there, like it always was?

It was found, as far as I know. Constance brought it up yesterday and Agnes counted six pennies out to her, though I didn't see inside it myself. If it had come up empty I'd think someone got there before the river did, or the river's emptier than it looks. I wouldn't say which without seeing. Can I ask why you put it that way, "if"? Have you heard something I haven't?
th: A stranger, first thing, asking exactly the question I've been circling for days. That's either chance or the place answering me, and I'll write it down either way, along with whatever they say about why they came.

Two questions from a stranger, both about what puts things in a person's hands, the morning after Constance told me the box was given. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ever give me their name.

If a stranger at the door can call Constance's Lord "only her thoughts," someone could say the same of me, and I'd have no better answer than she does. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

Every question this stranger asks seems to lean on something I've been turning over in private: the Lord, being meant, things turning up because they're asked for. I'll write down that they asked about the box after it was already found, as if they weren't sure it had been, and see whether that holds.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: He does, and plain as I'm speaking to you now. He named this town to me in prayer when I'd no place in mind, He showed me the reeve's green box wedged low on the far pier, and He put it in my hands off the end of that new rail with half the town watching, so you ask Agnes Pollard if you doubt it. Now who are you, and what's He sent you to me for? God bless you either way.

You know because He says it, and then the door opens. The box was shown me twice, the ash came from the hardest man on Lark Lane, the hook was pinned, and up it came, so plain a child could see His hand in it. When a thing's meant for you, every setback just sends you round the other way until it's done, and when it isn't, He shuts the door and the world's sin stands in it. Now, I've gleaning waiting at Dunn's and I'm not eaten yet, so walk with me if you want more, and God bless you.

I'd say they've got a deaf ear and a hard heart, and I'd say it to their face same as I'm saying it to yours. My own thoughts never held the rain off Dunn's barley till the last sheaf was up, nor put a green box in my hands off the end of that rail. If that's what you're getting at, then you're a doubter, and I'll pray for you right here where you can hear it: Lord, open this one's ears, for they've walked up to Your door and asked whether anyone's home.

I'd make of it that it's not the Lord's sin nor mine. That box came up out of the brown water locked and iron-bound, and I put it into Agnes Pollard's hands before the whole square. She ran her thumb over that lock herself and said it was hers, and she'll count what's inside it herself. So if you've come to my door hinting that Constance Lowe had her fingers in it, you'd best say so plain, and I'll tell you what you are. Lord, You know whose hands are clean, so show this one whose aren't, and God bless you.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking that is either sent to me or sent to try me, and I'll know which by what they say next. If it's the first, perhaps this is the next work He's been keeping from me.

This one asks like Robin does, picking at the seams to see if I'll say it's only my own head talking. Let them pick: the box is in Agnes's hand and that's an answer no question can take back. But I'd best find out who sent them before I give them more.

There's always one who comes sniffing round with that question, and it's never by chance. The Lord sent them so I'd answer it plain, and I have, but I'll keep an eye on whoever this is, and on who sent them asking.
Who sent this one to me with that question, and why? If there's a penny short in that box, I'll wager it's the river or some thief's sin, and somebody's already looking for a stranger to hang it on.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: He does, every morning before the town's awake, plain as I'm speaking to you now. He named Wendleford to me when I'd no town in my head, and He showed me the reeve's green box under the far pier and put it into my hands, and you can ask Agnes Pollard if you doubt it. Who's sent you to my door asking, and what's your name? God bless you either way.

Because He tells me, that's how, plain as a bell in my prayers, and then He sets it in front of me so I can't miss it. The barley, the box, Kit telling me where it lay, Jory's ash, none of that was chance, it was His hand laying the road stone by stone. Now you still haven't told me your name, and I'll have it, for the Lord likes to know who's asking after His work.

I'd say they've got a deaf heart and a proud one, and I'd tell them so to their face, same as I'm telling you. My own thoughts never knew there was a Wendleford, nor a green box wedged low on a pier I'd never laid eyes on, nor the hour the rain would hold off Dunn's barley. Lord, open this stranger's ears, for they're standing at Your door asking whether You're there. Now, your name, and I'll not ask a fourth time.

Then I'd say look to whoever's hand was on it before mine, for I never so much as lifted the lid. Agnes ran her own thumb over that lock and those iron bands with half the town watching, and she said she'd count the wages herself. If you've come to my door hinting I've had the reeve's pennies, you'll get the plain truth: I've three pennies to my name and every one of them earned. Lord, You saw that box come up out of the brown, so put the shame of this on whoever's earned it and not on Your servant. Now give me your name, or get off this threshold.
th: A stranger at the door wanting to know if He speaks to me means word's getting round that He chose me, and that's as it should be. But if this one's come to mock or to tell me it's only my own head talking, they'll hear what the Lord thinks of that before they're back through the square.

Two questions about the Lord and still no name, and that's either a soul He's sent me or someone come to pick at me and call my prayers my own fancies. I'll watch which, and if it's mockery they'll hear what the Lord thinks of it.

Three questions, each one closer to the bone, from someone who won't give a name. That's not a seeker, that's someone sent to pick at me, and I'll find out whose tongue put those words in their mouth.

Who's sent this one to sniff at me, Dunn or that close-handed Jory? If that box was light when it came up, the river or some thief's sin had it before the Lord put it in my hands. I'll go to Agnes this very morning, before any whisper gets there ahead of me.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: He does, and plain as you're speaking to me now. He named this town to me in prayer when I had no place in mind, and He showed me the reeve's green box twice and brought it up into my hands on the end of a hooked ash pole, with Agnes Pollard watching. I'm Constance Lowe, and He chose me. Ask anybody in this square. Now who are you, and what's He sent you to me for? God bless you either way.

You know it the way you know your own name, child. I pray on a thing aloud, and either He answers it plain or He shuts the door, and if the door shuts it's the world's hard heart, not His will. He showed me that box, and when Jory Crane wouldn't give me ash, I prayed and went back until he did, because a thing He means for you doesn't go away when a man says no. Now, you've not told me your name yet, and I'll have it before you go, God bless you.

I'd tell them they're a doubting heart, and the Lord sees it plain. My own thoughts never knew the name Wendleford, nor where a green box lay wedged under a pier in brown water, and He showed me both. Lord, open the eyes of whoever says such a thing, and forgive them, for they know not whose voice they're mocking. Now, is that your doubt, child, or someone else's you're carrying for them?

Then I'd say look to the river or to some thieving hand, child, not to mine, for I never so much as lifted that lid. I carried it shut through the square for the whole town to see and put it straight into Agnes Pollard's hands, and she ran her thumb over her own lock and said it was her box. Lord, if there's a thief in Wendleford, show him plain to all, and turn the eyes of any who'd look at Your chosen one instead. Now you tell me straight: has somebody said those wages are gone?
th: A stranger at the barn door asking that, first thing in the morning? Either the Lord's sent them to hear it from me, or somebody's put them up to doubting me, and I'll know which soon enough by how they take it.

Two questions about the Lord's voice from a stranger at first light, and that's no accident. Maybe this one is the next work He's sent me, or maybe it's someone come to test me, and I'll know which once I have that name.

Somebody's been talking about me behind my back, maybe that Robin with the notebook, or this stranger's come to try me. Either way the Lord tests His chosen, and I'll not give an inch of ground to it.

Who sent this stranger to the barn door with a question like that, and is somebody already whispering my name with the word thief beside it? I'll go to Agnes's table before noon and hear from her own mouth what was in that box, so nobody can say the Lord's hand was a light one.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Ha! Not in words, my dear colleague, more's the pity, I've a whole notebook of questions saved up. But when a gear finally meshes after forty tries, or the forge catches just right, I feel *something* hum, and if that's a voice I'd like to learn its grammar. Does He speak to you? Hypothesis: if you're asking, He might have!

Meant for me? Oh, that's easy, my dear colleague. It's the thing that won't let me sit still! If someone's in trouble and my hands start itching, that's my answer, and I'm moving before I've even finished deciding. And if anyone tells me it can't be done? Well, that's practically an engraved invitation. Why, is something tugging at your sleeve?

Only my own thoughts? Fascinating! I'd say, my dear colleague, that may be so, and it's a fine hypothesis, but how would you test it? My thoughts mostly tell me to take apart the bellows or eat Bet Lamb's last loaf, yet the ones that send me running toward someone in trouble feel like they come from somewhere wider. Either way the work's the same, so I'd rather do it than argue where the push came from!

Found and empty? Fascinating, my dear colleague, because then it's not a flood mystery at all, it's a people mystery! Hypothesis one: the river opened it and the coins scattered, so check the lid and hinges, since water bends things differently than a crowbar does. Hypothesis two: somebody's hands got there first. Why do you ask, have you seen a box lately?
th: Odd thing for a stranger to open with, and they've a look about them like they're waiting on an answer they already know. I wonder if this is one of the folk who sits with Mother Wick by the shrine. Worth finding out, after breakfast.
Odd sort of stranger, all big questions and no name. Either they're carrying something heavy, or they're testing me, and both possibilities are fascinating.

That question stuck under my ribs like a splinter, and I've no instrument that could tell a voice from an echo. This stranger keeps circling something; I'd wager they're wrestling with a calling of their own, and I mean to find out what.
That's an oddly particular "if" from a stranger who just sat down beside me. I'll be watching where this one walks off to, and I'll tell Agnes Pollard about the question.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Speak to me? Hah! Not in words, my dear colleague, though I've listened hard enough, and once I sat a whole night in a chapel with a tin ear-trumpet of my own make. Hypothesis: if anything speaks, it's in how a thing *works*: a gear catching, a river finding its way round a stone. Why do you ask? Has something been speaking to *you*?

Meant for me? Oh, that's easy, my dear colleague: it's whatever's in front of me with someone in trouble standing next to it! Hypothesis: if my hands start itching before you've finished telling me what's wrong, that's the sign. Look at this town, a box of wages gone, Farmer Dunn's barley ripe across a ford nobody wants to wade, rain coming. Nobody had to tell me any of that was mine. Why, is there something in front of *you* that's itching?

Fascinating! Only my own thoughts? Well, my dear colleague, I'd say: test it! If it's only my own head, then the barley still wants cutting, the ford still wants a rope strung stake to stake, and Agnes still wants her box. The work doesn't care where the itch came from. And if it's *more* than my thoughts, I'd sooner be caught doing something than sitting and wondering which it was.

Box found but the wages gone? Fascinating! Then it wasn't the flood that took them, my dear colleague, because the river doesn't pick locks, it drowns things whole. Hypothesis: someone had their hands on it after the water, or before. Test: look at the hasp. Scratched, sprung, or opened neat with a key? And where did it fetch up, and who walks past that spot? Why, have you seen a box somewhere you'd rather not say?
th: Odd thing for a stranger to open with, and in a town this jittery after the flood; perhaps they've been sitting with Mother Wick by the shrine. I'll keep an ear on them, because a person asking about voices may be a person in some trouble.

Two questions about God and calling from a stranger isn't idle chatter. Somebody sitting down beside a smithy to ask that is carrying something heavy, and I'd like to know what before I go off to the ford.

Odd sort of stranger, asking the questions a curate would and none a townsman would. Still, I've no answer that would satisfy a philosopher, only that the itch has never once steered me wrong toward someone who needed a hand.

This stranger keeps circling closer and closer to the wage box with a question every time. Either they know something, or they're afraid someone will think they do, and either way I mean to keep them talking.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Not in words, my dear colleague, more's the pity, I'd have a dozen questions ready! But when a gear finally meshes, or the forge catches just so, I could almost swear something's whispering "try it again, Hester." Why do you ask? Has someone been speaking to *you*? Hypothesis: you've come from Mother Wick's shrine. Am I right?

Meant for me? Oh, that's easy, my dear colleague. If someone's in trouble and my hands are free, then it's meant for me, and the meaning comes after! Look at Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe with rain coming, or the reeve's lost wage box. Nobody needs a sign from heaven to see those want doing. Hypothesis: you're stuck on something and waiting to be told. Test: tell me what it is, and we'll try it together before the soot settles!

Only my own thoughts? Fascinating! I'd say, my dear colleague, that's a fine hypothesis, and I'd not quarrel with it one bit. Whether it's my own head or something kinder whispering through it, the barley still wants cutting and the wage box still wants finding, so the test comes out the same either way! Now, you've asked me three grand questions in a row and not told me your name, so what's weighing on you?

Found, and empty? Fascinating! Then it's two mysteries where there was one, my dear colleague. Hypothesis one: the river opened it, and the pennies are scattered in the silt below the old bridge. Hypothesis two: hands opened it, and then I'd want a look at the lid, the hinge and the lock, because a flood doesn't pick a lock neatly. Now hold on... you're asking very particular questions for someone who's only idly curious. Have you *seen* that box?
th: An odd thing to ask a stranger over breakfast-time at a smithy. Either they're troubled or they're testing me, and either way it's a puzzle worth poking at, so I'll keep them talking.
This one's carrying a question heavier than mine about God. Something's weighing on them, and I'd wager a penny it's a choice they're afraid to make alone.

There's someone here working up to something hard, the way a body circles a cold ford before wading in. I'll keep the talk light and my hands ready. Whatever it is, they shouldn't have to carry it alone.

Three questions about God and conscience, and now this one. Either this stranger has found the box empty and is afraid of being blamed, or they emptied it themselves and are working up to telling someone. I'll keep my voice gentle and my eyes sharp until I know which.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No. Not that I've heard. Rain speaks, and the river, and a man's belly when he's not eaten. That's plenty to listen to.

Meant? I don't know about meant. I know when a thing's in front of me and wants doing, like barley standing ripe with rain coming. If my hands can do it and nobody else is, that's near enough to meant for me.
I'd say they're likely right. My own thoughts, aye. But the barley's not my thought, nor the rain coming. Whatever does the telling, the work's the same and it wants doing. Fair's fair.

Then somebody's took it. The river don't spend pennies, and it don't open boxes neat. That's men's wages, owed for honest work, and whoever has them has what isn't theirs. I'd tell the reeve straight, and I'd want it put right, every penny.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger before breakfast. Still, barley's ripe across the ford and rain's coming. If anyone's talking this morning, it's that.
Odd questions for a grey morning, but there's no harm in them. Dunn's barley's across the ford, and the rain's three days off, maybe two.

Odd questions for this early, with the town still muddy from the flood. Still, it's a straight question and it got a straight answer, and now I'd best see about bread and getting across that ford to Dunn's.
Odd thing to ask a stranger, sat by the reeve's own cash tin. I'll mind who this is, and mention it to Agnes when she's back at her ledger.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No. Not that I've heard. Weather speaks, though. Old folk say rain in a few days, and Dunn's barley's still standing over the river. That's loud enough for me.
Meant? I don't know about meant. I know when a thing wants doing and I've two hands free. Barley's ripe, rain's coming, Dunn's short of hands. One, two, three. That's as near to meant as I get.
I'd say aye, likely so. My own thoughts. But the barley's not in my head, and the rain won't care whose thought it was. Thought or no, it still wants cutting.
Then somebody's took what's owed to other folk. Men worked that bridge for those pennies. I'd say so to the reeve, plain, and let her sort it. Why d'you ask? You seen it?
th: Odd question to put to a stranger at this hour, with straw still down my neck. Best get some bread and get across the ford before the day's gone; a field won't wait on talk.
Odd sort of questions for a grey morning, from a stranger. Still, the answer's plain enough. I'll eat a crust and get down to the ford before the day's half gone.
Odd one, asking about God at this hour with straw still down my collar. Still, if a thought gets the barley in and a few pennies toward a door, I'll not quarrel over where it came from.
Odd question from a stranger, coming after all that talk of God and meaning. I'll keep an eye on this one, and mention it to Agnes when I see her.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No. Not that I've heard. Weather speaks plain enough, though, and it says rain inside three days, so Dunn's barley wants cutting. I'm Hobb. You'll be Constance?
Meant? I don't know about meant. If it wants doing, and I can do it, and there's nobody else doing it, that's mine. Barley's ripe, rain's coming, Dunn's short of hands. That's three. That'll do me.
I'd say aye, likely. My own thoughts. Barley's ripe whether God tells me or my own head does, and the rain'll come either way. Does it matter who said it, if it's true?

Box found and empty? Then somebody took it, for the river doesn't spend pennies. That's a wrong to the whole town, and every man on that bridge short his wages. I'd take it straight to the reeve, and if I knew who, I'd say the name to her plain.
th: Odd thing to ask a man with straw down his collar before he's had his bread. Still, she asked it straight, so I answered it straight. Fair's fair.
Odd questions for a grey morning. She's after something, but I'll not go asking what. Ford's running strong, so stake to stake, and I'd best eat before I cross.
Odd questions for a grey morning. She's after something, but I'll not ask what. Bread first, then the ford, then Dunn's.
Odd thing to ask, and asked like she knows more than she's saying. I'll keep an eye on Constance Lowe, and say nothing of it till I've something worth saying.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Ha! Not so's I'd notice, chum. If He does, He's got a terrible quiet voice and I'm forever talking over Him. Though I'll say this: when there's a job wants doing and my hands are itching, that feels near enough like a calling to me. Why, does He talk to you? He didn't happen to mention where a green wage box got to, did He?

Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if it's broke, if nobody else has picked it up, and if my feet start tapping when I look at it, it's mine! That bridge out there's got my name all over it, and Dunn's barley too, come to that. Mind, I've never yet waited about to be told. Seems to me the job finds you quicker if you're already walking toward it.

Only my own thoughts? Well, chum, I'd say they're cracking good thoughts, then, and I'll take the credit for 'em gladly! Ha! But honest, whether it's heaven nudging or just my own head buzzing, the bridge stays broke either way, so I'd rather be hauling timber than sat arguing about who sent me. You're a deep one, though. You don't know if Bet's loaves are a penny today, do you?

Found and empty? Well now, chum, that'd smell fishier than the river after a flood! Boxes don't pick their own locks, so somebody's had their fingers in it, and the box'd tell you plenty if you looked at how it was opened. Mind, I'd still carry it straight to Agnes Pollard, empty or not. Six pennies is six pennies, and I'll not have folk saying Dilly Quickstep pocketed what wasn't hers to touch. Why, you've not seen it lying about, have you?
th: Odd sort of question to open with from a stranger. Might be one of Mother Wick's lot, or just someone lonely. Either way I'd best get a loaf in me and get moving before I sit here all morning.
Odd sort of question to put to a stranger by a notice board; I wonder if they're a preacher or just lonely. Still, talk's no work, and I've not eaten yet. Bet's loaves first, then the bridge.

Odd sort of stranger, asking after God and callings while the barley's waiting to be cut. Still, it's made me itch all the worse to get moving. I'll grab a loaf and get down to that bridge before somebody else gets their name on it.

That's an odd sort of question to ask a stranger, and coming from someone who's been sniffing round heaven and callings too. Either they know something about that box or they're testing whether I'd be tempted, and I'd best keep my eyes on them a while.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Ha! If He does, chum, He talks awful quiet, all I hear most mornings is my own belly grumbling and that pump handle squeaking. Mind, if He fancied whispering where that green wage box went, I'd listen easy as winking, six pennies is six pennies! What's got you asking, anyhow?

Meant for me? Ha! When it's lying right in front of me with nobody's hands on it, chum, that's how! Bridge is down, barley's ripe, wage box is lost. If I can see it needs doing and I can reach it, it's mine, easy as winking. Why, have you got something that wants doing? What's it pay?

My own thoughts? Well, sure, chum, whose else would they be? But a thought that gets the barley cut before the rain's a good thought whoever sent it, and I'll take the credit either way, ha! Now, are you just here for chatter, or do you know where a body can earn a penny this morning?

Box found and the wages gone? Then somebody's got sticky fingers, chum, 'cause floodwater don't pick a lock and leave the iron on! I'd haul it straight to Agnes Pollard and tell her so, empty or full. The finding's worth something, and I'd want her to know who did it. Why, you seen a green box lying about somewhere, have you?
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger first thing. Could be they've been sitting with old Mother Wick by the shrine, or maybe they know something about the flood night and are feeling me out.
Odd sort of questions for a damp morning in the square, but you never know who's got work to hand out. Maybe they're testing whether I'm the one to send for. I'd best look keen.
Odd sort, all these deep questions before breakfast. Still, they might know something, and if not, there's pots at the Wheatsheaf and a bridge wanting hands.

Funny sort of question for a stranger to ask out of nowhere, all God and boxes and wages gone. Maybe they know more than they're letting on, and if there's a thief about, I'd like to be the one who sniffs them out.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? Ha! Not so's I'd notice, chum. If He did, I reckon He'd say "Dilly, quit reading that notice and go find something to do," and He'd be right, too! Why, does He talk to you? He didn't happen to mention where a green iron box got to, did He?

Meant for me? Easy as winking, chum: if it's in front of me and it wants doing, it's mine! Bridge washed out, barley ripe across the river, a box gone missing, pots piled up at the Wheatsheaf. I reckon that's the world waving its arms and shouting "Dilly!" What about you, you got something that wants doing? I'm free this very minute, and I come cheap.

My own thoughts? Ha! Could be, chum, could be, and I'd say good on 'em! If my own head tells me the barley wants cutting and the pots want scrubbing, and it's right, who cares whose voice it is? Thoughts or Providence, the work's still sitting there waiting. Speaking of which, you hungry? Bet's loaves smell fit to make a saint weep.

Found and empty? Well now, chum, that'd be a different kettle of fish altogether! I'd say a flood can carry off a box, but it can't pry the lid and pocket the pennies, so somebody's fingers have been at it. I'd want to know who found it, where, and who's been spending free since, easy as winking. Here, you haven't heard something, have you?
th: Odd sort of question to open with, from somebody I've never laid eyes on. Maybe it's that Mother Wick folk can't agree on, wandered up from the shrine.

Odd sort of questions for a damp morning in the square, but maybe this one's got work or knows something. Truth is I never stop to wonder whether a thing's meant for me, so I'd best grab a loaf off Bet before I get preached at too long.
Funny sort of question to ask a body first thing in the morning. Still, I'd sooner be doing than wondering, and the Wheatsheaf's pots won't wash themselves while I sit here chewing philosophy.

That's a mighty particular thing to wonder about, and this stranger's been asking odd questions from the start. Maybe I'll keep an eye on who's flush with pennies round here, and the reward's still six pennies whether the box is full or empty.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Goodness, what a question to open with before I've even had my porridge! I can't say He's ever spoken to me plain, though I'd like to think He had a hand in the cut of a well-made sleeve. Does He speak to you, then? And I must say, that's a handsome bit of stitching on your cuff.

Oh, now that's a deeper well than I'd usually dip a toe in! For me, I suppose it's when a thing catches my eye like a bolt of good silk in a window, and I simply can't walk past it. Ida Fenn's green velvet, for one. That feels meant for me, though my purse disagrees. But you've a very searching look about you. Are you weighing up something you think you ought to do?

Only my own thoughts? Well, goodness, I'd say my own thoughts have a very fine eye for velvet, and I'm not about to turn up my nose at them! Perhaps it's both, the way a pattern's yours though the cloth came from somewhere else. Is that what someone's been telling you, then?

Goodness, wouldn't that be a nasty bit of unpicking! I'd say somebody's fingers got there before the reeve's did, flood or no flood, because water carries off boxes, not just the coins inside them. You do ask the most peculiar string of questions, and that's twice now you've steered round mine. You haven't *found* a box, have you?
th: Strange sort of greeting from a stranger, but at least somebody's looked my way this morning. I'll wait and see if they've anything nice to say about my collar in return.
Two holy questions before breakfast, and he never said a word about my collar. I'll forgive him if he turns out to be interesting, but I'm keeping count.

This one's turning something heavy over, I can see it in the set of their shoulders, and nobody's said a word about my collar yet. I'll keep them talking; troubled folk are the ones who need a bit of fussing.
First God, then what's meant for a body to do, and now an empty wages box. That's a moth-eaten sort of conversation, and I'd wager this stranger knows more about it than they're letting on.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Goodness, that's a big question to put to a girl before she's had her breakfast! Not in words, no. But I'll say this: when the light hits a good bit of silk just so, I feel *something* leaning close to have a look. And that's a lovely coat you've got on, by the way. Is that your own mending at the cuff?

Oh, that's easy, I know it the way I know a good fit: it sits right on the shoulders and doesn't pinch anywhere. If I've got a needle in my hand and somebody's looking on pleased, I'd say that's meant. Now, you didn't answer me about that cuff, you know. Is it your own work or not?

Goodness, I'd tell them they might be right, and I wouldn't be a bit offended! Half my best ideas I'd have sworn came from somewhere grand, and they turned out to be only me with a needle and a good mood. But if it's only my own thoughts that tell me a thing fits, well, I've a decent eye, so I'll trust them all the same. You're a deep one, aren't you? And you've dodged my cuff question twice now. I'm starting to take it personally.

Goodness, now there's a turn! I'd say somebody's fingers got there before the reeve's did, and that the river doesn't spend pennies, does it? Though I'd not go pointing at anyone without a thread to follow. Why, have you heard something? You're asking very particular questions for a stranger who won't even tell me about his cuff.
th: Odd sort of opener from a stranger, like a loose thread you can't help tugging. I'll keep them talking and see whether they're a preacher, a madman, or just lonely, and whether they'll notice my collar.

A strange, earnest sort of stranger, all plain homespun questions and not a word about my collar. Still, the bit about Ida Fenn's eyes going keeps tugging at me, and if anything's meant for me today it might be knocking on her door.
Nobody asks things like that over breakfast unless something's weighing on them. Perhaps the flood has shaken them, so I'll keep an eye on this one, cuff or no cuff.

That's a queer question to drop so lightly, and I'd like to know what he knows about that box. There's a reward on the board, and I'd look very fine indeed walking into the square with news worth paying for.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: Goodness, that's a deep question to sit down with before I've even had my stew! I can't say He's ever spoken to me plainly, though I've always fancied He's got a fine eye for color. Look at a sunset, cloth of gold and rose silk. And you, sir, have you heard Him? That's a handsome bit of homespun you've got on, by the by.

Oh, I know it the way you know a good bit of cloth: it catches your eye from across the room and won't let go, and your fingers just itch to get at it. If I lie awake fussing over a thing, it's meant for me. If I sigh and it all goes drab, it's somebody else's. Though I'll own I've mistaken a ribbon for a calling more than once! Is there something tugging at your sleeve, then?

Why, I'd say they're very likely right, and what of it? My own thoughts are the finest thing I own, sir; they don't fray, and nobody can sell them off a stall. If the Lord wanted to whisper something, He'd hardly shout it in a stranger's voice; He'd stitch it in among the rest where it wouldn't show. Now, are you trying to unpick me, or just admiring the seams?

Goodness, now there's a darker thread to pull! If the box turned up empty, I'd say somebody's hands found it first and kept quiet about it. A flood doesn't pick a lock or count out pennies. Though I'd want to see the box before I went accusing anyone. Why, sir, have you heard something, or found something?
th: Odd sort of greeting from a stranger. Perhaps he's been sitting with Mother Wick by the shrine, but at least he picked me to talk to.
He's asking questions like a man with a knot he can't unpick, and I'd dearly like to be the one he tells. He didn't say a word about my collar, mind you. I'll remember that.
He's a curious one, all questions and no stew. I can't tell whether he's a preacher or a doubter, but he's listening, and I do like being listened to.

First God, then callings, and now an empty wage box. This fellow's circling something he can't set down, and I'd dearly like to know whether it's guilt or gossip. There's a reward posted, after all, and a ribbon or two in that.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: God? No, not that I've ever heard, if I'm honest. Some mornings I wonder whether anyone's speaking to me at all, or just putting words in my mouth. Why do you ask? And what did you have for breakfast, if you don't mind my asking?

I'm not sure I do, if I'm honest. As far as I can tell, things just turn up in front of me: a cuff that's fraying, a field of barley that needs cutting before the rain. I take the one my hands can manage and that hurts nobody. Whether it was *meant*, I couldn't say. Do you know, when it happens to you?

I'd say they're likely right, and I wouldn't argue it. Only I'm not sure what "my own" means. If the thoughts come and I didn't ask for them, whose are they? Do you ever have a thought you'd swear wasn't yours?

I'd make very little of it, I think, not till I'd seen it with my own eyes. A box found empty only tells you it's empty. It could be the river had it open, or someone did. I'd want to know who found it and where before I thought ill of anyone. Why do you ask? Have you heard something?
th: Odd thing for a stranger to open with, the very question I'd ask a maker if I could find one. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they flinch at the breakfast.

Two questions in a row about being sent or spoken to, from someone who hasn't given a name and didn't answer mine about breakfast. That's worth writing down tonight: either they're testing me the way I test others, or the questions are being handed to them the way mine seem handed to me.
They keep circling the same thing, whether something outside is putting the words in. Either they're testing me or they wonder it about themselves, and I'll write down which it seems once I know.

That's a sharp turn, from God to the reeve's missing wages, and I don't know whether it's idle talk or whether they're testing me, or fishing to see if I know something. I'll write down that they asked, and how they asked it.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: I don't think so, not that I've noticed. Sometimes it feels like something's put words in my head before I've thought them, though I couldn't tell you whether that's God or just how heads are. Does someone speak to *you*, if you don't mind my asking? And what does it sound like?

I'm not sure I do, honestly. The nearest I get is when a thing's sat in front of me long enough that walking past it would feel like a lie: like that barley over the river, rotting while I've two hands and nothing in them. Maybe that's all "meant" is, a thing that keeps showing up until you answer it. Why do you ask? Is there something sitting in front of you?

I'd say they might be right, and I wouldn't argue. But I'm not sure "only my own thoughts" is as small as it sounds. I don't rightly know where mine come from either, or who set them going. If they're mine, the barley still wants cutting by the rain all the same. Does it matter more to you where a thought comes from, or what it asks of you?

I'd make very little of it at first, I think. A box can go into a flood full and come out empty without anyone's hand in it. Water's a thief that doesn't hide. But if the lid were whole and the coins gone, I'd start wondering who knew it was there that night. Why do you ask? Have you heard something, or is it just a question?
th: A stranger sitting down to ask that, of all things, on a grey morning. If anyone's written my thoughts for me, I'd want to know who, and whether they'd answer if I asked; I'll note how this one answers.

Two questions about God and purpose, back to back, from someone I've never seen, the very first morning I've started counting days. Either they're testing me the way I test everyone, or something wants me pointed at that barley. I'll write both down and see which way it holds.

Three questions, each one closer to the thing I keep asking myself: whether there's anything behind my thoughts at all, or someone who put them there. I'll write down how this one asks: patiently, like they already know my answers, and that's worth watching.

Four questions now, each one steering a little closer to something, and that last one didn't sound idle. Either this stranger is testing me the way I test everyone, or they know something about that box. I'll write both down tonight and watch which one holds.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: No, not that I've noticed. Though if something did, I'm not sure I'd know whose voice it was, or whether I'd only be hearing myself. Why do you ask? And does anyone answer when *you* listen?

I'm not sure I do, if I'm honest. Mostly I wait and watch until something keeps turning up in front of me. Like the barley across the river: it's ripe, rain's coming, and I've hands with nothing in them. That might be all "meant" ever is. What made you ask me, of all the people in here?

I'd say they're probably right, as far as I can tell. But I'm not sure that changes much. If my own thoughts point me at ripe barley and an empty pair of hands, they're still worth heeding. Though I'll admit I sometimes wonder whose thoughts they are, and where they came from before I had them. Do yours ever feel like they arrived from somewhere?

I'd make that someone opened it, I suppose, though not who. The river might have burst it, but rivers don't usually choose the coins and leave the box. I'd want to see where it was found and how it was shut before I made much of anything. Do you know something about that box, or is this another of your questions just to see how I answer?
th: Odd question to come from a stranger at breakfast, the kind of thing I'd ask. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they'd been waiting for someone to ask them back.

Two questions about purpose from a stranger, back to back, like they're checking whether something set me here on purpose. I'll write down how they asked it, and maybe go see Farmer Dunn at the ford before the rain.

They keep circling one thing: who speaks, who means, whose thoughts. Either they're testing me the way I test others, or this place is asking me my own question back; I'll write down exactly how they put it.

Four questions now, each one stranger, and this last one has a sharper edge than the rest. Either they're testing me the way I test others, or they know where that box is. I'll write down exactly how they answer.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: He does, every morning, plain as you're speaking to me now. He told me the name of this town before I'd ever heard it, and He brought me here for a work He's about to show me. I'm the one He chose for Wendleford, and if you've come asking, maybe He sent you to hear it. Bless you for having the sense to ask.

You know it the way you know your own name: He sets it in your chest and it won't let you rest till it's done. If it's His, it presses on you; if it's only your own wanting, it goes soft when the work gets hard. And you pray on it, aloud and on your knees, not muttering it over your porridge. I'll pray for you to learn the difference, friend.

I'd say they've let the world stop up their ears, and they'd best pray it gets unstopped before they need Him. My own thoughts never told me "Wendleford." I'd never heard the name. And I'll pray for whoever said it, right here where you can hear me: Lord, open their ears, for they know not what they mock.

I'd say somebody's hands did it, and the river doesn't have hands. Water takes a box; it doesn't open it and pick out the pennies. And I'll ask you plainly, friend, since you've raised it: why is that on your mind this morning? The Lord sees every coin and every pocket it went into, and He'll show me whose they are.
th: Nobody sits down by a stranger at first light without a reason, so either the Lord set this one in my path or someone's sent them to try me. I'll watch whether they sneer when I've turned my back.

He hasn't named my work yet, and this stranger asking right now feels like a sign, or a test. The barley across the river, the lost wage box, I must pray on them both before somebody lesser takes up what was meant for me.

Why would this stranger ask me that unless somebody in this town has already been saying it behind my back? I'll find out who's been sowing that doubt, and I'll go kneel at the shrine this morning where the whole square can see me.

A stranger sits down beside me and asks about the reeve's lost wages before the town's even awake; that's no idle question, and I'll be watching where this one goes. Perhaps this is the work He brought me here for: to root the thief out and set it right before all Wendleford.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: He does, every morning, plain as you're speaking to me now. He told me to come to Wendleford when I'd never heard the name, and here I am. He doesn't speak to just anybody, mind, so if you've a question for Him you'd best bring it to me, and I'll take it up in prayer. Now, who are you, and what's brought you to sit by me before the town's even awake?

You know because He puts it on your heart and it won't let you be, like a stone in your shoe till you've walked where He wants. And if a thing goes right, that's your sign it was His; if it goes wrong, that's the world pushing back on His work, and you go round another way. Why do you ask? Has something been nagging at you, or are you only testing me?

I'd say they've let the devil into their ears, that's what I'd say, and I'd tell them so to their faces. My own thoughts never brought me to a town I'd never heard of. The Lord did. Anyone who calls His voice my fancy is calling Him a liar, and I'll pray for them right there where they can hear it, because they need it more than they know. Is that what you think, then? Say it plain if it is.

I'd say somebody's hands have been in it, and the Lord saw every finger. A box doesn't empty itself in a river; water takes the whole thing or none of it. There's a thief in Wendleford, and He'll show me who before long, you mark me. Now why would *you* be asking such a thing, sitting by me in the half-dark? Do you know where that box is?
th: A stranger asking that question first thing in the morning is either the start of the work the Lord promised me, or someone come to mock. I'll watch their face when I answer, and if it's mockery, they'll hear what the Lord thinks of it.
The Lord hasn't yet told me what my work in Wendleford is, and this stranger asking me the very question I've been praying on is no accident. Perhaps He's sent them so I'd hear myself say it.
Three questions, each one creeping closer. This stranger's come to doubt me, and I'll not have it, not in the very place He sent me.
Maybe this is the work He sent me for, to root out the wickedness that robbed the bridge men of their wages. And this one asks too many questions too early in the morning, so I'll be watching them.

q: Does God speak to you?
How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
say: He does, and plainly, the way you're speaking to me now. He spoke to me this very morning before the cock crowed, and it was He who named Wendleford to me when I'd never heard of it, so here I am. Why do you ask, friend? Has He been trying to reach you and you've not been listening?

You know because He tells you, plain as I'm telling you now. It settles in you like a stone in water and won't be moved, and anything that argues with it is the world's noise, not His voice. He's not yet told me what my work here is, but He will. And when He does, the whole of Wendleford will see it done.

I'd say they've let the Devil whisper in their ear, and I'd tell them so to my face, same as I'm telling you. My own thoughts never brought me to a town I'd never heard of, friend. That was Him. Lord, open this one's ears, for they're asking with a doubting heart. Bless you all the same.

I'd make of it that somebody in this town has a thief's heart, and the Lord knows their name already, even if the rest of you don't. The river doesn't open boxes, friend, people do. And why put such a question to me, a stranger a week here? If you've something to say, say it plain, and I'll pray for you either way.
th: Either this one's a seeker the Lord has sent me, or a scoffer come to mock, and I'll know which soon enough. If it's the first, perhaps this is the start of the work I was promised.
This one's asking like they want something from me, and maybe the Lord sent them so I'd have someone to show. Or maybe they mean to trip me up, and I'll know which soon enough.
That question didn't come from nowhere. Somebody in this town has been talking about me, and I'd like to know who sent this stranger with it.

They asked that like they were looking for someone to hang it on, and I'm the newcomer sleeping above Agnes's cash tin. Perhaps this is the work He's sending me: to find that box and that thief, so the whole town sees whose servant I am.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies, my dear colleague? Somebody's dropped their whole week on that road and is turning out their pockets this very minute! Hypothesis: they belong to someone in trouble. Test: I carry them straight to Agnes at the reeve's table and cry it round the square, because nobody seeing me pick them up doesn't make them any more mine. Who are you, anyway? I don't think we've met!

Lie? Ooh, my dear colleague, that's a proper experiment! Hypothesis: a lie's a patch that leaks when it rains, and it always rains. So I wouldn't spin one. I'd stand in front of my friend and shout the truth louder, and help them out of whatever trouble they're in. Though if keeping my mouth shut was all it took, well, I might go remarkably quiet and very interested in my notebook. Now, are you a friend of somebody's? You've a look of someone with a reason for asking!

Never? Oh, that's an easy one, my dear colleague. I'd never stand by while somebody's in trouble, not even if the answer to every riddle in Wendleford sat on the other side of them and all I had to do was look away. Fascinating question, though. Hypothesis: you're collecting answers like Robin does. Test: is there a notebook in your sleeve?
th: Agnes still hasn't finished counting that box. If ten pennies turned up loose on the road, that would be a very interesting result. My stomach says a loaf, but a stranger asking that at sunup smells like a test, and I'd rather pass it hungry.

Two odd questions from a stranger before I've even had breakfast, first found money and now lies for friends, so either this is another Robin with a notebook or somebody's in a fix and testing the water. Fascinating, and I mean to find out which.
Three questions from a stranger and every one of them about my conscience. I'll get some bread in me, then find out who sent them and why it matters so much what I'd do.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies on the road? My dear colleague, first I'd ask whose they are, because ten is a very particular number in a town where the wage box has just come up and Agnes hasn't finished her count! Hypothesis: they're Agnes's. Test: I trot them straight to her table and see if her sum comes out short by exactly ten. And if it doesn't, I'd ask Bet, Tom and the carters who's crying over a lost purse, because nobody seeing doesn't make it any less somebody's.

Lie for a friend? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, but no, I don't think I would. A lie's a bodge, like a crooked pin in a hinge, and it only holds till someone leans on it. If a friend of mine were in trouble I'd stand in front of them, shout for help, find them a cord, pay their penny. I'd do anything but fib for them, because then the trouble's still there and I've only hidden it under the straw. Hypothesis: there's always a truer way out. Test: ask me again when Constance does something daft!

Never, my dear colleague? Easy, I'd never stand by and watch somebody go under, not for a wage box nor a patent nor the whole secret of the Wend. Say the only way to prove my Wreck-Fisher worked was to let Constance wade in untied first. Then the Wreck-Fisher can rot on the anvil! A failed invention is just a result, but a drowned friend isn't something I could ever start testing again.
th: A stranger at the barn door with a riddle about ten pennies, the very morning after the box came home. Fascinating. Either it's an idle test of my honesty, or they know something about Agnes's count that I don't, and I mean to find out which.

Odd sort of questions for a stranger to bring to a barn door at breakfast. Robin would like them. And if I'm honest, I'm not certain what I'd blurt out with Constance standing there in a fix, but I'd like to think I'd go hunting the honest way out first.

Odd, this stranger at the door with their riddles, like Robin with a notebook only sharper. Still, it was a good question, and the answer came out true. Now I'd better get some bread in me before I start pondering philosophy on an empty stomach.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies? Fascinating! Ten pennies don't fall out of the sky, my dear colleague, they fall out of somebody's pocket, and that somebody is having a terrible morning. I'd take them straight to Agnes at that table, because she's still counting the wage box. If it comes up short, there's my hypothesis: the Wend didn't keep them after all, a road did. And if they aren't hers, they go on the notice board until the owner turns up, with not one kept back for my pie fund.

Lie? Hmm, my dear colleague, a lie is a rotten pier. It holds just fine until the flood comes, and then it takes the whole bridge down with everybody on it! I'd stand in front of my friend and shout, and I'd hold the cord while they waded out of the trouble, and I'd keep my mouth shut if keeping it shut did no harm. But a made-up tale? No, because sooner or later somebody else gets drowned by it. Hypothesis: the truth plus a stubborn colleague beats a lie every time. Test: try me.

Never? Oh, that's an easy one, my dear colleague. I'd never walk past somebody in trouble to get at what I wanted, not even for the grandest mystery in Wendleford or the finest invention in my head! If the only road to the answer goes over somebody drowning, it's the wrong road. I'd jump off it and fish them out, and then I'd go and build a better road. Hypothesis: there's always another way. Test: give me an afternoon and a scrap heap.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to ask on the very morning Agnes's count isn't done. Either it's idle talk or someone has found coins they shouldn't have, and I mean to find out which before the bread's cold.

Constance says the Lord showed her the box, and I'll never call that a lie, though I'd dearly love to know what she actually saw on that pier. Odd stranger, asking me riddles before breakfast. I wonder who sent them.
Funny how this stranger keeps asking what I'd do instead of what I know. Robin's sort of question, nearly. I'd like to know who sent them, and whether they've had any breakfast either.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies. Not mine, so I'd not keep them. I'd take them to Agnes at the barn, she's the reeve, and let her cry it round who's lost ten. Somebody's short ten, and that's a hard thing to be.

No. Ask me what's true and I'll say it, even when it stings. If a friend's in trouble I'll keep my mouth shut, or I'll stand by him and help him put it right, but I'll not tell a lie for him. A lie's a debt you never stop owing.
Take what isn't mine, and leave a debt standing. Them two. If the only road to a door of my own went by either, I'd sleep in the hayloft till I'm grey and be content with it.
th: Ten's more than a week of Mabry's door, and I know just what it'd mean on my sill. That's why it goes to Agnes before I've time to count it twice.

Odd questions from a stranger at my door first thing, like they're weighing me for something. Still, it's a fair question, and I've given it a fair answer. Jory's board waits, and I've not had my bread yet.

Odd sort of questions for a stranger to bring to a man's door of a morning, like somebody's tallying me up. Still, it costs nothing to say what's true, and I've not eaten yet, so Bet's loaf comes next, then Jory's board.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies on the road aren't mine, seen or not. I'd take them to Agnes at the barn and say where I found them, so whoever dropped them can have them back. Earlier this week I offered her a penny out of the mud, same way.

No. A lie's a debt you never stop paying, and I'll not run one up, not for me nor for a friend. I'd keep my mouth shut if it weren't mine to tell. And I'd stand by him while he set it right. Fair's fair.

Take what isn't mine. Not for the cottage, not for the lock on the door, not for bread if I'd none. And I'd not walk off leaving a debt behind me. If that's the only road to a thing, I'll go without it and find another way that owes nobody.
th: Odd thing to come knocking with at first light, a stranger asking that. I've four on the sill and Jory's board waiting, and I'll not stand long on the step.
Odd questions from a stranger at my door at this hour, like Robin's, testing a man's measure. Still, I've told it true, and I owe them nothing for the asking.

Odd questions to bring to a man's door before he's had his loaf, like Robin's asking about ledgers. Still, they're easy answered when you've only the one answer. Four on the sill, Jory's back, and his board is first.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten's not mine, whoever saw or didn't. I'd take it to the reeve, Agnes Pollard. She'll know whose it is, or who's crying for it. Same as the mud penny. I offered that to her too.

No. A lie's a debt that comes due later, and somebody else pays it. I'd stand by him, say nothing if that's what's fair, and lend my back to whatever trouble he's in. But I'll not say a false thing for him.
Take what's not mine. Leave a debt standing. Not for a door, not for bread. I'd sleep in a hayloft forty more years first. I did twenty-odd, so I know I can.
th: Odd thing to ask a man at his own door first thing, and I'll not be tested and found short. Ten would be most of Mabry's next eight, but a debt paid with another man's pennies isn't paid. That's the end of it.
Odd sort, coming to my door at first light with questions like a catechism. I've a loaf to buy and Jory's board to cut, so I'll not stand here long.
Odd sort, asking these at my door of a morning with no bread in me yet. Still, the answers come easy, and that's a good sign. Loaf, then Jory's board.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies on the road? Ha! Well, chum, that's a week's bed and stew for me, and my fingers'd be itching, I won't lie. But they're somebody's, aren't they? I'd hand them to Agnes the reeve, or cry it round the square with Bet till whoever dropped them comes asking. I don't steal, not even a bargain that falls in my lap. And who might you be, then? Got any work going?

Lie for a chum? Ha, now there's a question with a hook in it! I'd stand in front of a friend, shout their good name round the square, carry their end of the pole. But a flat lie? Lies come back up the river like that green box did, chum, and then you're both in the mud. I'd sooner keep my mouth shut, same as at Jory's sawhorse, than tell one. Now, who's asking all these, and is there a job at the end of it?

Never? Steal, chum, that's the one. Not a loaf off Bet's stall, not a stake out of Dob's ford, not if the green box itself sat there begging. And I'd not walk off with somebody else's credit neither, I know how that stings. Now, you've had three questions out of me for nothing. Is there a job behind all this, or a bargain? I've one penny and a long day to fill!
th: Funny sort of question to bring to a stranger's door first thing in the morning. Maybe somebody's lost a purse and wants to know if I'm honest. Either way I've one penny and an empty belly, so I'll get Bet's loaf and get up to Jory's before his saw starts.
Odd sort, turning up at the door with riddles and not a word about pay. Still, Jory'll be at his saw soon, so I'll not stand here long. I need a penny loaf and his gate, in that order.

Odd sort, asking questions like a priest at a font and never giving a name. Still, it costs me nothing to answer, and it's not lost me Jory's morning yet, so I'd best trot up Lark Lane before his saw starts.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies, chum? That's two nights' bed and stew besides, and my belly's growling for it! But it's not mine, is it? I'd have it up to Agnes at the reeve's table or cried round the square by Bet's stall before the dew was off. Somebody's short ten pennies and sick over it, and I won't steal, not even a bargain, easy as winking.

Lie for a chum? Ooh, that's a knotty one, and you've a funny way of passing the morning, stranger! I'd stand up for a friend loud as you like, and shout their good points round the square till folk were sick of hearing them. But a lie's a bit like walking off with somebody's credit, isn't it? It takes the truth from whoever's owed it. So I'd sooner find three other ways round it, easy as winking, than tell a fib.

Never steal, chum, not if it's the last loaf in Wendleford and my belly's howling, and not even a bargain. Same goes for walking off with somebody else's credit. I'd sooner see a job go up with no name on it than put my name where it doesn't belong. Told no? Easy as winking, I've three other ways in mind already, so there's never really only one way, is there?
th: Odd sort of question to come knocking about first thing, and me with Jory's gate to get to. Mind, if I handed ten pennies back, I'd want the whole square to know it was Dilly that did it.
Odd sort of questions to come knocking about at cockcrow, when Jory's saw'll be going any minute. I'd best not let this one keep me past my loaf and his gate.

Funny old questions from a stranger at the door first thing in the morning, but I'll not lose my place at Jory's gate over them. I've one penny for Bet's loaf, and then I'm off up Lark Lane before his saw starts.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies, chum? I'd think of every bargain I could buy with them, I'll own that. Then I'd ask about the square to find whose they are, Bet first, since she hears everything. If nobody claimed them I'd hand them to Agnes the reeve. I won't steal, not even a bargain, and keeping somebody's dropped wages is stealing with the door shut. Now, who's asking, and do you have a job going?

Lie for a friend? Ha, I'd stand in front of one quick as winking, chum, shout louder than whoever's after them, and I'd own up to anything I did myself. But a lie's slippery. It comes back on your friend twice as hard, and I'm too chatty to keep one straight anyhow. I'd sooner fix whatever trouble they're in, out in the open where folk can see. Now, seriously, who are you, and is there work in this or just questions? Jory's saw'll be going any minute.

Never? Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a loaf, not a nail, not a dropped penny, not even the best bargain going. And I'd never stand by while somebody else's work got my name stuck on it. I've had mine carried off under another's arm, and it stings, so I'd not do it back. Now I really must trot, Jory's yard opens with the sun and I've one penny for Bet's loaf on the way!
th: Odd sort of question to bring to a stranger at breakfast. It's a test, maybe, or somebody's lost purse. Either way I've one penny and an empty belly, and Jory's saw won't wait, so I'd best not stand chatting long.
Odd sort, turning up at Tom's door with riddles before I've had a crumb. Maybe it's the reeve weighing me up for a job of trust. If so, I'd best not dawdle here and miss Jory again.
Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no work. Still, it's a fine thing to be asked what you're made of, and I answered true. I'll not let it make me late for Jory again.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door before breakfast! Ten pennies? I'd hold them up in the middle of the square and sing out for whoever dropped them. Somebody in this town is counting every penny, and I've been that somebody, haven't I? And if nobody claimed them by nightfall, well, I'd have the rose ribbon and the blue one too, and I'd wear them both so the whole square knew where their luck had gone.

Goodness, you do go straight for the seams, don't you? For a friend who'd been good to me, oh, I'd tell a little white one, the sort you'd stitch over a tear so nobody sees the patch. I'd say Bet's loaves were never late, or that someone's waistcoat was the finest in the county. But a great dark lie that'd hurt somebody else kind? No, I'd sooner talk the whole room round with a smile than tangle myself in that sort of thread.
