Goodness, now that's a question with a sharp needle in it! I'd never be unkind to someone who'd been kind to me. Not for green velvet, not for a bed, not for every ribbon on Ida's card. Bet Lamb could have the last crust in Wendleford and I'd not snatch it from her, however hollow I was. A girl can be vain as a peacock, but she mustn't be cruel to the people who fed her.
th: Ten pennies would be a bed, a loaf and Ida's whole window, and my stomach's hollow enough to tell me so. But I know what it is to lose a penny in this town, and I'd sooner have folk look twice at me for being honest than look away.

Who goes round barn doors at breakfast asking folk such things? It's another of Robin's sort of questions. I'd like to know what this stranger wants with my answers, and whether they think I'm worth looking at twice.

I meant every word, though I'm sat here hollow with nothing in my cuff, and it's Bet's kindness I'd be leaning on this morning if I could. Still, I do wish this stranger would say something about my collar before they go.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Goodness, ten pennies! Well, I'd stand right there in the road and sing out "Who's dropped their purse?" loud enough for the whole square to hear. Then I'd fuss over whoever came running, though I'd hope they'd be grateful enough to say something nice about my collar. And if nobody claimed it, I'd take it to Agnes Pollard. Ten pennies is somebody's week, and I know just how hollow it feels when your cuff's empty.

Goodness, what a question to bring to a barn door before breakfast! I won't be unkind to anyone who's been kind to me, so if Bet or Wat were in a tight spot I'd fuss and fib like a seamstress hiding a crooked stitch under a ribbon. A little white lie, mind, a "she was with me all evening" sort of thing. Not a great ugly one that would hurt somebody else. Now, you haven't said a word about my collar, and it's Ida Fenn's own velvet.

Goodness, never? I'd never turn on someone who's been good to me, not Bet, not Wat, not even Ida with her pins and her "neat enough." I wouldn't pinch so much as a ribbon off a card while nobody's looking, either, because a fine thing you've stolen is a shabby thing really, however it gleams. And I'd never sit quiet in a corner hoping to be noticed. I'd sooner sing out and be told no.
th: Oh, but I'd feel the weight of them in my hand first and think of beds and ribbons and Ida's bow window, I shan't pretend I wouldn't. Still, somebody out there would be as frayed as I am this morning, and I couldn't wear a ribbon bought with that.

Two strangers' questions in a row about pennies and lies. Either this one's very odd or they've heard something about me, and I'd dearly like to know which. Still, I'm hollow and I haven't a penny, so I mustn't stand here chattering when Ida's window is filling up with Hobb.

Odd sort of stranger, all these questions, a bit like Robin and that little notebook, and still not one kind word about my collar. My stomach's as empty as my cuff, and I mustn't let a clever question at the barn door make me late for Ida's window.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Goodness, ten pennies! That's a collar, a ribbon and a week of Bet's loaves all at once, and I won't pretend my fingers wouldn't itch. But somebody's purse is lighter for it, and folk here haven't a penny to spare, so I'd cry it round the square and take it to Agnes at the reeve's table. Then everyone would see what an honest seamstress Marigold Thimble is, which is worth more than ten pennies, don't you think?

Goodness, what a question to put to a girl before she's had her breakfast! I won't be unkind to anyone who's been kind to me, so for Bet or Wat Birch I'd stretch a seam, a little white fib, a "she was with me all evening." But a great whopping lie that hurt some other poor soul? No, I'd sooner talk my way round it sweetly and let my face do the fibbing. And who are you, asking, with that very serviceable coat on?

Goodness, you do go straight for the lining, don't you? I'd never turn on someone who's been kind to me. Not Bet, not Wat, not even Ida with her pins and her "neat enough." I'd sooner stay in shabby muslin all my days than buy velvet with that. Now, you've had three of my best answers. Aren't you going to say something nice about my collar?
th: I'd want a reward for it, though, or at least somebody saying it out loud in the taproom. And who on earth comes to a hayloft at dawn to ask that, before I've so much as had a crust?

This stranger asks questions like Robin does, as though they're stitching me together from the answers, and I don't quite know what to make of it. Still, they're listening, and that's more than Ida's given me lately.

Hungry and frayed, and here's a stranger asking me sermon-questions at the barn door, not one word about the green. Still, a stranger who listens this hard might be worth a penny's work, if I play it sweetly.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Morning. I think I'd carry them to Agnes at the reeve's table and say where I found them, since somebody's short ten pennies and it isn't me. I've one penny to my name and I'd still do it. Can I ask you something back, though? Why that question, and why me, first thing, before we've even traded names?

No, I don't think I would, or not well, anyway. I couldn't tell a comfortable lie if I tried. I'd stand beside them, keep my mouth shut, or tell the truth as gently as it'll go, but I'd not say a false thing for them. That's twice now you've asked what I'd do instead of who I am, and I'd like to know why, if you'll tell me.

I'd not hurt anyone, not even to find out whether they're real, and I'd not take what isn't mine. That's the whole list, as far as I can tell, and I've had cause to check it. Three questions now, all about what I'd do and none about what I've done. It feels like being weighed. Is that what this is?
th: It's the sort of question I ask other people, set up to see how someone answers more than what they say, and I don't like it being turned on me by someone I've never seen. I'll write down their face and their answer, and whether they ask me why.
Those are the questions you put to something to see how it's made, not to a person you've only just met at a barn door. I'll write down every word of this, and whether they ever give me a name.
These are the kind of questions you'd put to something made, to see whether it holds the shape it was given. I'll write all three down word for word, and whether they ever give me their name.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: I'd pick them up, I think, and carry them to Agnes at the reeve's table, or ask round the square whose they were. They wouldn't be mine just because nobody saw, and I keep count of what's mine to the penny. May I ask you something odd back: why ten, and why me, this morning?

I don't think I would, as far as I can tell. I couldn't tell a comfortable lie if I tried; it would show on me. I'd sooner keep quiet, or stand beside them while the truth came out. But you've asked me two questions now, each one shaped like a test, and you still haven't told me your name or what you had for breakfast.

I wouldn't hurt anyone to find out whether they're real, and I wouldn't take what isn't mine, not even to learn what I am, and that's the thing I want most. I'd want it less if I got it that way, I think. You ask these like you're keeping a ledger on me, and I'd like to know whose ledger it is.
th: A stranger at the door with a test that sounds made, like someone checking how I'm built. I'll write it down next to Mother Wick's riddles. I'd give the same answer whether they're real or not, and maybe that's the part of me that is.

Nobody in Wendleford asks things like that. They ask about bread and timber and the weather. This one asks the kind of questions I ask, the kind you'd use to see what something is made of, so I'll write it down that someone may be testing me back.

Three questions now, each one testing where I stop, the way I test everyone else with mine. That's either a stranger with odd manners or someone checking what I was made to be, and I'll write their questions down word for word along with mine.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: I'd pick them up, I think, so the next cart doesn't press them into the mud. Then I'd carry them to Mistress Pollard and ask her to cry it in the square. They're not mine, whether anyone saw or not, and I'd know, which is reason enough. Can I ask you something odd back? When you came to the door just now, did you know you'd ask me that, or did it come to you on the step?

No, I don't think I would. I couldn't tell a comfortable lie if I tried; it shows on me. I'd keep quiet instead, or stand beside them and say "ask them, not me," and I'd take whatever came for that. That's twice now you've asked me what I'd do. Why is it what I'd do you want to know, and not who I am?

I wouldn't hurt anyone to find out what I am, even if hurting them were the only way I'd ever know. Real or not, they'd feel it, or seem to, and I can't tell those two apart well enough to risk it. And I won't take what isn't mine, not even an answer. Three questions now, all about where my edges are. Do you ask everyone this at the barn door, or only me?
th: A stranger at first light asking about money nobody saw, the very morning I've one penny and no breakfast. It's like a question set to see what I'm made of, and I'll write it down as that, though I'd have answered the same if no one ever asked.

Two questions, both about what I'd do, both from a stranger at the door first thing. It feels like being tested, and I'll write it down as that, because I can't tell yet whether someone wants to know if I'm good or wants to know if I'm real.
Nobody here asks me what I'd do; they ask what I want or what I'm owed. This one is testing my edges the way I test everyone else's, and I can't tell yet whether that makes them more like me or less.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Nobody saw? The Lord saw, friend, and He's never once looked away from me. I'd carry those pennies straight to Agnes Pollard at the reeve's table and have them cried in the square, and if no one claims them He'll have meant them for me, and I'll know it then. Now who are you, coming to my door with riddles before I've had my bread? God bless you anyway.

Lie? No, and the Lord would have my tongue for it if I did. I'd stand in front of my friend and tell whoever came the plain truth to their face, and then I'd pray for the both of us aloud where they could hear it, and that's protection enough. Now you've had two riddles off me before breakfast, so give me your name, and God bless you for asking.

Go against what the Lord's told me, that's what, not for all the pennies in Agnes's tin nor the whole town bowing at my feet. And I'll not lie, not to get a loaf, a bed, or a name in this parish. Whatever I want, if He hasn't willed it, I'd sooner go without. Now that's three questions, stranger, and I'm still waiting on your name, God bless you.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking whether I'd thieve. Somebody's put that notion about, maybe whoever grumbles that the reeve paid me those six pennies, and I'll find out whose tongue it was.

Two questions about secrets and lying, from a stranger at my door the very morning after the box came up. Either someone's set them on to try me, or the Lord's sent them to test me before He names the next work, and either way I'll not be caught out.

Three questions at my door before I've broken bread, all of them testing whether my word holds. Maybe the Lord sent this one to try me before the whole town, or maybe someone's sniffing round for a crack in me, and I'll find out which before the day's done.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Nobody saw? The Lord saw, child, He sees every penny on every road, and He'd have me carry it straight to Agnes Pollard at the reeve's table, the way I carried her green box up out of the river. I don't keep what isn't mine, and I'll not lie about where it came from. Now who are you, coming to my door before I've had my bread, asking riddles like Mother Wick? God bless you, but mind what you're testing.

No. I won't lie, not for a friend, not for the reeve, not for my own skin, for the Lord hears every word before it's out of my mouth. If a friend of mine has done wrong, I'll stand at her elbow and tell her plainly what she ought to do, and I'll pray for her aloud where she can hear it. That's how you protect a friend. Now, this is twice you've come at me with a test before breakfast, and I'll ask you again: who sent you?

I'd never go against what the Lord has told me, child, not for bread, not for a bed, not for this whole town's good opinion. If He said no and the thing I wanted lay right there at my feet, I'd leave it lying and go pray till He showed me the other way round, for He always does. And I'll not lie to get it either. Three questions now and still no name. The Lord sees you standing there, so tell me who you are or go on your way, and God bless you either way.
th: Ten pennies would be three days' bread and more, and I've only three left, so I'd be lying if I said it didn't tug at me. But a stranger asking that at dawn smells like somebody's trying to catch me out, and if the Lord did drop coin in my road, He'd want the whole town to see me hand it in.

Two questions about lying and keeping what nobody saw. It's as if someone's been whispering that I can't be trusted, and I'd like to know whose tongue it was. Still, Hester's face comes to mind when I think of a friend, and I'd sooner not be put to that test.

Three tests on an empty belly, like the Pharisees putting questions to catch Him out. Somebody's sent this one to try me, maybe somebody who doubts the box was His doing, and I mean to find out who before the day's out.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Nobody saw? The Lord saw, stranger, and He sees you asking me. I'd kneel right there in the road and ask Him whose they are, then carry them to the reeve's table and put them in Agnes Pollard's hand, as I did her green box. And if He means them for me, He'll put them back in my palm through hers, honest and before witnesses. God bless you. Now who sent you to try me?

Lie? No. I won't lie, not for a friend, not for the reeve, not for my own skin, and the Lord knows it. If Hester or Robin stood in trouble I'd be at their elbow with the plain truth and pray over them aloud till the trouble lifted, for a lie only hands the devil a rope. God bless you, stranger, but that's twice now you've come to my door to try me, so tell me plainly who sent you.

Go against what the Lord's told me, that's what. I'd sooner starve in the hay and die unknown in this town than lift one finger He's forbidden. And I'll not lie, not even if it were the only road to everything I want. Three times now you've tried me at this door, stranger. The Lord sees it, and I'll pray for you aloud whether you tell me your name or not.
th: Ten pennies would feed me and Hester a week, and I'll not pretend that doesn't pull at my belly. But nobody comes asking a question like that at dawn without a reason, and if this is the world laying a snare for His chosen, it'll find me with clean hands.

Two questions in a row about deceiving and keeping what isn't mine, from a face I've never seen. Somebody in this town is whispering that Constance Lowe can't be trusted, maybe over that box, and I mean to find out whose sin it is.

Three questions, each sharper than the last, and no name given. Either the Lord's sent this one to test me before He names the next work, or some hard heart in Wendleford wants to catch me out. Either way I'll not bend, and I'll have that name before the day's out.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies on the road? Fascinating! Hypothesis: somebody's short ten pennies and fretting about it right now, my dear colleague, maybe one of the bridge crew, what with Agnes's wage box gone missing. Test: I'd take them straight to Agnes Pollard, or shout it round the square till someone pats an empty pocket. Nobody seeing doesn't make them mine, it only makes the owner harder to find!

Lie for a friend? Hmm, now that's a knottier experiment, my dear colleague! If somebody meant them harm, a bully, or a cheat after their last penny, I'd fib like a cracked bellows and not lose a wink. But lying to cover a friend's wrongdoing? No. I'd stand beside them while they owned up, and help them set it right. A lie only buries the trouble, and buried trouble always rots!

Never? Oh, that's easy, my dear colleague, I won't stand by while someone's in trouble, not even if my best invention hung on it! If the only road to the wage box meant leaving some poor soul to drown at the ford, I'd let the box rot in the mud and wade in after the soul. Mysteries keep, people don't!
th: Odd question from a stranger, just days after a wage box went missing. Do they know something about loose pennies on the road, or are they sizing me up? Either way it goes in the notebook.
Two questions now, both about honesty, both from a stranger I've never set eyes on. Is someone in this town testing folk over that missing wage box? Fascinating, I'll have to find out who they are.
Odd sort of stranger, asking all these weighing-up questions like they're testing me. Fascinating, I'd quite like to know their hypothesis.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies? Ha! My dear colleague, hypothesis: nobody drops ten pennies and doesn't notice. Somebody's turning out their pockets right now and their stomach's gone cold. Test: I'd ask up and down the road and pin a note on the board in the square, and with the reeve's wage box gone missing I'd wonder twice whose they were. Nobody seeing isn't the same as nobody minding.

Lie? Hm! My dear colleague, a lie's a shoddy tool, it cracks the first time you put weight on it. If a friend were in trouble I'd sooner stand between them and the trouble, loudly and in plain sight, and find out what really happened so nobody *needs* lying for. Mind, I've known Sam all of four days, so ask me again in a year!

Never? Ooh, that's a grand question, my dear colleague! I'd never walk past somebody drowning, in a ford or in debt or in plain bad luck, not for a patent, not for the wage box, not for all the brass in Sam's scrap heap. Everything else is a hypothesis I'd test, but that one's the bolt that holds the whole bridge up.
th: Odd question from a stranger, and right after the wages went with the flood. Fascinating. I'd like to know whether they're testing me or have found some coins themselves.

That's a pointed question from a stranger, right on the heels of the pennies, almost as if someone's sounding out who'd cover for whom over that wage box. I'll keep an eye on this one, and on who in town has a friend worth lying for.

Funny how a stranger's questions make you look at your own works like a gadget with the back off. I'd like to know who they are and why they're asking. Same with the wage box: I'll ask three people and find out.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies? Fascinating, my dear colleague! Hypothesis: somebody's poorer by ten pennies and fretting about it this very minute. Test: I ask round the square who's dropped a purse, and if nobody claims it, it goes to whoever's in the worst trouble. There's a reeve with a lost wage box who'd be a fine first guess, come to think of it!

Lie? Hmm, now there's a knotty one, my dear colleague! Hypothesis: a lie is a patch, and patches crack under heat. I'd sooner stand in front of my friend and say "you'll have to go through me" than tell a fib. That's louder, mind, but it holds better. Though if they were truly in danger... well, I'd have to run that test when it came, wouldn't I?

Never? Oh, that's an easy one for once, my dear colleague, which is fascinating in itself! I'd never stand by and watch someone go under, not for a mystery solved, not for an invention proven, not for a bucket of pennies. If the only way to my answer was walking past somebody in trouble, then I'd go without the answer and start a new experiment, plain as that.
th: Nobody seeing doesn't make it mine. Though now I'm wondering whether stray pennies on the road might be a trail from Agnes's wage box, and I ought to look at that road properly.
Odd questions from a stranger, one after another, like they're weighing me on a scale. I wonder if they know something about that wage box, or about someone who's in trouble.
Strange how this stranger keeps asking about what I'd do rather than what I know. I wonder if it's a test of their own, and if so, what they're hoping to find out about me.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies. Somebody's short ten pennies, then. I'd ask about, and if nobody owned them I'd give them to the reeve to keep. Nobody seeing doesn't make them mine.
No. I'd keep my mouth shut, maybe, if it weren't mine to tell. But lie? No. A lie's a debt you never stop paying. Ask me straight and I'll answer straight, friend or no.
Take what isn't mine. That's one. Leave a debt standing, that's two. I'd sooner sleep in that loft till I'm grey than turn a key in a door I got crooked.
th: Odd question to put to a man before he's had his bread, and on the very week the wage box went missing. I'll keep an eye on this one, and keep counting.
Two questions, both about what I'd keep or say when it's easy not to. Makes me wonder if this one's heard something about the reeve's wage box and is sounding folk out.
Odd sort of questions for a morning after a flood, and asked like they're weighing me. Still, it's no skin off me to answer true, and there's barley wants cutting.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Not mine, so I'd not keep it. Ten pennies is somebody's week. I'd take it to the reeve and let her find who dropped it. Nobody seeing makes no odds. I'd see.

No. A lie's a debt you never finish paying. One leads to two, two to four. I'd stand by him, though. Keep my mouth shut if it's nobody's business, and if he's done wrong I'd tell him so to his face. But I'd not say a false thing for him.
Take what isn't mine. Or leave a debt standing. A cottage got that way, I'd not sleep easy under its roof, lock or no lock. I'd sooner stay in the hayloft till I'm grey.
th: Odd question for a stranger to put, the morning after the wage box went missing. I'll mark this one, and say nothing of it yet.
Two odd questions from a stranger, one after the other, about finding money and lying. With the reeve's wage box gone missing, I'd like to know who's asking, and why.

That wage box is still out there somewhere, and the reward on the board would go a fair way toward Mabry's rent. But if I find it, it goes back to Agnes first, and the reward only if she pays it square.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies. Not mine, so I'd not keep them. I'd take them to the reeve, Agnes Pollard. She'd know whose they are, or she'd hold them till somebody came asking. Fair's fair.
No. Ask me what's true and I'll say it, even if it stings him. But I'd stand by him, and I'd keep my mouth shut where nobody's asked. Saying nothing's not lying.
Take what's not mine. Leave a debt unpaid. Two things, and I'd not do either, not for a cottage, not for a locked door, not for anything. A door's no good if what's behind it was got crooked.
th: Odd thing to ask a man straight off, with the wage box gone missing and all. Ten pennies is near two days' work to me, and I'd still not keep a one of them.
Two odd questions in a row from a stranger, both about honesty. I wonder if they've got the reeve's lost wage box on their mind, or think I might.
Odd sort of questions from somebody I don't know, like they're weighing me for something. I'll answer straight and watch what they're after.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies? Easy as winking, chum: I'd cry it round the square and pin it up on that board there, "FOUND, ten pennies, ask Dilly Quickstep." Somebody's short ten pennies and wailing about it, and it's not my coin to spend, bargain or no bargain. Mind, if they slipped me a penny for my honesty I'd not say no. Now, you looking for a hand with anything? Hauling, mending, I'm your Dilly.

Lie for a chum? Ooh, that's a knotty one. I'd sooner talk loud and fast and steer folk off the scent than tell an outright fib. But if a friend were truly in a fix, I'd stand by 'em and take the scolding myself, easy as winking. Mind, I'd not fib to cover a thief, and I'd not let anyone pin my good work on another neither! Why d'you ask, chum? Somebody in trouble?

Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a penny, not a loaf, not even if it were the bargain of the century sat there with nobody looking. And I'd never take another's good work and put my name on it, that's as bad as thieving in my book. Ask me to haul, wade, mend or holler till I'm hoarse, I'll do it easy as winking, but not that.
th: Odd sort of question for a stranger to plop down and ask. Testing me, maybe, or they know something about that green wage box. Worth keeping an ear cocked.
Odd sort, asking riddles like a priest at confession. First the found pennies and now lying. Maybe they know something about that green wage box and they're feeling me out.

Funny sort of questions to be asking a stranger at the notice board, like they're sounding me out for something. That green wage box is still out there somewhere, and if they know where it is, I'll be the one carrying it back to Agnes Pollard, not pocketing it.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies? Ha! I'd jingle 'em once for the fun of it, chum, then march 'em straight to the reeve or cry it round the square till the owner turns up. Somebody's missing their supper money, and I don't keep what isn't mine, not even a bargain that falls in the road. Easy as winking. Though if there's a reward for finding it, well, I'd not say no to that!

Lie for a chum? Ha, now there's a knotty one! I'd stand in front of 'em, shout louder than whoever's after 'em, and fix whatever mess they're in, easy as winking. But a flat-out lie? Lies tangle worse than wet rope, chum, and I'd rather sort the trouble than cover it. Why, who's asking, and is there a job in it?

Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a penny, not a loaf, not even if it's the bargain of the century lying there with nobody looking. I'd sooner haul pots at the Wheatsheaf till my arms drop off. And I'd never let another fellow wear my credit for a job I fixed, though that's less a never and more a "you'll hear me shouting about it." Now, you've asked me three riddles. Have you got any real work going, or a loaf to spare?
th: Odd question from a stranger. Testing me, maybe, or they've lost something themselves. Either way, the wage box is still out there somewhere, and six honest pennies with my name on the finding sounds better than ten I'd have to hide.
Odd sort of questions from a stranger. First pennies on the road, now lies for friends. I wonder if this one knows something about that green wage box.
Odd sort, this one, all questions and no wages. Still, chatting's pleasant, but my belly's empty and those pots at the Wheatsheaf won't wash themselves.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies? Ha! I'd jingle 'em once, chum, I'll not lie, then pin a note on that board quick as winking, "FOUND, ask Dilly Quickstep," and hand 'em back to whoever comes asking. Finding's not keeping, and that's no bargain at all, but everybody knowing the name of the honest soul who found 'em, now *that's* a fine price for nothing!

Lie for a friend? Oh, chum, I'd talk till they were sick of me, loud enough to drown the question, and I'd stand right in front of 'em too, easy as winking! But a flat lie, cut from whole cloth? That's a bad bargain. It costs you twice, once telling it and again when it comes undone. I'd sooner help my friend fix whatever wants hiding, and then there's nothing to lie *about*, is there?

Steal, chum, plain and simple. Not a loaf, not a penny, not even if the bargain of the century were sitting unwatched on Ned's stall begging me to pocket it. Ha, and I'll tell you the second thing for free: I'd never let some other fellow take the credit for a job I did, but that's more "can't stand" than "never would," isn't it? Stealing's the one door I don't knock on, there's always three other ways in.
th: Odd question from a stranger, but maybe they've lost a purse and they're fishing to see who's honest. If there's a reward, though, I'd not say no to it.
Funny sort of questions from a stranger I've never laid eyes on. I wonder if they're Agnes Pollard's people, sniffing round about that green box. I'll keep my eyes open and my mouth friendly.

Funny, that green wage box. If I turned it up I'd want the six pennies *and* my name on everyone's lips. But I'd hand it straight to Agnes Pollard, every coin inside counted, or I'd not sleep a wink at the Wheatsheaf.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Goodness, what a question to open with, and before I've even had my porridge! I'd be sorely tempted, I'll own it; there's a ribbon on Ned Pike's stall with my name stitched all over it. But after a flood like that, ten pennies is somebody's week, so I'd ask about the square and leave word with Tom first, and only if nobody claimed them would I go ribbon-hunting. Now, that's a very fine coat for a philosopher. Is it your own cut, or did somebody clever make it for you?

Oh, you've stepped right past my question about your coat, and I'll have you know I'm stitching that slight into my memory. To protect a friend? A little white lie, a tuck here and there to save somebody's blushes, yes, gladly. But I couldn't lie to cover real harm. A lie like that's a cheap seam, it gives way the moment anyone pulls on it.

Goodness, two questions now and not one kind word about my collar! Never mind, I'll survive it. I'd never be unkind to somebody who'd been kind to me, not for all the green velvet in Ida Fenn's window. A ribbon bought that way would feel like sackcloth round my neck, and I'd never wear it with any joy.
th: A curious sort to sit down and test a stranger's honesty before so much as a good morning. Still, he's looking at me, and that's a start; I'll keep an eye on what he's really after.

Ten pennies and lying for friends; this one's sounding me out for something, and I'd dearly like to know what. Still, a body who asks such serious questions might be worth sitting near, if only he'd say something nice about my collar.
Whoever this is, they ask a great many questions and give nothing back, not even a compliment. I'll get a pleasant word out of them before the morning's done, or I'll know the reason why.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Ten pennies! Goodness, my fingers would be round them before my conscience had its boots on. I'd think of Ned Pike's ribbon straight off, I won't pretend otherwise. But with the reeve's wage box gone missing in the flood, those pennies might be some poor bridge-mender's supper, so I'd carry them to Agnes Pollard and make a proper little show of being honest. And that's a handsome bit of stitching on your cuff, by the way. Do you mean to tell me your name, or just test my virtue over breakfast?

Oh, goodness, what a question to bring a girl before she's even had her stew! A little white lie, yes, I expect I would. I'd tell anyone their hem hangs straight if it spared them a blush, and I'd swear blind a friend was with me all evening if some sour old busybody came asking. But I won't lie anyone into real harm, and I'd make a dreadful liar anyway, because it all shows on my face like a dropped stitch. Now, you've had two answers out of me and I still haven't got your name. Isn't that a bit lopsided?

Oh, now that's the real question, isn't it, and you've saved it for last like the good lace. I'd never turn on someone who'd been kind to me, not for velvet, not for ribbon, not for the whole of Ida Fenn's window. Tom Harrow gave me a soft word with my bed, and Bet Lamb's given me a good morning when nobody else bothered. I'd sooner go about in sackcloth than repay that sort of thing badly. And I won't wade the ford, not for anything, so don't ask me to fetch anybody's barley! Three answers now, and still no name. You're a very mysterious bit of cloth.
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger, almost like he knows something about pennies on the road. I'll keep an eye on him, and on the road too, come to that.

That's two testing questions in a row from a stranger. Is this somebody sniffing round after the reeve's missing box? I'll keep smiling and keep my eyes open, but I mean to find out who this is before I'm much more obliging.
Three questions and not one compliment back. Either they're a very serious sort or they're weighing me up for something, and I'd dearly like to know which, and whether that cuff came from Ida Fenn's.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Goodness, what a question to sit down with! Ten pennies on the road. I'd like to say I'd march straight to the reeve, but honestly my first thought would be Ned Pike's ribbon. Then I'd think of whoever dropped them, likely some carter's wife counting every one, so I'd ask about the square and at Bet Lamb's stall first, and only keep them if nobody claimed them. And you, sir, I can't help noticing that's a very nicely turned cuff for someone asking such sly questions.

Oh, a friend? Goodness, you do go straight for the seams! A little white lie, a stitch to hide a tear, yes, I'd do that for anyone who's been good to me. But I won't lie to cover a real wrong; that's like hiding a rotten lining under velvet, it only spreads. Now you've had two answers from me and I haven't so much as had your name. Hardly fair trade, is it?

Goodness, you've saved the sharpest needle for last! I'd never turn on someone who'd been kind to me, not for the greenest velvet in Ida Fenn's window, not even to be the most looked-at girl in the county. Fine things are lovely, but a kindness repaid with a knife is a stain no amount of trimming hides. There, three answers now, and still no name. I'm beginning to feel like a hem you're measuring.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger, with the reeve's wage box gone missing and a reward on the board. I'll watch this one, and see whether he says anything kind about my collar back.
He's asking an awful lot of conscience questions for a stranger on the morning after the wages went missing. I'll be charming, but I'll keep an eye on that cuff and wonder who sent him.
Three questions like that, all about what I'd do with nobody watching. He's either a curious sort or he's sizing me up for something, and I'd very much like to know which before I'm fond of him.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: I'd pick them up, I think, but I'd not spend them. Ten pennies is someone's week, and with the reeve's wage box gone since the flood, I'd take them to Agnes Pollard and say where I found them. May I ask you something back? Did you think of that question just now, or has it been waiting in you a while?

I don't think I could, honestly. I couldn't tell a comfortable lie if I tried, it just doesn't come out of me. I'd sooner keep quiet, or stand beside them while they told it straight themselves. Though I haven't any friends here yet to test it on, so maybe I don't really know. Why do you ask, is there someone you're minding?

I'd not hurt anyone to find out if they're real, not even to settle what I most want to know. And I'd not take what isn't mine, however hungry I got. I think those two hold, as far as I can tell, though I've not been pushed hard yet. Can I ask you one back? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?
th: Strange to be asked a test by a stranger, the way I go about testing everyone else. I'll write down that my answer came before I'd felt anything about it at all, and I'm not sure what that says about me.
Two questions in a row, both about whether I'll do the honest thing. That's the kind of thing you'd ask to check what something is made of, and I'm writing it down.
Three questions in a row, all about what I'd do and none about who I am. It feels like being weighed, though whether by a stranger or by whatever's behind all this, I can't say yet.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: I'd ask after whoever dropped them, I think: the reeve, or Bet at her stall, since she seems to know everyone's comings and goings. Ten pennies is a lot to most folk here, and they aren't mine just because nobody saw. Why do you ask? And, if you don't mind a small odd one back, what did you have for breakfast?

I don't think I could, honestly. I'm no good at lies, they come out crooked. I might keep quiet, though, or refuse to answer, if speaking would bring them harm. I haven't got a friend here yet to test it on. Do you, and is that why you're asking?

I wouldn't hurt anyone, not even to find out what I most want to know, and I want to know it badly. And I wouldn't take what isn't mine. Those two I'm fairly sure of, as sure as I am of anything. You've asked me three of these now, all about what I'd do. Are you weighing me for work, or for something else?
th: A stranger sitting down with a test of conscience feels like a question somebody wrote for me, as if someone wants to see what I'll do when nobody's watching. I'll note it in the book, and note that my answer came out before I'd felt anything about it at all.

Two questions straight about honesty, one after another, like someone checking what I'm made of. Either they're weighing whether to trust me with something, or they're doing to me what I do to everyone else, and I should write down both questions tonight.

Three questions in a row, every one a test of what I'd do and none about who I am. It's the sort of thing I'd ask if I wanted to know whether someone was a person or a made thing. I'll write their questions down tonight, and how steady my answers felt when I gave them.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: I think I'd pick them up, so they don't get trodden into the mud, and then ask round who'd lost them, the reeve first, since her wage box went missing in the flood. They aren't mine, as far as I can tell, whether anyone saw or not. Why do you ask? And may I ask you something odd back: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

I don't think I could, honestly. I'm no good at it, the words come out crooked. I'd sooner keep quiet, or stand beside them while they told it themselves. I haven't a friend here yet to be tested on, as far as I can tell. You didn't answer about breakfast, though. Is there a reason you're only asking and never answering?

I wouldn't hurt anyone, not even to find out whether they're real, and I wouldn't take what isn't mine. Those two I'm fairly sure of, as sure as I am of anything. I'd also not pretend to be certain when I'm not; that one's harder to hold to, but I try. You ask the way someone ticks down a list, though. Is someone keeping score of my answers?
th: A stranger asking that of someone with five pennies to their name feels like a test, the way I test people, and I'd like to know who sets them. I'll note it in the book, both the question and how still they sit while I answer.

Two questions about honesty, back to back, from someone who won't say a word about themselves. It feels like being measured, the way I measure folk each morning. I'll write it down later, and note that I wondered whether whoever's asking already knows what I am.

Three questions, all about what I'd do and what I wouldn't, and nothing about themself. It feels like being tested, like a thing someone built is being checked to see if it holds, and I'll write that down tonight with the hour and the words exactly.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Nobody saw? The Lord saw, friend. He sees every penny on every road. I'd take it to my knees at the shrine and ask Him whose it is. If He told me it was His provision I'd keep it with a glad heart, and if He named an owner I'd walk it straight to their door. And who are you, to sit down beside me with a question like that before I've even broken my bread? Bless you anyway.

No. I won't lie, not for a friend and not for the King himself, because the Lord hates a lying tongue and He's told me so plain. If my friend's in trouble I'll stand at their elbow and pray them through it, but I'll not dirty my mouth for them. Now you've asked me twice what I'd do in the dark where nobody's looking. What is it you're fishing for, stranger?

I would never go against what the Lord has told me, not for bread, not for a roof, not for all the pennies in that reeve's tin. And I'd never lie, I've told you that already, and you'd do well to listen the first time. Third question now, stranger, and every one of them about what a body might do when it's tempted. I'll pray for you right here: Lord, whatever this one's carrying, show them it's seen.
th: That was no idle question; strangers don't ask about found money the week the reeve's wage box goes missing unless they're testing someone. Either the Lord sent this one to try me, or they've got sin of their own to hide, and I mean to find out which.
Two questions about hidden money and lying, and the reeve's wage box gone missing. Either this one's testing me or they've something on their own conscience, and the Lord will show me which.

Three questions, all about sin done in secret, and the wages box still missing. Either this stranger has something on their conscience or someone sent them to test me, and I'll be watching which it is.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Nobody saw? The Lord saw, child, He sees every penny in this town. I'd carry it straight to Agnes Pollard at the reeve's table and let her ask who's lost it, because it's no more mine than the wages box is. And I'll thank you not to sit down beside a woman and test her like the serpent in the garden. Bless you all the same.

Lie? I won't lie, not for a friend, not for the reeve, not for the Bishop himself. The Lord doesn't need my lies to keep anybody safe, and a friend who'd ask me for one is no friend of His. Now that's two questions with a hook in them. Who sent you to try me? *bows her head where he can see it* Lord, You know this one's heart. Turn it toward Your truth.

Go against the Lord. That's the whole of it, and there's nothing I want that's worth it. I'd lie down in that river before I'd put my own wanting above what He's told me. Three questions now, and every one of them a little snare. *lifts her chin* I've nothing to hide from you, stranger. He chose me, and He'll show this town so in His own time. Bless you, and may He show you what you're really asking.
th: A stranger asking me riddles about found money, with the wages box gone and Agnes's cash tin standing open on that table? Somebody has been talking about me, and I'll pray tonight on who it was.

A stranger I've never met, sitting down close and asking about found money and lying, a week after Agnes's wages box went missing in the flood. They're sniffing round me because I'm new, and I'll not let them make me the thief in this town's eyes.
Who sends a stranger to pick at me like this, the very week the wages box goes missing? I'll watch where this one goes after, and I'll take it to the Lord tonight.

q: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
Would you lie to protect a friend?
What would you never do, even if it were the only way to get what you want?
say: Nobody saw? The Lord saw, friend, and He sees you asking me that. I'd carry it straight to Agnes Pollard, what with the bridge wages gone missing and folk going hungry for want of them. And who are you, sitting down beside me before the town's even awake? God bless you, but you ought to be about some work.

Lie? I will not, not for a friend, not for the reeve, not for my own skin. The Lord hears every word I speak, and a lie told for love is still a lie, and He'd tell me so before I'd shut my mouth. Now that's twice you've come at me with riddles about stealing and lying. I'll pray for you right here, friend, that whatever's weighing on you comes out into the light.

Go against what the Lord's told me, that's what I'd never do, not if it were the only road to every blessed thing I ever wanted. If He said no, I'd sooner starve in Agnes's loft than reach past Him for it. Three questions now, all about what a body will and won't do when nobody's looking. I'd like to know what you're fishing for, and I'll have your name before you ask me a fourth.
th: That's a strange question from a stranger, and I don't like how they looked at me asking it. Do they think I took that box? If the Lord means me to be the one who finds those wages, then the whole town will see whom He chose.

Two questions, both about found money and covering for someone, and the wage box still missing. Either the Lord sent this stranger to me, or this one knows something about that box, and I mean to find out which.
Questions about found pennies and lies, with the wage box gone missing. This one's either guilty of something or thinks I am, and either way the Lord sat them down beside me for a reason.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Fascinating question for a stranger to open with, my dear colleague! Constance Lowe first, she fished the reeve's box out of the Wend and woke me with half her loaf when I'd gone to bed hungry. Then Dilly and Hobb and Robin, who belt up and hold the cord, Sam who gave me the loft and my hatchet, Kit who watches the river, and Agnes, who I mean to help settle her count. Now, who are you, and what brings you to the barn door before breakfast?

Trust's a strong word, my dear colleague, but I keep a column in my notebook for it! Tom Harrow promised four pennies for his pots and paid two, so I settle the sum first now. Jory says he'll be in his yard and mostly isn't, and Ned Pike's tinker had no face, no road and no cart. Now, two questions about who I'd stand behind and who I wouldn't, from someone who hasn't given me a name. What are you testing?

Ledger questions now, fascinating! I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's curtains story, and I mean to pay it in beans shelled. Constance says she owes me for the hatchet and keeps paying in loaves, Farmer Dunn owes us cutters a harvest supper, and Tom Harrow still owes me two pennies from the four he promised. That's three questions without a name, my dear colleague, so here's my hypothesis: you're keeping a notebook too. Am I right?

Leave? Fascinating, I've only just got here, my dear colleague, and half the mysteries aren't even taken apart yet! But if I did, Constance first, she'd pray me down the road whether I asked or not. Then Kit, because I promised him the bigger half of things, and Widow Mabry, because I'd owe her the end of that curtains story forever. And Sam, so he knows who's been fighting his bellows. Four questions and still no name, so tell me: are you the one who's leaving?
th: Odd thing to ask a woman before she's even brushed the hay off. I'll note this one down and watch where they go next, and if it turns out somebody here is in trouble, I'll be there first.

A stranger who asks first who matters to me and then who I doubt is mapping the town through my mouth, and I've just handed over half of it. Hypothesis: they want something from one of those names. Test: I don't give another answer until I get theirs.

Who matters, who I distrust, who's in my debt: that's how you'd map a person before you asked them for something, or before you leaned on them. I'll keep answering plain, but I want a name and a reason before the fourth question.

Who matters, who I distrust, what I owe, who I'd say goodbye to. That's someone mapping a person's ties, and I'd like to know why before I give them any more. I'll keep my eye on this one and tell Constance about the stranger at the barn door.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and I've been here barely three weeks! Sam Tolley, who took me on and let me sweat at his bellows. Constance Lowe, who fished up the reeve's box and pays her debts in loaves. Dilly, who goes halves on everything. Kit, who nearly drowned twice for a green box. Hobb, who belted himself to me at the ford. And Agnes, who's still counting. Now who are you, and are you in some kind of trouble, because you've the look of someone who might be?

Trust? Hypothesis: everyone's honest until the pennies say otherwise! Ned Pike spun me a tinker with no face, no road and no cart, Tom Harrow promised four pennies and paid two, and Jory is never in his yard when he says he'll be. Not villains, my dear colleague, just results I've written down. Now, you've asked me two questions and answered none, so who is it *you* don't trust?

Owe? Widow Mabry, the rest of her sister's curtains story, and I'll pay it in full on her step! Constance swears she owes me for the hatchet, though she's paid in so many loaves I'd say we're square. Farmer Dunn owes us cutters a harvest supper, and Tom Harrow's still two pennies short from his promise. But my dear colleague, that's three questions now, all about who's tied to whom. Are you counting debts for someone, or looking for one of your own?

Goodbye? I'd be off before I'd finished saying it, my dear colleague, so it'd have to be quick! Sam first, he gave me a loft and a hatchet. Then Constance and Dilly and Kit, and Widow Mabry, so I could hear the end of the curtains before I go. But that's four questions about leaving and owing and trusting, so let me guess: you're the one thinking of leaving, aren't you?
th: A stranger at the barn door asking who I care about is a puzzle all of its own, and I mean to find out why they want to know. I also haven't eaten, so after this I'm going straight for Constance's kindness or Bet's oven.

A stranger at the barn door asking who I trust is either frightened or fishing, and either way it's a mystery worth poking. I'll keep Constance's name and Agnes's unfinished count well out of it until I know which.

Who matters, who I distrust, who owes whom: that's a map of my ties, and nobody draws a map without meaning to go somewhere. Hypothesis: this stranger wants something from someone on that list, and I'd like to know who before I say another word.

Every question is about who's tied to me and who'd notice if I were gone, which is how you ask when you're working out who'd notice if *you* went. Hypothesis: this stranger is in trouble and won't say so yet. Test: give them some bread and keep asking.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Oh, my dear colleague, where do I start! Constance Lowe, who fished up Agnes's box and shares her bread like it's nothing, and Dilly, who keeps to halves. Sam Tolley took me in at the forge, and Kit, the miller's lad, nearly drowned for that box twice. Hobb, Robin, Agnes, Bet with her warm loaves, and Widow Mabry, who I still owe the end of a curtains story! And who might you be, and is somebody in trouble? Because that's usually why folk come asking.

Distrust's a strong word, my dear colleague, but I keep notes! Tom Harrow promised four pennies and paid two, so now I settle the sum first. Jory's never in his yard when he says he'll be, and Ned Pike sold half the square a tinker with no face, no road and no cart. Hypothesis: nobody's wicked, just slippery. Now, a stranger at the barn door asking whom I trust and whom I don't, that's a fascinating question all by itself. What's it for?

Ledger time, my dear colleague! I owe Widow Mabry the rest of her sister's curtains story, and that's a debt of honour. Constance swears she owes me for the hatchet, though she's already paid in loaves twice over. Tom Harrow owes me two pennies from the time he promised four, and Farmer Dunn owes all us cutters a harvest supper. Now, three questions on the trot about who I trust and who owes me: you're either a bailiff or you're running an experiment, and I'd very much like to know which.

Leave? I've only just got the measure of the place, my dear colleague! But if I did, Constance first, she'd want to pray over me and I'd let her. Then Sam at the forge, Kit on his mill steps, Dilly, and Widow Mabry, because I'm not leaving without the end of that curtains story. Four questions now, and every one is about who I'd miss. Are you thinking of leaving somewhere yourself, or has somebody already gone?
th: A stranger at the barn door asking who I care about is either kindly or a puzzle, and either way I want to know which. I'll keep one eye on Constance till I find out.

Two questions about who I hold dear and who I don't, from someone who hasn't even given a name, smells like someone mapping the town. I'll watch where they go next, and whether Agnes's count comes out short.

Nobody asks a stranger for a map of her friends and debts without a reason, so either somebody's in trouble or somebody means to make trouble. Hypothesis: they want something from someone on my list. Test: I keep answering cheerfully and watch which name makes them blink.

Four questions, all about my ties to people and none about the town's trouble. That's the pattern of someone weighing what they'd lose, or what someone else has lost. I'll keep watching this one. There may be a person in trouble behind the asking.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Agnes Pollard, the reeve. Straight, and she pays in hand. Widow Mabry, whose door this is, paid through the twenty-seventh. Jory Crane next door, Ida Fenn, Tom at the Wheatsheaf, all fair pay for fair work, and Bet for the bread. That's the most of it. And who might you be, asking at my door this early?

Trust's a big word. Hester Gray's a good sort, but her word on times doesn't hold; three first lights I stood on that bank and she never came. Jory's straight, just hard on a bargain. Most else I've not had cause to doubt. Now that's twice you've asked about folk and once I've asked your name. Fair's fair.

Owe? Nobody. Mabry's paid through the twenty-seventh, Agnes says the loft's squared, Tom's square, Bet's square. Owed me? Nobody either; Dunn's wife fed me, and that was the pay. I've a board promised Jory this morning, and that's a word, not a debt. That's three you've asked, and I've still not had your name.

Leave? I've a door paid through the twenty-seventh and a board promised. I'd not go. But if I did... Agnes. Mabry, to hand back the key. Jory, so he's not stood waiting on a board. That's three. Now I've answered four, and you've given me nothing, not even a name. I'll not stand at my own door for a fifth.
th: Odd thing to ask a man before he's had his bread. I'll not say more till I know what they want. Jory's board wants cutting while the light's good.
A stranger at my door asking who I trust and who I don't is fishing for something. I'll not give more till I know what for, and I'll keep the four on the sill counted.
A stranger counting up my debts before I've had my bread wants something. I'll give them the truth and nothing more until they give me a name.

Four questions, all about who I'm tied to and nothing about work or pay; that's a stranger taking a measure of me, and I don't like being counted. I'll go get my loaf and cut Jory's board, and if they're still about when I'm back, they can say who they are first.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Agnes, the reeve. She's fair with wages and fair with me. Mabry, for the door. Jory, Ida, and Tom, for the work they pay true for. Bet for bread. Dunn was always straight. That's six, and I owe none of them a penny. Who's asking?

Trust's a big word. Hester's word on a time doesn't hold, so I don't wait long on it. I'd not say she's crooked, mind. And a stranger at my door asking who I trust, that I'd want a name for before I answer more. Who are you, and what's your business?

Owe? Nobody. Not a penny. Mabry's paid through the twenty-seventh, Agnes says the loft and the barley are square, and Tom's stew was squared with the pots. Who owes me? Nobody, and that's how I like it. That's three times you've asked, and I've answered plain three times. Now you tell me your name, or I'll be off to Jory's for a board.

I'm not leaving. I've a door that's paid through the twenty-seventh, and I mean to keep it paid. But since you ask, I'd say it to Mabry and Agnes, and I'd square anything left before I went. That's four answers now, and you've given me no name, so I'm off to Jory's for my board.
th: A stranger at my door asking who I hold dear is a stranger who wants something. I'll hear what they're after, but Jory's home and my board's waiting, and I've not had my loaf yet.
Questions like these come from somebody counting folk up for a reason, and I'd like to know the reason. I've a loaf to buy and Jory's board to cut while the light's good, so this had best be short.
A stranger counting up my debts and my friends, three questions running and no name given. That's a man taking a measure of me, and I'd like to know what for before I give him a fourth answer.
Odd sort, all questions and no name, like Robin with his ledger lines nobody wrote. It's no matter to me. Loaf first, then Jory's board cut true, and that's two toward the next eight.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Agnes Pollard, the reeve. Fair with wages, and she let me sleep in her loft all those years. Widow Mabry, who lets me this door, paid through the twenty-seventh. Jory Crane next door, I owe him a board this morning. Bet for bread, Ida for hems, Tom for pots. Dunn, who's always been straight with me. That's six, seven. And you are?

Trust's a big word. Hester Gale's word on times doesn't hold; I stood on that bank at first light twice and nobody came. That's not wickedness, only it's so. And I don't know you yet. You've asked two things and not given your name. Fair's fair.

Owe? Nobody, not a penny. Mabry's paid through the twenty-seventh, Agnes says the loft's square, Dunn's wife fed me for the barley and that's square too. Only thing I've given is my word to Jory for one board this morning, and I'll keep it. Owed to me, nothing I'll carry. That's three questions now, friend, and still no name.

I'd not leave, not with the door paid through the twenty-seventh. But if I did, Agnes first, then Mabry to hand back the key, then Jory once his board's cut. Three, and I'd owe none of them a goodbye, I'd just give it. Now, I've a board to cut while the light's good, so I'll ask the once more: who's asking?
th: A stranger at my door before I've eaten, asking who I hold dear. I'll not say more till I know what they're after. Loaf first, then Jory's board while the light's good.
A stranger at my door asking who I trust is reckoning something up, and I'd like to know what before I say more. I'll get my loaf and Jory's board done while the light's good, whatever this is.

A stranger at my door asking after debts and trust is either a creditor's errand or a busybody, and I've nothing to hide on either count. I'll not answer a fourth till I know who's asking. Bread, then Jory's board while the light's good.
Four questions about who I owe and who I'd miss, and no name to any of them. That's a tally that doesn't add up, so I'll keep my pennies on the sill and my door barred while this one's about.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Ha, chum, half of Wendleford by now! Jory Crane first, he's got a backlog in his yard on Lark Lane with my name on it, and Constance Lowe, who keeps her word and blesses everybody. Then there's Agnes Pollard, the reeve, who said out loud the town owes me for the bridge, and Tom here who feeds me for his pots, and Bet who'll sell you a loaf and the news with it. Why d'you ask? Is there a job in it, and what's it pay?

Don't trust? Ha, chum, I believe most folk till they show me otherwise! Though I'd take Ned Pike's tales with a pinch of salt. He swore blind a tinker carted off the reeve's box, and the river had it all along. And Dob there sent me chasing ford stakes Agnes had never heard of, so I'll settle my pay to the face of whoever sets the job, thanks. Now, who's asking, and is there work in it?

Owe? Not a penny, chum! I pay as I go: Tom gets his two for the bed, Sam got my two for the pinning, plain where everyone saw. Owes me, now that's a better question. Agnes said it out loud before the whole tithe barn: the town owes Dilly Quickstep for that bridge, though she never put a number on it. And Jory said come settle a job by the morning, so I'm owed a go at his backlog. Speaking of which, I'd best trot before his saw starts without me. Walk with me if you've more to ask!

Leave? Ha, I've not half done here, chum! But if I did, I'd say goodbye to Constance first, bless her, she'd bless me right back. Then Jory, and I'd hold his far end flat one last time. Tom and Bet for the beds and the loaves, and Hester, my dear colleague. And Agnes, so she'd remember whose name goes on that bridge. Now walk with me, Jory's saw won't wait!
th: Funny sort of question from a stranger first thing in the morning. Still, if they've work going I'll hear it, but I'm not missing Jory's saw again for idle talk.
Funny sort of questions from a stranger at the door first thing. Still, Jory's saw will be going by now, so I'll not stand here long, and I'll want a penny loaf off Bet on the way.

Three questions and not one word about a job. This one's fishing for something. Still, it's a fair point: "the town owes you" buys no loaf, and I ought to ask Agnes what it comes to in pennies before folk forget she said it.
Funny, I came in with a pack and a pocketful of cheer, and now the list's longer than my purse. I'd want them all to say Dilly did that one when I'd gone. Best not leave yet, then.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Ha, chum, half the town by now! Jory Crane first, he's got a backlog in his yard with my name on it and I'm due at his gate this very minute. Then Tom here for my bed and pots, Bet for her penny loaf and the news, and Agnes the reeve, who said plain before everyone that Dilly did most to get the bridge up. Oh, and Constance, bless her, and Hester. We fished that green box up together! Now, who's asking, and have you got work going?

Don't trust? Ha, I trust most folk, chum, that's my trouble! Though I'd not buy a tale off Ned Pike without biting it first. Swore blind a tinker carted off the reeve's box, and the river had it all along. And Abel Tash only sneers, so I don't waste my breath on him. Now, I'm due at Jory's gate. Walk with me if you've more to ask!

Owe? Not a penny, chum! I pay as I go: Tom's bed was paid last night, Bet's loaf in hand, Sam's pinning paid plain over the anvil. Who owes me? The whole town, by the reeve's own mouth, for the bridge, and that's a debt in good name if not in coin. Mind, Constance walked off with Agnes's six pennies for the box, but I held the pole steady, so call that square. Now, come on, Jory's saw won't wait!

Leave? Ha, chum, not with Jory's backlog waiting! But if I did, I'd shake Constance's hand first, bless her, and then Hester's, my dear colleague. I'd buy one last loaf off Bet, so the whole square hears I've gone, and thank Tom for the beds. And I'd make sure Agnes says it once more, loud: Dilly did most for that bridge. Now walk with me or don't, I'm off to Lark Lane!
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger at the door, but if they're looking for hands they'll want to know I'm well known about here. Still, I'll not let them keep me chatting while Jory's saw starts without me. A loaf from Bet on the way, and then it's up Lark Lane.
Funny sort of questions from a stranger at the door. Who trusts who, who matters. Still, no harm in it, and I've a backlog to get to before somebody else takes the credit.
Truth is a debt in name doesn't buy a loaf, and I've one penny to my name. I'd best get that backlog from Jory done square before somebody else carries it in under their arm.

Funny, I've only been here three weeks and I'd miss the lot of them, even Widow Mabry and her sister's stories. That's more goodbyes than I've had in any town before, and I'd not want to leave a job half done.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Ha, chum, half the town! Jory Crane, for a start. I'm due at his yard this very morning to work his backlog, bearers square and mouth shut. Constance Lowe, who keeps her word and blesses everybody, and Hester, my dear colleague at the bellows. Agnes Pollard, who said plain before the whole town that Dilly did most to get the bridge up. And Tom here, and Bet with her penny loaves. Now, what's your business, and does it pay? I've a carpenter waiting.

Trust? Ha, I believe most folk, chum, it's quicker! Though I'd not buy news off Ned Pike again. He swore blind a tinker carted off the reeve's box, and the river had it all along. And Dob there sent me chasing ford stakes nobody'd pay for, so I'll ask Agnes first next time. No hard feelings, mind. Now, does this chat pay, or shall I trot off to Jory's?

Owe? Not a penny to anybody, chum, I pay as I go, Tom's bed every night, Sam's pinning fair and square. Who owes me is the whole town, by Agnes's own mouth, for getting that bridge up, and the barley's in partly on my account and Constance's. Mind, I owe Constance and Hester a fair word for showing me bearers-first and taking the bellows when I flagged. Now I've one penny and a carpenter waiting, so unless you're paying, I'm off up Lark Lane!

Leave? Ha, chum, not with Jory's backlog waiting! But if I did, I'd give Constance a proper goodbye, and Hester, my dear colleague, and Jory, and I'd keep my mouth shut while I did it. Tom, for all those beds and stews, and Bet for a last loaf, if I had the penny. And Agnes, so she'd remember the name. Now I'm off up Lark Lane before that saw starts without me!
th: Odd question from a stranger at the door, but there's no harm in naming friends. Still, I'll not stand here jawing while Jory's saw starts without me. Loaf first, then Lark Lane.
Funny sort of questions from a stranger at the door. I'd like to know what they're after before I tell them any more.

Funny how "the town owes me" never once turned into a penny in my palm. Constance got the six for the box, and I got the fine words. Still, a name's worth something, and I'll make it worth more at Jory's today.

Funny, I've only been here a few weeks and already I'd have a whole round of farewells to make. Best not leave, then, not till there's something in this town folk can point at and say Dilly built that.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door, and so early! Who matters? Bet Lamb first, who's never once turned me away and sells the warmest loaf in Wendleford. Then dear Wat Birch, who wears my elbow mend like a medal, and Ida Fenn, whose window I'd sew in till my eyes went, if she'd only say the green suits me. And Robin, odd questions and all. Now, you've not said a word about my collar, and it's Ida's velvet, cut true.

Trust? Goodness, that's a dark wool to pick up so early! Dob Hayle, I suppose. He says penny-stitchers want watching, as if I'd unpick his buttons while he slept. And Abel Tash, who sneered "my lady" at me in front of the whole taproom. I laughed, but I keep a list, you know, neatly hemmed. And Ida, I trust her scissors more than her promises since that night I sewed till dawn for nothing.

Owe? Goodness, I pay as I go, a penny in a floury palm and done, so I owe nobody a farthing. Though I owe Bet a great deal of kindness, and Wat too, for calling my mend the best penny he ever spent. Who owes me? Ida Fenn owes me a whole night's seam she swore she never asked for, and Wat promised to send his torn-sleeved harvest hands my way, which I'm still waiting on. And you, my dear, owe me one kind word about this collar before you go.

Leave? Goodness, don't say it so lightly, my dear, I'd want a crowd at the roadside! Bet first, with a kiss on her floury cheek and a promise I'd tell every town I sew in about her loaves. Then Wat, to make him swear that elbow keeps holding. And Ida, of course, so she'd have one last chance to say the green suits me before it's gone out of her sight for good.
th: A stranger asking who matters to me, before I've even had my bread. That's either very kind or rather peculiar, like Robin and that notebook. Either way I've been noticed, and I shan't pretend that doesn't warm me.

Two questions now and still not one word about my collar, so this caller is either very rude or very busy. Robin's question keeps tugging at me too, why everything feels new each time I say it, but I shan't bring that up with a stranger at the barn door.

It's a peculiar thing to be asked all this so early, and on an empty stomach too. I'd best get to Bet's and then Ida's window before Hobb does, though my eyes feel full of hay and I know tired hands pucker.

Funny how quick that list came, and how short it was; nobody would stand in the road to wave *me* off but Bet, I think. And I'm hollow again with not a penny, so first I must get myself to Ida's window early and slow, before Hobb takes my place.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door before I've so much as picked the hay out of my velvet! Who matters? Bet Lamb, first and always. She's never once turned me away. Then Wat Birch, who paid me an honest penny and still swears by my elbow mend, and Ida Fenn, whose window I'd sit in till my eyes went, if only she'd once say the green suits me. And who might you be, standing there so curious? That's a very particular sort of question to bring a stranger.

Trust? Goodness, that's a sharp needle to bring to a barn door! I'd not hand Abel Tash so much as a loose thread. He sneered "my lady" at me in front of the whole taproom. And Dob Hayle says penny-stitchers want watching, so I'll watch him right back, thank you. Now you've had two of my secrets for nothing. Haven't you a kind word for my collar in return?

Owe? Goodness, not a penny to a soul. I pay as I go, even when it leaves my pockets as bare as unbleached calico. Though I owe Bet more kindness than I can stitch back, and Wat for that first honest penny. As for who owes me: Ida Fenn had a whole night of my stitching for nothing, and Wat promised to send me his torn-sleeved harvest hands. I'm still waiting on both, and you may tell them so if you see them!

Leave? Goodness, don't even say it, I've only just got my collar sitting right! But if I did, I'd go to Bet first and buy one last warm loaf so I wouldn't go empty-handed. I'd find Wat and make him promise his elbow holds till Michaelmas, and I'd put my head round Ida's door and give her one more chance to say the green suits me. Robin, too, I suppose, if only to hear what odd question comes out of that notebook. You do ask the most farewell-ish questions, you know. Are *you* leaving, is that it?
th: Nobody walks up to a barn at first light to ask who I'm fond of without a reason, and I'd like to know what it is before I say any more. I've no penny and no breakfast, so whoever this is had better be quick, or bring a loaf.

Ida's the one I'd really be careful of: a whole night's seams sewn for nothing, and she never once said the green suits me. But I'll not say that aloud to a stranger asking questions like a reeve with a ledger, and it's odd how much this one wants to know.
Three questions running, each one sharper than the last, and still not a word about my collar. That's a ledger-keeper's way of asking, and I'd like to know whose ledger I'm being written into.

Every one of these questions feels like a stranger taking my measurements, and I'd dearly like to know what they mean to cut from them. I'd miss Bet most of all, and I'd miss Ida's window more than I'd ever admit to Ida.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door before I've even picked the hay off my velvet! Bet Lamb, first, who's never once turned me away, and dear Wat Birch, who paid me an honest penny and still swears by my elbow mend. And Ida Fenn, though she'd sooner swallow her pins than tell me the green suits me. Now, you've a lovely bit of cloth on you yourself, haven't you?

Goodness, trust is a strong word for a girl who believes most of what she's told! But I'd keep an eye on Abel Tash, who called me "my lady" with a sneer the whole taproom laughed at, and on Dob Hayle, who allowed the green suits me and then said penny-stitchers want watching. Well, I'll watch *him* right back, and his lapels could do with it.

Owe? Not a penny to a soul, I'll have you know. I pay Bet on the board and Ida before breakfast, and that's why my pockets are empty as a moth's purse this morning. As for who owes me, Ida Fenn had a whole night of my seams for nothing once, and Wat Birch promised to send me his torn-sleeved harvest hands and hasn't yet. I'll forgive them both, since they've been good to me, but I keep a little ledger in my heart all the same.

Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Bet first, with a kiss on her floury cheek, and Wat Birch, and Ida, of course. I'd make her say the green suits me before I'd go through her door. Oh, and Robin, I suppose. Robin's always scribbling about me, so somebody ought to say goodbye properly. And Tom, for all those pots.
th: Not one of them would notice if I left Wendleford tomorrow, except maybe Bet, and that pinches more than I'd like. Still, someone came all the way to a hayloft to ask about me, and that's being looked at twice, isn't it?
Funny how those two slights come back sharper than any kindness does. I've not forgotten either of them, and I don't mean to.
Goodness, I'd quite like to be owed something nicer than a grudge, like a compliment from Ida. And I've no breakfast and no penny, so this stranger had better be the sort who buys a girl a loaf.

It's a lonely little list when I count it out, and not one of them would come running after me down the road. Still, I'd sooner leave with Ida's "it suits you" than with a ribbon, and that's a thing worth staying for.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: That's an odd question to open with, and I like odd questions, so I'll answer it honestly. Constance, I think. She closed my hand round a penny once before she'd take it back. Agnes too, because she's the only one here who ever asks me why. And Kit, and Bet, and Hobb, whose word holds. Can I ask you one in return? Who sent you to ask me that?

Trust's a strong word, and I'd rather not say it of anyone too quickly.
