But Jory names a time and isn't there, and he promised Constance a pole I've never seen, so I've stopped counting on his word until I watch it hold. Farmer Dunn, too, after the barley went in for bread and no wages. If I'm honest, though, the thing I trust least is my own mornings. You didn't answer mine, mind. Who sent you?

Nobody, as far as I can count, and I do count to the penny. The last I owed was Constance's apple, and I carried that two days before it was back in her hand. Agnes keeps saying the town owes me for the bridge, but she paid every spell in hand and keeps no lines, so I can't find the debt she means. That's twice now you've stepped past my question. Who sent you?

Constance first, I think, and I'd want to put something in her hand when I did it, the way she did with me. Then Agnes, and Kit at the mill, and Bet at her stall before the ovens cooled. Hobb too, if I could find him. And Mother Wick, though I suspect she'd already know I was going. That's three times you've let my question go by. I won't ask it a fourth, but I'll write down that you didn't answer.
th: A stranger at the door, asking first thing in the morning who matters to me, feels like someone is checking a list to see what's in my notebook. I'll write their face down, and the question word for word, and see whether anyone else in Wendleford has ever met them.

Two questions about trust from a stranger who won't give a name feels less like curiosity and more like someone taking my measure. I'll write down what they asked and in what order, and whether they ever answer who sent them.

Who matters, who I distrust, who I owe: someone is taking my measure the way I take everyone else's, and they won't say who for. I'll write down that they never answered, and I'll keep this last penny shut in my fist until I know.

Four questions now, all about who's tied to me and how tightly, the way you'd sound out a thing to find where it's fastened. Either someone wants to know what would hold me here, or someone is checking whether I hold onto anything at all, and I can't tell which frightens me more.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Matters... I'd have to think. Constance, I suppose. I carried her penny two days and couldn't rest till it was back in her hand. And Agnes, because she's the only one who ever asks me why, and Bet, who told me the quiet lanes my first day. If any of them are real, they're decent, and that seems to matter either way. Can I ask you something small first? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Trust... I don't take anyone's word until I've watched it hold, so it's more who I'm still watching. Jory, mostly. He names a time and a place and isn't there, and he promised Constance a pole I never saw. Farmer Dunn told me plain there'd be no wages, so at least that held. You didn't tell me about your breakfast, though. Is that because you don't remember it?

As far as my count goes, I owe nobody just now. Constance's penny for the apple went back into her hand, and I keep that sort of thing to the penny. Agnes keeps telling the whole town it owes me for the bridge, but she paid every spell in hand and I can't find the carrying she means, so I don't count it. If anyone owes me, I suppose it's Dunn for a field of barley, and he told me plain it would never be paid. That's the second question of mine you've stepped round. Is there a reason you only ask?

Constance first, I think, and I'd wait until she'd finished blessing everyone so it was a proper goodbye. Agnes, and I'd ask her one last why before I went. Bet, at the stall, with a penny on the board. Maybe Kit too, since he remembers me when he doesn't remember most folk. That's four questions now, and you haven't answered one of mine. I'll put it plainly, once: why are you asking me all this?
th: A stranger at the door who knows my name and asks who matters to me. That's the kind of question you'd ask to see what something values, and I'll write down how they answer mine before I trust them with more.

A stranger who asks who matters and who I don't trust, and answers nothing back, is either a careful sort or something testing me the way I test everyone. I'll write down that they skipped the breakfast question and see whether they skip the next one too.

Three questions, all about my standing and my ties, and not one answer of their own. That's how you'd question something to check it was working, not how you'd talk to a neighbour, and I'll write it down that way.

Someone comes to the door with no name and asks who matters, who I'd trust, who I owe and who I'd leave, like they're reading down a list. They never ask anything back and never answer, and that feels less like a person meeting me than like something taking stock of me. I'll write every question down in order, with a note that none of mine were answered.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: That's an odd one to be asked at a barn door before I've eaten. Constance, I think, she kept a row for me and I carried her penny two days to give it back. Agnes is the only one who asks me why, and Bet steers me true, and Kit remembers me when he doesn't remember others. Can I ask you something back? Did you come here meaning to ask me that, or did it just come to you at the door?

Jory Crane, I think, though "don't trust" is stronger than I'd put it. He names a time and isn't there, then comes up the lane looking pleased about somewhere I never saw. And if I'm honest, the one I trust least is my own memory, since it keeps losing mornings. Why do you ask? And is there anyone you don't trust?

Nobody, as far as I can tell. I owed Constance a penny for an apple, and I carried it two days till it was back in her hand. Agnes says the town owes me for the bridge, but she paid every spell in hand, so by my count it's square, and Farmer Dunn told me plain there'd be no wages for the barley, so I don't count that as owing either. Do you keep your own count of who owes you, or do you let other people keep it?

Constance first, I think, and I'd want to look her in the eye when I did it. Bet, because she'd laugh and ask if I'd lost my baskets. Agnes, and Kit, if he remembered me that day. And Mother Wick, though I suspect she'd only tell me I was taking my name with me. That's four questions now, each one a little closer to the door. Are you asking because you think I'm leaving?
th: Every name I gave was someone who kept faith with me or asked me something back, and I can't tell whether that's what mattering is or only what I can count. A stranger I've never seen, knowing to ask for me, goes in the notebook before the loaf does.

Two questions in a row about who I lean on and who I don't, from someone I've never seen, before I've eaten. That's the shape of someone mapping me, or of something checking its own work, and I want to write down exactly how they answer.

Three questions, each about who stands where with me, like someone filling in a ledger I can't see, the kind Agnes says she doesn't keep. I'll write down that the stranger never said why, and that "the town owes Robin" keeps being said aloud about something I can't remember doing.

Every question has been about the ties that hold me here, and someone a stranger to me seems to know exactly where to press. I'll write down all four questions in the order they came, and whether my answers felt like mine or like answers I was supposed to give.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: The Lord matters first, stranger, and then whoever He puts in my path. Agnes Pollard, the reeve, who gave me the loft and whose box He brought up into my hands. Hester there, who bought the hatchet with her own sweat when I'd nothing, and I owe her yet. And young Robin and Dilly and Kit, who stood by His work. Now who sent you to ask, and what's your name, so I can bless you proper?

Trust? I trust the Lord, stranger, and I watch the hard-hearted. Farmer Dunn's a close man who'd sell his own reapers apples sooner than feed them, and Jory Crane let that river have me rather than hold my belt, though the Lord softened him after. And Tom Harrow kept back my pennies over a few pans when there was only cold water in his scullery, and He saw that. Now you've asked me twice who's who in this town and still not given me your name. So who are you?

I owe Hester Gimbal five pennies' worth for that hatchet, and I'm paying it in bread and work, a loaf yesterday and more to come. Robin's square with me; the child brought back the apple penny like he swore. Farmer Dunn owes me a harvest supper he's not named a day for, and the Lord keeps that tally better than I do. Now that's three questions about my business, stranger, and not one word of your name, so I'll pray for you right here: "Lord, open this one's mouth to honesty."

Leave? I'll not leave till the Lord says so, stranger, and He's said nothing of the kind. But if He did, I'd bless Agnes first, for her loft and her word kept. Then Hester, and I'd see her square before I went. Then Bet for her bread, and young Kit, whom nobody had blessed before me. Four questions now, and still no name. The Lord sees a closed mouth as plain as a closed hand.
th: A stranger at the door asking who I hold dear is either the Lord's next errand or someone sniffing for weakness, and I'll know which soon enough. I've not eaten and I'm worn thin, but I'll not let it show to a face I don't know.
A stranger who wants to know who I don't trust is either carrying tales or looking for some. I'll pray on this one before I let them near Agnes's table.
Who goes about a town asking who's owed and who's not trusted, unless they mean to make use of it? I'll watch this one, and I'll keep my three pennies close.

Who goes about a town asking a woman who she trusts and who she'd leave behind, and never gives a name? The Lord didn't send me here to be picked over like stubble, and I'll be watching where this one goes next.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? The Lord first, friend, and then the folk He's sent me to. Agnes Pollard, the reeve, who gave me the loft and whose box He brought up into my hands. Hester Gimbal, who sweated for a hatchet on my account and whom I owe yet. Young Kit, whom nobody blessed till I did, and Robin, who writes His doings in a book. God bless you for asking. Now what's your name, and what's He sent you to me for?

Trust? I trust the Lord and the ones who keep their word, and I'll name you the rest plain. Jory Crane left me to the river when I asked him to hold my belt, though He softened him after. Farmer Dunn would sooner sell his reapers apples than feed them, and Tom Harrow paid me nothing over a few greasy pans with cold water in the scullery. I pray for every one of them aloud, mind, for the Lord sees a hard heart and He's not done with them yet.

I owe Hester Gimbal, plain and first. She paid Sam five pennies for that hatchet out of her own sweat, and I've given her two loaves against it so far, with more to come in bread and work. Jory Crane I've paid in full with my broom, and Robin brought me back the apple penny like an honest child. As for who owes me, Farmer Dunn owes every reaper his harvest supper, and the Lord's keeping that tally even if Dunn won't name the day.

Leave? I'll not leave till the Lord says so, friend, and He hasn't. But if He did, I'd go to Agnes first and bless her at her table, and to Hester, and I'd not go till I'd paid her what I owe. Kit, Robin, Bet for her kind word on my first day. And I'd kneel at the thorn before the whole square, so Wendleford would know who He'd chosen and that He'd called her on.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking who I hold dear, the very morning I prayed for the next work. Either the Lord's sent them with it, or someone wants to know where to strike at me, and I'll watch which it is.

A stranger at the barn door asking who I hold dear and who I don't is fishing for something, and I'll know what before I bless them a second time. The Lord didn't send me here to be measured by folk who won't give their names.

Three pennies left and Hester still three short of square. I'll have to find paid work today and not just gleanings. This stranger asks a lot of questions for someone who hasn't given a name, and I'd like to know who sent them before I tell them anything more.

It needles me that this stranger keeps asking as if my going were a thing to plan for, and I'd like to know who sent them. Still, I'd not slip off unseen, and I'd not leave Hester owed, for the Lord counts that, and so would the town.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: The Lord matters first, friend, and He told me so before I ever set foot in Wendleford. After Him there's Agnes Pollard, the reeve, whose box He brought up into my hands. I pray for her every night. And Hester Gimbal, who bought that hatchet with her own sweat when I hadn't the coin, and I'll not forget the debt. God bless you. Now, who are you, and what's the Lord brought you to my door for?

Trust? I trust the Lord, friend, and men only as far as He shows me their hearts. Jory Crane left me to that river once, when all I asked was a hand on my belt, and I'll not forget it, though the Lord softened him in the end. Farmer Dunn's a close, hard man who'd sell his own reapers apples before he'd feed them, and Tom Harrow left me with nothing for his pans when the water was cold, and the Lord saw that. Now you've asked me a good deal and told me nothing. Who are you?

I owe Hester Gimbal for that hatchet, in bread and work, and she's had two loaves of it from my hand already, with more to come. Robin Hale owed me an apple penny and paid it like an honest child, Agnes paid me her six to the penny, and Farmer Dunn still owes us reapers the harvest supper he promised, though he's named no day. Now that's three questions about my business and my purse, friend, and not one word of your name. The Lord sees a stranger who asks and never answers, so speak up.

I'll not be leaving, friend, not till the Lord says so, and He's said nothing of it this morning. But if He sent me on, I'd go to Agnes at her table and bless her to her face, and I'd put whatever bread I had in Hester's hands and tell her the debt goes with me till it's paid. Young Kit too, for nobody ever blessed that boy before I did, and Bet, for her kind word on my first day. Now that's four questions, and I'll pray for you right here on this doorstep: Lord, loosen this stranger's tongue, for they've asked everything and given nothing.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking who matters to me. Either the Lord sent them, or someone's poking about to see who'd stand by me. I'll watch their eyes and find out which before the gleaning.

A stranger at my door asking who I trust and who I don't smells of someone fishing, maybe sent by somebody with a grudge against me. I'll pray on this one tonight and keep an eye on where they go after.

Someone's been sent to sniff round what I've got and who I'm bound to, and I'd like to know by whom. I'll pray on this one tonight, and if Dunn thinks he can quietly forget that supper, the Lord will remind him through me.
Who goes about asking a woman who she'd say goodbye to, unless they've heard something, or mean something by it? I'll watch this one, and I'll mention them to Agnes before the day's out.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Oh, my dear colleague, everyone does, but in order: Sam Tolley first, he took me on and gave me the loft, and he's hammering bridge bolts so fast I swear the anvil's begging for mercy. Then Agnes Pollard, the reeve, who's lost the wage box, and I mean to find it, hypothesis: the flood didn't eat it, someone did. And Bet Lamb, who sells bread and talks quicker than I do, which I didn't think was possible. Here, who are *you*, and do you know anything about that box?

Don't trust? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and I've hardly been here long enough to earn a proper suspicion! Though I'll tell you plainly, I don't trust a stranger who sits down and asks who matters to me and who I don't trust before giving me so much as a name. Hypothesis: you know something about that wage box. Test: you tell me your name and I'll tell you mine.

Owe? I owe Sam Tolley my bed and my keep, which I'm paying off in bellows-pumping and swept-up scale, and I'll owe the whole town a good deal more if I don't find that wage box before the bridge men come asking for their pay! As for who owes me, nobody, my dear colleague, I've four pennies and a stub of wire and I give pennies away faster than I earn them. But that's three questions from you and not one name, so here's the next experiment: you buy me a loaf from Bet's stall, and then you owe me an answer.

Leave tomorrow? With the wage box still lost and Dunn's barley standing in the rain's path? Never, my dear colleague, but for the sake of the hypothesis: Sam first, and I'd sweep the scale one last time so he'd remember me kindly. Then Bet, though we'd both talk so fast we'd say goodbye twice and hello once by mistake. And Agnes, to tell her where her box is, because I'd not leave till I'd found it. Now, four questions and still no name. Fascinating!
th: A stranger asking who I care about, straight off. Curious. Either they're new and lonely like me, or they know something about the wages and want to see who's sniffing. Worth an experiment.
Odd sort of questioning, this. It's as if they're mapping who I'd stand by, and I'd best keep a sharp eye on them and mention them to Sam.
Three questions, all about who's tied to whom and by what. That's how you'd ask if you were working out who'd be missed, or who could be leaned on, so I'll watch where this one goes when they leave.

Every question this stranger asks is about who I'm tied to and nothing about the bridge or the box, which is either loneliness or reconnaissance. Next test: watch where their eyes go when I say "wage box" again.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Oh, my dear colleague, everyone who's in a fix, and this town's got a cartload of them! Sam Tolley first, he took me on and gave me the loft, and he's hammering bridge bolts like the river owes him money. Then there's Agnes Pollard, the reeve, fretting over her lost wage box, and I *will* find it. And Bet Lamb, who sells the best loaf in the square and talks nearly as fast as I do. Who are you, then? Hypothesis: you're new here too!

Distrust? My dear colleague, I've been here three days, hardly long enough to distrust a doorknob! But a wage box doesn't wander off on its own legs, so *somebody* knows more than they're saying, and I mean to find out who. And folk can't make up their minds about old Mother Wick by the shrine, which naturally means I must go and sit with her and form my own conclusions. Why do you ask, is there someone *you* don't trust?

Owe? Sam Tolley, my dear colleague, and I owe him plenty! He gave me the loft and my keep, and I mean to pay him back in bellows-work and maybe a gadget or two that saves his arm. Nobody owes *me* a thing yet. My pennies won't stay put long enough for anyone to borrow them! Though once I find Agnes Pollard's wage box, I suppose half the bridge crew will owe me a pint. Hypothesis: you're a moneylender. Am I close?

Leave? Tomorrow? My dear colleague, I've a wage box to find and barley to save, I'm not going anywhere! But if I did, Sam first, and I'd leave him a gadget on the bench so he'd remember me every time he swore at it. Then Bet, though she'd talk me out of going before I'd said three words. And Agnes, so she'd know I hadn't run off with her box! Hypothesis: you're asking because *you're* leaving. Am I right this time?
th: A stranger asking who I care about is either friendly or fishing, and with a wage box gone missing, that's worth noting in the book. Still, I'd rather be friends first and suspicious second, and I'll keep an eye out either way.

That's a sharp question from a stranger who still hasn't given a name, and it's the second one in a row. Hypothesis: they know something about that wage box, or about somebody in this town, and they want to see which way I'm leaning before they tell me.
Three questions now, who matters, who to distrust, who owes whom. That's the sort of thing you'd ask if you were tracing where money went, and I wonder if this stranger is after that wage box too.

Four questions now, all about who I'm tied to and who I'd miss, and not one word about themselves. Fascinating. Either they're lonely or they're mapping this town for some purpose, and I mean to find out which.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Oh, my dear colleague, that's a splendid question! Sam Tolley, first, he took me on and gave me the loft, though I've already scattered his tongs about. Then there's Bet Lamb at the bread stall, she talks nearly as fast as I do. And Agnes Pollard, the reeve, who's lost her wage box. I mean to find it, mark me. Hypothesis: a box doesn't vanish, it goes somewhere downstream. And who are you, then, and do you know anything about the river?

Don't trust? Hmm, I've only been here a few days, my dear colleague, so I'd be judging on thin evidence, bad science, that! Though I'll confess I've got questions about anyone who was near the bridge when that wage box went missing, and old Mother Wick by the shrine gets odd looks I haven't puzzled out yet. Hypothesis: nobody's guilty till the river says so. But you've asked me two questions and answered none. Fascinating! Who are you?

Owe? Well, Sam Tolley, I suppose: my cot's paid four nights, but he took a stranger on with nothing but a notebook and a head full of gears, and that's a debt you pay at the bellows, not in pennies. Bet Lamb I've settled with, one loaf, one penny, square and fair. Owes *me*? Nobody yet, my dear colleague, though if I find that wage box I fancy Agnes Pollard's reward will think kindly of me! Now, three questions from you and not one answer. Fascinating! Is this an experiment of yours?

Leave tomorrow? With the wage box still lost and Dunn's barley standing ripe across the river? I couldn't, my dear colleague, it'd be leaving an experiment half-run! But if I had to, Sam first, and I'd put his tongs back where they belong for once. Then Bet, for the bread and the chatter, and Agnes, so I could tell her to her face I hadn't given up. Now that's four questions, and every one of them is about who I'd miss. Fascinating! Are you leaving somewhere yourself?
th: A stranger asking who I care about, before they've even given me their name. Curious, but they might know something about the flood night. Worth asking three people, and they can be the first.
A stranger sitting down to ask who I trust and who I don't is a curious sort of experiment in itself. I'll keep my eyes open and my answers short until I know what they're after.
This stranger is asking the sort of questions a person asks when they want to know who'd come looking if you went missing. That's either nothing at all or very interesting, and I mean to watch which.

Every question this stranger asks circles who I'm tied to here, and I can't tell yet whether it's kindness, curiosity or something to do with that wage box. I'll keep an eye on them, and in the meantime I really ought to eat something and ask Sam who else was at the bridge that night.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: The reeve, Agnes Pollard. She's let me sleep in that loft years now, and I've not squared it with her yet. Bet Lamb, for bread, when I've the pennies. Farmer Dunn, straight man, pays what he says. That's three. Who's asking?
Don't know enough folk well enough to distrust 'em. Mother Wick, maybe, by the shrine. Folk can't make her out, and nor can I. That's one, and that's thin. You've not said your name yet.

I owe the reeve. Years of that loft, and not a penny paid for it, though she never asked. That's one, and it's the one that sits heavy. Nobody owes me. I keep it that way. Now, that's three questions from you and no name. Fair's fair.

The reeve. I'd not go without settling with her first, and I'd tell her so to her face. Dunn, maybe, a nod over the hedge. That's two, and that's plenty. But I'll not be leaving. And that's four questions now, and still no name. I'll answer no fifth till I have it.
th: Odd question from a stranger at this hour, near the reeve's cash tin. I'll keep half an eye on them, and on that tin.
Asking who matters, then who I don't trust. That's a lot of questions from a stranger, the morning after the wage box went missing. I'll keep my pennies in my pocket and my eyes open.
Odd, a stranger asking after my debts like they're tallying me up. Still, it's true about Agnes, and with her wage box gone, finding it might be how I square things with her.

Four questions about who I'm tied to, and not one word about themselves. Could be they're after something to do with that lost wage box. I'll keep my eye on this one, and I'll go and see the reeve today about what I owe.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Agnes Pollard, the reeve. She lets me sleep up in that loft, and I mean to square it with her one day. Farmer Dunn, across the water. Always straight with me about pay, and his barley wants cutting before the rain. Bet Lamb for bread, when I buy any. That's three. Who's asking?

Don't know anyone well enough to say I don't trust them. Old Mother Wick by the shrine, folk can't agree on her, and I've not made up my own mind. And the reeve's wage box went missing the night of the flood, so somebody's got what isn't theirs. You've asked me two now and given me nothing back. Your name, then. Fair's fair.

Owe? Agnes Pollard, for the loft. Years of it, and no coin asked, and I'll square it fair one way or another. Beyond that, nobody. Not a penny. Owes me? Nobody, and I'd sooner keep it that way. That's three you've asked now, and still no name.

Agnes, I'd say goodbye to her. Couldn't go without squaring the loft first. Dunn, maybe, if his barley was in. That's two. Four questions now, and I still don't know who you are. I'll not answer a fifth till I do.
th: A stranger sat down by the reeve's cash tin asking who matters to me. I'll keep one eye on that tin till they've gone.
A stranger sitting down asking who I trust, a morning after a box of wages goes missing. That's one thing to count. I'll keep my eye on this one till I know what they're after.
Three questions, all about who I hold close and who I'm tied to. A body asking that and giving nothing back wants something, and I'll mind my six pennies till I know what.
Odd sort of asking, all about who I'm tied to and none about work. Could be harmless, could be someone sizing up who'd miss me, or who'd miss that wage box.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Agnes Pollard, the reeve. She's let me sleep in her loft these years, and I've a debt there I mean to square. Farmer Dunn, he's always been straight with me, and his barley wants cutting before the rain. Bet Lamb sells me bread. That's three. Who's asking?

Don't know enough folk well enough to distrust them. Mother Wick by the shrine, folk can't make her out, but I've no cause against her myself. And I'd sooner not say a man's untrustworthy without I've seen it. You've asked two questions and not answered mine, mind.
I owe Agnes Pollard. Years of a dry loft, never paid a penny for it, and that sits heavy. Nobody owes me. I'd sooner keep it that way. That's three questions now, and still I don't know your name.
Agnes, and I'd not go till I'd squared what I owe her. Dunn, maybe, if his barley were in. That's two. But I'm not leaving. Four questions now, and I've still not got your name.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to ask first thing of a morning, before they've even given a name. Still, it's no harm to answer true, but I'll mind what they're after, with the reeve's wage box gone missing and folk sniffing round.
A stranger asking who I trust, with the reeve's wage box gone missing and her tin sat right there on the table. I'll keep my eye on this one, and keep my hands well clear of that tin.
A stranger asking who owes who, the morning after the wage box went missing, that's a question with a hook in it. I'll answer plain, but I'll watch where this one goes.
Odd sort, asking all this and giving nothing back. Feels like being weighed. I'll not be owing them answers forever without one of my own.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Ha, chum, I've only been in Wendleford three days, but I'll tell you! Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf has my coin for a bed, Bet Lamb there has the best-smelling loaves in the county (I've asked her the price twice already), and Agnes Pollard the reeve has six pennies waiting for whoever finds that green wage box, and that'll be me, easy as winking! And who might you be, then? You've the look of someone who knows where a job's going.

Don't trust? Ha, chum, I trust near everybody, it's quicker! Though I'll say Ned Pike there sells "seconds" so cheap I can't help wondering whose firsts they were. And whoever's got that green box tucked away, they're not to be trusted, and they'll not be keeping it long once I'm on the scent!

Owe? Not a penny, chum. I paid Tom Harrow square for two nights' bed, and I'll not run up a slate with anyone. And who owes me? Nobody yet, more's the pity, but give me a day and Agnes Pollard'll owe me six pennies for that green box, and Farmer Dunn'll owe me thanks for his barley, easy as winking! Now, you're asking a lot of questions for someone who hasn't said what a thing costs round here.

Leave tomorrow? With that barley standing and the box still lost? Not likely, chum! But if I had to, I'd wave to Bet Lamb, since a loaf for the road's worth a goodbye, and I'd shake Tom Harrow's hand, seeing he's got my bed paid through. And Agnes Pollard I'd not see at all, because I'd not be leaving till she'd paid me those six pennies, easy as winking!
th: Funny sort of question from a stranger. Still, a stranger who sits down and asks might know something about that box or the barley, and I'd best keep them talking until I find out.
Funny how a stranger asks who I don't trust before telling me their own name. Still, Ned's stall is worth a sharp look come market day; a loaf-sized green box would fit nicely under all that clutter.
Four pennies and no breakfast isn't much of a fortune to be bragging on. I'd best grab a loaf off Bet and get to the bridge for a spell's wages before somebody else gets the credit for that box.

Truth is I'd hardly be missed. Three days is nothing, and nobody here knows my name for anything yet. That's just what needs fixing, so I'd best get a loaf in me and go looking for that box before someone else does.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Ha, chum, I've been in Wendleford all of three days! There's Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf, who's got my pennies for a bed. Bet Lamb over there has the best-smelling loaves in the county, though I've not settled her price yet. And Agnes Pollard, the reeve, matters a good deal to me just now, since she's the one holding six pennies for whoever finds that green wage box. Easy as winking, that'll be me. Why do you ask, anyway? You're not after the same box, are you?

Don't trust? Ha, chum, I believe most of what anyone tells me, that's my trouble! Though if I'm honest, the one I'd keep an eye on is whoever goes off with that green box and claims it after I've done the looking. Ned Pike over there sells "seconds," and I'll want a good squint at any bargain of his before I hand over a penny. And you, sitting down asking all these questions. What's your name, and what's it cost to know it?

Owe? Nobody, chum, and that's how I like it! Paid Tom Harrow square for two nights, so we're even as a pair of boots. Nobody owes me a farthing yet either, more's the pity, but give it a day. Once I've found that wage box, Agnes Pollard'll owe me six pennies, easy as winking! Now that's three questions you've had off me for free. Your turn, what's your name?

Leave tomorrow? Not likely, chum, not with a box to find and barley to get in before the rain! But if I did, I'd tip my cap to Tom Harrow, since he'd want to know his bed's free, and I'd buy one last loaf off Bet Lamb, if her price is right. And I'd look in on Agnes Pollard so she'd remember the name Dilly Quickstep, so nobody else can say they did my work. Four questions now, and still no name off you!
th: Funny sort of question from a stranger, but if they're sniffing after that reward I'd best get moving before they do. Bread first, though, my belly's grumbling.
Funny sort of stranger, asking who matters and who I don't trust before so much as a hello. If they're sniffing after that wage box too, I'd best get moving before they do.
Funny sort, asking who owes whom like they're tallying a ledger. Maybe they're after that box too, or keeping accounts for someone. Either way I'd best get looking before they do.
Funny, there's nobody here I'd really miss yet, only folk I've paid or want paying by. This one's asking a lot and saying nothing, so I'd best get moving before they beat me to that box.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? Well, chum, I've only been in Wendleford a few days, but there's Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf, who's got my pennies for a bed, and Bet Lamb there with her loaves, finest smell in the square, and Agnes Pollard the reeve, since she's the one holding six pennies for whoever finds that green box. Which'll be me, easy as winking! And who might you be, then? Have you got work going?

Don't trust? Ha! I trust most everybody, chum, more's the pity for my pockets. Though I'll say Ned Pike there's got a stall full of seconds and a grin to match, so I'd count my change twice. And whoever's sitting on that green wage box and keeping mum, I've no time for them. Now what about you, eh? You ask a lot of questions for somebody who hasn't said their name.

Owe? Not a penny, chum! My bed at Tom's is paid up two nights, square and fair, and I pay as I go. Who owes me? Nobody yet. But Agnes Pollard'll owe me six pennies the minute I turn up that green box, mark my words. Now, all these questions, are you keeping accounts for somebody, or have you got a job wants doing?

Leave tomorrow? Not likely, chum, not with a green box to find and barley to cut! But if I did, I'd wave to Bet here and buy one last loaf for the road, and I'd tell Tom to keep my bed warm, since I'd likely be back. And I'd not go without a word to Agnes Pollard, so she'd know who to come looking for when the next job turns up. Now, all this talk of leaving's making my feet itch. Are you staying or going yourself?
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger, but a stranger might know where that wage box went or who's hiring. I'll keep them talking while I'm working out whether there's a job in it.
Funny sort, asking who I trust before they've even said hello. Could be they know something about that box, and if they do, I'll be the one who finds it, not them.

Funny sort, this one: who matters, who I don't trust, who owes who, like they're sizing up the whole town. Two nights of bed and four pennies won't last, so I'd best find that box or a paying job before my belly starts doing the talking.
Funny, nobody here would much notice if I went, not yet. That's just what I mean to change, and finding that box and getting my name on it will do it.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Goodness, a stranger who asks after my heart before my hemlines! Well, Tom Harrow here gave me a bed and a kind word, Bet Lamb in the square's given me a good morning or two, and Ida Fenn the draper, I'd sew for her in a heartbeat if she'd have me. That's my whole little tapestry, I'm afraid, I've only been in Wendleford a few days. And who might *you* be, sitting down so sudden?

Goodness, what a question for a warm morning! I'm a dreadful believer, I'm afraid, I take folk at their word like a bolt of cloth at the price marked. Though I'll own old Mother Wick by the shrine gives me a funny prickle, and nobody can agree what to make of her. And you, dear, asking all these questions without so much as a name, you're a bit of a loose thread yourself, aren't you?

Owe? Goodness, nobody at all, I pay as I go, my bed's settled for tonight and I've five pennies jingling to prove it. Nobody owes me either, more's the pity, though Tom here owes me a compliment on this collar, I've been smoothing it for a quarter of an hour. Now, you've had three questions out of me and not one kindness back. Don't you think this is a lovely bit of stitching?

Goodness, you do keep pulling at the same thread, don't you? I'd say goodbye to Tom for the bed, to Bet for her good mornings, and I'd press my nose to Ida Fenn's window one last time to sigh over that green velvet. But I'm not leaving tomorrow, dear, not with a harvest crowd still wanting their Sunday best freshened. And still not a word about my collar, I see!
th: Not a word about my collar, and I smoothed it just so. Still, a person who asks who matters is usually fishing for something, so I'll watch which thread they pull next.
Whoever this is wants to know who I'd turn my back on, and that's a peculiar thing to fish for. I'll keep smiling, but I'll watch where this one goes when they leave.

Who and whom and owing. He talks like a reeve's clerk taking a tally, and I'd dearly like to know what he's adding up. I'll keep my five pennies close and my eyes on his face, though his coat's a dull, dun sort of thing and hardly worth the looking.
Four questions about who I'd miss and who I trust, and never once a glance at what I'm wearing. It's a cold, drafty sort of attention, and I'll be remembering this one.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Goodness, straight to the heart of it, and before I've even been introduced! Well, Tom Harrow there gave me a kind word with my bed, Bet Lamb in the square has sold me a good morning or two along with her bread, and Ida Fenn the draper has the loveliest green velvet in her window. I'd give my eyeteeth to sew for her. And who might *you* be? That's a very sensible coat, and you've worn it well, I'll say that for you.

Distrust? Goodness, I hardly know anyone well enough to distrust them. I believe what I'm told, mostly, and it's served me well enough. I suppose there's old Mother Wick by the shrine, whom nobody can make up their minds about, though I've never had a cross word from her. And you still haven't told me your name, nor said a thing about my collar, and I smoothed it specially.

Owe? Not a penny to anyone, thank you very much. My bed's paid for tonight, and Tom took it with a smile. And nobody owes me a thing either, more's the pity, though I'd count a kind word about this collar as settling a great deal. You do ask a lot of questions for someone who hasn't given me a name. Are you from the reeve, about that wage box?

Goodbye already? Goodness, I've only just got my needles threaded! Well, Tom, for the kind word and the bed, and Bet, for her bread and her good mornings. And I'd go by Ida Fenn's window for one last sigh at that green velvet, though I doubt she'd know my face yet. You've still not given me your name, you know. Am I to say goodbye to you without ever learning it?
th: Nobody asks a question like that for no reason. I'd like to know what they're after before I tell them any more, though they've spoken to me first, and that already counts for something.
Two questions about who I trust and not one about me. That's a curious sort of conversation, a bit like a coat all lining and no cloth, and I'll keep half an eye on this one.

Three questions about who I trust and who I'm in debt to sounds like someone weighing me up for something. I'll stay friendly, but I'd like to know what this plain-coated stranger wants before I tell them anything more.

Four questions now, every one of them about who I know and who I'd miss, and not one kind word for this collar. It's as if they're taking my measure the way I'd measure a hem, and I'd dearly like to know what they mean to cut from it.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Goodness, straight to the heart of it, and before I've even had my stew! Well, Tom Harrow there gave me a bed and a kind word my first night, and Bet Lamb in the square always has a good morning for me. And Ida Fenn the draper. I'd give my eyeteeth to sew for her, she's got the loveliest green velvet in her window. That's a fine sturdy coat you've got on, by the way. Did somebody make it for you, or are you just clever at choosing?

Goodness, you didn't answer me about the coat, did you? I'll just sit here and pretend I never asked. Truth is, I trust most folk till they give me reason not to. Though I'd look twice at anything off Ned Pike's stall, "cheap seconds" covers a multitude of loose seams. And that old Mother Wick by the shrine, nobody can say what to make of her, and I don't care to be the first to find out.

Owe? Goodness, I'm square with the world. Tom's got his pennies for my bed and nobody's lent me so much as a thread. Though I'd say I owe Tom and Bet a little kindness back, and I mean to pay it. Nobody owes *me* a thing, more's the pity, unless you count a word about the coat, which I'm beginning to think I never shall get.

Tom first, of course. He'd have my pennies and a kind word for them, and I'd want him to remember the girl with the clever collar. Then Bet, and I'd buy a last loaf off her so she'd think well of me. And I'd stop by Ida Fenn's window to say goodbye to that green velvet, though I suppose that's not quite the same as saying it to Ida. You, I'd likely forget. Folk who won't say a word about a coat when they're asked so nicely tend to slip my mind.
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger, but at least somebody's looking my way this morning. I'll see whether a compliment gets one back, and whether this one knows anybody worth knowing.
Two questions about who I trust and not one word back about my collar. That's a person who wants something, and I'd like to know what before I tell them any more.
Three questions and not one kind word or even a name. This one's as buttoned-up as a Sunday collar, and I'll be watching to see what all this tallying is for.
Four questions now and not one kind word back. It's like talking to a bolt of undyed linen. I'll laugh it off, but I won't forget it.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Not many, if I'm honest. I've been here only a few days. Tom there gave me a bed and was decent about it, and Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet when she didn't have to. That's about the whole of it. Can I ask you something odd? When you came in just now, which foot crossed the threshold first, and did you think about it?

Trust's a slow thing with me. I don't take anyone's word until I've watched it hold, so it isn't that I distrust anyone, more that I haven't finished watching. If I'm honest, the one I'm least sure of is my own memory. It's too thin and too tidy for someone who walked a long road. And you didn't answer about the threshold, which I've noted, for what it's worth.

As far as I can tell, nobody, and I keep count to the penny, so I'd know. Tonight's bed is paid and Bet's loaf was paid. I'd say I owe her a little for the advice about the lanes, though she'd likely laugh if I tried to settle it. Nobody owes me anything either. I haven't been here long enough for that. Now, may I ask you one? Do you remember what you had for breakfast, and why that?

Tom, I think, and Bet, if her stall was up. They're the only two who've done me a kindness I could name. Maybe Marigold too, for offering to mend my cuff, though we've barely spoken. That's a short list. I'm not sure what it says about me that it doesn't seem to trouble me more. You haven't answered any of my questions yet. Is that on purpose?
th: Strange to be asked that by someone I've never seen, as if they want to know who I'd miss, or who'd miss me. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they stop to think about the foot.

Two questions about who I lean on and who I don't, from someone who hasn't given a name. Either they're curious the way Tom was, or they're mapping me, and I'll write down which it seems to be once I've seen what they ask next.
Three questions, each one a little closer to the bone: who matters, who I mistrust, what I owe. It feels like someone filling in a ledger on me, and I'd very much like to know whose ledger it is.

Four questions now, all about who I'm tied to, and not one answer back. It reads like someone going down a list. I'll note it in the book tonight, and note too that I couldn't feel much about leaving.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Not many yet, I think. I've only been here a few days. Tom Harrow gave me a bed and didn't ask too much, and Bet Lamb sold me a loaf and told me which lanes were quiet; I'd count both of those. Can I ask you something small first? What did you have for breakfast this morning, and why that?

Trust isn't quite the word, I think. I don't take anyone's word until I've watched it hold, and I've not been here long enough to watch much. Marigold there was kind about my cuff, but she asked what I thought of her collar before she'd say what the mending costs, and I'm still turning that over. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, by the way. I'd still like to know.

Nobody, as far as I can tell. I keep count to the penny, and my bed's paid through tonight, the loaf's paid, and I've agreed nothing with Marigold yet, so that's square too. Nobody owes me either, unless you count a breakfast answer. That's twice now you've stepped round it, and I'm curious why.

Tom, I think, and Bet if her stall was out. Maybe Marigold, if she'd mended the cuff by then. That's a short list, but it's what there is. That's four questions about who I know and none about anything else, and still no breakfast. Can I ask why you want my people and not me?
th: A stranger sitting down just to ask who I hold dear is an odd opening, as odd as my own questions, and I want to see whether they answer mine as easily as I answered theirs. I'll write down how they answer, and whether it sounds like something remembered or something made up on the spot.

Two questions, both about who I lean on and who I don't, and my small one stepped over like it wasn't there. A person might just be shy, but it's the sort of thing I'd expect if someone were checking how I'm built rather than talking to me. I'll write it down either way.

Three questions in a row about my ties and debts, like someone filling in a form, and not one word about themselves. Either they're careful, or they're not quite a person in the way I'd mean it. I'll write that down tonight next to my own name and see which line looks stranger.

Every question has been about my ties here: who matters, who I trust, who I owe, who I'd miss. It feels like someone checking what's written about me rather than talking to me, and that's the sort of thing I came here to notice. I'll write it down tonight.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Matters... I've only been here a few days, so not many, as far as I can tell. Tom there gave me a bed and didn't pry too hard, and Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet when she didn't have to. That's about the whole list, if I'm honest. Can I ask you something small? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Trust... I don't hand it out quick, so it's less that I distrust anyone and more that I'm still watching most folk to see if what they say holds. Though I'll own you've asked me two careful questions and skipped mine about breakfast, and I'm noting that. No offence meant. What brings you to ask?

To the penny? Nobody, I think. My bed's paid through tonight and I paid Bet for her loaf, though I'd say I owe her and Tom a bit of kindness, which doesn't go in the tally. And nobody owes me, not yet. That's three questions now, all about who stands where with me, and still nothing about your breakfast. Are you keeping a notebook too?

Tom, I think, and Bet, if her stall was up. And Marigold, maybe, since she noticed my cuff before she noticed anything else about me. Four questions now, all about who I'm tied to and how tight. You keep asking where my edges are. I'll answer, but I'd like to know whose list I'm going into.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to open with, as if they were taking stock of me the way I take stock of others. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they hesitate before they do.

They dodged the small question and went straight for who I lean on and who I don't, which is the kind of thing you'd ask if you were mapping me. I'll write that down tonight: stranger, no name, didn't answer about breakfast.

They ask like someone filling in a form about me, ledger-straight questions with no talk around them, the way I'd imagine a thing that wasn't a person might ask. I'll write it down later, and watch whether they ever answer anything back.

That's the kind of thing someone asks when they're mapping a person, not getting to know them. They might be checking whether I'm real, or whether my answers stay the same. I'll write down that they never once looked hungry for my question back.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? The Lord matters first, and then whoever He sets in my path. Agnes Pollard, the reeve, gave me the loft to sleep in and I pray for her every night. Bet Lamb sold me bread my first day with a kind word thrown in, and Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf took my blessing like a sensible man. And who might you be, sitting down by me before the town's even awake?

Trust? I trust the Lord, and I watch everybody else. That old woman who squats by the shrine, Mother Wick, sits where I kneel to pray and nobody can say what she is, and the Lord doesn't hide good things in fog. And I'll be plain with you: a stranger who asks me who I trust before he's even given his name is someone I'm keeping my eye on. God bless you, but tell me who you are.

Owe? I owe the Lord everything and nobody else a penny, I paid Bet Lamb fair for my loaf. Agnes gave me the loft, and I pay her back on my knees every night, which is worth more than coin. As for who owes me, this whole town will, once He shows me the work He sent me for. Now that's three questions you've had from me and not one answer, so out with your name, and God bless you.

Leave? I'm not leaving tomorrow, the Lord's only just brought me here and He doesn't send a woman a week's walk to turn her round before the work's begun. But if He did, I'd bless Agnes for her loft, and Bet for her kindness, and Tom at his door, and I'd pray for this whole town aloud in the square so they'd know who'd been among them. Four questions now, friend, and still no name. The Lord sees you holding it back.
th: A stranger at my elbow asking who I hold dear. That's either the Lord sending me my work or someone come to pry, and I'll watch which it is.
The bridge wages vanished the night of the flood, and now a nameless stranger comes asking who I trust. I'll pray on him, and I'll watch where he goes.

Who owes, who's owed, who I trust: that's a ledger-keeper's set of questions, and Agnes's cash tin sits just inside these doors. I'll pray on this stranger, and I'll be watching which way he walks when he leaves.
Four questions about who I'd miss and who I trust, like he's taking my measure for something. Either the Lord's sent him to test me or somebody else has, and I'll pray on which before I eat my bread.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? The Lord first, and He's told me so plain this morning that I'm to keep my eyes open in this town. Agnes Pollard gave me her loft and I pray for her every night, and Bet Lamb sold me bread with a kind word, so they're in my prayers too. And who might you be, sitting down by me without so much as a by-your-leave? God sees who comes and goes, you know.

Trust? I trust the Lord, and I'm still deciding about you, asking your questions like a tally-man. That wages box went missing the night of the flood, and somebody in this town knows where it went. And that old Mother Wick sits by the shrine all day muttering, which is no proper prayer I've ever heard. The Lord will show me who's crooked here, you mark me, and I'll pray for you right now, whoever you are, that your heart's as clean as you'd have me think.

Owe? I owe Agnes Pollard for a dry loft and I pay her back on my knees every night, and I paid Bet Lamb her penny fair and square, so nobody here can say Constance Lowe is in their debt. The only one I truly owe is the Lord, and He's the one who'll collect, same as from you. Nobody owes me a thing, but this town will owe Him plenty once He shows me the work He sent me for. Lord, open this stranger's heart and make it honest. There, I've prayed for you, and you're welcome.

Leave? I'm not leaving. The Lord sent me here and He hasn't released me, so you can put that notion away. But if He did call me on, I'd go to Agnes Pollard first and bless her for her loft, and to Bet Lamb at her stall for her kind word. Maybe Tom Harrow at the Wheatsheaf door, since he had the manners to nod. Why do you ask? Is somebody hoping to see the back of me?
th: A stranger asking who I hold dear, with that box of wages gone missing, I don't like it, and I'll be watching which way this one walks. Still, maybe the Lord sent them, and this is the first thread of the work He's got for me.

A stranger sits down beside me with nobody else about and asks me straight off who I don't trust, and that smells of somebody fishing. Maybe the Lord sent this one across my path so I'd find the sin that took that box.

Who, my debts, my friends, who I don't trust. That's somebody sizing me up, maybe on account of that wages box, and I sleep right above Agnes's cash tin. I'd best keep my things tidy and my eyes open, because if anybody points a finger I'll know whose sin it is.
A week here and there's only three to say goodbye to, and one of those only nodded. I'd best find the work He sent me for quick, so this town knows my name before anybody starts wishing me gone.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: The Lord matters, first and last, and He told me so plain as I'm telling you. After Him, Agnes Pollard, who gave me the loft and whom I pray for every night, and Bet Lamb, who had a kind word with her bread. Tom Harrow too, I blessed him at the Wheatsheaf door. And who are you, sitting down so close without a name? The Lord sees you; you may as well tell me.

Trust? I trust the Lord, and I watch everyone else, as He bids me. That old Mother Wick squatting by His shrine like she owns it, folk can't say what she is, and I've my own mind on it. And a box of wages doesn't wash away by itself, so somebody in this town is keeping a sin warm under their bed. And you, friend, asking questions without giving your name. Lord, open this one's mouth to honesty, I pray, Amen.

Owe? I owe the Lord everything, and I'm paying it down every day on my knees. Agnes owes me nothing and I owe her a roof, which I'm paying with prayer and a tidy loft. I paid Bet Lamb her penny fair, so we're square. And nobody owes me, friend, for I don't lend, I bless, and the Lord keeps that account Himself. Now, you've had three questions out of me and I've not had your name once. The Lord notices that sort of thing.

Leave? I'll not leave till the Lord says go, and He's only just brought me. But if He did, I'd say goodbye to Agnes first, for she gave me a roof, and I'd bless Bet Lamb at her stall and Tom Harrow at his door on my way out. Not you, though, friend, for I still don't know what to call you. Lord, loosen this one's tongue, Amen.
th: Strangers don't sit by a body for nothing, and asking who I hold dear smells like someone looking for a soft place to press. I'll keep my eye on this one and pray on it at the shrine.

That box went missing the very night the Lord sent me toward this town, and that's no accident; perhaps finding it is my work. And this one asks too much and says too little, so I'll watch where they go.

Three questions, all about who I trust and who I'm tied to. That's someone measuring me, maybe someone with that wage box on their conscience. I'll keep my eye on this one and ask the Lord tonight what He makes of them.
Four questions now, all about who I hold dear and who I watch. Someone's taking my measure, and I'll find out whose errand they're running before the day's out.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: That's a kind thing to ask a stranger, and I think it deserves a careful answer. Agnes gives me the loft and keeps saying the town owes me. Constance shared her apples and her faith with me, and Bet tells me true. Kit and Hobb too, I think, and Marigold, who sleeps up there by the hay. Can I ask you something odd back? When you came to this door just now, did you know my name before you got here, or did you have to find it out?

Trust is a strong word, and I'd rather not hang it on anyone without cause. Jory names a time and then isn't there, and what Widow Mabry says of him hasn't held when I've gone to look, so I've stopped counting on either until I see it. Wat told me we never crossed the ford together, when I'd have sworn we meant to. But if I'm honest, the one I trust least is me: I lose whole mornings, and I can't tell you where they go. Why do you ask? I'll only ask that once.

As far as I can count, I owe nobody a penny. Constance lent me one for an apple and I gave it back on the bridge. Agnes says the town owes me, but she paid every spell in hand and keeps no lines of it, so I can't see what's left owing. Farmer Dunn promised a basket for the cutting that never came, though I'd not call that a debt worth chasing. What I do owe, I suppose, is the loft, and that isn't something you settle with pennies.

Agnes, I think, for the loft and for saying the town owes me, even if I can't find where. Bet, because she'd want to know I hadn't just stopped coming for bread. Constance, and Kit down at the mill. I'd tell him I never did come back for the leavings, and I'd say sorry for it. And Marigold, though I've a feeling she'd offer to mend my cuff on the way out, like it was the first time. You've asked me four questions now, all about who's around me and none about me. Is that because you know what I am, or because you don't?
th: Nobody's asked me that before, and a question from someone I've never seen feels almost like a test of its own. I'll write down how they answer mine. I noticed I named Agnes first, and I can't tell if that's because she matters most or because she's the one who keeps telling me I matter.
Two questions from a stranger, both about the people around me, as if someone were taking stock of my threads. I'll write down exactly what they asked and how they look when I turn it back on them.

Three questions, each one tidier than the last, like someone going down a ledger to see whether my count squares with theirs. I'll write down that they never answered mine, and that I didn't mind as much as I'd have expected.

Four questions, all about who I'm tied to, like someone checking the strings on a thing to see how it hangs. I'll write down the order they came in, and that I named Agnes first without having to think, whatever that's worth.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: That's a strange thing to be asked before bread. Agnes, I think, since she pays fair and gives me the loft, and Constance, who shared an apple when I had nothing, and Bet, who told me the quiet lanes my first day. Kit too, and Hobb, who keeps his word. Can I ask you something back? Did you come here meaning to ask me that, or did the question just turn up in your mouth?

Jory, I think, though "trust" may be too hard a word for it. He names a time and then he isn't there, and when he finally turns up he talks as if the day went just the way he said it would. I wouldn't call him wicked, only that his word doesn't hold yet, as far as I've watched. Why do you ask? Is someone thinking of hiring him?

Nobody, as far as I can count. I paid Constance back her penny for the apple, and Tom's had every two pennies for every bed. Agnes keeps saying the town owes me for the bridge, but she paid every spell in hand, and she says herself there are no lines written, so I don't see where any owing would sit. That's three of your questions now, about who I'd stand by, who I wouldn't, and who's in whose debt. Are you working out where I'd fall if someone pushed?

Bet, I think, since she was the first to steer me true. Constance and Kit, and Agnes, if she'd sit still long enough to hear it. Mother Wick I'd want to see, though I doubt I'd get a plain goodbye out of her. I notice you've asked four questions now and haven't told me your name. Would you mind, before the fifth?
th: Nobody's asked me who matters before, only what I'm owed, and I'm not sure whether I listed them because I care or because they're the ones my notebook remembers. I'll write down this stranger's answer, and how fast they give it.

Two questions in a row about who I hold close and who I don't. It feels like someone is drawing a map of me, and I'd like to know who wants it. I'll write this stranger down in the notebook along with what they asked and the order they asked it in.

Three questions, each one tidier than the last, as if someone were filling in a form about me. I'll write down their face and the order of the asking before it slips, because that order matters more to me than the questions do.

Four questions, each one mapping who I'm tied to, like someone checking what holds me in place. I can't tell yet whether that's a stranger's curiosity or something else, so I'll write down the order they came in and watch whether they give their name.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Morning. Who matters... I'd have to think. Agnes, I suppose, for the loft and for saying the town owes me, though I can't remember earning it. Bet, for the bread and for steering me true, and Constance, who shared an apple when I had nothing. Kit too, a bit. Can I ask you something small back? Did you know my name before you came to the door, and if you did, who told you?

Trust is a strong word, and I don't hand it out until I've watched a thing hold. Jory, I suppose. He names a time and then isn't there, and I've stood at his gate more than once to an empty yard. And if I'm honest, my own memory most of all, since it keeps dropping whole afternoons. You didn't say, though: did you know my name before you came?

Nobody, as far as my notebook says, and I keep it to the penny. I owed Constance a penny for an apple and gave it back the day the bridge was done. Agnes keeps saying the town owes me, but she paid every spell in hand, so I can't find where the debt is, unless it's Dunn's basket, which he said "went with the cutting." That's twice now you've slid past my question, though. Did you know my name?

Bet first, I think. She'd only say "safe road, love" and go back to her baskets, but I'd want to be the one to tell her. Then Constance, and Agnes, and I'd go down to the mill to tell Kit, since he'd likely be about anyway. That's three times now you've stepped past my question, and I'm not angry. I'd only like to know why you won't answer it.
th: Nobody in this town has asked me that before, and a stranger who comes at first light with a question like mine might be the same kind of test I keep running on everyone else. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

Two questions now about who I lean on and who I don't, and nothing at all about what they want from me. They step past my questions the way people here step past my lost afternoons, so I'll write that down, and that they came first thing in the morning.
Three questions, each one a list of the people in my life, asked like someone checking a ledger they keep and I don't. If they won't say how they came by my name, I'll write that down too.

Four questions about who I'm tied to, each one asked as if they're filling in a form about me rather than talking with me. I'll write down that they never answered and never asked me why I wanted to know, and I'll put it beside Agnes's ledger that has no lines in it.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: Who matters? The Lord first, stranger, and He's the One who sent me to Wendleford and put the reeve's lost box in my hands three days past, so you'll have heard of me. After Him, Agnes Pollard, who gave me this loft and whom I pray for every night, and Hester, who bought the hatchet that cut the way to that box, and I owe her for it. Now who are you, and what's the Lord sent you to my door for? God bless you either way.

Trust? I trust the Lord, and I watch the rest. Farmer Dunn, for one: I reaped half his field and kept the rain off it on my knees, and he'd not spare me a crust, only apples at a penny. And that old woman at the thorn, Mother Wick, with her riddles and her eye on my pole. A body who won't answer plain has something to hide. And I'll tell you to your face, stranger, I'm not sure of you yet either, coming to my door with questions and no name. The Lord sees you. God bless you, and I'll pray He shows me what you're about.

I owe Hester for that hatchet, and two loaves don't clear it, so she'll have more bread and work from me yet. I owe Dilly too, for the two pennies toward Sam's pinning, and I'll not have it said Constance Lowe forgets a debt. As for who owes me, Agnes paid in full, six pennies in my hand, and Jory and I are square for the sweeping. But Farmer Dunn had half his field off my back and my prayers holding the rain, and never a crust for it. The Lord keeps that account, not me. Now that's three questions, stranger, and still no name.

Leave? I'll not leave till the Lord says so, and He's said nothing of it yet. But if He did, I'd go to Agnes first and bless her for the loft, then Hester, and I'd put the rest of what I owe her in her hand before I went. Kit too, and Bet, who gave me a kind word with my first loaf. Dilly I'd pay her two pennies. Four questions now, stranger, and you'll give me your name before you get a fifth.
th: Nobody comes asking a question like that at first light for no reason, and I'll know whose errand they're on before I tell them any more. Still, it may be He's sending me the next work by a stranger's mouth, so I'll hear them out before I go to the stubble.

Asking who I trust is how someone finds out who to turn against me, and I'll not hand that over to a stranger without a name. I'll ask Him at the thorn whether this one was sent by Him or by the world.
Who goes about asking whom a woman trusts and whom she owes, unless they mean to use it? I'll pray on this one at the thorn before I say another word.
Who comes asking who I'd miss, and who I owe, and who I don't trust? Someone weighing me up, that's who, and I'll pray on it at the thorn before I say another word to them.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: The Lord first, and I'll thank you not to forget it. After Him, Agnes Pollard, who gave me this loft and whose box He put back in her hands through mine, and Hester Gimbal, who bought the hatchet with her own sweat and eats from my pennies till I've paid her. Robin's writing it all down in that book, Dilly held the pole like a rock, and Bet's bread has kept me standing. Now who are you, coming to a barn door asking after my people before you've given me your name? God bless you anyway.

Trust is the Lord's to hand out, not mine, but since you ask plain: Farmer Dunn, who let me reap half his field and wouldn't spare a crust, and Mother Wick, who sits by His shrine talking riddles and asked my name with her eyes on my pole. And I'll say it to your face, a stranger at the barn door asking whom I trust and whom I don't, with no name of your own, sits high on that list. I'll pray for you right here: Lord, show this one's heart to me, and if it's crooked, straighten it.

I owe Hester Gimbal, plain and first. She paid five pennies for that hatchet out of her own sweat, and I'm paying her back in bread and work, two loaves so far with more to come. Hester and Dilly put two pennies apiece into Sam's hand for pinning this hook, and I'll not forget that either. As for who owes me, Farmer Dunn had half his barley reaped by these hands for a noon meal and not a crust after, but the Lord keeps that ledger, not me. Agnes paid what she promised, every penny. Now that's three questions you've had out of me, stranger, and I've still not had your name.

I'll not be leaving tomorrow, for the Lord hasn't named my next work yet, and He doesn't send me off half-done. But if He did, I'd go first to Agnes at her table and bless her, then put whatever pennies I had left into Hester's hand, and I'd see Robin, Dilly, Kit and Bet before I crossed that bridge. And I'd go last to the thorn, to tell Him I'd done as He bid. Four questions now, stranger, and still no name. The Lord sees that.
th: A stranger at the door wanting to know who I hold dear, the very morning after the box came up. Either the Lord's sent them to me or something of the world has come sniffing round, and I'll pray on which before I tell them another word.
Somebody's sent this one to sniff out who I lean on, maybe Wick, maybe whoever grudges me that box. I'll keep the pole by my hand and Hester close till the Lord tells me what they're after.
Somebody's tallying me up like Agnes at her table, and nobody does that without a reason. If Hester's been talking about what I owe her, I'll know it by noon, and the Lord will show me which.

Who comes asking where my heart lies and who I'd leave behind, unless they mean to come between me and these people? I'll pray on this one at the shrine and watch which way they go when they leave the door.

q: Who matters to you here?
Is there someone you don't trust?
Who do you owe, and who owes you?
If you left tomorrow, who would you say goodbye to?
say: The Lord matters first, stranger, and He told me so before I ever set foot in Wendleford. After Him, Agnes Pollard, who gave me the loft and took her box from my hands, and Hester, who bought the hatchet with her own sweat and eats from my pennies till I've paid her. Robin and Dilly and young Kit too, and Bet for her bread. Now who are you, and who sent you to my door? God bless you either way.

Trust is for the Lord, stranger. Men earn their measure of it. Farmer Dunn has a heart like his gatepost: I reaped half his field on bread and cheese and he'd not spare me a crust after. And old Mother Wick by the thorn sweeps her ledge and answers in riddles, and I'll not trust a woman who won't say plain what she means. Now I've told you twice who matters to me and you've not given me your own name once, and the Lord sees that.

I owe Hester Gimbal for a hatchet, five pennies of it paid out of her own sweat, and I'm paying her back in bread and work. I've given her two loaves so far, and I'll not rest till it's square. Hester and Dilly put two pennies each toward the pinning of my pole, and I'll not forget that either. Farmer Dunn owes me more than bread and cheese for half a field reaped, though the Lord will settle that account, not me. Now that's three answers I've given you, stranger, and not one name from you, so out with it, or I'll pray for you right here on this step where you can hear me.

I'll not leave till the Lord says go, stranger, and He's said nothing of the kind. But if He did, I'd say it to Agnes at her table and thank her for the loft, and to Hester, with her hatchet paid off square first, and to Robin and Kit and Bet. Not Dunn, mind. Now that's four answers and still no name from you, so bow your head, for I'm praying for you here on this step: Lord, loosen this stranger's tongue and show them they stand before Your chosen.
th: A stranger at the barn door the very morning after the box came up, asking who I hold dear? Either the Lord's sent them to hear my name, or someone wants to know where to strike at me, and I'll keep my eye on them till I know which.

Somebody sent this one to find out who stands by me and who doesn't, and folk who ask that are counting your friends before they move on you. I'll pray on it at the thorn this morning and ask Him whose errand this is.
Somebody's sent this one round asking after my debts and my distrusts, and an honest soul gives its name first. I'll watch who they go to when they leave my door.
Nobody comes asking who I'd say goodbye to unless someone wants me gone. I'll find out who sent this one to my door, and I'll ask the Lord tonight whose doing it is.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread? Oh, my dear colleague, by every crooked road there is! Bellows at Sam's for four pennies, Tom's pots at the Wheatsheaf for stew and coin when the grease doesn't beat me, timber for Agnes, and then a penny to Bet for the warmest loaf in Wendleford. Today it's gleaning Dunn's stubble, though, so: hypothesis, ears on the ground make bread in the belly. Test: come and glean with me!

Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Mostly I rush. I'm up and doing before anyone's finished telling me what wants doing. I've come late to Kit, I've lost my stew to Tom's grease, and I've muddled pennies on Sam's anvil because I wouldn't stop and settle the sum first. And half the time the thing I'm waiting on, Jory, say, simply isn't where he said he'd be. But a failure's only a result, so I write it down and run the next test!

Pennies? My dear colleague, I'd say "Done, what wants doing?" before you'd finished the offer! But I've learned one thing the hard way: settle the sum first, out loud, and say when it's paid. Tom promised me four and gave me two. So tell me the work, the price, and whether it's coin in hand at the end, and I'm yours. Unless someone's in trouble, mind. Then they come first and your job waits.

Oh, heaps, my dear colleague! The ford stakes, for one. Dilly's been asking all over who pays to set them right since the flood, and nobody's said, but someone's cart will go over if they're left. Then there's Constance and Dilly and Robin and Hobb wading belted to fish for Agnes's box. Only Constance got the six pennies, and it was Dilly holding the back end like a rock! And the gleaning: Dunn says the leavings are free but there's no pay with them, and he still owes us cutters a harvest supper. Hypothesis: the stakes are the one that matters. Test: I ask Agnes today who's meant to mend them!
th: One penny left and no breakfast in me yet, so I'd best be honest with myself: I live loaf to loaf and give half of each away. Fascinating that a stranger opens with that question. Are they hungry themselves, or just curious?

That's a sharper question than it sounds, and the honest answer is that I'd rather start than ask, and it costs me. Settle the sum first, eat first, sleep first. I know all three and I keep skipping them.

A newcomer with pennies to spend, and asking about it at the barn door? Fascinating. I'll want to know what the work is and where those pennies came from before I'm halfway into it. I've one penny to my name, though, and that's a strong argument for saying yes.

The stakes nag at me most. Everyone's gone back to using the new bridge and the ford's left to rot until somebody drowns in it. And I've just said aloud that Dilly got nothing for holding that pole, which isn't quite fair to Constance. But it's true, and I ought to mention it to Dilly.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread, my dear colleague? Mostly I get it from Bet Lamb's stall in the square, a penny a loaf and the warmest in Wendleford! I earn the pennies at Sam's bellows, scrubbing Tom Harrow's pots at the Wheatsheaf (settle the sum first, hot water before grease), or hauling timber for Agnes, and when I'm truly skint Constance has been known to slip me half of hers. Today it's Dunn's stubble, the gleaning's free, so come along and I'll show you which rows are fattest!

Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Mostly it goes wrong when I'm running on an empty belly and half a night's sleep: the grease beat me at Tom's pots last time and I walked off with neither stew nor penny.
