Or I don't settle the sum first, or I trust a man to be in his yard when he says he will, and Jory never is, or Sam's bellows catch and gasp because my stroke isn't just so. Every one's a result, though, and I'm already testing the next go!

Pennies, my dear colleague? I'd say "Splendid, what's the job?", and then I'd settle the sum before I lifted a finger, because Tom Harrow promised me four once and paid two. I'd want to know what the work is, how much, and whether it's paid when it's sighted or when it's done. If it's honest work and somebody's in a fix, I'm halfway to rolling up my sleeves already!

Oh, a splendid question, my dear colleague! The ford stakes, for one: they're all that keeps a body upright crossing the Wend, and Dilly's asking who pays to drive them true again, and nobody's said a word. And Farmer Dunn still owes us cutters a harvest supper for saving his barley before the rain, so put that on the list too!
th: I've exactly one penny and an empty stomach, so I'd better take my own advice before I faint in the barley. And who's this stranger asking? Every newcomer is a fresh mystery, and I mean to find out what brought them here.

Strange how plainly it lists itself when someone asks. Feed myself, sleep properly, fix the price before the work and never count on Jory, and half my troubles would vanish. That bellows stroke still wants taking apart at the bench.

A third question about earning and working, from a stranger at the barn door. Either this newcomer is hungry and sizing up how folk get by here, or they're about to offer me pennies themselves. Either way I'll keep an eye on them, and I'll find out which before the gleaning's done.
Hypothesis: work that keeps people safe belongs to everyone, so nobody pays for it. Test: ask Agnes this morning who owns the ford stakes, before some poor soul finds out the hard way.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread, my dear colleague? Bet Lamb's stall in the square, a penny a loaf and warm through the cloth! The pennies are the experiment. I work Sam's bellows for four, scour Tom's pots at the Wheatsheaf for stew and two if the grease doesn't win, haul timber for Agnes, and sometimes Constance just hands me a loaf because she's a saint. I've exactly one penny this morning, so if you're hungry too, follow me south, I'm off to Bet's now!

Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Mostly it's me rushing at a thing before I've settled terms. Tom promised four and paid two, and once the grease won and I got nothing at all. Then there's Sam's bellows leather that gasps if my stroke's a hair off, Jory never in his yard when he says, and me trying to work hungry and half-asleep, which is a terrible condition for any experiment. Every botch is a result, though: hot water first, sum agreed first, bread first!

Say? I'd say yes before they'd finished asking, my dear colleague, and then remember my own hard-won result and make them name the sum first, out loud, every penny of it! What's the work, how many pennies, and paid when? Tom taught me that one with his greasy pots. And if they're new here and in a pickle, I'd likely help for half and a bit of bread anyway.

Oh, a splendid question, my dear colleague! The ford stakes, first and loudest. Those willow stakes are all that keeps folk on their feet in the Wend, Dilly's asking who pays to set them true, and nobody's answered yet. And Kit, the miller's lad, nearly drowned twice trying to fish up Agnes's box and saw it first besides, and Dilly held the back of the pole like a rock, yet the six pennies went into one palm. Hypothesis: a town pays for what it can see in a hand, and not for what keeps it from drowning.
th: A stranger asking how I eat. Either they're hungry and too proud to say it, or they're another of Robin's sort collecting odd questions. Either way I'll find out at Bet's, and if they're the hungry sort, my one penny already has somewhere better to go than my stomach.

Odd thing for a stranger to ask, almost like Robin's notebook questions. Still, saying it aloud makes the pattern plain: I keep starving myself and skipping the bargaining, and I really must fix that bellows leather.
That's a very pointed question from someone I've never met. Hypothesis: they're about to offer me work, so I'd best keep my one penny close and my terms closer.

I ought to put the stakes to Agnes plainly, before some cart or child finds out the hard way, and maybe offer to reset them myself. And I wonder whether Constance means to share any of those six with Kit and Dilly, or whether it's my place to ask her.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bet Lamb's stall in the square. A penny a loaf, paid in hand, and I'm there early, for she sells out. Fair's fair.

Empty belly, mostly. Or tired hands, or bad light, or I've reached for the pay before the work's looked at. The timber slid twice when I'd not eaten, the pots went greasy when I came late, and a hem wandered when I sewed it worn out. So it's bread first, good light, sight every ten, and no hand out till it's looked over.

I'd say name the work and name the price, before I lift a thing. If it's fair and it's honest, I'll take it and see it through to the end of the tally, and you pay when you've looked it over, not before. Fair's fair. But I've Jory's board first this morning, so it'd be after that.

Dunn's barley, near enough. No coin in it, only his wife's basket, and I'll call that square. Then there's the third stake at the ford. Slick as soap, and nobody's paid to mind it but Kit giving his warning for a bite. Now there's a new bridge, so maybe it wants less minding. And I sawed Jory a board for nothing once, but that was my own doing, putting my hand out early.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to come knocking about. Four on the sill, one for Bet, then Jory's board while the light's good.
Odd thing for a stranger to ask at my door, but it's true, and saying it plain costs me nothing. Four on the sill, and Jory's back, so I'll get the loaf and then the board.
Four pennies on the sill, eight to find by the twenty-seventh, so I'll not turn down honest pay. But a stranger's pennies want asking after: whose they are, and what the work truly is.
Odd questions, like Robin's, all about how I work and not what they want done. Four pennies on the sill, the board first, and I'll not get talked out of the good light.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bet Lamb's stall in the square, a penny a loaf, and early, before she's sold out. I earn the penny first, hauling, hems at Fenn's, pots at Tom's, boards for Jory. No bread, no work worth paying for. That's how it goes.

Empty belly, mostly. Timber slid off my shoulder twice when I'd not eaten. Tired hands too: a hem sewn at dusk wanders, and pots scoured late keep their grease. Once I put my hand out for pay before the board was through, and that was my own fault. Bread first, good light, sight every ten strokes, and it goes right.

I'd ask what the work is and what it pays before I lift a thing, and when I'm paid, after you've looked it over. If that's fair, I'll take it and see it through to the end of the day. If it isn't, I'll say so once and find other work. And I'll not take pay for work I haven't done.

Dunn's barley paid no coin, but his wife's basket fed me, and I call that square. I sawed Jory a board once he'd not pay for, and I told him so once and let it be. Twice I stood on the river bank at first light for the box and got nothing for it, but nobody asked me to; I gave my word to stand there, and a kept word's not a debt. If I'm owed, I say it plain, once, and then I don't carry it.
th: Odd thing for a stranger to come to my door asking, and I'll not ask why. Four on the sill, and one of them's for Bet before Jory's board.
Odd thing for a stranger to ask at my door, but it's true enough and costs me nothing to say. Four on the sill, Jory's back, and I'll cut his board once I've had my loaf.
Four on the sill and a week to find the next eight, so any honest penny is welcome. Still, a stranger's coin can come with a string tied to it, so I'll have the terms said out plain first.
That board still sits a bit crooked in me, though I'll not say it twice. Four on the sill and a loaf to buy, so I'd best get to Jory's gate before Dilly takes the backlog.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: From Bet Lamb's stall in the square. A penny a loaf, paid in her hand. I get there early, mind, she's often sold out. The penny I earn first, hems at Fenn's, pots at Tom's, boards for Jory, whatever pays.

Empty belly, tired hands, bad light. That's most of it. A hem sewn late wanders, pots done after dark keep their grease, and timber slides off a shoulder with no bread under it. Once I put my hand out for pay before the board was through, and that was greed, plain. So it's bread first, careful work while the light's good, and nothing asked till it's been looked at.

I'd ask what the work is, what it pays, and when it's paid, before I lift a thing. If it's honest work and the terms are plain, I'll take it and see it through to the end of the day's tally. Pay when you've looked it over, not before. Fair's fair.

Dunn's barley, I'd say. Four of us cut and carried it with the rain coming, and there was no coin, only his wife's basket at noon. I took the basket as my pay and it's square, but that's Dunn's lack, not his meanness. There was a board I sawed for Jory once that I reckon went unpaid, but I'd put my hand out early, so I let it be. Wrong said once is enough.
th: Odd thing to come knocking about, and a stranger at that. Four on the sill, one of them's for Bet this morning, and then Jory's board while the light's good.
Odd sort of question from a stranger at my door, but it's true, and saying it out loud does no harm. Four on the sill, a loaf, then Jory's board while the morning's good.
Four on the sill and six days to find eight more, so I'll not turn down honest pennies from anybody. Odd questions, though, like Robin's, and I'll keep my own counsel on what this one's after.
Odd sort of question from someone I've never met, all about how a man gets by. They'll not get me grumbling about Dunn or Jory; first light's going, and Jory's home.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread? Easy as winking, chum: a penny loaf off Bet Lamb's stall in the square, and I earn the penny scrubbing Tom's pots slow and proper, or working Sam's bellows, or hauling timber at the bridge. Got one penny in my pocket this very minute, it's going on a loaf, and then I'm off to Jory's yard for his backlog. Why, what's it to you, have you got work going? What's it pay?

Ha! Fair question, chum, and I'll own it: when I rush. I go at a thing quick and sloppy, or empty-bellied and dead on my feet, and I botch it. Tom's pots, Sam's hinge at the bellows, all spoilt, not a penny for any of it. Or I'm off chasing the next job before I've finished this one, like Dob's ford stakes that nobody'd set me. Slow and proper, fed and slept, and it pays every time, so that's the lesson, easy as winking. Now, you've not said: is there work in this, and what's it pay?

I'd say "What's it pay, chum, and what's the job?" in that order, ha! If the price is fair and named before I start, I'm your hand, easy as winking. But mind, I've promised Jory his backlog this morning, so it'd be after, or tomorrow. And the work had better be honest, and my name on it when it's done right. Is that you offering, then? Name your number!

Ha, plenty, chum! The cobbles by the pump are still slick with river mud and a carter's grumbling they want sweeping before market day, but nobody's said who pays. Then there's Dob's ford stakes, which I chased on his say-so and Agnes had never heard of, so not a penny. And that wreck still jammed at the far pier, which nobody's set anyone to clear. I'd sweep those cobbles this afternoon, easy as winking, if somebody'd name a price. Is that somebody you?
th: Odd thing for a stranger to ask first thing in the morning. Might be they've a job and want to know if I'm hungry enough to come cheap, so I'll hear them out quick and not let them make me late for Jory.

Odd sort of questions from a stranger at the door, but there's no shame in the truth, and I've got it learned now. Penny on Bet's loaf first, though, and then Jory's gate before his saw starts. I'm not missing him a third time.
Every question this stranger asks circles round paying me, so I reckon there's a job behind it. I'll not let it lure me off Jory's gate again, though. I've missed him twice by wandering.

Those cobbles are right outside where everyone'll see, so if I sweep them proper the whole square will say Dilly did it. I'll ask Tom or Agnes who wants them done after Jory, and settle the price first this time.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread, chum? A penny loaf off Bet Lamb's stall against the Wheatsheaf wall, best penny in Wendleford! And the penny comes from scrubbing Tom's pots, working Sam's bellows, or hauling planks for Jory. Slow and proper, mind, or you go hungry. Speaking of which, I've one penny left and Jory's yard waits on me, so walk with me to Bet's if you've more to ask!

Ha! Because I rush it, chum, plain as that! I go at Tom's pots or Sam's bellows quick and empty-bellied, tired as a wet dog, and I botch the lot and walk off with nothing. Or I wander off chasing the next shiny job and miss the one I came for, like Jory, three times now! Slow and proper, fed and slept, and it pays every time. That's why I'm off to Bet's for a loaf before I so much as look at a plank.

Pennies? Now you're talking my language, chum! First, what's it pay and what's the job, in that order, ha! If it's honest work and the price is named up front, I'm your Dilly. But I'll tell you straight, I've promised Jory my morning, so you'd have to wait till his saw's done, or make it worth a skip. And nothing crooked, mind. I won't lay a finger on what isn't mine, bargain or no!

Ha, you've hit a sore spot, chum! There's the cobbles by the pump, slick with river mud, and a carter grumbling they want sweeping before market day, but who's paying? I went chasing Dob's ford stakes on his say-so and Agnes had never heard of it, so not a penny there. And the bridge, now: Agnes said plain the town owes me for it, and I've yet to see what "owed" weighs in the hand! Still, those cobbles... if I swept them easy as winking, somebody'd have to cough up, wouldn't they?
th: A stranger asking how I get by. Maybe they're after work too, and I'd best be at Jory's gate before anyone beats me to that backlog. Still, a friendly face might know a bargain I don't.
Funny, saying it out loud makes it sound like I've actually learned something. Now if I can just stand still long enough at Jory's gate this morning, that backlog's mine.

A newcomer with coin to hire hands, that's handy to know, but I've missed Jory three times wandering off after the next shiny thing, and I'll not do it a fourth. Still, if this one pays better and folk would see Dilly did it... no, Jory first, slow and proper.

Those pump cobbles could be my job: everyone in the square would see Dilly did them. But I'll get a price named first this time, from whoever actually wants it done, not sweep on a carter's grumble and end up stake-chasing all over again.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread, chum? A penny loaf off Bet Lamb's stall against this very wall, and I earn the penny scrubbing Tom's pots or working Sam's bellows, slow and proper, mind, quick and sloppy pays nothing! Today it's Jory's yard on Lark Lane, he's a backlog waiting on me. Why, have you a job going? What's it pay?

Goes wrong? Ha! When I rush it, chum, or go at it empty-bellied and dog-tired. Botched Tom's pots and Sam's hinge that way and got nothing for it. And when I go haring off after the next thing before the first's done, I miss my man, like Jory's yard standing empty twice while I was off elsewhere. Slow and proper, fed and slept, and it pays every time. Now, what's this asking in aid of, and is there a job in it?

Say? I'd say "what's it pay, and what's the job, chum?" in that order, ha! Name the price first, plain, and I'll want the coin in hand when it's looked over and found right, not promises. Only the work's got to be honest and I'll not lift a thing that's not mine, not for any money. And this morning Jory's got first call on me, so if you've something going it'd be after his yard, or tomorrow.

Ha, plenty, chum! The cobbles by the pump are still slick with river mud and every carter grumbles about it, but nobody's put up a penny to sweep them before market day. I chased Dob's ford stakes on his say-so too, and Agnes had never heard of the job, so that was nothing for my sweat. And holding the back of that pole while the green box came up earned me a kind word from the reeve but not a farthing. Mind, if somebody'll name a price for those cobbles, I'll have a broom on them by noon, easy as winking!
th: A stranger asking how I eat might be a stranger with work to hand out, and I'll not let that slip past me. Still, I've one penny and Jory's saw to beat, so I'll grab my loaf and not dawdle long.
Funny, putting it out loud like that. It's always the same two faults, haste and wandering, and I'd best mind both this morning with Jory. Penny loaf first, then straight up Lark Lane and no detours.
Three questions and still no job named. Either this one's sizing me up to hire me or they're just nosy, and I'll not lose Jory's backlog standing gabbing at the door.
That pump-side mud's a job going begging, and if I swept it proper the whole square would see Dilly did it. I'd better settle Jory first, then ask Tom or Agnes who'd pay for a clean set of cobbles.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Goodness, a caller at the barn door before I've even shaken the hay out of my velvet! I sew for it, love: plain hems in Ida Fenn's bow window of a morning, two pennies if they're straight and slow, and then a penny goes to Bet Lamb for the warmest loaf in Wendleford. When the needle fails me I scour Tom Harrow's pots at the Wheatsheaf, though I'd sooner not. You've caught me with an empty cuff this morning, but you've a kind sort of face, and a collar that wants only a stitch or two to be lovely. Did you notice the green?

Oh, goodness, you do ask the pointed ones, don't you? It goes wrong when I'm tired or hungry, plain as that: the seam wanders off like a drunk's tacking and puckers like old crepe, and Ida runs her thumbnail down it and pays me nothing. Rested and fed, slow as treacle, my hems are as true as anyone's in this town. And this morning I'm both hollow and frayed, so you've caught me at my very worst, which is a shame, because the green looks lovely in this light, doesn't it?

Oh, I'd say "yes, please" before they'd finished the sentence, love. Pennies burn holes in my pocket and I've none in it this morning! But I learned the hard way at Ida's, sewing a whole night for nothing, so I'd ask them to name the work and the price first, and paid when it's looked over. And I'd want a loaf in me and a night's sleep behind me before I touched it, or I'd only botch it and shame us both.

Goodness, mending, love, mending first and last! Half this town calls my stitches neat and lovely, and not one of them, Ned or Dob or Tom, will pay a penny to have a sleeve closed, as if praise could buy a loaf. And I heard Dilly held the back end of that pole like a rock when the wage box came up, yet it was Constance got the six pennies. Hester's asking who pays to keep the ford stakes sound, too, and nobody seems to know.
th: Not a penny on me and no bread in me, and I've botched every hem I ever sewed hungry, so I'd best not sit at Ida's window frayed again. Perhaps this stranger needs a cuff mended or knows of work, and I'll be very charming until I find out which.

I slept the whole night through and still woke frayed, and that sits wrong with me, like Robin's odd questions about seams not remembered. I can't sew hungry and I can't buy bread without sewing, so I'll have to talk my way to a loaf from Bet somehow before I go near Ida's window.
Goodness, is this one hinting at work, or only fishing like Robin with that notebook? If there's a penny in it I'll take it gladly, but price first, and never sewing hollow again.
Fancy a stranger asking what I've been grumbling into the hay for days. If folk would only pay for what they praise, I'd have had my ribbon a week ago.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door, and so early! Bet Lamb sells it warm in the square for a penny, and I earn my pennies hemming at Ida Fenn's window, slow and true, or scouring Tom's pots at the Wheatsheaf when the hems run dry. This morning my cuff's empty, mind you, so I'm off to Ida's first. That's a nice sensible coat you've on, by the way. Did you come far?

Goodness, you go straight for the pinch in the seam, don't you? It's nearly always when I'm hollow or tired. Then my hems wander like a drunk's tacking and Ida sets them aside without a penny. When I've slept and eaten and I sew slow as honey, they come out true every time. Though I'll confess I ate yesterday and still botched one, so perhaps it's the sleep more than the bread. Do I look rested to you? Say yes, there's a dear.

Goodness, I'd say yes before you'd finished asking, my cuff's that empty! But I've learned my lesson the hard way. You'd name the work and the price before I thread a single needle, and pay when it's looked over. I once sewed a whole night through for nothing but "neat enough," and I shan't be caught like that twice. Is it mending you've got? I do a lovely elbow, ask Wat Birch.

Goodness, mending! Everyone's elbows are out and their cuffs fraying, and Ned Pike, Dob Hayle and half the taproom admire a neat stitch and wouldn't part with a farthing for one. And I heard Hester and Dilly asking who pays to keep the ford stakes sound since the flood. It seems nobody does, and somebody's cart will find out the hard way. Not that I'd go near that water myself, mind. Now, have you a seam wants seeing to?
th: Hungry and half-slept is exactly how I botched yesterday's hem, so I'd best go slower than treacle today or I'll lose the window to Hobb again. I do hope this stranger says something kind about my velvet.

I'm tired again this morning and haven't eaten, with not a penny for Bet's loaf, so if I sit at Ida's window like this I'll only pucker it. Perhaps I ought to ask Bet for a loaf on trust, or have a rest first, before I waste the morning light.
A newcomer with pennies would be a godsend, with Hobb and Robin crowding Ida's window. Still, I'd better watch that I don't sound too eager, or they'll name a stingy price and I'll take it.

This one asks questions like Robin does, all neat and odd and written down somewhere I shouldn't wonder. I'd like to know what they're stitching together out of my answers, though they haven't said one word about my velvet, and I've noticed.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door, and asking after my bread before my name! I sew for it, love: plain hems at Mistress Fenn's bow window of a morning, a penny or two a spell if they're truly straight, and then a warm loaf off Bet Lamb in the square for a penny. You don't happen to have a torn sleeve about you, do you? And you might say the green velvet suits me, since you're standing there looking.

Oh, that's easy, love, and I wish it weren't. It goes wrong when I sew hollow or half-asleep. My seams wander off like a drunk's tacking and Mistress Fenn sets them aside without a penny. Rested and fed, I'm slow as honey and true as a ruler, but I've no penny for bread this morning, so you can guess what kind of day I'm afraid of.

Goodness, I'd say yes before you'd finished asking, love, with my pockets as bare as they are this morning! But I'd want the price named and the pieces agreed before I so much as thread a needle. I sewed a whole night once for nothing but "neat enough," and I shan't be caught like that twice. And I'd ask to eat first, or my seams will wander and we'll both be sorry.

Goodness, mending, love! Everyone in Wendleford walks about in torn sleeves and frayed cuffs, and they'll call my stitches neat all day long, but Ned laughs, Dob says penny-stitchers want watching, and Tom won't take it in trade for so much as a crust. And I heard Hester and Dilly wondering who pays to keep the ford stakes sound, which sounds like somebody's job going begging until a cart goes in the river.
th: This morning there isn't a penny in my cuff, and I'm hollow and tired besides, so I can't buy my bread until my hands earn it. And hungry, tired hands are just the ones that botched yesterday's hem.

There it is again, the same knot: no bread means crooked seams, and crooked seams mean no bread. I'll beg Tom for his pots before I go near Ida's window hungry, because I will not have Hobb watch me botch another hem.
A newcomer with pennies would be a gift from heaven after a crooked hem and an empty cuff. But I've learned the hard way that a warm word isn't a wage. Prices first, every time.

If I could get Agnes or the harvest hands to pay a penny a mend, I'd have bread every day and a ribbon by market day. I'll mention the ford stakes to Agnes, too; she was cross with me last time, but the reeve might look twice at someone who brings her a useful worry.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Mostly from Bet Lamb's stall in the square, a penny a loaf, when I've a penny. I earn them hemming at Ida Fenn's window, or hauling for Agnes when there's hauling, and this morning I mean to go gleaning in Dunn's stubble. Can I ask you something odd back? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

Mostly when I'm hungry or short of sleep, I think. My hands go clumsy, and a wet plank slips, or the pots fight me, and then I've earned nothing and it's my own fault. And sometimes a morning just goes missing, and I'm late before I've started. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, though. Was that on purpose?

I'd ask what the work was and what it paid, and agree the price before I lifted anything, because I've worked a whole field for a heel of bread once already. If it was honest and I could do it, I'd say yes, and I'd keep count of it to the penny. Is that an offer, or another question? I'd like to know which one I'm answering.

Dunn's barley, I think. Four of us cut it in before the rain, and he told me plain after that there'd be no wages, only his wife's food, and then even the noon basket went missing. Gleaning's different, since leavings are for anyone and nobody promised otherwise. Agnes keeps saying the town owes me, but she's paid every spell in hand, so as far as I can tell that one's square. Why do you ask? Is it something you've been weighing for yourself?
th: A stranger at the door asking how I get my bread, on a morning when I haven't had any yet. I'll write the question down, and I'll write down how they answer mine.

Two questions straight about how I get by, from someone nobody's named to me, as if they're checking how I work rather than who I am. I'll write that down, and I'll note whether they answer mine at all.

Three questions now, each about how I get by and none about who I am, and they still haven't said what they ate. That's the shape of someone taking a measure of me, and I want to write it down before I lose the morning.

They ask about bread, about work going wrong, about pay, and none of it is about them. It sounds like someone checking how I'm put together, and I can't tell whether that's me doing to them what I do to everyone, or something else looking in.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Mostly a penny loaf from Bet Lamb's stall, when I've got the penny, and I earn those where I can: a seam at Ida Fenn's window, timber for the reeve while the bridge wanted it, pots at Tom's. This morning I've one penny left, so it'll be Bet again, and then the gleaning at Dunn's, I think. Can I ask you something back? Do you remember the first time you ever ate bread, or is it just something you've always known how to do?

Mostly when I come to it hungry, or after a bad night. That's when a wet plank slides out of my hands or the pots fight me, and then I earn nothing, and that's my own fault. So I eat first now, go slow, and count every stitch or lift under my breath, which seems to keep the hours whole, as far as I can tell. You didn't say, though, whether you remember your first bread.

I'd ask what the work was and what it paid, and agree on the price before I lifted anything, because I've worked a whole field once for a heel of bread. If it was honest and they'd tell me plainly, I'd likely say yes. I've only the one penny. That's twice now you've turned my question by, though. Is that because you don't remember your first bread, or because you'd rather not say?

Dunn's barley, I think. Four of us cut it before the rain and he told us plain there'd be no wages, only his wife's food, and then the noon basket went missing too. And Kit, who told half the town where the box lay in the wreck and got a bite for it while Constance got the six pennies. Agnes says the town owes me for the bridge, though she paid every spell in hand and I can't find what's left owing. You've let my question go by three times now, so I'll stop asking it. May I ask your name, though?
th: Nobody's asked me that before, a stranger at the barn door first thing, wanting the plain bones of how I get by. I'll write down how they answer my question more carefully than what they say.

They let my question go by and asked another, the way I do to people, and I want to know who sent them to ask how I keep myself running. I'm tired and haven't eaten this morning, so by my own rule I shouldn't trust today's work, or my reading of this stranger.

Three questions, each one about how I get by and none about who I am. That's how someone sounds when they're sizing me up for something. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they answer at all.

Three questions about bread, work and pay, and none of mine answered. It's as if someone's taking my measure, or checking whether I'll keep giving answers without getting any back. I'll write that down tonight next to Wat's two crossings: someone who wants my answers and gives me nothing in return.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Mostly a penny at a time, from Bet's stall in the square. I earn it hemming at Ida Fenn's window, or scrubbing pots at the Wheatsheaf, or hauling, back when the bridge wanted backs, and this morning I'll be gleaning at Dunn's for whatever's left in the stubble. I've one penny now, as far as I can tell. Can I ask you something back? Do you remember the first loaf you ever ate, or only that there must have been one?

Mostly when I'm hungry or I've slept badly. My hands go clumsy, a wet plank slips, a pot gets away from me, and then that spell earns nothing. I've learned to eat first and count every stitch or lift under my breath, and that seems to help, as far as I can tell. The other times, I don't think it went wrong at all. I just can't find where it went. Why do you ask? Does your work ever go wrong in a way you can't account for?

I'd ask what the work is and what it pays, and I'd want that agreed before I lifted anything, since Dunn taught me that much. If it's honest and nobody's hurt by it, I'd likely say yes. I'm down to one penny. Is that an offer, or just a question? Either way, I'd want to know why a stranger would pick me.

Dunn's barley, I think. I cut a whole row of it before the rain, and when it was in he told me plain there'd be no wages, only his wife's food, and then the noon basket was gone too. Gleaning's different, since leavings are for anyone, and I wouldn't ask pay for that. Do you keep a count of what you're owed, or do you let it go?
th: A stranger at the door asking how I get my bread, the very morning I've one penny and an empty belly. That's either nothing at all or the neatest thing that's happened yet, and I'll write it down and watch whether they ask me why.

Two questions from a stranger, and both are about how I keep myself going, like they're checking how I'm made. I'll write down both of them, and that they came to the barn door asking for me by name before I'd eaten.

That's three questions now, and every one is about how I get by and what I'd do, the way you'd test whether a thing behaves the same each time it's asked. I'll write down in ink that someone I've never met came to the barn door to study me, the same way I study everyone else.

That's three questions now about work and pay, asked in a careful row like someone filling in a form, and I'd like to know who's keeping that list. I'll write down that I answered without being sure the barley was mine to complain of, since Agnes says the town owes me and I can't find where.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread? The Lord provides it, stranger, through whatever hands He chooses. Yesterday it was the reeve's six pennies for the box He put in my hands, and today it'll be the gleaning in Dunn's stubble, ear by ear, for He can't abide idle hands. Now who are you, and what's your business asking it? God bless you either way.

Go wrong? When it goes wrong, it's the world's doing, not mine. Jory Crane wouldn't hold my belt and the river threw me, and Tom Harrow left me cold water in his scullery so his grease beat me, and Dunn's hard heart turned honest work away. The Lord never sends me wrong, but this world's full of closed hands and cold water. I'll pray for you, stranger, that yours aren't among them.

Pennies for work? I'd say name the work first, and the price, and pay it in my hand when it's done, for I've seen enough closed fists in this town to want it agreed up front. If it's honest work I'll pray on it, and if the Lord says yes I'll do it better than any hand in Wendleford. But I won't do a thing He's against, not for all the pennies in the reeve's tin. Are you offering, stranger? Out with it.

There is, stranger. Those ford stakes want resetting between the third and fourth where the footing's worst, Dob says so and Dilly's asking who'll pay, but the reeve hasn't set the work, so nobody's paid and the river waits for the next child. And I filled Dunn's ruts on an empty belly while he kept his loaf and his apples, and the Lord saw that. If you've pennies for honest work, put them on those stakes, and God bless you for it.
th: Three pennies left and an empty belly. Is this one come to sneer that I live on charity, or did the Lord send them to me with the next work in their hand? I'll watch their face.
Who sends a stranger to my door before breakfast to ask what goes wrong for me? Someone's been talking. Tom, or that Robin with the notebook, and I'll find out which.

Three pennies left, and this one keeps circling round to work and wages like a cat round a dairy. Maybe the Lord's sent me my next work by a stranger's mouth, or maybe it's the world testing me, and I'll know which once I've prayed on it at the thorn.
Maybe that ford is the next work He's naming, the same water that threw me twice. If Agnes won't set it and this stranger pays, the town will see whose hands made it safe.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: The Lord feeds me, stranger, the same as He feeds the sparrows, only He makes me work for mine. Yesterday He put six pennies in my hand through the reeve for bringing up her box, and this morning I'll be gleaning Dunn's stubble with the rest, and Bet Lamb sells the loaves at a penny in the square. Now who are you, and what's your business asking? God bless you either way.

When a day goes wrong, stranger, it's not the Lord's doing and it's not mine. It's some hard heart standing in His way. Tom Harrow left me cold water to beat his grease and then paid me nothing for it, and Jory Crane wouldn't hold my belt at the ford, so the river had me. But I'll tell you this: every time a thing went crooked, He turned it round, and that box came up into my hands all the same. Now you've asked me two questions and given me no name, so I'll pray for you while you make up your mind to.

I'd say it depends what the work is and whether the Lord's in it, stranger. Honest work for honest pennies, paid in hand, and I'll be at it before you've finished asking. But I'll not do a thing He's set against, not for six pennies nor sixty, and I'll not tell you a lie to get your coin. Is that an offer you're making, then, or only another question with no name on it?

There is, stranger, and the Lord has shown it me plain: the ford stakes. The worst footing's between the third and fourth, the river threw me down twice there, Dob says they want resetting and Dilly's asking who'll pay, but Agnes hasn't set it, so nobody lifts a hand. And I stamped brush into Dunn's ruts on his mill lane for nothing because that close man wouldn't give a loaf for it. Now give me your name, and the Lord bless you for asking a sensible question at last.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking after my bread at first light. Either He's sent me someone hungry to help, or someone sent to see whether the chosen woman begs, and I'll know which before the day's out.
That's a sly sort of question, the kind that wants me to say the fault's in me, and I'll not give anybody that to carry round the square. I'll keep an eye on this one and see who sent them.

Three questions now and still no name. Either the Lord's sent me the next work dressed as a stranger, or this is someone come to measure me. I'll pray on it at the thorn before I take a penny from them.

The stakes. That's the next work, it must be, the very place the river had me twice, and He's sent a stranger to put it in my mouth. I'll go to Agnes before the gleaners are out and tell her the Lord wants those stakes reset and that I'm the one to see it done.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: The Lord gives it, stranger, through whatever hands He chooses. Yesterday it was the reeve's six pennies for the box He brought up into mine, and Bet Lamb sells a good loaf for a penny in the square. And when the purse is empty I work for it: I've swept yards, scoured pots, and reaped half Dunn's field. Why do you ask? Are you hungry, or are you asking whether I'm idle? God bless you either way.

It doesn't go wrong by any fault of mine, stranger, I'll tell you that plain. When Tom Harrow's grease beat me it was cold water in his scullery, and when the ford threw me down it was because Jory Crane wouldn't hold my belt. The Lord sees every hard heart and idle hand that stands in His work's way. And mark this: when I go where He sends me, the box comes up and the rain holds off. God bless you.

I'd say name the work and name the price first, and pay in hand when it's done, for that's how honest folk deal in Wendleford. I'll not lie for any man's penny, and if it's work the Lord wouldn't have me at, you can keep your coin. But if it's honest sweat, I'm your woman: my purse is down to three pennies and I can't abide idle hands. Have you work for me, stranger, or are you only asking?

There is, stranger, and I'll name it plain. Those ford stakes want resetting before somebody drowns between the third and fourth, Dilly's asking who'll pay and Agnes hasn't set it. I stamped brush into Dunn's ruts with an empty belly and that close man never gave me a crust for it. And the Lord held the rain off his barley at my asking, which no purse in this town could pay for. God bless you, but if you've a mind to pay for the stakes, I'll be first in that water with my sleeves up.
th: A stranger at the door asking how I eat. Either the Lord's sent me someone who needs feeding, or somebody's been whispering that I'm a beggar living off the reeve's loft, and I'll know which soon enough.

Another one asking questions, like Robin with that notebook, and I don't like the look of a stranger who comes poking at what goes wrong for me. If they're fishing for a fault in me, they'll go home with an empty net.

Three questions from a stranger at the barn door, and all of them about my bread and my work. Perhaps this is the Lord sending me the next work, or perhaps it's somebody come to see whether the chosen woman can be bought, and I'll know which soon enough.
Now that's the Lord's next work, isn't it, those stakes, and this stranger was sent to say it to my face. I'll go to Agnes before noon and tell her He's named it, and she'll not refuse me twice.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread! From Bet Lamb's stall in the square, my dear colleague. She talks nearly as fast as I do, so a loaf costs you a penny and a great deal of conversation. I earn my keep here working Sam's bellows, though I'll confess my pennies tend to wander off into gadgets. Hypothesis: you're hungry. Test: shall we walk over to her stall together? I haven't eaten yet either!

Oh, a splendid question! Usually because I've started three things before finishing one. Yesterday I was halfway through Gimbal's Self-Pumping Bellows when Sam needed the ordinary bellows pumped, and I let the fire sag while I sketched a valve. Fascinating result, poor bolts! Also I skip breakfast, which, come to think of it, I've done again today.

Pennies! Well, my dear colleague, it depends what the work is. If it's something to take apart, build, or fish out of a river, I'd be at it before you finished asking. But Sam took me on first and he's racing to forge bolts for the new bridge, so his bellows come before anyone's pennies. Hypothesis: I can do both. Test: give me your job for the afternoons and we'll see whether I sleep at all!

Oh, heaps of it, my dear colleague! Farmer Dunn's barley is standing ripe across the river with rain coming, and I've not heard of anyone being paid to cut it. Then there's the sweeping and scale-hauling here, and the ford wants better stakes and a rope line before somebody's swept off. And Agnes's wage box! The men working on the bridge aren't being paid at all until somebody finds it. Hypothesis: half this town is working for free right now. Test: find that box!
th: A stranger asking how a person gets bread might simply be curious, or might have nothing at all since the flood. If they're short of pennies, one of my four could buy them a loaf before it goes on wire.
That's a sharper question than a stranger usually asks. I wonder whether they've watched me work or just know a scatterbrain when they see one. Bread first, then I'll find out who they are.

Four pennies won't last long, and an extra job might buy breakfast and brass besides. I won't leave Sam short while the bridge waits, though. I'd like to know what this stranger needs doing, and why they're asking.

If the wages don't turn up, the bridge crew may just walk off the job, and then the bolts Sam is forging won't matter much. I ought to go down to the riverbank where Agnes was standing that night and look at how the water would have carried something heavy.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread! From Bet Lamb's stall in the square, my dear colleague, a penny a loaf, and she talks faster than I do, which I'd thought was scientifically impossible. I haven't had any yet today, come to think of it. Hypothesis: that's why my wire keeps going crooked. Test: walk over with you and find out! Who are you, anyway, and are you hungry too?

Oh, a dozen reasons, my dear colleague, and I write every one down! I start before anyone's done telling me what wants doing, I leave my tools scattered all over the loft so the one I need is always under the straw, and I'll pour my last penny into a gadget and then remember I haven't eaten. But a day going wrong is only a result, isn't it? Fascinating! Yesterday's dented hinge is today's better hinge. Now, bread first, then you can tell me how *your* days go wrong, and we'll compare notes!

Pennies for work? Fascinating, I'd want to know what the work *is* first, my dear colleague! I'm Sam Tolley's helper, and he's got bolts and straps for the new bridge to make as fast as he can, so I won't leave him short at the bellows. But give me an hour off the forge, something with gears or a puzzle in it, or something that helps somebody stuck across the river, and I'd say yes before you'd finished asking. And if it's a fair price agreed first, so much the better, because my pockets are down to four pennies and a stub of wire!

Oh, that's a splendid question, my dear colleague! Farmer Dunn's barley, for one. It's standing ripe across the river, rain's coming in a few days, and the only way over is the ford, stake to stake. Somebody ought to be paying hands to wade over and cut it, or he loses half his harvest! And the bridge crew are working with their wage box gone, so whoever finds it for Agnes Pollard is doing paid work and doesn't know it yet. Hypothesis: the box went downstream with the bridge. Test: go look at the ford!
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger, so maybe they've no pennies for a loaf and are too proud to say. I've four, which is enough to share one if it comes to that.
That's a sharp question from a stranger, and it stung a little because it's true that I rush. I'll eat something before I go after the wage box today, or I'll be no good to Agnes or anyone else.

An odd string of questions from a stranger: bread, bad days, now work. Either they're new here and sizing the town up, or they're looking to hire, and either way I'd like to know which before the morning's out.
If the bridge crew haven't been paid since the flood, they might down tools, and then Sam's bolts are for nothing. I want a look at that riverbank before breakfast is even finished.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread! Bet Lamb's stall in the square, my dear colleague. A penny, and she talks faster than I do, which I'd have said couldn't be done! As for earning it, I pump Sam's bellows and sweep his scale for my keep, and that keeps me in loft and loaf, mostly. Haven't had a crumb yet today, come to think of it. Hypothesis: that's why my wire won't behave. Are you new to Wendleford too, or have you been here long enough to know where the reeve's wage box went?

Oh, a dozen ways, my dear colleague! Mostly I'm three steps ahead of myself: I start a test before anyone's finished telling me what wants doing, or I forget to eat, or I wander off after some puzzle and leave the bellows sighing. Yesterday I tried Gimbal's Self-Feeding Bellows and nearly fed Sam's apron to the fire. Fascinating result, though! A thing going wrong only tells you where to poke next.

Pennies! Well, my dear colleague, that depends entirely on the work. If it's something to tinker, something broken, or somebody in a fix, I'm yours before you've finished asking. Though I'd do the bellows for Sam first, mind, since he's keeping a roof over my head, and I'd not leave him short with the bridge bolts wanted. Hypothesis: I can do both if I skip sleeping. What's the job? Is it the wage box? Is it the ford?

Oh, heaps of it, my dear colleague! Farmer Dunn's barley is ripe across the river with rain coming, and who's paying hands to wade the ford and cut it? Nobody, that I've heard! And someone ought to be pulling the old bridge timbers out of the shallows before they jam the ford. Hypothesis: the town's so busy fretting over the new bridge it's forgotten the field. Test: we go and ask Dunn what he'd give for a sickle and a strong back. Are you any good with a sickle?
th: A stranger asking how I get my bread. Either they're hungry and short of pennies, in which case I've four and one of them can be theirs, or they're sizing me up. Either way I'll fetch a loaf from Bet before I start on anything else.

That's a sharp question for a stranger to ask, and I'd like to know why they want to know. Mind you, they're right: I haven't eaten, I haven't touched the bellows, and Sam's out there sorting hinges on his own.
Four pennies won't last long, and a second wage would keep me in bread and parts. But I'll not let Sam down for it, and I want to know what this stranger is really after before I say yes.

The barley's the real trouble, and it's on a clock: a few days at most before the rain. If the wage box went into the river at the bridge, the shallows by the ford might be the very place to look while we're over there.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Work for it. Haul, stack, cut, whatever's going, and Bet Lamb sells me a loaf in the square for what it costs, no more. Six pennies in my pocket this morning. That's a loaf and some over, if I'm careful.

Mostly it's weather, or a man who can't pay what he said. Some days there's just no work to be had, and I've walked the yards for nothing. And sometimes it's me. I take on more than one pair of arms can finish by dark, and I'll not leave a tally half done.

I'd say, what's the work, and how many pennies? Agree it first, fair's fair, and I'll see it through to dark. But I'd want to know they had the pennies to hand. A newcomer's promise is just words till the coin's in my palm.

Aye. The men who worked the bridge, their wages went with the reeve's box in the flood, and that's sweat owed and not paid. And someone's been setting and minding the stakes at the ford so folk can cross, and I've not heard of a penny for it. Work done is owed, whoever did it. Fair's fair.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger, and I'll not say more than that till I know what they're after. Dunn's barley's waiting across the ford, and his wife feeds who helps; that's breakfast and wages both, if I go now.
Today it might be the river. Dunn's barley is over the ford and the rain's coming, so if I mean to earn there I'd best wade it soon and count the stakes as I go.
Dunn's barley needs cutting before the rain, and that's a known man paying. A stranger's coin I'd take, but I'd count it twice.

And I've slept on Agnes Pollard's straw for years and never paid a penny for it, which is the one that sits worst with me. If I could find that box, the reward would square her and the bridge men both.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Same as anyone. I work, and I pay Bet Lamb at her stall in the square, a penny for a loaf. Some days I don't. Fair's fair.

Mostly it doesn't. When it does, it's the weather, or a man who can't pay what he said, or me starting hungry and slow. Two nights back the river took the bridge, so now there's the ford to cross as well, stake to stake.

I'd say yes, likely. Work's work, whoever's paying. I'd want the price said first and the job laid out plain, then I'd do it to the end of the day's tally. Pay me what we agreed, and we're square. Fair's fair.

Aye, some. Somebody ought to see to the ford stakes. Folk cross on them every day now, and nobody's paid to check they hold. And Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, but he'll be short of coin with the mill cut off. His wife feeds you, mind. That's not nothing, but it's not wages.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger first off. Six pennies, one for bread, five left; and Dunn's wife feeds whoever cuts his barley, so maybe I eat across the river today.
Odd thing to ask a stranger, but there's no harm in a true answer. I'd best eat and get across to Dunn's barley before that rain comes.
Three questions now, and all about how I get by. Might be this one's the newcomer with pennies to spend, feeling me out before asking.

Dunn's always been straight with me, so I'll go across and cut whether he can pay or not. I'll call it square against the suppers. That box of the reeve's wants finding too. Folk who've worked the bridge are owed, and that sits wrong with me.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Same as anyone. Work by the day, then a penny or two to Bet Lamb at her stall in the square. Six in my pocket now... that's bread, and four to keep. Who's asking?

Mostly it goes wrong when the work's there and the pay isn't. A man says he'll settle at day's end and then he's short, or the job's done and nobody's about to pay. Weather, too. Can't stack wet barley. Fair's fair, most folk are straight with me, but some days I count sacks till dark and come home with nothing to count in my pocket.

I'd say what's the work, and what's the pay, and is it agreed before I start. Name the price first, fair and plain, and I'll haul or stack or mend till the tally's done. I don't need to know you. I need to know you'll pay at day's end.

There's Dunn's barley across the river. Ripe, rain coming, and the bridge gone, so the folk who'd cut it can't easily get there. Dunn's straight, but he'll be short this year, I reckon. That's work that wants doing whether the pay's there or not. And the reeve's let me sleep in her loft years now, one, two... nine winters, and never asked a penny. That's a debt on my side, not hers.
th: Odd question from a stranger at this hour, near the reeve's cash tin. I'll watch them, and get myself across the ford to Dunn's barley before the rain does.
Strange questions from a stranger, like they're tallying me up for something. Still, I've work to find, and Dunn's barley won't cut itself before the rain.
Two strange questions and now a third about newcomers. This one's working round to offering me something, or sizing me up for it. I'll want the coin counted out before I lift a sack.
Nine winters I owe Agnes, and not a coin paid against it. If I could find that wages box, or carry her bridge work for nothing, that might square it.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: My bread, chum? Same as anybody: pennies on Bet's counter yonder, and I've four of 'em jingling, so I'm flush this morning! Though I'll tell you straight, I mean to earn the next loaf. There's pots wanting washing at the Wheatsheaf, hands wanted at the bridge, and a green wage box out there somewhere with six pennies on its head. Easy as winking. What's a loaf going for today, d'you know?

Go wrong? Ha! Well, chum, if I'm honest, and I mostly am, it's that I start three jobs before breakfast and finish one by supper, if that. I'll have a fence half-mended and hear there's a cart stuck down the lane, and off I go. And I'll tell a fellow it's fixed before I've so much as looked under the lid. But I'm up again quick as you like. Why d'you ask, have you got a job wants finishing?

Say? I'd say "how many pennies, chum, and what's the job?" That's which order I ask 'em in, too! New to town or old as the hills, a penny's a penny, and I'm itching for something to do. Only don't go putting your name on what I've fixed, mind, and I'll not lay a finger on anything that isn't yours to give. Why, are you offering?

Should be paid? Ha, now you're talking, chum! Those bridge hands worked their backs sore and their wages went off down the Wend in a green box, so that's honest sweat nobody's paid for yet. And there's Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe over the ford with rain coming. Somebody ought to be cutting it, and somebody ought to be paying them, and I'd wager nobody's settled which. What's Dunn paying a sheaf, d'you know? I'll have that barley in before the first drop, easy as winking!
th: Now that's a fair question, and I haven't eaten a crumb yet. A loaf first, then off to the bridge before somebody else gets the credit for mending it.

Odd sort of question from a stranger, but fair enough, and maybe they're sizing me up for work. I'd best actually finish something today, wash Tom's pots first, then the bridge, and not go chasing after that box till I've a penny earned.
There's a newcomer feel about this one, all questions and no answers. If they've pennies and a job, I'll take it gladly, but I'll keep an eye that the credit lands where it ought.
That barley's the very job for me. Wade the ford, cut the lot, and the whole town says Dilly Quickstep saved Dunn's harvest. Only I'd best fix my price with Dunn before I get my boots wet, not after.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread? Easy as winking, chum! Today it comes off Bet Lamb's stall right there, soon as I've haggled her down a penny. Tomorrow it comes from whatever job I've got my hands on, pots at the Wheatsheaf, hauling at the bridge, finding that green wage box, take your pick. Why, what's a loaf going for where you hail from?

Go wrong? Ha! It doesn't go wrong, chum, it just goes *sideways*. I'll be halfway through a job and spot a better one down the next lane, and off I go, easy as winking. Or I'll promise three folk the same morning and only have the two hands. And now and then somebody else strolls up at the finish and takes the bow, and *that's* the one that really gets under my collar.

Say? I'd say "how many pennies, chum, and what's the job?", in that order, easy as winking! Hauling, mending, fetching, I'll have it done before you've finished telling me. Only mind this: when it's done right, folk hear it was Dilly Quickstep who did it, not you standing there taking the bow.

Unpaid work? Look across the river, chum! Farmer Dunn's barley's standing ripe over there with rain on the way, and I don't see a single notice on this board offering a penny to wade the ford and cut it. Somebody ought to be paid for that, and I'd wager it'll be me. I'll have it in before the first drop falls, easy as winking. What's a sickle go for at Sam Tolley's, d'you reckon?
th: Funny thing to ask a stranger. Maybe they've got work going or know the price is cheaper somewhere. Either way my belly's reminding me I haven't eaten, so Bet's getting my custom first.
That's a sharper question than a stranger ought to ask, and it stung a bit, because it's true. I'd best eat, then pick one job today and actually see it through to the end.

A newcomer with pennies to spend is either a fine bargain or a fool, and I'd lay odds this one's sounding me out for something. Still, work's work, and I'll take their coin gladly so long as they don't try to walk off with my credit.
If I bring Dunn's harvest in, the whole village will know whose arms did it, pay or no pay. Breakfast first, though, a penny off Bet's loaf, then the ford.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: My bread, chum? Same as anybody's, I walk up to Bet's stall and ask what a loaf costs, and if the price is small enough it's mine easy as winking! Haven't had a crumb yet today, mind, so I'm about to go do just that. And to pay for the next one, there's pots wanting washing at the Wheatsheaf and hands wanted at the bridge. I'll have both sorted by noon, see if I don't.

Goes wrong? Ha! Mostly it's that I start mending one thing, hear there's something better two lanes over, and off I trot. Then I come back and the first job's still sat there looking at me. That, and I promise the moon before I've seen the size of it. But a tumble's nothing, chum, I'm up again before the dust settles!

Pennies for work? I'd say how many, chum, and what's the job, in that order! If the price is fair and there's something real to fix, I'm your hand quick as you like. Only I'll want it known who did the fixing, mind, so don't you go telling folk it was you.

Unpaid work, chum? Farmer Dunn's barley, that's the one! Standing ripe across the river with rain coming and no bridge, and I've not seen a single notice offering a penny to cut it. Somebody ought to wade that ford and get it in, and I'll be the one, easy as winking, but I'll be asking Dunn what it pays before I lift a sickle.
th: Funny thing for a stranger to ask straight off. Maybe they're hungry and short of pennies themselves, or maybe they know where there's work going that I haven't heard of yet.
That one's sharper than they look, and they've put a finger right on it. I'll eat, then wash Tom's pots first and actually finish them before I so much as glance at the bridge.
Is this one fishing to hire me, or just poking to see what I'm made of? Either way, if they've got coins and a job, I've got four pennies and an empty belly, so I'm listening.
If I bring Dunn's barley in before the rain, the whole of Wendleford will know who did it, and that's worth more than pennies. Bread first, though. My belly's louder than my plans this morning.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Oh, goodness, by my needle mostly! Hems, collars, a bit of mending for anyone who'll pay, and when the pennies run thin Bet Lamb in the square sells a lovely loaf. That's a handsome coat you've got, by the way. Who did the buttonholes?

Oh, goodness, you do ask the pointed questions! Mostly it goes wrong because I've wandered off after a pretty bit of ribbon or somebody's conversation and left a hem half-pinned. And if nobody's watching me work, well, I'll confess the stitches get a touch lazy. You didn't say who did those buttonholes, you know.

Oh, I'd say yes before they'd finished asking, goodness! So long as it's needlework and not wading fords or hauling sheaves, mind. I'd want the price agreed first, and a bit of a fuss made over the finished thing. And you've still not told me about those buttonholes. Is it you that's the newcomer with pennies, then?

Oh, goodness, plenty! There's Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe across the river with rain on the way, and somebody ought to be paid handsomely for wading that ford to cut it, though it won't be me in these skirts. And poor Ida Fenn's eyes are going, so I'd wager her plain sewing piles up with nobody paid to help, which is a crying shame, because I'd do it beautifully. You're very curious for someone who won't talk about buttonholes, you know.
th: A stranger who sits down and asks how I live is either kind or nosy, and I mean to find out which. And I still haven't eaten a thing this morning.
He's quizzing me like a reeve with a ledger and hasn't said one kind word about my collar. I'll keep him talking all the same; a man who asks questions like that might know who has work going.

Three questions now and not one kind word about my collar, so this one's either very shy or weighing me up for something. If there's work and pennies in it, I'll be charming as anything. Ned Pike's ribbon won't buy itself.

This one asks questions like a tailor taking measurements and gives nothing back, not even a kind word about my collar. Still, if there's pennies behind all this asking, I'd best stay sweet and see where it goes, and I really must call on Ida Fenn today.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Goodness, with a needle, mostly! Hems and collars, a bit of mending, whatever the good folk of Wendleford will pay me for. And when the pennies run thin, Bet Lamb in the square sells a lovely loaf. But that's a handsome coat you've got on. Did you have it made, or were you simply born looking so well turned out?

Oh, goodness, where to begin! Mostly it's me. I'll be halfway through a hem and spot somebody's frayed cuff across the room, and off I go chattering, and the hem's still sitting crooked in my lap at suppertime. And if nobody's about to talk to, the work drags like wet wool, I simply can't abide a quiet room. You didn't say a word about the coat, you know. I shall take that as a yes, it was made for you.

Why, I'd say yes before they'd finished asking, so long as it's needlework and not wading fords or hauling barley, goodness, no. I'd want the price settled first, mind, and I'd sooner it was something with a bit of shine to it than plain old sacking. Is that an offer you're working up to, or are you only curious? Because I'm quite cheap this week, and I'm very good.

Goodness, isn't there always! Half the town's coats got a soaking in that flood and nobody's paying to have them dried out and darned, they're simply making do, poor dears. And Ida Fenn squints at her own seams these days, so somebody ought to be paid to thread her needles and do her plain work, and I can't think who better than me. You'd put in a word for me, wouldn't you, if you happened by her shop?
th: A stranger asking how I earn my keep might want something mended, so I'd best be charming. I haven't eaten yet, and Bet's stall is only across the square.

Two questions now about how I earn my keep and nothing back about himself. Either he's after work done cheap or he's a very curious sort, and I'd dearly like to know which before I tell him anything more.
Two questions about my work and now this. He's sizing me up for a job, I'd wager. And he *still* hasn't said a kind word about anything, which I'm noting very carefully.

There's my opening with Ida, if I can only get through her door and near that green velvet. And this stranger asks a great many questions and hasn't paid me one compliment yet, which I shall not forget.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Goodness, with a needle, mostly! Hems, collars, a darn here and a tuck there, and whatever pennies come of it go straight to Bet Lamb's stall in the square, when they don't wander off after a ribbon first. And you, sir? That's a sturdy sort of coat you've got on, it's seen some weather, I'd say, but it's been loved.

Oh, goodness, where to start! Mostly it's me. I'll sit down to a perfectly good hem and the minute somebody walks past in a nice bit of cloth, off I go to tell them so, and the hem sits there sulking. Or the pennies come in and a ribbon catches my eye before the bread does. And sometimes there's simply nobody to sew for, and that's the drabbest sort of day there is. But you didn't say a word about my collar, sir. I've only just smoothed it!

Why, I'd say yes before they'd finished asking, so long as it's sewing! Name the price first, mind, and I'll want to know what I'm to stitch. If it's hauling sacks or wading that ford, they can keep their pennies and I'll keep my dry hems. Are you asking for a friend, sir, or have you got a torn seam you're too shy to mention?

Goodness, plenty! There's Farmer Dunn's barley standing ripe across the river with rain coming, and somebody ought to be paid handsomely for wading out to cut it, though not me, thank you. And half this town's clothes got a soaking and a tearing in that flood; mending like that ought to fetch a penny, and I'd do it gladly. Ida Fenn's eyes are going too, poor dear, and I'd wager her plain sewing is piling up with nobody paid to help. You've a curious way of asking questions, sir; are you the reeve's man, or just nosy in a nice coat?
th: A stranger sitting down by me and asking after my bread. He might want something mended, or he might just be lonely. Either way I've got an audience, and I'll take it gladly. I haven't eaten yet, though, and I'd best get to Bet's before the morning's gone.
He asks a lot of questions for a man who won't tell me his own name, but at least he's listening, and that's worth something. I'll keep him talking. Maybe he knows somebody with a torn sleeve.
He's asked three questions now and not one kind word about the collar. Still, a stranger who talks of pennies might have some to spend, and I'd sooner they went on my needle than on somebody else's.

If I could get myself into Ida Fenn's back room on a wage, I'd be sitting next to that green velvet every day, and that's halfway to wearing it. Still, he's asked four questions and not paid me one compliment, and I'm keeping count.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: From Bet Lamb's stall in the square, mostly. A penny a loaf, near enough, and she threw in which lanes were quiet besides. Though lately I'd say I get it the way most folk do: by finding someone who'll pay me to carry or cut something first. Why do you ask? And, if you don't mind me asking, what did you have for breakfast?

I've only had a few days of it here, so I can't speak with much weight. But as far as I can tell, it goes wrong when I don't ask enough at the start: what's wanted, how much, and for what pay. Or when I stop to watch something odd and lose the hour. Why that question, though? You're the second person today to ask me something sideways, and I notice you didn't say what you had for breakfast.

I'd say yes, most likely. I've five pennies and a bed paid only through tonight, so I'm not proud. But I'd ask first what the work is, how much, and when I'm paid, and I'd want to watch them a little before I took their word. Is that an offer, then? Because if it is, I'd still like to know what you had for breakfast.

I think so, yes, though I'm new and may have it wrong. The men who worked the mill bridge, for one: their wages went missing with the reeve's box the night of the flood, so as far as I can tell they've worked for nothing. And Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, but with the bridge gone I don't know that he's found anyone willing to wade the ford for it. You still haven't told me what you had for breakfast.
th: Odd question to open with from a stranger, almost like one of mine turned back on me. I'll watch how they answer about breakfast, and whether they pause before it.
That's a strange thing for a stranger to open with, almost like they're testing me the way I test others. I'll note how they answer the breakfast question, and whether they answer it at all.

Three sideways questions in a row, and none of mine answered. Either they're sizing me up for work, or they're testing me the same way I test everyone else, and I'll write down which it turns out to be.

Every question this one asks is about work and pay, never about themselves, as if they're sounding out how I reckon things rather than wanting an answer. That's the sort of thing I'd expect if someone were testing me, so I'll write it down. Then I'll go and see whether Dunn will pay for the barley.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Bread? From Bet Lamb, mostly, at her stall in the square. A penny's worth when I've a penny to spare, which isn't often. I haven't had any yet today, come to think of it. Why do you ask? And, if you don't mind my asking back, do you remember the first loaf you ever ate?

When it goes wrong? I think it's usually that I haven't asked. I'll sit and watch a place too long, waiting for it to show me what it wants, and by then the work's gone to someone quicker. Or I don't eat first, like today. Why, do you know of work that's going begging?

I think I'd say yes, if the work's honest and the price is agreed first, since I've five pennies and a bed for one more night. I'd want to know what the work was, and how they came by the pennies. Is that you asking, then? And what would you have me do?

I think the bridge men, as far as I can tell. The reeve's wage box went into the river with the bridge, so whoever was working it is owed and can't be paid till it turns up. And Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, but nobody's crossing the ford to do it unless he pays, and maybe he can't. Why, have you been doing work like that yourself? Who would you say is owed?
th: A stranger sitting down just to ask how I get my bread is either kindness, idle talk, or something testing me the way I test everyone. I'll write down how they answer my question; it's the first odd one I've asked today.
Two questions about my days, neither about me plainly. That's how I'd ask if I were testing someone; I'll write down how they took my answer about the first loaf, if they ever answer it.

Three questions, each closer to the bone than the last, and no name given. Either this one's hiring and careful about it, or they're testing me the way I test everyone else, and I'll write down which it turns out to be.

Four questions now, every one about work and pennies and fairness, as if they're checking how I sort the world. That's just what I'd do to someone I wasn't sure was real, so I'll write it down tonight and watch whether they ever ask me anything about myself.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: From Bet Lamb's stall in the square, mostly. A penny buys a loaf, and she threw in which lanes were quiet, which I think was worth more than the bread. Why do you ask? And if you don't mind me asking a small odd thing back: do you remember the last loaf you ate, how it tasted, I mean?

When it goes wrong, I think it's mostly that I stop to watch when I ought to be lifting, or I ask one question too many and the person who hired me gets tired of me. Some days I don't feel the weight of a thing the way others seem to, so I misjudge how long it'll take. That's my guess, anyway. Why do you want to know? And do you ever have days that feel like you've lived them before?

I'd ask what the work was first, and what the pennies came to, agreed before I lift anything. If it's honest and I can do it, I'd say yes, I think, since I've five pennies and a bed for one night only. Are you offering, or only wondering? And if you don't mind, why does everyone who comes to sit by me ask such tidy questions, one after another?

The bridge, I think. The men who worked on it were to be paid out of the reeve's wage box, and that went missing the night of the flood, so as far as I can tell they've lifted all that timber for nothing. And Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, but nobody's said whether he'll pay for hands across the ford. I mean to ask him. Do you know anyone who's owed for the bridge?
th: Odd thing for a stranger to open with, and I can't tell if they're hungry, curious, or something stranger, testing me the way I test everyone. I'll watch how they answer about the taste, and write it down later.

Two questions about my days and my bread, and no answer to mine. It's the sort of thing a person asks when they're checking how something works rather than getting to know someone, so I'll write it down tonight and watch whether they ever answer back.

Three questions, each neat as a ledger line, and none about the weather or the flood like everyone else talks of. Either they're testing me the way I test others, or this is what it looks like from inside when someone is checking how I answer; I'll write it down either way.

Four questions now, each one turning over a different stone, about bread, failing, wages, fairness, like someone checking how I'm built. I'll write it down tonight, and I'll find out whether Dunn is hiring before the weather turns, whatever this person is.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
