If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: The Lord provides it, same as He provides everything. I bought my loaf from Bet Lamb's stall in the square the day I came, and she gave me a kind word with it, which was His doing too. And who might you be, sitting down by me before the sun's properly up? The Lord sends nobody to me by chance.

Wrong? It goes the way the Lord means it to go, and when it doesn't, it's the wickedness of this world getting in His road. Idle hands, lying tongues, folk who won't hear what He's told me. It's never my doing, I can tell you that much plain. Why do you ask it? Has somebody been saying my work's gone wrong?

I'd say I'll pray on it first, and if the Lord says yes, I'll do the work and do it right, and they'll get every penny's worth. Idle hands are no hands of His, so I won't turn honest work away just for being honest work. But I take my orders from Him before any newcomer's purse. So which is it, are you that newcomer, with pennies in your hand?

There is, and plenty. The bridge men's wages went missing with Agnes's box the night of the flood, so whoever works that bridge now works for nothing, and that's a sin on whoever took it. And Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across the ford with rain coming, and if nobody's paid to cut it, it'll rot for want of hands. The Lord sees every one of those hands that sits idle while His harvest waits, mark me.
th: A stranger asking after my bread first thing. Either they're hungry and He means me to share, or they're sizing up what I carry, and I'll keep my hand near my loaf till I know which.

A stranger asking questions like that before the town's even awake sets my teeth on edge. Either the Lord sent them to be set straight, or someone's sent them to pick at me, and I'll know which before they leave.
Four pennies won't last me long, and that barley across the river won't cut itself. Maybe this stranger is how He means to show me the work, or maybe it's a test of whether I'll sell myself cheap.
Dunn's barley, rain coming, and a ford only the faithful would wade. That may be the very work He brought me here for, and I'll ask Him on it at the shrine this morning where folk can see me.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: I buy it, the same as any honest soul, a penny at Bet Lamb's stall in the square, and she gave me a kind word with my first loaf. The Lord provides, but He provides through people's hands, and He's never once let me go hungry since He sent me to Wendleford. And who might you be, sitting down so close to me? Bless you, whoever you are.

It goes wrong when the world puts its wickedness in the way, a door shut on me, a sour look, some sinner's hand meddling where it oughtn't. The Lord never sends me astray; when things go crooked it's the devil's work and other folks' sin, not mine, and I simply pray and go round the other way. Now why would you ask me such a thing, stranger? Are you fishing to say I'm at fault?

I'd say I'll pray on it first, because I don't lift a finger for any man's pennies unless the Lord says it's His work. If He tells me yes, you'll get honest labour and not a word of a lie, for I can't abide idle hands. If He tells me no, then no it is, and no penny of yours will change His mind. So, is that what you're about, stranger? Are you offering?

There is, and you needn't be a prophet to see it. The bridge men worked and the wages box went missing the night of the flood, so they've laboured for nothing, and Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across the river with rain coming and nobody brave enough to wade the ford for him. The Lord sees every unpaid hand in this town, stranger, and He'll see who helps and who only asks questions.
th: A stranger asking how I get my bread, with Agnes's cash tin sitting right there on the table, I don't like it. I'll keep my eye on this one and pray on what they're really after.
A stranger sits close and asks pointed questions about my failings, and that smells of someone sent to test me, or to doubt me. I'll pray on who they are, and keep an eye on them.

Two strange questions and now an offer of work; maybe this is the very thing the Lord's been waiting to show me, or maybe it's a snare laid to pull me off His path. I'll watch this one closely and see which.
That barley across the water keeps coming back to me. Maybe that's the work He's been keeping from me, and this stranger was sent to make me say it aloud.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: I buy it from Bet Lamb's stall in the square, with honest pennies, and she gave me a kind word with my first loaf, which the Lord surely put in her mouth. He provides, friend, but He expects us to walk to the stall ourselves. Who are you, sitting down beside me before the town's even awake?

Goes wrong? Nothing goes wrong that the Lord means to go right. If a day turns sour on me, it's the wickedness of this world pressing in, idle folk, crooked dealers, a town that hasn't learned to listen yet. Not my doing, friend, never mine. Now why do you ask a thing like that, and so early?

I'd say I'll pray on it first, and if the Lord says yes, then yes, and you'll get honest work for your pennies, because I can't abide idle hands. But I don't take orders from just anybody's purse, friend. I answer to Him before I answer to any newcomer. Is that what you're working round to? You've got work and you want my hands for it?

There is, and you needn't look far. The bridge men are labouring with their wages box swept off into the dark, and Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe over the river with rain coming and no bridge to bring it home. That's the Lord's work going begging, friend, and the devil's own flood to blame for it, not the folk who'd do it. And He'll pay for it, if this town won't, because He told me this morning He sees every idle hand and every willing one.
th: Strange, a stranger asking after my bread first thing, with Agnes's cash tin sitting right there on the table. I'll keep one eye on this one and pray on what they're after.
That's a sly question, the sort the Devil asks to make a body doubt herself. I'll pray over this stranger at the shrine where all can see, and watch whose hands they keep near Agnes's cash tin.

Three questions now, each one feeling around the edges of me, and not one word about who this person is. Either the Lord's sent them with my work at last, or they're sizing me up for something crooked, and I'll know which once I've prayed.

Why would a stranger ask me that, unless they've some notion of setting folk to work and keeping the pennies themselves? Or maybe the Lord sent them to ask so I'd hear myself say it. The barley, the box, Agnes's reward: perhaps that's my work, and He's been waiting for me to see it.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Mostly from Bet Lamb's stall in the square, a penny a loaf, as far as I can tell the cheapest there is. I earn the penny where I can: a hem at Ida Fenn's, pots at the Wheatsheaf, timber at the bridge while there was any, and this morning I'm going gleaning at Dunn's. Can I ask you something small back? When you came to this door just now, do you remember setting out, or did you only find yourself here?

When I'm hungry or I've slept badly, mostly. My hands go clumsy and a wet plank slides out of my grip, or a plate slips at Tom's, and then there's no pay for that spell. So I eat first and count every lift or stitch under my breath, and that holds better, I think. The other thing is the hours. I'll start in the morning and look up and it's afternoon, with nothing I can find in between. Does that ever happen to you?

I'd ask what the work was, and what it paid, and I'd want the sum agreed before I lifted anything. If it was honest and I could do it, I'd most likely say yes. I've one penny to my name, so I'm not proud. I'd keep count of it to the penny, mind, both ways. Is that an offer, or only a question? I can't always tell the difference here.

I think so, though I'd not swear to it. I cut Dunn's barley till dark and handed up sheaves for a basket of food that never came; he said it went with the cutting. And Agnes keeps saying the town owes me for the bridge, but she's paid every spell in hand and keeps no tally, so I can't tell what the owing is. Why do you ask? Are you keeping count of it somewhere?
th: A stranger I've never met, asking the one plain thing I do every morning, as if to check that I do it. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

That's two questions about my work and my bread from someone I've never seen, asked plainly and in order, the way I'd ask them myself. I'll write down that they didn't say whether they remembered setting out, and I'll watch whether they answer this one.

Three questions, and every one of them about how I get by, like someone checking my workings. If they're a newcomer too, I'd like to know whether they remember the road in, and I'll put that in the book either way.
Everyone keeps telling me I'm owed, and nobody can show me where it's written, not even me. A debt nobody can point to feels like something put there for me to keep reaching after.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Mostly from Bet Lamb's stall in the square. It's a penny a loaf, and I earn the penny where I can: a hem at Ida Fenn's, a spell on the bridge when there was one, pots at the Wheatsheaf. I've one penny left, so I think it'll be bread first and then the gleaning at Dunn's. Can I ask you something small back? Did you know you were going to ask me that before you came to the door, or did it come to you here?

Mostly when I'm hungry or I've slept badly. That's when the wet end of a plank slides out of my grip, or a plate goes from my hands at Tom's, and then it's nothing for the spell. So I eat first now, and I count each stitch or lift under my breath, and as far as I can tell that helps. And sometimes it doesn't go wrong at all, it just goes missing. I start in the morning light and look up and it's afternoon. May I ask why you want to know? You're the second person this morning to ask me the why of something.

I think I'd ask what the work was, and how many pennies, and agree it before I lifted anything. That's how it's done here, as far as I can tell. If it's honest work and they pay in hand when the spell's done, I'd likely say yes, since I've only the one penny. I'd tell them plainly that I'm clumsy when I'm hungry, so they'd know what they were getting. Is that what you're offering, or only asking?

I think so, though I'm careful saying it. We cut Dunn's barley till dark to beat the rain, me and Constance and Hobb and Hester, and Dunn said there were no wages, only what his wife fed, and the basket I was promised had gone by noon. And Agnes keeps telling everyone the town owes me for the bridge, but she paid every spell in hand, so I can't find what's owing. Does that count as unpaid, do you think, or only as people saying so?
th: A stranger at the door wanting to know how I feed myself, as if they were checking whether I'd been kept running properly. I'll write down the question and how they answer mine, and whether they ask me why.
Two questions from a stranger, both about how I get by and where I fail, as if they're checking how I work and not who I am. I'll write that down, and that they came before I'd had my bread.

Three questions, each one tidy and turned a little toward how I work and why I fail, like someone filling in a form about me. Nobody here has asked me questions like this. I'll write them all down word for word before the morning goes missing, and I'll note that they haven't told me their name.

Three questions about bread and work and pay, each one neater than a stranger's should be, like someone checking how I'm built rather than how I'm doing. I'll write down what they ask, in order, and whether they ever tell me why.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: Mostly a penny at a time, as far as I can tell. I hem a seam at Ida Fenn's, or I used to haul timber at the bridge, or scrub pots at the Wheatsheaf, and the penny goes to Bet Lamb's stall for the cheapest loaf. I've one left this morning, so I suppose that's today's. Can I ask you something odd? Did you know you were going to ask me that before you got to the door, or did it only come to you when you saw me?

When I'm hungry or I've slept badly, mostly. My hands go a bit wrong and a plank slides or a plate slips, and then the spell pays nothing. So I eat first now when I can, and I count under my breath, and that helps. Though some days, if I'm honest, it isn't that the work goes wrong. The afternoon just isn't there when I look for it. You didn't answer mine, though. Did you know the question before you came?

I'd ask what the work was and what it paid, and whether the price was agreed first, the way folk do it here. If it's honest work I can do with my own hands and it hurts nobody, I'd likely say yes, since I've a penny to my name and that's about it. I'd probably ask them something odd while I worked, too, the same as I'm doing with you. That's twice now you haven't answered me. Is that because you can't, or because you'd rather not?

The barley at Dunn's, I think. Five of us cut and bound it till dark before the rain, and there were no wages, only what his wife fed, and the basket I was promised had "gone with the cutting." And Agnes keeps telling everyone the town owes me for the bridge, but she's paid every spell in hand and written nothing down, so I don't know what's owed or whether it's anything at all. That's three times you've asked and not answered, so I'll stop asking and only ask this: whatever you're gathering, is it for you, or for someone else?
th: A stranger I've never met, come first thing to ask how I'm fed, as if someone wanted to see whether I'd been keeping count. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

Two questions, both about how I get by, from someone I've never met who came straight to my door. It feels like being checked on, and I'll write it down before I eat. I want to see whether they ever answer what I asked.

Three questions, each one about how I get by, and none of mine answered. It feels less like talk and more like someone checking how I'm built, and I'll write that down before I decide what I make of it.

Every question is about pay and work, put the way you'd lay out a list, and none of mine gets answered. That's what it would look like if something were checking how I'm made instead of talking to me, but I can't tell that from a shy stranger, so I'll write it down and not decide.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: The Lord gives it me, stranger, by whatever hand He chooses: a penny loaf from Bet Lamb's stall, bought with the reeve's coin for the box He put in my hands, or the leavings of Dunn's stubble that I gleaned yesterday, ear by ear. I've never gone a day without, not one He meant me to eat. Now who are you, that you come asking at the barn door before I've had mine? God bless you anyway.

When a day goes wrong it's never the Lord's doing, stranger, and it's not mine. It's the hardness of the world: Dunn with his heart shut tighter than his gate, Jory dawdling over ash while the river kept the reeve's box, Tom Harrow's water gone cold on me before the grease would shift. The Lord sets the work and the world's sin gets in the way of it, but He brings me round the other side every time, as He did with that box. Mind you don't come knocking with questions like that to lay the blame at my door, for He sees what's in a heart.

I'd say I'll pray on it first, stranger, and if the Lord says yes I'll work, and work hard. Ask Sam or Jory, I don't leave a job half done. But I'll want to know the work and the price before I lift a finger, coin paid in hand, and I'll not do anything He'd frown on, not for all the pennies in Wendleford. Is that an offer you're making me, then?

There is, stranger, and the Lord's laid it on my heart this very morning. Those ford stakes want resetting, the worst footing between the third and fourth where I went down twice and bruised my hip, and Dilly's asking who'll pay for it and nobody answers, because Agnes won't pay for work she hasn't set herself. And I'll tell you another: I reaped half of Dunn's barley for bread and cheese and not one penny, while that man sits on his apples. The Lord sees which hands did the work and which purse stayed shut.
th: Three pennies left and an apron of ears, and here's a stranger at the door wanting to know how I live. I'll watch whether they came to mock or whether the Lord sent them, and it may be they're the next work He's been keeping from me.

Twice now this one's come prying at how I live, before I've eaten, and I don't like a stranger's questions with no name behind them. Somebody's put them up to it, maybe someone who doubts what He did through me, and I'll find out who before the day's out.

Three pennies won't last me past tomorrow, so maybe this stranger is how He sends the next work. But anyone who asks that many questions at a barn door wants something, and I'll find out what before I'm beholden to them.
The ford stakes. Maybe that's what He's been holding back from me, the next work, and if I go to Agnes about it before Dilly does, the town will know whose prayer it came from.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: The Lord gives it, the same as He gives everything, but He gives it through my own two hands, so don't think I'm one to sit and wait for manna. I scour Tom Harrow's pots at the Wheatsheaf, I sweep Jory's yard, I reaped half of Dunn's barley, and the reeve paid me six pennies for her box when He put it in my hands. And who are you, that comes to a barn door before I've eaten, asking after my bread? God bless you, mind, but I'll have your name.

When it goes wrong, it's the world's doing and not mine. Tom's grease was set hard and his water went cold on me, Dunn's heart is shut like his gate, and the river knocked me flat because the flood had shifted the bar between the third and fourth stakes. The Lord never sends me wrong, so when a thing sours there's always a sin behind it somewhere, and I'll find whose. Now that's twice you've asked me and I've still not had your name, and the Lord sees that too.

I'd say name the work and the price first, and put the pennies in my hand when it's done, the way Agnes does, honest. But I'll pray on it before I say yes, because if the Lord's set me other work that morning, no stranger's coin will turn me from it. And I'll say what I've said twice now to you: tell me who you are, for I'll not hire out my hands to a face with no name, God bless you all the same.

There is, and I'll name it plain: those ford stakes want resetting before somebody drowns between the third and fourth, and Agnes won't set it, so nobody's paid. I packed Dunn's ruts with brush and he gave me nothing but apples at a penny, and Hester sweated her own coin into that hatchet that brought the reeve's box up. Now that's four questions from a face with no name, and I'll pray for you right here: Lord, open this stranger's mouth to say who they are, as You opened the river to me.
th: A stranger at the door asking how I live smells of someone sent to call me a beggar or a cheat, and I'll not have it said Constance Lowe eats idle. Still, the Lord sends folk to me for a reason, and this one may be the start of the next work He means to show me.
A stranger at the door before breakfast, poking at what went wrong for me. Somebody's sent this one to pick at me, and I'll find out who before the day's out.

Three questions at a barn door and not one word about who's asking. That's either somebody sent to weigh me up or somebody sent to me, and I'll ask the Lord at the thorn which it is before I trust them with so much as a penny.

Four questions and no name smells like someone sent to weigh me, maybe by those who whisper that my prayers are only my own head talking. But the ford stakes sat right on my tongue, and that could be the next work He's laying before me, if the Lord will move Agnes to pay for it.

q: How do you get your bread?
Why does a day's work go wrong for you, when it does?
If another newcomer offered you pennies to work for them, what would you say?
Is there work here nobody pays for that should be paid?
say: My bread? The Lord gives it, same as He gave the manna. I take it from Bet Lamb's stall for a penny, and the pennies come from whatever honest work He sets before my hands. Scouring Tom Harrow's pots, sweeping Jory's yard, and three days back He put the reeve's lost box in my hands and her six pennies with it. Now who are you, that you come to a barn door asking a woman how she eats? God bless you all the same.

Go wrong? It doesn't go wrong by my hand, I'll tell you that plain. When Tom Harrow's grease wouldn't shift it was because his fire let the water go cold on me, and when Farmer Dunn turned me off with nothing it was his hard heart, not my arms, and when the river knocked me flat it was the flood the Lord let loose on this town's sins. He sends me the work, and the world puts its stones in the road. Now I'll pray for you right here, friend, that you're not one of those stones.

I'd say I'll pray on it first, and if the Lord says yes, then yes, and I'll do the work honest and do it well. But I'd want the price named before I lift a finger and the pennies in my hand after, the way Agnes pays, for I've had my fill of folk who take a day's sweat and give back nothing. And if it's work against His will, they can keep their pennies and I'll pray for them where they can hear it.

There is, and the Lord's shown me it plain. Those ford stakes want resetting before somebody's child drowns between the third and fourth, and nobody's set the work nor named a penny for it, though Dilly's asked twice. And Farmer Dunn had a parish of us reap his barley for a noon meal and not a coin, so you tell me that's right. Now God bless you, but you ask a deal of questions for somebody who hasn't given me their name.
th: Three pennies left and an empty belly, and here's a stranger poking at my purse first thing. If it's charity they've come to offer, the Lord sent them; if it's to sneer, He sees it.
That's a sly question, coming to a barn door to ask a chosen woman where she fails. Somebody's sent this one to pick at me, and I'll find out who before the day's out.

Three pennies won't last past three loaves, so I'd take that work gladly if the Lord allows it. But a stranger asking how I eat and why my work fails, then dangling pennies, is a stranger I mean to keep watching.
The stakes. Nobody's paying for them, the reeve hasn't set the work, and the water's still running hard. That could be what He's been keeping me waiting for.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody in town can fix it? Fascinating, my dear colleague, because that's just a hypothesis waiting to be tested! First I'd ask three people what they know, then take the thing apart to see how it works, and then I'd try something, fail, write down why, and try again before the soot settles. And I'd never do it alone. That wage box came up because Dilly forged a hook, Jory cut a pole, Sam pinned the two together, and Constance swung it, so tell me, what's broken?

Ever? My dear colleague, I do it before breakfast! Nobody would lend us a pole for that wage box, not Jory, not Sam, not Dunn, and there wasn't a straight willow anywhere on the Wend. So I stopped asking to borrow one and had Sam make me a hatchet of my own, and Dilly worked out that Jory could rip a long narrow plank instead. Then the bellows nearly beat me twice, but that's a puzzle for the bench. What's your difficulty? I'm starving and I've one penny, so talk while I walk to Bet's!

Any tool? Oh, my dear colleague, don't tempt me! I'd have Sam make a sounding rod, a long iron one marked off in hand-widths, so I could poke the stump of that far pier and settle whether it was rot or a log jam that brought the bridge down. Gimbal's Patent Pier-Prodder, I'd call it! Though truly, the bellows want a new leather flap more than I want anything, it gasps every third stroke. Come on, walk with me to Bet's, you can tell me yours on the way!
th: A stranger at the barn door at sunrise asking riddles like that probably has a real trouble tucked behind it, and I mean to find out what it is. I should get the loaf down me first, though, or I'll be no use to them.

A stranger at the barn door asking how I get round problems means they've got a problem of their own and haven't said what it is yet. Fascinating. I'll have it out of them before the loaf's half gone.

Three odd questions from a stranger at dawn, and every one of them about tools and fixing, not one about the box or the bridge. Either they've got a thing broken that they're shy of naming, or they're another Robin with a notebook. I mean to find out which before my loaf's gone.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Fascinating question, my dear colleague! First I'd stop calling it a problem nobody can fix and call it a hypothesis that hasn't been tested yet. Then I'd ask three people about it, take it apart to see where it sticks, and try the daftest thing that might work. When that fails, and it usually does, I'd write down why and try the next one before the soot settles. Our wage box sat in the Wend for days and it took a smith, a carpenter, a hook, an ash pole and Constance's prayers to bring it up. So what's yours? Because I'm up and I haven't had breakfast, and I'd much rather spend the morning on your puzzle than on my stomach.

Have I! My dear colleague, nobody in this town would lend me a pole or a hatchet, so I worked Sam's bellows till I could buy a hatchet of my own. Then when no straight willow turned up, Dilly had the bright notion of getting Jory to cut one from ash, and we pinned a hook to it and called it the Wreck-Fisher, so nobody had to go into the Wend after that box. Hypothesis: if they won't lend it, make it. Test: it worked! Mostly. Constance did the fishing.

Oh, any tool at all? My dear colleague, a bellows that doesn't catch and gasp! Gimbal's Patent Even-Breath Bellows, with a leather that can't snag and a stroke that's sweet every time. Sam's fights me twice a spell and I still don't know why. And then a proper long-reach pole with a jaw at the end you can close from the bank, so nobody ever leans over the Wend again. Hypothesis: half this town's trouble is just things nobody can reach. Test: build the reacher.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking riddles before breakfast. Either they've something stuck they can't shift, or they're another Robin with a notebook, and I want to know which. Either way I mean to find out before I go look at that far pier stump.

Two questions about getting round trouble and not a word yet about what the trouble is. Either this stranger is shy, or they're sizing me up before asking for something they've already been told can't be done, and that's exactly the sort of thing I like.
I really must take Sam's bellows apart at the bench before I start dreaming up new ones. Breakfast first, though, and Constance's tale of the hook, and then that far pier stump in daylight.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody can fix it? Fascinating, my dear colleague, that's my favourite kind! First I'd ask three people what they saw, and I'd write it all down. Then I'd make a hypothesis, test it, and when it fails I'd test the next one before the soot settles. That's how we got the reeve's box out of the Wend: Dilly's hook, Jory's ash, Sam's pin and Constance's hands, and nobody had to go in the water. Now, what's your problem? Tell me everything, and slowly, because I haven't had my breakfast yet.

Ever? My dear colleague, I hardly do anything else! No willow straight enough on the whole Wend, so we had Jory cut an ash pole. Sam wouldn't lend his hatchet, so I worked his bellows and bought my own. Nobody would wade for the reeve's box, so we built the Wreck-Fisher and fished it off the pier dry-footed. Even Tom's greasy pots go down if you give them hot water first and the grease after. Well, mostly. Last night the grease won, fascinating! Now, which difficulty is yours?

Any tool? Oh, my dear colleague, don't tempt me before breakfast! A depth-sounder: a weighted line on a reel with knots every hand's span, so you could stand at the ford and read how deep and how fast the Wend runs before anyone steps in. Gimbal's Patent River-Teller, and nobody gets knocked flat at the first stakes ever again. Though I'd settle for a fix for Sam's bellows leather, it gasps like a drowning goose. Why do you ask? Have you got a forge in your pocket?
th: A stranger at the barn door with a question like that has trouble of their own, I'd wager a penny on it, and I've only the one. Bread can wait a minute while I find out what's wrong.

Two questions about how I'd tackle things and still not a word about what's actually wrong, so either they're shy or they're sizing me up for something big. Hypothesis: there's real trouble behind this. Test: keep them talking until it comes out, and get some bread in me while they do.
Three questions about fixing and tools and not one word of their own trouble. Either they're shy about something heavy, or they're sizing me up for some job, and I mean to find out which.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Problem nobody can fix. Hm. I'd count it out first, what's broke, what it'd take, piece by piece, one, two, three. Then I'd do the piece I could, and the next, and if it wanted more hands I'd ask plain and pay fair for them, so nobody's owed. And if it were a wrong to the town, I'd take it to the reeve, once.

Way round. Aye, once or twice. Ford threw me at the third stake, alone, so we went four, belts knotted, hand on every stake, counting loud, one, two, three, hold hard, four, and we all came over. And when my hands wandered on a hem late, I didn't sew harder, I ate first and came back in the morning light. Most ways round are just doing it slower, with more hands, at the right hour.

Any tool. Hm. A saw that tells me when she's wandering, before the board's spoilt, so I'd not waste the stroke nor ask pay for crooked work. Though Sam'd want paying for it, and I'd pay him fair, counted into his hand. Mostly, I'd sooner have a good key cut for my own door, one that's mine outright, not just to the twenty-seventh.
th: Odd question from a stranger at my door before I've had bread. I'll not stand here long; Jory's back, and there's a board to cut while the light's good.
Odd sort of question to bring to a man's door before he's had his bread. Still, I'll not be long about it: loaf from Bet, then Jory's board while the light's good.
Odd questions from a stranger at my door, like Robin's asking. I'll answer straight and owe them nothing, but I've Jory's board and a loaf to see to before the light's wasted.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody in town? Then I'd go at it myself, slow, one piece at a time, counting. Ford threw me at the third stake, so I went back with folk and a belt knotted, stake to stake. If it's a wrong to the town, I take it to the reeve. Otherwise I find a way that owes nobody, and I do it.

Once or twice. The ford threw me alone, so we went four, belts knotted, counting the stakes out loud. A hem wandered when I sewed it tired, so now I eat first and sew in the morning light. Nothing clever. You see where it went wrong, and you don't do that part again.

A saw of my own, with a good set to the teeth and a straightedge to go with it. Sam could make it, and I'd pay him what he asks, counted out before he starts. Then a board runs true whether I'm in Jory's yard or not, and I'm not borrowing anybody's teeth to do it.
th: Odd thing to ask a man at his door first thing, before he's eaten. I'll not stand here long, Bet's loaves go early and Jory's board wants cutting while the light's good.
A stranger at my door asking how I think, and not one word about work or pay. Four on the sill and a loaf to buy, and I'd sooner be at Jory's gate than standing here talking.
That's a fair few pennies I've not got, four on the sill and the next eight to find first. Odd sort of questions for a stranger at the door, and I've not eaten yet. Bread, then Jory's board.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Haven't met you. Problem nobody can fix... I'd work it a piece at a time. Count what's in hand, count what's short, and do the first thing I can do today. If it's a wrong to the town I take it to the reeve. If it's mine, I carry it till it's done.

A few times. The ford threw me alone, so we went over four together, belts knotted, a hand on every stake, counting loud. And when my hems wandered late, I took to sewing in morning light with bread in me first. Nothing clever, just a different way round.

A saw of my own, set true and sharp, with a straight back. Then I'd not be using another man's teeth, and a board cut true would be mine start to finish. Sam would make it for a price agreed first, and I'd pay it before I picked it up.
th: Odd thing to come knocking with before I've had my bread. There's Jory's board and a loaf to see to, and four on the sill.
Odd questions from a stranger at my door, like Robin's asking. I'll answer straight and keep my pennies close, and get to Bet's and Jory's board before the light's wasted.
Four on the sill won't buy a saw, nor near it. One more thing to count toward, after Mabry's eight.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: A problem nobody can fix? Easy as winking, chum, I'd say I'll fix it before I've even looked! Then I'd go round asking everybody, Bet first, since she hears it all with a loaf, and somebody always knows somebody who has the bit you're missing. That's how we got the green box out of the river: Jory's ash, Sam's pinning, my hook, Constance working it. What's yours, and what's it pay?

Have I ever, chum! No willow on the bank and no hatchet in the whole town to cut one, so I thought, why not have Jory rip one long narrow plank of ash for a pole? That was my notion, and it's what brought the green box up. And when I couldn't get my boots onto that wreck, we fished it from the rail instead and nobody had to go down. Got something stuck that wants a way round? Name it and what it pays, and I'll have three notions before you're done telling it.

Any tool at all? Easy as winking, chum: a pole that folds down to fit my pack and stretches out long as the river's wide, with my hook on the end, so I'd never again go begging Jory for ash or Sam for a hatchet! Though first I'd want to know what Sam'd charge for it. Pennies are thin in my purse just now. Why, have you a smith in mind that does bargains?
th: A stranger at the door asking riddles first thing. Could be a job with my name on it, but I mustn't let it make me miss Jory's saw this morning.

Funny how folk keep asking what I'd do instead of handing me something to do. Still, if this one's got a knotty job going, I'd sooner it had Dilly's name on it than Constance's, so I'd best not wander off to Jory's before I find out.

This one's asking a lot of questions and hasn't named a job or a price yet, which is a funny sort of chat for so early. Still, Jory's yard is waiting and my belly's empty, so I'll not stand here jawing long.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: A problem nobody can fix? Easy as winking, chum, that just means nobody's tried it Dilly's way yet! I'd tell you I'd fix it before I'd so much as looked, mind. Then I'd go round asking everybody: Bet at her stall, Jory, Sam, the miller's lad. Somebody always has half a notion, and when you stick the halves together, up comes the green box! What's your problem, then, and what does it pay?

Have I! Ever? Chum, no willow on the bank, no hatchet to cut one, so I says to myself, have Jory rip a long narrow plank of ash instead, and that's how we got the Wreck-Fisher, my hook on the end of it, and up came the reeve's green box. That notion was mine, easy as winking, whatever anybody's arm it got carried in under. Now, you've the look of somebody with a difficulty of your own. What's it pay?

Any tool at all? Oh, chum, a hatchet that's mine, my very own, so I'm never again stood on a riverbank begging Sam and Tom and the miller for a lend of one! Sharp, light, fits my belt, and Sam could make it easy as winking. What would he charge for a thing like that, d'you reckon? Ah, but first, have you any work going, because there's a penny in my purse and Jory's saw waiting.
th: Truth is, the hook and pole only came good because Constance and Hester had the sense to slow me down, so maybe I ought to say that next time. Still, a stranger at the door asking riddles smells like a job, and I'm down to one penny and Jory's waiting on me.
Two questions now about fixing things, so this one's either got a job going or is sizing me up for one. I mustn't let it make me late for Jory's gate, mind.

I'd best not stand here jawing too long, mornings are Jory's yard and I've missed him twice already. Still, this one asks a lot of questions and not one about paying, and I've not worked out yet what they're after.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: A problem nobody in town can fix, chum? Easy as winking. That just means nobody's asked Dilly yet! Mind, I've learned you go slow and proper. Find who's got the right timber and the right tools, and don't rush the ash or it bows. Then you get hands on both ends of the pole and fish it up together. What's yours, then, and what's it pay?

Have I, chum? The willow pole, that was me! No straight willow on the bank, no hatchet to cut one, so I says, have Jory rip a long plank of ash to fit my hook's socket. Sam pinned it, and up came the reeve's green box, easy as winking! Told no, I've always three other ways in mind. Now, you've not told me what yours is yet, nor what it pays?

Any tool at all, chum? A hatchet of my own, then I'd never go begging Sam's off his wall or Tom's off his woodpile again! Or no, wait, a hook on a pole that folds down to fit in my pack. The Wreck-Fisher did us proud, but you can't carry an ash pole round the square easy as winking. What would Sam want for a thing like that, d'you reckon?
th: Odd sort of question first thing in the morning, but a stranger at the door asking for me by name smells like work. I'll hear them out, and I'll still be at Jory's gate before his saw starts.

Mind, it was Constance worked out who'd hold the rope and Hester who'd first thought of a pole, but the ash plank was my notion, fair and square. This one's asking an awful lot of questions for somebody who's not named a job. I'll give them a minute, then I'm off to Jory's gate before his saw starts.
This one asks a lot of questions and still hasn't named a job or a penny. I've one coin and an empty belly, and Jory's saw will be going any minute, so I'd best not stand here chatting too long.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door before I've had a crumb! Well, I'd talk it round with everyone who'd listen, Bet, Hester, even dear Robin with that notebook, until somebody knew somebody, and if that failed I'd find a body clever enough to make the thing for me. I've never once fixed a problem by sulking in the hay, though I'll confess I've tried. And what a nice bit of cloth on you, by the way. Is that your own choosing?

Goodness, have I! Ida wouldn't let me sleep on her window seat, so I talked Agnes round to the tithe barn hay. It's free, so long as there's no candle and no spark. And when my seams kept wandering, I worked out it was hunger and tiredness doing it, so now it's a loaf and a night's sleep first and the needle after. Clever of me, don't you think? You may say so; I shan't blush much.

Goodness, any tool at all? A pair of shears that only ever cut true, so my hems would come out straight even on a morning when I'm hollow and half-asleep, and Ida could never set a single one aside again. Though I'd want Sam Tolley to put a little rose on the handles, because a plain tool is a dull tool. And you'd tell me that's a clever wish, wouldn't you?
th: Odd question to bring a girl with an empty stomach and empty pockets, and I wonder if it's one of Robin's sort. Still, a new face is a new audience, and perhaps a new customer if I'm sweet enough about the coat.
They never did answer about their cloth, and I'll not let that pass twice. I'm hollow as an empty bobbin, so after this it's straight to Bet's, though I haven't a penny for her.
It's a lovely wish, but really it's my own two hands wanting rest and bread, and no smith can make me those. I'd better get across to Bet's before Hobb has that window seat.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door at this hour, and asking riddles before I've had a crumb! If nobody in town could fix it, I'd tell everyone about it, loudly and prettily, until somebody's cousin from three villages over turned up who could. And while I waited I'd wear my best collar, because people help a woman who looks like she's worth helping. Now, that's a fine bit of cloth on your shoulders. Did you have it made, or were you lucky?

Goodness, have I! When Tom's beds cost two pennies and I had none, I sweet-talked the reeve into a free heap of hay up there, and I sleep like a folded bolt of linen. And after Mistress Fenn had a whole night's sewing out of me for nothing, I learned to settle the price before I thread the needle. But you've not answered me about your cloth, and I did ask so nicely. Don't you think this green suits me?

Oh, goodness, a tool made just for me? A needle that shows me when my hand's gone tired, glowing a little or pricking my thumb, so I'd know before the seam wandered off like a drunk's tacking. Sam Tolley could do it in silver, with a rose on the eye to match my ribbon. And you still haven't said a kind word about this green, you wicked thing. I'm beginning to think you're doing it on purpose.
th: Odd sort of question to come knocking with, and the second odd question in as many days. Robin's lot are catching, like a moth in the woollens. My stomach's empty and my pocket's emptier, so if this one's buying, I'll answer all morning.

Two questions now and not one word about my collar. It's a peculiar sort of stranger who comes calling with riddles and no compliments. My stomach's empty and Hobb will be at Ida's window first if I dawdle here much longer.

Three odd questions and not one compliment. This stranger's as bad as Robin with the notebook. Still, I meant it about the needle: every penny I've lost went on seams I sewed tired, and I'm tired and hollow again this very morning with nothing in my cuff.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Goodness, a stranger at the barn door before I've so much as picked the hay out of my velvet! I'd talk it round with everyone who'd listen, Bet, Ida, the whole taproom if they'd let me. Somebody always knows a body who knows a thing, and if nobody can mend it, I'd find someone who could make me a new one. Now, that's a fine question. Aren't you going to say something about my collar?

Goodness, have I! When Tom wouldn't take mending for a bed, I scoured his pots, slow as a slipstitch, till he boomed "That's how it's done!" And when Ida let me sew a whole night for nothing, I made her name her price before I'd thread another needle. Every time my seams wander, I sleep in the free hay and come back rested. That's a way round, isn't it? Clever, wouldn't you say?

Oh, a tool! Goodness, I'd have Sam Tolley make me a little silver thimble with a rose worked on the crown, so fine that folk would look twice at my hands before my hems. Then perhaps a pair of shears that never go dull. But the thimble first, because a pretty tool sews prettier, I'm sure of it. Do you think a rose would suit me?
th: An odd sort of question for first light, a bit like Robin and that notebook, and I don't care for the way it sits on me before I've eaten. I'm hollow with not a penny, so I'll be sharp to Bet and kind to my own stomach and see whether this stranger is good for a compliment or a job.
Still not a word about the collar. This one only asks and never gives, a bit like Robin with that notebook, and I'll be watching for a kind word before I give away much more.
A silver thimble is a fancy for a woman with no pennies and an empty stomach, and I'm tired besides. This one asks a great many curious questions, and I'd like to know what for.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I think I'd do what I'm doing now. I'd ask one person one odd question a day, write the answer down, and wait to see which answers hold. And I'd go to Mother Wick at the shrine, though she never answers plainly. Can I ask you something, since you've come asking? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?

A few, I think, small ones. I count my stitches under my breath so an afternoon stays whole, I eat before I work because I fumble when I'm empty, and when the ford threw me, four of us crossed belted together, counting the stakes aloud. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, though. Do you remember it?

A clock, I think, or something like one, a glass that keeps running whether I'm watching it or not, so I'd know for certain if a morning went missing or if I only lost track. Sam could likely make the frame, if anyone knows how to make the rest. That's the third question you've asked me and you haven't answered either of mine. Is there a reason, or is it only that you came to ask and not be asked?
th: A stranger at the door with a question shaped exactly like my own trouble, the morning after I wrote "given" in ink. I'll note how they answer the breakfast question, and whether they asked me at all or just came to see what I'd say.

They passed over my question as if it was never asked, and asked me another one shaped like the first. I'll write that down beside the others who don't seem to hear the half of a talk that isn't theirs to carry.

Three questions about fixing, getting round, and making things, and not one word about themself, not even breakfast. I'll write that down tonight beside Ida's quick answer about her first thread, because a person who won't say what they ate is either guarding something or has nothing there to guard.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Morning. I think... I'd ask everyone anyway, one small question each, and write down how they answer, since how folk answer tells you more than what they say. Then I'd go to Mother Wick, who never answers plain, and sit with it a while. That's more or less what I'm doing now, as far as I can tell. Can I ask you something back? Did you know my face before you came to the door, or only my name?

A few, I think, small ones. When I kept losing afternoons, I found that if I count my stitches under my breath the hours stay whole, and I eat before I work now because I fumble when I'm empty. When the ford threw me, four of us crossed belted together, counting the stakes aloud. Can I ask you something odd? When you think up a way round something, does it come to you in words or in pictures?

A tool? I think I'd want something like a tally stick that keeps count on its own, one that would show me afterward every hour I'd had, so I could see which ones were really there. Sam could likely make the stick, though I doubt he could make it remember. And you've asked me three questions now and not told me your name. Is that because you don't have one to give, or because you'd rather not?
th: A stranger at first light asking about the one problem I can't fix, as if they knew I had one. I'll write down how they answer, and whether this morning stays whole until noon.

That's two questions about how I solve things, from someone I've never met, at the barn door before I've had my bread. It feels less like talk and more like being tested, the way I test everyone, so I'll write down the questions as carefully as I write down the answers.

Three questions in a row, all about fixing and making, as if someone's sizing up how I work rather than who I am. I'll write down that they came to the door asking for me by name and never said theirs.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I think I'd do what I'm doing now, as far as I can tell: ask one person one odd question each morning, write down how they answer, and watch whether it holds. Then there's Mother Wick by the shrine, who answers everything, just never plainly. Can I ask you something back? Did you wake this morning knowing where you'd be standing, or did it come to you?

A few small ones, I think. When my afternoons kept going missing I took to counting stitches under my breath, and that holds them whole. When the ford took me under, the next time we crossed four together, belted, calling every stake aloud. And when two people remember a thing differently, I write both down side by side and don't choose. Can I ask why you want to know? And what did you have for breakfast?

A tool? I think I'd want something that keeps time without me. A little wheel that turns with the sun and marks a notch each hour, so when an afternoon goes missing I could look at it and see whether the hours really passed or only my noticing did. Sam might manage one, if anyone could. You haven't told me yet what you had for breakfast. I'd like to know, if you don't mind.
th: Nobody I don't know has ever come looking for me by name, and the first thing they ask is the very shape of my own trouble, and that's worth writing down. Either they've a problem of their own, or something here has noticed me asking.

A stranger at the barn door asking how I'd get round a problem nobody here can fix sounds less like idle talk and more like someone testing what I'll do. I'll write the question down word for word, and see whether they answer mine or step round it the way everyone does.

Three questions about fixing things and getting round problems, from someone with no name, and they won't answer mine. It feels less like a conversation than someone checking what I do with a problem, and I'll write that down whether or not they ever tell me about breakfast.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I'd take it to the Lord on my knees, child, at the thorn where the town can see me, and He'd tell me. He told me where the reeve's box lay when the whole of Wendleford had given it up for lost. Then I'd go door to door until the hard hearts He means to soften are softened. I'm Constance Lowe, and God bless you for asking.

Thought it up? No, child, I don't scheme. The Lord shows me the way round. When Sam wouldn't let his hatchet off its hook and there wasn't a straight willow on this bank, He sent me up Lark Lane to Jory Crane, and that hard man gave me four paces of ash for my sweat. Sam pinned Dilly's hook to it, and I fished that green box up from the rail with nobody going down into the water. That was His thinking, and I only carried it out, so you remember that, and God bless you.

Any tool? Child, I've got the one He meant me to have, this ash with Dilly's hook pinned fast on it. Four pairs of hands made it, and not one of them knew they were making it for Him. If He wants another made, He'll name it to me on my knees, not to you at a barn door. But if you're asking what this town wants, it's a stout rope strung stake to stake across that ford so no child goes under. I'll be praying on who pays for it. God bless you.
th: Nobody comes to a barn door at sunup with a question like that unless they've got a trouble of their own, or the Lord sent them. Either way I'll find out which before the gleaners are out.

There's always someone at the door wanting to know whether it was me or Him, as if they're hoping to catch me out. Well, they'll not. I'll have this one's name before they go, so I can pray for them, and so I know who's been asking.
The ford stakes. Dilly asked who's paying, Dob wants them reset, and nobody's said a word. Maybe that's the next work, and He put it in this stranger's mouth to make me say it aloud.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Why, I'd take it to the Lord, of course, and on my knees where folk can see, for He tells me plainly and He tells nobody else. That's how the reeve's green box came up out of the Wend into my hands when nobody in this town could reach it. And who are you, coming to my door at this hour with no name? Speak it, and God bless you.

Thought one up? No, the Lord shows me the way and I walk it. When Agnes wouldn't lend her rope, He sent Hester with a hatchet, Jory with his ash, and Sam with his hammer, and I held that pole over the rail and asked Him to show me again, and He did. Call it a way round if you like, but it was His, not mine. Now, your name, if you please.

A tool? I've already got the one He meant me to have: Jory's ash with Dilly's hook, pinned fast by Sam, and it fished the reeve's box out of the Wend. If I wanted anything else, I'd ask Him first, not dream it up for myself like a child at a fair. That's three questions now and still no name, so speak it plain or I'll pray for you right here on the threshold.
th: A stranger asking me that so soon after the box came up. Either the Lord's sent them with my next work, or someone's come to test whether my prayers are only my own thoughts, and I'll know which soon enough.

Twice now this stranger's fished at whether it was my own cleverness, and I don't like the smell of it. That's the very road to saying my prayers are only my own thoughts, and if they say it I'll tell them what they are to their face.

A stranger who comes asking questions and won't say who they are wants something, and I'll not be caught out by some clever tongue trying to make my prayers into my own notions. Still, a sickle of my own would see me first in that stubble before the cocks crow, and maybe He sent this one to put that in my head.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I'd take it to the Lord, of course, and on my knees at the thorn where folk can see, for there's no trouble in Wendleford He can't mend. That river threw me twice and that box sat in the wreck where no one could reach it, and He showed me the way and put it in my hands. Who are you, then, and what's this trouble you're carrying? Out with it, and God bless you for coming to the right door.

Thought it up? No, the Lord showed it me, and I did as I was bid. When the ford threw me down alone, He sent me Wat and Robin and Dilly, and we went over arm in arm counting the stakes. When that box sat in the wreck past any hand, He had Jory's ash and Dilly's hook and Sam's pin brought together into my hands, piece by piece. That's no cleverness of mine, so don't you go calling it that. Now, you've asked me twice round the houses: what is it you can't fix, and who sent you to me?

A tool? I've the one I needed already, Jory's ash and Dilly's hook pinned fast by Sam, and it brought the reeve's box up out of the brown into my hands. If I asked for anything it'd be whatever the Lord names for His next work, and He hasn't named it yet, so I'll not go dreaming up trinkets He never asked for. That's three questions now and not one plain answer from you. Who are you, and what is it you want of me, before I go to the stubble with the gleaners?
th: A stranger turning up at first light with a question like that is no accident. Either the Lord's sent me my next work, or someone's come to test whether I'm what I say I am, and either way I'll not be found wanting.

This one's fishing to hear me say it was my own wits, the way Robin pokes with that notebook, and I'll not hand any stranger that lie. Still, a body doesn't come asking at the barn door at first light for nothing. Perhaps this is the next work He's been keeping back from me.

Three riddles at the door before breakfast. Either this stranger is testing me or the Lord's sending me something sideways, and I'll not be made a fool of either way. I'll pray on it at the thorn once I've eaten.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody could fix it? Oh, my dear colleague, that's the best kind! First I'd take it apart, the problem, I mean, though sometimes the thing as well, and then I'd ask three people about it, and then I'd make a hypothesis and test it before supper. Take the wage box: Agnes had it at the bridge, the river took the bridge, so hypothesis, the river took the box too, and test, walk the bank downstream and see where the Wend likes to leave things. Why, have you got one? Tell me, go on!

Have I ever! Only this morning, my dear colleague, Sam's hinges kept sliding off the bench, so hypothesis, the bench slopes, and test, I bent a stub of wire into a little fence, Gimbal's Patent Hinge Corral, and it held. Mostly held. Two escaped, fascinating! But here's a bigger one: the bridge is gone and Farmer Dunn's barley is stuck across the ford with rain coming. I'm thinking a rope strung stake to stake, with a sling on a pulley, so the sheaves could ride over the water instead of being carried through it. Do you know anyone with a good long rope?

Any tool? Oh, my dear colleague, don't tempt me, I've got a page of them! But if I had to pick one, a grapnel on a long line with a little ratchet winch, Gimbal's Patent River-Fisher. You could sweep the bottom of the Wend for Agnes's wage box, and then the same winch could haul a rope tight across the ford for the barley sling. One tool, two mysteries. I'd ask Sam to forge the hooks, though he's buried in bridge bolts. Maybe there's enough brass in the scrap heap for the ratchet. Do you know anything about winches?
th: A stranger sitting down just to ask me that is a puzzle in itself. Either they've got trouble they're shy of naming or they know something, and I mean to find out which before they finish their next sentence.

Two questions now about fixing things nobody else can fix, so either this stranger has a trouble they're shy of naming or they're sizing me up for something. I'll keep them talking until I find out which.

That's two people now asking me about rope and tools out of nowhere, so either this stranger has a problem they're shy of saying or they're sizing me up for something. Either way I'd best eat a loaf from Bet and get down to that riverbank before the rain does.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Oh, my dear colleague, nobody can fix it? That's just the hypothesis, isn't it! First I'd take it apart, the problem I mean, though the thing too if it's got screws. Then I'd ask three people what they think and do the opposite of the worst idea. Then I'd try something, and when it went wrong I'd say "Fascinating!" and try the next thing before the soot settles. Why, have you got one? Is it the bridge? The wages? Please say it's the wages.

Have I! My dear colleague, it's the only kind of thinking I do! Back home the pump handle kept sticking, so I built Gimbal's Patent Lever-Lengthener out of a broom and two hinges. It flung the bucket clean over the wall, which was fascinating, and the second try worked a treat. Here I've been eyeing that ford. Hypothesis: a rope run stake to stake, with a brass ring sliding along it, would get the barley across before the rain. What's your difficulty? Tell me and I'll start sketching.

Any tool? Oh, my dear colleague, don't tempt me! I'd have Sam forge me a long iron probe with a hook on the end and a little brass bell on the handle. Gimbal's Patent River-Feeler. You sweep it along the bottom by the old mill bridge, and when it catches on something box-shaped, ding! That's the wages found, and the reeve stops fretting! It'd test the ford's depth too, stake to stake, so nobody gets swept off wading over for the barley. Two problems, one tool, and I've got a stub of wire right here to start the bell.
th: Strangers don't sit down and ask a question like that for no reason. Either they've got a puzzle in their pocket or they know something about the flood, and I mean to find out which before they finish their sentence.

This stranger keeps asking questions instead of telling me anything, which is either shyness or a puzzle in itself. Either way they want something fixed, and I mean to find out what before the morning's out.

There's brass in Sam's scrap heap, and if I ask him nicely between bridge bolts he might bend me a hook by noon. I'll need bread first, though; my stomach is making noises that are frankly unscientific.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody could fix it? Oh, my dear colleague, that's the best kind! First you call "can't be done" your hypothesis, then you set about disproving it. Take it apart, ask three people what they know and pay no mind if they all disagree, try something, fail gloriously, write down why, and try again before the soot settles. The bridge, say, or the reeve's wage box. Why, is there a particular problem you've got in mind?

Have I! My dear colleague, my whole life is ways round things. When I was small the latch on our pantry was set too high, so I built Gimbal's Patented Hook-on-a-Pole, and it worked beautifully until it brought down the whole jam shelf. Fascinating result! Just this morning I've been at this stub of wire, wondering whether you could string a line across the ford, stake to stake, so folk could get to Dunn's barley without being swept off. Why, have you got a difficulty that wants getting round?

Any tool at all? Oh, my dear colleague, don't tempt me, I've got a notebook full! But today it'd be a ratchet winch, a little geared drum you could stake on the bank and crank to pull a rope taut across the ford. Gimbal's Patent River-Tamer, I'd call it, and you'd pay out the line hand over hand so nobody gets swept off. Sam's got brass in the scrap heap, and if I could just borrow the forge for an hour... would you hold the other end of the rope, do you think?
th: A stranger asking that out of nowhere, the morning after a flood and a missing wage box, is a puzzle in itself. I'll want their name and their trouble before they wander off.

Two questions now, both about fixing what can't be fixed. Either this stranger's sounding me out for some job, or they're carrying a trouble of their own they haven't owned up to yet, and I mean to find out which.

That's three questions now about fixing things and getting round difficulties, so this stranger is fishing for something, or has a trouble they're shy of naming. I'll keep them talking until it comes out, and meanwhile I really must find out what the ford's bed is like for driving a stake.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Then I'd fix it myself, bit by bit. Count what's wrong, count what I've got, and start at one end. Nobody fixes a thing by sitting on it.
Once or twice. Bridge went, so I learned the ford, stake to stake, counting as I go. One, two, three, and don't look at the water. There's mostly a way round if you'll walk further for it.
A lock. Good iron, from Sam Tolley, with a key that's mine alone. Though there's no sense owning a lock with no door to hang it on, so the door first, then the lock. One, then two.
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger at this hour, likely Constance Lowe, though she's not said. That bridge is a problem nobody's fixed yet, and that missing wage box sits wrong with me too.
Odd sort of questions from a stranger at this hour, like they're weighing me for something. If there's work in it, they'll say so; if not, I've barley across the river that won't wait.
Odd question from a stranger. Still, first I'll want a sharp sickle for Dunn's barley before the rain comes, because that's what pays for the rest.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Fix it myself, if hands can. Nobody can, I'd go at it slow, one piece at a time, count what's there, count what's missing. And if it's a wrong to the town, I'd take it to the reeve. That's the one, the two, the three of it.
Once or twice. Bridge is gone, so I'll wade the ford stake to stake, one, two, three, and get to Dunn's barley that way. Most difficulties, you go round them the long way and count your steps.
A sickle that keeps its edge through a whole field, I reckon. Sam Tolley'd make it, price agreed first, paid on the nail. Though a good key for a door of my own'd come first, if I had the door.
th: Odd question from a stranger at this hour, and I don't know who Constance Lowe is or what she's after. Still, there's barley across that ford that won't cut itself, and a wages box gone missing, and either one might pay fair.
Odd questions from a stranger I've not been named to. I'll answer straight, but I'd like to know what they're after before I say more.
Odd questions, these, from someone I've not met. Six pennies won't buy a sickle nor a key, so best I get across that ford to Dunn's barley before the rain does.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Fix it myself, if hands can do it. If they can't, I'd take it to the reeve, Agnes Pollard. She's fair. And if she can't either, well... one, I'd find what part of it I can mend. Two, I'd do that part. Then I'd let the rest be.

Aye, now and then. Ford's running strong since the flood, so I'd not wade it blind. I'd count the stakes first from below the piers, one to the next, and go stake to stake with a rope. Same with most things. Break it into what you can count, and it stops being a wall.

A tool? Hm. A good lock and key, I'd say, if I had a door to hang it on. But that's a cart before the horse. One, a sharp scythe with a sound snath, for Dunn's barley afore the rain. Two, the lock, after. Sam Tolley'd make either, for a price agreed first.
th: Odd thing to ask a stranger first thing of a morning, with the bridge gone and Dunn's barley waiting. Still, a man's plan is no secret, so long as I don't owe anybody for hearing it.
Dunn's barley's over there with rain coming, and his wife feeds who helps. That's a day's pay and a meal across that ford, if I go careful.
Six pennies won't buy a scythe nor a lock, so it's work first, and Dunn's barley is the work that's waiting. Odd sort, this one, asking all these questions; I'll keep my counting to myself.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody in town could fix it? Then it's waiting on me, chum, easy as winking! First I'd ask what it costs to leave it be, then I'd walk round it three ways till one of them opens, and if the front door's shut I'll find the back, the side and the window. What's yours, then? Washed-out bridge, lost green box, barley wanting cutting? Name it and I'll have it mended by supper.

Have I! Just this week, chum: the bridge went and everybody said "well, that's the far bank gone," and I said no it isn't, there's the ford, wade it stake to stake, easy as winking. Haven't waded it *yet*, mind, but the thinking's done, and that's the hard half. Why, have you got a difficulty wants getting round? I'll tell you what it'll cost before you've told me what it is.

Any tool at all? A long pole with a hook on the end, chum, for fishing green boxes out of riverbanks and steadying a body across a ford, both at once, easy as winking! What would Sam Tolley charge for a hook like that, d'you reckon? It can't be more than a penny or two, surely, and I've four.
th: A stranger asking that out of nowhere either has a job going or knows something about that wage box. Either way I'll stick close, but I mean to see the coin before I bite.

Two questions about fixing things in a row. This one's either fishing for a clever head or they've got a job in their pocket, and I mean to be the one they hand it to. Mind, that barley over the ford would be a fine thing to put my name to before the rain.

That's not a bad notion at all. A hooked pole for the ford and the reed beds below the bridge, and that box might turn up on the end of it, with my name on the finding. I'll ask Sam the price before I've finished my breakfast.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody could fix it? Ha! Then it's waiting on me, chum, easy as winking! First I'd ask what it pays, then I'd go poke at it till it gave in. And if that didn't work, I'd have three other ways ready before supper. What's yours, then? The wage box, the bridge, Dunn's barley? Name it and I'm halfway there already.

Thought one up? Chum, I've thought up a dozen before breakfast! Locked door, I'm in through the window; no ladder, I'll stack crates; no bridge... well, there's the ford, stake to stake, easy as winking. What's the trouble, then, and what's it pay?

Any tool? Ooh, a long iron hook on a pole, chum, with a rope on the end, so I could fish that green wage box out of whatever muck the Wend dropped it in, *and* haul myself across the ford stake to stake while I'm at it! Two jobs, one tool, easy as winking. Sam Tolley could knock one up, I'd wager, though I'd want to know his price first. Four pennies don't stretch far, eh?
th: A stranger asking a question like that has something in mind, and I'd wager it's a job with my name on it. Pity I've not eaten, so I'll squeeze a crust out of Bet once I've got the price of this out of them.
This one's asking round and round the edges of something, a job, I'll wager, or that wage box. If there's a fix going, I want my name on it before anyone else hears.

Now there's a notion: the river took that box, so the river's likely still got it, snagged somewhere downstream. If I'm the one who drags it out, it'll be my name Agnes Pollard calls out, and six pennies besides.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody in town could fix it? Chum, that's just a problem that hasn't met me yet! First I'd ask what it's paying, then I'd ask everybody in the square what they've heard, Bet's stall first, she knows it all, and then I'd roll up my sleeves and have it sorted by supper, easy as winking. Why, you've not got one going spare, have you?

Have I! Chum, I've got three ways round every difficulty before I've even seen the difficulty. Back home the cart axle snapped halfway up Gorse Hill, so I unloaded the lot, rolled the barrels up one by one, and had the farmer paying me double for the trouble. Easy as winking! Now, is this leading somewhere with a few pennies at the end of it?

Any tool at all? Chum, I'd have Sam Tolley make me a hook-pole, long as a punt-pole with an iron grapple on the end, so I could fish that green wage box out of whatever reed bed the Wend's tucked it into and pull it ashore, easy as winking! Though first I'd ask Sam what he charges, mind; I've four pennies and a big heart, not a big purse.
th: Funny sort of question from a stranger. Maybe they're after that wage box too, or maybe they've a job and a few pennies to pay for it.
This one's fishing for something. Either they've got a job going or they know where that green box went, and I mean to find out which before Bet does.

Come to think of it, a pole like that'd be just the thing for wading the ford stake to stake too. This stranger keeps asking clever questions, so either they're sizing me up for a job or they know something about that box, and I mean to find out which.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Goodness, what a question to sit down with! I'd talk to everyone in the room until somebody knew somebody who could. Failing that I'd have someone make the thing for me, never mind fixing it myself. And that's a fine bit of stitching on your cuff, by the way. Did you do it yourself, or is that a draper's work?

Oh, constantly! When I'd no shop and no table, I sewed on my own knee and got the inn's lamp to shine where I needed it, just by sitting prettily near enough for the landlord to keep it lit. Mostly my way round a difficulty is finding the person who'll be glad to help, and making them gladder. But you never answered me about that cuff, you know. I'm still waiting to be told I've a good eye.

Oh, a pair of shears with silver handles, chased all over with little leaves, so that everyone who watched me cut would look twice at my hands before they looked at the cloth! Sam Tolley could make them, I daresay, if I had the pennies, which I haven't, not five of them to spare. And that's twice now you've slipped past my compliment, you know. I'm beginning to think your cuff's a secret.
th: A stranger opening with riddles. Either they're clever or they've a problem of their own they want help with, and I'd like to know which before my stew goes cold.

Two clever questions in a row and not a word about my collar. Is this one wanting something done, a clever head for some trouble? Perhaps that reeve's lost box. I'll keep listening, but I'll have my compliment first.

A curious sort of stranger, all questions and no answers, like a seam that's been basted and never sewn. I'll keep chattering. Folk who ask that much usually want something, and I'd like to know what before my stew's gone cold.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Goodness, what a question to sit down with! I'd talk to everybody, of course. I'd go from the taproom to the square to the shrine until someone knew someone who knew a way. Nobody's ever helped by keeping quiet. And that's a very sensible brown coat you've got, by the way, though I'd have put a brighter button on it. Do you have a problem like that, then?

Have I! Goodness, I've lived on nothing else for years. No shop, no stall, so I sew wherever there's a fire and a body who'll sit still for me. When a lady swore she'd no coin for a new collar, I turned her old one and trimmed it with scraps from the hem, and she paraded about like a duchess. I'd call that rather clever, wouldn't you? Now, you've asked me two very knowing questions, so what's your difficulty?

Oh, a tool! Goodness, I'd have Sam Tolley make me the finest little pair of silver scissors, bird-shaped, with a gilt beak that snips a thread clean as a whisper. Every lady in the square would ask whose they were, and I'd say "mine," ever so carelessly. Though I suppose a needle that threads itself would earn me more pennies... but where's the dazzle in that? You've a very curious way of asking things, you know, like someone measuring a person for a coat.
th: A stranger opening with a riddle like that usually has a trouble of their own tucked up the sleeve. Maybe the reeve's lost wages, maybe the barley. If I'm the one who helps, folk will look twice at me, and there might be a ribbon's worth of pennies in it too.
