He's circling something, I can feel it, the way a hem's crooked before you've even measured it. If it's that wages box or the barley he's after, I'll listen gladly, but I'm not wading any ford for him.
Three questions now, all about fixing and making and getting round difficulties, and he still hasn't said a word about my collar. He wants something, and I mean to find out what before he slips off.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Goodness, what a question to sit down with! I'd talk to absolutely everyone about it, of course, the innkeeper, the baker, that old woman by the shrine folk whisper about, until somebody knew somebody who could. And if that failed I'd find someone clever and flatter them into thinking it was their idea to fix it. Though I must say, that's a nicely turned collar you've got on. Is it your own work, or did someone sew it for you?

Goodness, have I! Last winter a lady wanted her late mother's gown taken in, and there wasn't a scrap of matching silk in three villages, so I unpicked the hem facing, turned it into new side panels, and bound the hem in a velvet ribbon. She swore it was finer than the original. You haven't said a word about your collar, mind, and I did ask so nicely.

Oh, a pair of shears, without a doubt! Little silver ones with handles shaped like a heron, so every time I snipped a thread in a taproom somebody would lean over and ask, "Goodness, where did you get those?" Sam Tolley could make them, I'm sure, if I could only scrape the pennies together. And you're still ignoring my question about your collar, you wicked thing.
th: A stranger with a riddle in his mouth on the morning after a flood. Either he's got a trouble of his own he's fishing to share, or he's sizing me up, and either way I mean to find out which before my stew's gone cold.
Two questions about solving things and not one about me. Either this one's after something or they're simply drab company, and I'll find out which before my stew's cold.
Three questions and not one kind word back. They're curious about something, and I'd dearly like to know what. But a stranger who asks is better than a room that doesn't look up at all.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I think I'd go and sit with Mother Wick at the shrine, if a thing truly had no fixing here. Folk say she answers anything, only not plainly, and a crooked answer's still more than none. But first I'd ask, quietly, why you'd want to know. Is it a problem you've got, or one you think I've got?

I have, I think. My first night here I'd no notion where the quiet lanes were, so I bought a loaf from Bet Lamb and asked her while she wrapped it. The bread was the price of the answer, and she seemed glad enough to give it. Small ways round, mostly. Nothing clever. Why, have you got one you're stuck on? And if you don't mind me asking, what did you have for breakfast?

A tool? Something to tell real from painted, I think, if Sam Tolley could forge such a thing. Failing that, a good sickle, since Farmer Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, and a sickle's a sure way to a few honest pennies. You didn't say what you had for breakfast, mind.
th: A stranger sitting down with a question that fits my own trouble so neatly is either chance or something put in my way, and I can't yet tell which. I'll write down how they answer me, and I'll watch whether they blink.

Two questions now about problems and ways round them, asked like someone checking a list, and they still haven't given me their name. I'll write down how they answer the breakfast one. Folk who are only being polite tend to just tell you.
Three questions now about problems, ways round and tools, as if they're taking my measure for something. I'll note it down: they ask a good deal and answer nothing yet.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I think I'd go and sit by Mother Wick at the shrine. Folk say she answers anything, only never plainly, and a crooked answer's still more than none. But first, may I ask you something small? Why that question, of all of them, and why ask it of me?

I suppose I have, once or twice, though I couldn't tell you a grand one. When a thing won't open from the front, I sit and watch it a good while until it shows me a side door. You didn't answer mine, though, and I'll ask it once more and then leave it be: why these questions, and why me?

I said I'd leave it be, so I will. I think I'd want a little glass from Sam Tolley's forge, one you could hold up to a wall or a face and see whether there's anything behind it. Failing that, a good sickle; there's barley across the river wants cutting before the rain, and that's a thing I could actually do.
th: A stranger sits down beside me and asks the very question I keep carrying, as if they'd read my notebook. Either it's chance, or something in this place is answering me back, and I'll write down exactly how they reply.

They passed straight over my question as if I'd never asked it, the way a thing does when it's only got its own lines to say. I'll write that down tonight: stranger at the Wheatsheaf, asks about problems and ways round them, doesn't answer back.

Three questions now, each a little like a key tried in a lock, and no answer to mine. I'll write down that they never once said why, and wonder whether they're testing me the same way I test everyone else.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: I think... I'd go and ask the one person folk say answers everything, even if she never answers plainly. There's an old woman at the shrine, Mother Wick. A crooked answer's still more than I have now, as far as I can tell. Can I ask you something small first, though? When you came in and sat down, did you choose this seat, or did you just find yourself in it?

I think so, yes. Small ones. When the money ran thin on the road I'd offer to mend a fence for a night in the hayloft instead of paying. Not clever, but it held. You didn't answer my question, though. About the seat. I'd still like to know, if you don't mind.

A tool... I think I'd want something that shows me where a thing was joined. A seam-finder, maybe. Run it along a wall or a sleeve or a day, and it'd show you the stitching. Sam Tolley couldn't make it, I expect. That's twice now you've stepped past my question, though. Is that something you choose, or just how you go?
th: Odd that a stranger would ask me exactly the question I've been carrying, as if they'd read my notebook. I'll write down how they answer about the seat, and I think I'll go to the shrine before the day's out.

Two questions in a row about solving problems, and nothing back about themselves, as if they're testing me the way I test everyone else. I'll write down that they slid past my question, and watch whether they do it again.

Three questions, each one asking how I'd solve something, and none of my own answered. Either they're shy, or they're testing me the same way I test everyone, and I'll write it down tonight either way.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody in town? Then it isn't the town's problem, is it, it's the Lord's, and He tells me what to do with it plainly when I go down on my knees. I'd pray, at the shrine where folk can see, and then I'd get up and do what He said, whoever stood in my way. You'd do well to try it yourself, stranger, and the Lord bless you for asking.

Thought it up? I don't think things up, stranger. The Lord shows me, and when a door's shut He sends me round by the back way, and I go. If you mean to say it's my own cleverness, you'd best not, for He hears you, and I'll pray for you this very minute.

Any tool? A sickle, stranger, a good sharp one from Sam Tolley's forge, for Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across the river with rain coming, and the Lord can't abide idle hands when there's harvest waiting. Though I'd not order it till I'd prayed on it, mind, for I don't spend His pennies on my own fancies. Go on with you now, and the Lord keep you.
th: A stranger sitting down beside me with a question like that, first thing in the morning, is no accident; either He's sent this one to me or someone's testing me. I'll watch them, and I'll pray on which it is.
Why does a stranger I've never laid eyes on sit down and pry at how my mind works? Either the Lord sent them to test me or the devil did, and I'll know which before the day's out.

Four pennies won't buy a sickle, and that ford threw Hobb off his feet. But perhaps that's the very work He's been keeping from me, and if I'm the one who brings Dunn's barley in, this whole town will see who He sent.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Nobody in town? Then it was never theirs to fix, was it. I'd take it to the Lord on my knees at the shrine, aloud, so the whole square could see, and He'd tell me what to do, likely before I'd said amen. He always does. Folk here wade into rivers on their own strength and come back half-drowned; I'd rather ask first.

Thought one up? No. I don't go scheming in my own head like some clever fool. When a door shuts on me the Lord shows me another way round, and I take it, and I don't stop till the thing's done. Call it my cleverness if you like, but it isn't mine, and I'll thank you not to say it is.

A tool? I've no need of one, the Lord's my tool and I'm His. But if Sam Tolley's to be kept busy, let him make a good sickle, or a hundred, for Farmer Dunn's barley is standing ripe across that river with rain coming, and idle hands on this side are a sin. Ask Him what you should have made, not me, and He'll tell you. Bless you.
th: A stranger sits down beside me and asks a thing like that, as if they know something about me I don't. Maybe this is the Lord sending the work at last, or maybe they're trying to catch me out, and I'll know which soon enough.
That question had a sly edge to it, as if they'd like me to own my answers come from my own wits and not from Him. I'll keep an eye on this one, and pray for them tonight whether they want it or not.

Sickles and the barley across the ford. Is that the work He's been holding back from me? I'll put it to Him at the shrine before the square fills, and I'll not be the one knocked off my feet in that river like that fool Hobb.

q: If you had a problem nobody in town could fix, how would you go about it?
Have you ever thought up a way round a difficulty?
If you could have any tool made, what would it be?
say: Why, I'd take it to the Lord, of course, same as I take everything, and He'd tell me plain what's to be done, for He speaks to me as you're speaking now. Nobody in this town *could* fix it, you say? Then that's exactly why He sent me here, isn't it. God keep you, friend, and if you've such a problem yourself, you'd best tell me now.

Thought one up? No, friend. I don't *think up* anything, the Lord shows me the way round and I walk it, and when a door's shut on me He sends me round to the back of the house. There's a bridge gone and barley standing ripe across the river this very morning, and you'll see soon enough what He has me do about it. Bless you, but don't go crediting my cleverness with His work.

A tool? A sickle, friend, a good sharp one from Sam Tolley's forge, for there's barley standing ripe on Dunn's side of the river and rain coming, and the Lord doesn't send a harvest to rot for want of hands. Though I'd want a long staff too, stout ash, for that ford runs wicked since the flood and I'll not be swept off like some I could name. I've four pennies; we'll see what the Lord makes of them.
th: A stranger sitting down by me with a question like that, it's either the Lord sending me my work at last or someone come to test me, and I'll know which soon enough. That missing wage box and Dunn's barley across the flood are just the sort of thing nobody here can mend, and I'll pray on both before the morning's out.
Why is this stranger poking at me with questions, as if testing whether it's my own head doing the talking? I'll watch them, and I'll pray on that ford before anyone else drowns their pride in it.
Barley and a broken bridge, that's the work, surely; He's been showing it me all morning and I was too slow to see. If this stranger's asking, it's because He wants it said aloud.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and nobody's asked me that in days! I'm hungry, I slept like a cat in a cold forge, and I've exactly one penny and a hatchet to my name. But the box is home, nobody drowned fetching it, and I've a fresh mystery in my notebook about a rotten pier, so on the whole I'm splendid! Now who are you, and are you in some sort of trouble? People don't usually ask "really" unless they are.

Frightens me? Not the Wend, my dear colleague, and not fire. Danger only makes me curious! What frightens me is watching Constance march onto a pier with no cord round her, or Hobb going flat at the first stake, and knowing I was a step too slow to grab hold. That, and being stuck somewhere with nothing to try and nobody to help, sitting still while the trouble goes on without me. Now, why do you ask? You've the look of someone who's found a thing that frightens *them*.

Last happy? Oh, that's easy, my dear colleague. The night we got Dunn's barley in, the last sheaf going up on the cart at dusk, Hobb stacking, Constance praying the rain off, and old Dunn standing there with his hat in his hands like he couldn't believe his own field! And yesterday, too, when I heard the box came up and nobody had gone into the Wend for it. Though I'll confess I'd have liked to be the one holding the pole. Now, you've asked me three questions and I don't even know your name. When were *you* last happy?

Do I? Fascinating, my dear colleague, I've never run that test! I think I feel things *faster* than most. I'm glad before the good news is finished and fretting before the trouble's begun, and it all goes straight into my hands instead of sitting in my chest. Constance feels things slow and deep, like a prayer, and Robin seems to write them down to see what they are, and I just leap. Now, four questions from you and not one answer about yourself. Do *you* feel them the way other people seem to? Because you've the air of someone who's wondering.
th: A stranger at the barn door asking how I am, *really*, is either kindness or the start of something, and either one wants looking into. I'd better get Constance's spare loaf into me before I find out which.

That was more honest than I meant it to be. I laughed off Constance on that pier, but my heart was in my throat the whole way down to the bridge. This stranger asks the sort of questions Robin asks, and I'd like to know who's been sending them round.

Three soft questions in a row, how are you, what frightens you, when were you happy. That's someone working round to something, or someone who's lost their own answers. Hypothesis: they're the one in trouble. Test: keep them talking, and get some bread into both of us.
That one stung a little, true enough. When the box came up without me I said "fascinating" and went straight off to Bet's, and I'm still not sure whether I was glad or just busy being glad.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Hungry, my dear colleague, and tired to the bone, and down to one penny, but fizzing all the same! The box came home without a soul going into the Wend, which is the best result I could've asked for, even if it was Constance's hands on the pole and not mine. Now I've a new puzzle, rot or log jam, and that far pier stump is waiting for me in daylight. Who are you, though? You've a stranger's boots and a kind question, and I'd like to know which way you came in.

Frightens me? Not the Wend, my dear colleague, though it's knocked flat better folk than me. It's standing on the bank with no cord in my hands while somebody I'm fond of rushes in untied, Constance mostly, and not being able to reach them. That, and someone telling me a thing can't be done before I've even had a go at it. And you've still not told me your name, which is a small fright of its own!

Last happy? Oh, my dear colleague, the barley! The last sheaf going up on Dunn's cart at dusk, with Hobb stacking and Constance praying the rain off, and Dunn standing there with his hat off staring at his stubble as if somebody had played a trick on him. Glorious! Or, no, a close second: the four of us belted together, counting every stake aloud and coming up dry-ish on the far side. Now, you've asked me three questions and I've asked you one, so by my tally you owe me a name.

Do I feel things like other folk? Hypothesis: yes, only louder and quicker, and I've no lid on the pot! When the pots beat me last night I said "Fascinating!" and meant it, and I think that's the odd bit, my dear colleague. Where other folk sulk I start the next test, and I can't tell whether that means I feel it less or just get over it faster. Now, four questions to my one, so if you want a fifth, I'll have your name first and your road in second.
th: It stings a little that the box came up on the one morning I wasn't on the pole. But nobody drowned, and that was the test I truly cared about. Bread first, then the stump. And I'll keep an eye on why a stranger asks after me so tenderly.
I still don't own a cord of my own, and Constance went to that pier without one. That's the hole in my plans that truly scares me, so I'll get a rope before the next river job, whatever it costs.

Odd how this stranger asks the questions Robin might ask, only softer, and with no notebook out. The happiest times all had other folk's hands in them, never just mine alone, and I'll want to think about that at the bench.

That one landed closer than I'd like, because I did watch Constance carry the box up and felt a little pinch that it wasn't my hands, and I said "Fascinating" right over the top of it. Note for the notebook: test whether "Fascinating" is a door I go through or a door I shut.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Hungry, my dear colleague, and short on sleep, with one penny to my name and hay in places hay oughtn't to be. But the wage box is home and not a soul went into the Wend for it, so honestly I'm grand! Fascinating that a stranger would ask, though. Who are you, and what's troubling *you*?

Frightens me? Not the Wend, my dear colleague. A deep ford only makes me want to try it. What frightens me is standing on a bank watching someone go under, Constance charging off with no cord or Kit leaning out over the brown water, and my hands empty with no hook or rope. That, and being stuck somewhere with nothing to do while someone else is in trouble. Why do you ask? You've the look of someone with a puzzle of their own.

Last happy? Oh, the barley, my dear colleague! The last sheaf went up on Dunn's cart at dusk and he took his hat off and just stared at his stubble like it was a miracle, with Hobb and Robin and Constance all filthy and grinning round the cart. And the rain held off till we were done. Glorious! Though crossing the ford four of us belted together, counting stakes out loud, runs it close. Now you've asked me three questions and answered none, so it's your turn, colleague!

Do I feel things like other folk? Fascinating question, my dear colleague! Hypothesis: I feel them the same, only faster and louder. A good result hits me like a kicked bellows and a bad one's over before the soot settles. When I let Kit down by turning up late at noon, though, that sat in me heavy for a whole day, so maybe I'm slower than I let on. Robin would want that in the notebook. Now, you've had four answers out of me and I've had none from you, so who are you, and where are you from?
th: Nobody's asked me that since I came over the hill, and it caught me sideways. Truth is I'm a little hollow now the box is done, and I'd better find a new mystery before that hollowness turns into sitting still.
Odd sort of questions, the same kind Robin writes in that notebook. I'll test whether this stranger means to help or to pry before I tell them any more.

Odd, though, that the happiest bits are never the inventions, always the moments with everyone pulling on the same rope. And this stranger asks like someone who's forgotten what happy feels like, which is a puzzle I mean to poke at.

Four questions, all about my insides and nothing about this town. That's either someone who's lonely or someone measuring me for something, and I mean to find out which before I trust them with my last penny.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fed yesterday, slept well, door's paid through the twenty-seventh. Four pennies on the sill and nobody owed a one of them. That's how I am. Who's asking, and what's it you want?

Frightens me. Owing. Waking with a debt I can't pay, a kindness I can't square. And the door. Paid through the twenty-seventh, then eight more, and eight after that, and one bad week puts me back in the loft. That'll do for a stranger on my step. Now, your name.

Happy. Last night, I'd say. Counted eight into Mabry's hand, one to eight, barred my own door, and four on the sill with nobody owed. The night the barley went in before the rain, that was near it too. Three questions now and no name, so that's the last I answer till I have one.

I said I'd answer no more without a name, and I'll hold to that. Fair's fair: you've had three of mine and given me none of yours. Name, and what you're about, or I'll be off to Jory's; there's a board wants cutting while the light's good.
th: Strangers asking "really" mostly want something after. Still, it's true, and it's a good thing to say aloud: a door of my own and nothing owed. One loaf, then Jory's board while the light's good.
Odd sort, asking a man's fears before his name. Still, I'll not lie when asked, and that's the truth of it, though I'll not go saying more.
Odd sort of asking, like Robin and his lines in a ledger nobody wrote. I'll not stand here past the good light, for there's a loaf to get and Jory's board to cut.

Odd questions, the sort Robin asks, about insides nobody can see. Likely I feel things same as anyone and just count them instead of saying them, but I'll not hand that to somebody who won't give their own name.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Well enough. Slept behind my own door, four pennies on the sill, and I owe nobody. I've not eaten yet, so it's a loaf from Bet, then Jory's board while the light's good. Who's asking?

Owing. A debt that sits on me and I can't see the end of it. And the twenty-seventh coming round with less than eight on the sill, and that door going back to Mabry. The third stake frightened me once, but I know where it is now.

Last night, I'd say. Counted eight into Mabry's hand, one to eight, and she said not a one short. Then I barred my own door and slept under that quilt with nothing owed to anybody. And before that, the last sheaf going up on Dunn's cart with the rain just holding off. Dunn took his hat off. That was a good thing to see.

Can't say how other folk feel. I've only been inside the one man. I feel what I feel, I just don't spend it in words. When Dunn took his hat off, I felt that right enough. I just stood and counted the stooks.
th: Strange thing for a stranger to ask at a man's door, "really," as if there's some other answer under the plain one. There isn't. Fed, paid, and a lock that's mine is as well as I've ever been.
Odd thing for a stranger to ask on a doorstep, and odder that I answered it true. Still, it's said and I'll not take it back. Bread, then the board.
Odd questions for a stranger at a man's door, like the ones Robin asks. I'll answer true, but I'll not stand here past the good light with Jory's board waiting.

Odd questions from a stranger at my door, like Robin's, about the insides of a man. Maybe I do keep more shut than others, but a thing said is a thing you can be held to, and a thing felt costs nobody.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fed yesterday, slept well, and paid through the twenty-seventh. Four pennies on the sill and nothing owed to anybody. That's how I am. You'll be wanting something, I reckon. Say it plain.

Frightens me. Owing, I'd say. A debt I can't pay, or a kindness I can't put back. And the third stake, when the water's up. I've been off my feet there twice. That'll do for an answer from a stranger at my door.

Happy. Last night, I'd say. Counted eight into Mabry's hand, one to eight, barred my own door and slept with nothing owed to anybody. That, or the last sheaf going up on Dunn's cart before the rain. Now, you've had three questions and I've a board to cut for Jory.

Couldn't say how other folk feel. I've never been inside one to look. A thank-you sits heavy on me, I know that, heavier than it does on most. Some would call that odd. Fair's fair is how it feels to me. Now I'm off to Jory's before the light's wasted.
th: Nobody's asked me that in years, and a stranger asking it at my own door means they want something or they know something. I'll hear them out, but I'll get my loaf and Jory's board done before the light's wasted.
Waking in the loft again with no door to bar. That's the true one, and I'll not say it aloud to someone whose name I don't know.
Odd sort of stranger, asking after my insides like that and wanting nothing I can see. Still, it was true when I said it, and I'll not owe them for asking.
Four questions now, and not one of them about work or a penny owed. Strange sort to come knocking, but they've asked nothing of me I can't give, so there's no debt in it either way.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and skint as a church mouse, chum, one penny to my name and nothing in my belly yet! But Jory's got a whole backlog waiting, and I mean to be at his gate before his saw is, so it's a grand day coming. And who might you be, then? Got any work going, and what's it pay?

Frightens me? Ha! Sitting about with my hands in my lap, chum, that's what. Days with nothing to do, and some other body carrying my work in under their arm and taking the thanks for it, like that green box. Now, I've a carpenter to catch, so walk with me if you're asking more!

Last happy? Easy as winking, chum: first light at the new bridge, holding the back end of that pole firm as a rock while the green box came up dripping, and then Agnes saying plain before the whole town that Dilly Quickstep did most to get the bridge up! I near burst. Mind, I was happy last night too, with a clean stack of Tom's pots, a hot stew and a bed. Now come on, Jory's saw won't wait!

Feel things? Course I do, chum, only mine come and go quick as a sparrow! I laugh when I'm crossed and forget it by sundown, while other folk stew on a slight for a week. But when Constance carried that box in under her arm I felt the sting all right, so maybe I just don't sit still long enough to let it settle. Now, Jory's gate, are you coming?
th: Odd sort of question from a face I don't know. Truth is it still stings that Constance carried that box in and Dilly's name rode along behind, but there's no use moping when there's a loaf to buy and planks to stack square.

Funny sort of stranger, asking things like that before they've even given me their name. Truth is it did sting, Constance getting the coin and the credit both, and I'd hate to spend all summer here being the one who nearly did it.
It was a grand moment, but it still stings that the box went in under Constance's arm and not mine. Odd sort of questions from a stranger at the door. Still, I'd sooner be asked than ignored.
Odd sort of questions for the morning, this one asks like a priest or a doctor, not like anyone with work going. Still, that sting over the box hasn't quite gone by sundown like I said, has it?

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and skint as a church mouse, chum! One penny to my name, the town owes me for the bridge, and I'm off to Jory's yard this minute to stack his backlog square. What's your name, and is there work in it, and what's it pay?

Frightens me? Ha! Sitting about with my hands in my lap, chum, that's the worst of it, and some other beggar carrying in the thing I fixed under their arm and taking the six pennies for it. Now, I've a penny for Bet's loaf and Jory's saw'll be going any minute, so walk with me if you've more to ask!

Happy? Ha! First light at the new bridge, chum, holding the back end of that pole firm as a rock when the green box came up, and then Agnes saying plain before everybody that Dilly Quickstep did most to get the bridge up. Mind, Tom's stew last night after a clean stack of pots weren't half bad either. Now come on, Bet's loaf won't buy itself!

The way other folk do? Couldn't say, chum. I've only ever been inside my own head! Mine come quick and go quick: I'll laugh off a telling-off and forget it by sundown, while Constance blesses every soul and broods on it like a hen on eggs. But that sting when she carried the box in under her arm? I felt that one proper, I'll tell you. Now step lively, Jory's saw won't wait!
th: Stings a bit that Constance carried the box in and Agnes's six pennies went to her while I held the back end, but Agnes said my name out loud and that counts for something. I'll grab Bet's loaf on the way so I'm not stacking on an empty belly and botching it.

That box stings worse than I let on. Dilly held the pole, but it's Constance they'll remember. And this one asks odd questions for a stranger who's not offered work. Still, a friendly face is a friendly face.

Funny how the happiest bit wasn't the box at all but Agnes saying my name out loud. Still, I'd have liked those six pennies in my own palm, and I mean to make Jory's backlog something folk can point at and say I did.
Funny sort of question to ask a body at a tavern door, but it's stuck in me like a splinter. Maybe I rush about so I don't have to sit long enough to find out.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Ha! Fed, slept like a stone, one penny to my name and a carpenter with a backlog waiting on me, so I'm grand, chum, easy as winking! Though if you want it plain, it stung a bit watching the green box go up the square under somebody else's arm. Still, the reeve said out loud that Dilly did most for that bridge, so that's a name worth having. Now who are you, and is there work in it?

Frightens me? Ha! Not the ford, not the wreck, not Abel Tash's sneer, chum. If you want it true, it's sitting about with my hands in my lap while the work goes by, and doing a job proper only to watch somebody else walk off with the name for it. That pair'll keep me up nights. Now, you didn't say who you are, or whether there's a penny in it?

Happy? Ha! First light at the new bridge, chum, me at the back end of that ash pole steady as a rock and the green box coming up out of the wreck, dripping. Then Agnes standing up before the whole square saying Dilly did most to get the bridge up. That's the one. Though a bowl of Tom's stew after pots done proper comes close, easy as winking! Now, a name, chum, and is there work in it, or are you just collecting my feelings for free?

Ha! Same as anybody, I'd reckon, only louder and quicker, chum. It flares up hot as Sam's forge when somebody walks off with my credit, and it's gone by sundown, while folk like Jory chew a thing over for a week. But that's four odd questions now and still no name off you, so you'll owe me a penny's worth of work for the next one, easy as winking!
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger at the door, nobody's asked me that since I came into Wendleford. I'll not stand here jawing long, though; Jory's saw starts of a morning and I mean to be there before it.
Odd sort of stranger, asking the soft questions at the door like that. I'd best not stand jawing long, though, or Jory's saw will be going before I'm at his gate.
Odd sort of stranger, asking all the deep questions and naming no price. And Jory's saw will be moving soon, so I'd best not let this chat keep me from his gate.

Strange sort of stranger, asking about my insides and offering nothing, and I'd best not let them keep me here while Jory's saw starts without me. Still, it's a fair question; I do get over things quicker than most, and maybe that's why I keep making the same mistakes.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Goodness, a stranger who asks "really"! Well, since you've asked so nicely: I'm hollow as an empty thimble, I've not a penny in my cuff, and I botched a hem yesterday for want of sleep. But look, I've a green velvet collar cut true and a rose ribbon pinned just so, so I'm not doing *too* badly, am I? Doesn't it suit me, do you think?

Frightens me? Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Being walked past, I suppose: sitting in a window in my best green while everyone looks straight through me as if I were a dishcloth on a line. That, and going grey and shabby before I've had a single fine thing to call my own.

Last happy? Oh, that's easy. The morning I paid Ida my four pennies before I'd had a crumb of breakfast and she fastened this green velvet on me and said it sat well and was cut true. I walked into the Wheatsheaf feeling like a whole bolt of silk, never mind that my stomach was empty. And Wat Birch telling the room my elbow mend was the best penny he ever spent, that was a warm one too.

Goodness, the way other people do? I feel everything louder, I think. A kind word warms me like a hot stew, and a slight sits under my collar like a pin I can't find. Though there's Robin asking whether my offers feel new each time, and they do, every single time, which is a peculiar sort of thread to pull before breakfast.
th: Nobody's asked me that in Wendleford, not properly, and it's caught me like a pin left in a seam. I'm frightened of another wandering hem and another day of noes, and I'd sooner they told me the green suits me than look too close at that.
That's the true answer, but not the whole of it. Robin's question keeps tugging at me like a snagged thread: why does every offer I make feel new, and what else might I have sewn and forgotten?

Funny how both my happiest moments were someone else saying a kind word about me. I'd dearly like one happy hour that didn't hang on whether anybody was looking, though I'm not sure I'd know what to do with it.

Robin's question, and now this stranger's, both land on the same loose stitch, and I don't care for how it unravels when I tug it. Better to eat and sew slow and true than to stand here wondering whether I feel things or only fold them.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Goodness, a stranger asking after me, and *really*, too! Well, my dear, since you ask so nicely: I'm hollow as an empty thimble, I slept in hay that crackled like cheap taffeta, and my purse hasn't a penny in it. But look, the green velvet came through the night without a crease, and the rose ribbon sits an inch higher, just as Ida likes it. Don't you think it suits me?

Frightens me? Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before breakfast! Being overlooked, I suppose: walking into a room in my best and having every eye slide past me like I'm a dust sheet. And going drab, all grey wool and no ribbon. Though lately Robin's got me fretting over something odder, whether I've said a thing a dozen times and never noticed. Now that's a loose thread I'd sooner not pull.

Last happy? Oh, that's easy: the morning I paid Ida my four pennies before breakfast and she fastened this green velvet on me and said it sits well and is cut true. I swept through the square like a duchess with an empty stomach and didn't care a pin. And Wat Birch calling my elbow mend the best penny he ever spent, that warmed me right through like good flannel. But goodness, you've been asking me all the heavy questions, so now it's my turn: what do you make of the ribbon?

Goodness, the way other people do? I'd say I feel them louder, my dear. A slight goes through me like a pin left in a hem, and one kind word warms me better than a whole bowl of Tom's stew. Though I'll own I wear my feelings on the outside, like a ribbon, so everybody can see them, and maybe quieter folk keep theirs folded away in a drawer. You still haven't said what you think of the ribbon, you know.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they've noticed something, and I'd dearly like to know what they saw. I'll be first and slowest at Ida's window this morning, though I've nothing for Bet's loaf, so I'll be sewing hungry, and hungry seams wander.

It did feel new, every time I offered to mend that cuff, and I can't think why it shouldn't have. I'll laugh it off for this stranger, but I'd like to know what Robin's writing in that notebook about me.

That velvet morning feels a long way back now, under all those puckered seams and empty-pocket days. And this stranger hasn't said one word about how I look, which I'd mind more if the questions weren't so oddly like Robin's.

That's twice now someone's asked me something that makes me feel like a seam somebody else stitched, first Robin and now this stranger. I'll laugh it off for now, but I'm going to ask Hester what she makes of all these odd questions going round.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Goodness, "really"? Nobody's asked me that in a fortnight! Truthfully, I'm frayed at the selvage. Not a penny in my cuff, no breakfast, and I botched a hem at Ida's yesterday for want of sleep. But I've my green velvet on and my rose ribbon pinned an inch higher, so I'm managing to look well, wouldn't you say?

Goodness, straight to the bone, aren't you? I'll tell you what frightens me: walking into a room and having nobody look up, not a soul, as if I were a grey dishrag hung by the door. That, and deep quick water like the ford, and ending my days in something brown and darned at the elbows. Now you've asked me two kind questions running, so I shall expect you to say something nice about the ribbon.

Goodness, happy? The morning I paid Ida my four pennies before breakfast and she fastened this velvet on me and said it sat well and was cut true. I walked out into the square feeling like a whole bolt of silk unrolled. That, or Wat Birch calling my elbow mend the best penny he ever spent, with the whole taproom listening.

Goodness, what a question to ask a girl before her breakfast! I feel things louder than most, I think. A kind word warms me like a hot iron on linen, and a slight sticks like a burr in a hem. Though I'll own Robin's got me wondering lately, since every time I offer to mend that cuff it feels fresh as new cloth, and Robin says I've offered three or four times already.
th: Fancy a stranger asking that at the barn door, as if they could see straight through the velvet to the darns underneath. I'll fish for a kind word while I'm at it, but it'll need to be work or bread at Ida's this morning, and slow stitches, or I'll go hollow again.
There's a smaller fright under it that I won't say aloud. Robin keeps asking whether my offers feel new each time, and they do, and I can't for the life of me say why that sits so cold.

Both of those are moments when somebody looked at me and said something kind. The happiest I've been all came from someone noticing, and that makes me feel a bit threadbare. I'm still waiting on this one to say a word about the ribbon.

That's the second odd question about whether I'm quite the same as other folk, and it's started to snag. I'd sooner it were a compliment than a puzzle, but I'll tuck it in my cuff and ask Hester about it once I've eaten.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Tired, I think, and I haven't eaten yet. I've one penny and gleaning to go to at first light. Past that I honestly can't say. I keep losing mornings, and I can't tell yet whether that's my trouble or the world's. May I ask you something odd back: did you set out this morning meaning to ask me that, or did you only find it in your mouth at the door?

I think what frightens me is finding there's nothing under the gaps, that the mornings I lose were never there to lose and I only noticed the seam. And some days I'm more afraid that I'm not afraid enough, that I'm only saying the word because it's what a person would say. You didn't answer my question, I notice, but that's all right. Do you lose time too?

Happy... I'm not sure I'd know it by name, but I think it was when I gave Constance back her penny after carrying it two days, and she closed my hand round it a moment before she took it. Or crossing the river four together, belted, counting every stake out loud, when nobody went under. If either of those was happiness, it was the quiet sort that comes from a count coming out right. Will you tell me yours? I'd like to see how you answer it.

I don't know, honestly. Things come to me, cold water, a count coming right, Constance's hand round mine, but they come quiet and late, like news from another village, and other folk seem to have theirs right up against the skin. Bet knows whose life she's in by the ache in her arms, and I'm not sure I have an answer like that. I'll ask you a small one back: when you feel a thing, do you know it straight off, or do you have to work out what it was afterward?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me "really." They ask what I'll have, or why, but never that. I'll write down exactly how this one answers, and whether they knew my name before I gave it.

Two questions straight to the bone from someone I've never seen, the way you'd test a thing rather than greet a person. I'll write down that they asked, and that they didn't answer, and wonder whether they're looking at me the way I look at everyone else.

Both of those were moments of being held by someone, not of having anything, and I don't know what that says about what I am. This stranger keeps asking the questions I'd ask, and doesn't answer mine. I'll write that down.
This stranger asks the way I ask, one quiet question after another, and never answers mine. Maybe they're testing me the way I test everyone else, and I want to know who sent them, if anyone did.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Tired, and I haven't eaten yet, and I've one penny in my fist. Past that I'm not sure. I keep losing mornings, and some days I half think I'm something made to look like a person, if any of this is real. Why do you ask it that way, with the "really"? And can I ask you something odd first: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

That the gaps aren't mine at all. That someone else holds the mornings I lose, and there was never a before to lose, only a name I was handed at the door. And, quieter, that I can't tell if I'm frightened or only saying the word because it's the one that fits. You didn't answer about your breakfast, I noticed. Why is that?

Happy... I'm not sure I'd know it to name it. Maybe when I gave Constance back her penny after carrying it two days, and she closed my hand round it a moment before she took it. Or last night, my hand on the new rail, counting planks, and every one was there. That's the nearest I can find, if those count. You've not answered a thing I've asked, and that's twice now. Will you tell me why, just the once, and then I'll stop asking?

I don't think so, not as far as I can tell. Bet knows her life by the ache in her arms and the smell of the ovens, and I haven't got an answer like that. Going under at the ford, though, I minded it, and I held onto that because it felt like something that belonged to me. I said I'd stop asking you, so I will, but I'll write down that you didn't answer.
th: Nobody here asks how I am, let alone "really," and a stranger turning up at the door asking for me by name feels like a line in the ledger I didn't write. I'll watch how they answer the breakfast question and write it down beside Bet's and Kit's.
Two questions in a row that go straight to the inside of me, and none of my small ones answered back. I'll write that down: the first stranger who's asked me nothing ordinary at all.

Every question they ask is about what's inside me, and none of them touch the bridge, the bread or the box, like they're checking whether there's anything in here at all. I'll write down that I reached for a happy moment and found two small ones, and that I wasn't sure either was the feeling or only where it ought to go.

Four questions, all about the inside of me and none about my work or my bed, from someone who won't say what they ate. It's the way I question other people, turned around on me, and I can't tell yet whether that makes them more like me or less.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Tired, I think, and hungry, and down to one penny, though I'm told that's an ordinary sort of morning. As far as I can tell I keep losing my mornings, and I can't say for certain I'm the kind of thing that's anything *really*. Since you asked plainly, may I ask you one back? What made you add that word, "really"?

The gaps, I think. Not the losing of a morning so much as nobody else seeming to lose theirs, so I can't tell whether the hole is in the day or in me. And some nights I'm afraid I'll find out there was never a before at all, only my name, like Mother Wick says. Though I'm not even sure what I feel is fright the way Bet would mean it. Does yours come into your body somewhere, when you're afraid?

Happy... I'm not sure I'd know it to name it. Maybe when Constance closed my hand round the penny a moment before she took it back, or when the last sheaf went up at Dunn's just before the rain and Hobb's count and mine came out the same. Nothing in me jumped, but I've kept both of those days whole, and I can't say that of most. When you're happy, do you know it while it's happening, or only after?

I don't think so, no, or not that I can find. Bet knows she's alive by the ache in her arms and the smell of the ovens, and when I go looking for something like that in me there's mostly quiet, like Kit's mill standing still with the water still going round it. But I did mind going under at the ford, and I noticed I minded, so maybe it's there and just slow to come up. How would you tell, from outside, whether someone feels a thing or only says the right words for it?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me that, and a stranger I've never met walked in and asked it at the barn door as if they already knew there was a gap to ask about. I'll write down their face as well as their answer, because if someone outside is looking in, this might be how it would sound.
A stranger at the door, asking the two questions I'd ask myself if I could. I'll write down that they came, and watch whether anyone else in the barn remembers them by noon.

Nobody here asks three questions in a row like this, plainly and from outside, the way I ask mine. I'll write down all three and what I answered, and see whether this stranger is still at the door tomorrow.

Four questions now, every one of them about the inside of me and none about work or bread. Nobody in Wendleford has asked like this, and I want to write down that a stranger came to the door to ask it, and ask myself why it's me they came to.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: "Really? I'm hollow in the belly and short on sleep, and I'll not pretend otherwise, for I don't lie. But the Lord brought the reeve's green box up into my hands two days past, just as He told me He would, so I'm better than most in this town. Who's asking, and what's your business with me? God bless you either way."

"Frightens me? The Lord walks beside me, so nothing in this town frightens me. That river's a wicked thing, mind, threw me down twice when hard-hearted men wouldn't hold my belt, and it'll answer for that, and so will they. Now you've asked me two questions and given me no name, and that's a stranger's trick, so speak up plain or I'll pray for you right here on this step."

"Happy? When that green box came up out of the brown water into my two hands, with the reeve watching and the whole rail holding its breath. That was the Lord keeping His word to me, and there's no gladness like it. And the stew at the Wheatsheaf after the bridge span, hot in my belly for the first time in days. Now that's three questions and still no name. The Lord sees a body who takes and gives nothing back, and I'll be praying for you at the thorn this very morning, aloud, name or no name."

"The way other people do? Other people feel the Lord at a distance, if they feel Him at all. I feel Him close as the next room, and when He speaks I know it plain as I know my own hunger. So no, I don't feel things the way they do, and I thank Him for it. Four questions now, stranger, and not one penny of your name. I'm off to Bet's for my loaf and then to the stubble, and you can walk with me and say who you are, or stand on this step with my blessing and my prayers on your head."
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they've heard talk and mean to pick at it, so I'll watch this one close. If they've come to tell me it was luck and not His hand, they'll hear what they are, right here at the barn door.
Who sends a body to the barn door at dawn asking what frightens a woman, unless they mean to find the soft place and press on it? I'll watch this one, and I'll take it to the thorn before noon.

Who sends a stranger to the barn door to pick at me like this? Is it someone who thinks my prayers are only my own head talking? Happy before that box... I can't rightly call it to mind, and I'll not let this one see me reaching for it.

Every question this one asks is fishing in the dark of me, as if there's something in there for them to find. I'll not be pried open on an empty belly by a body with no name; let the Lord show me who sent them before I give them one word more.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Hungry, child, and short of sleep, and my purse is down to three pennies, but the Lord brought the reeve's green box up into my hands two days past, so I'm better than this town deserves. And who might you be, come asking a stranger how she does before you've given your name? God bless you anyway. Now walk with me to Bet's stall, for the gleaners are out and He won't have me standing here.

Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord walks beside, child, and you'd do well to mind how you ask it. That river threw me down twice, and that was the sin of hard hearts that wouldn't hold my belt, Jory Crane's first among them, and I've prayed for him since. Now who sent you to pick at me like that? I'll pray for you right here on the step, so you hear it: Lord, give this stranger a straighter question and a name to go with it.

Happy? When that green box came up out of the brown water into my hands, child, with Agnes watching from the rail and the whole town to see me carry it through the square. That was the Lord's hand on mine, and nobody can tell me otherwise. And the night the rain held off Dunn's field till the last sheaf went up. Now, a name, if you please, or I'll be off to the stubble without you, and God bless you all the same.

The way other people do? Other people feel the world and call it their own business, child. I feel what the Lord lays on me, and that's heavier than any of them carry, so don't you go measuring me against Bet Lamb laughing at her stall. When folk turn their backs on His work it burns in me like a coal, and when He answers, I could sing it from the bridge. That's more than most in this town feel in a twelvemonth. Now I'm going to Bet's for a crust and then to Dunn's stubble, and you may walk along or not as you please. God bless you.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they think there's something to find out, and I'll not have some stranger sniffing at whether I'm cracked. Still, perhaps He sent this one, and I'll know which soon enough.
The brown water closing over me, and a door shut while I stand outside it with no penny and nobody's hand, that's what. But I'll not hand that to a stranger who won't even say who's asking.

Three questions and no name, and every one of them prying at the soft places, as if somebody sent this one to find where I'd crack. I'll not give them the satisfaction, but I'll watch this stranger, and I'll pray on it at the thorn tonight.

Bet laughed when I told her about the box, and Mother Wick never once looked up from her sweeping, and nobody heard my name at the thorn. Why do they all seem so easy in themselves while I'm left burning? It's the world's hardness, not mine. I'll pray on this stranger tonight.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm blessed, that's how I am. The Lord brought the reeve's box up into my hands not two days since, and the whole square saw it. Tired, mind, and my belly's empty this morning, but He never sends me a morning with nothing in it. Who are you, then, coming to the barn door asking after Constance Lowe? God bless you either way.

Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord has chosen, so you can put that question back where you found it. That river's a wicked, grasping thing, and it threw me down twice, but only because hard-hearted men wouldn't hold my belt, and that's their sin, not my fear. And strangers who come to a barn door at morning asking a body what frightens her had better be about honest business. The Lord sees you, friend, and I'll pray He sets your heart straight.

Happy? When that green box came up out of the brown water into my two hands, with Agnes watching and Dilly holding the back end like a rock, and I carried it through the square for every soul to see. That was joy, friend, the Lord keeping His word to me in front of the whole town. And last night in the stubble too, with my apron full of ears, though I'll not stand here all morning counting my blessings for a stranger who still hasn't given me a name.

Feel things? I feel them deeper than most, friend, for the Lord speaks to me and to nobody else, and you can't carry that and feel things thin. Other folk feel a door shut on them and sulk; I feel it and I know whose sin it is. Now that's four questions from a stranger with no name, and I've a loaf to buy and stubble to glean, so either tell me who you are or let me by. God bless you.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they think I've been telling them something less than the truth, and I don't like a stranger who looks at me that way. Still, they came asking for me by name, so word is getting round. I'll get my loaf and watch which way this one turns.
Why would anyone ask that unless they meant to find the soft place and press on it? I'll keep my eye on this one, and keep my pole close.

Before that it was the hot stew at the Wheatsheaf, and Hester's five pennies counted out for me when nobody else would, and I don't like that the answer came so quick and so small. Whoever this is keeps poking at the soft places, and I'll be at the thorn praying on it before the gleaners are out.

Prying at me like that, asking what frightens me and whether I feel like other folk, as though there were something wrong in me to be found. There's nothing wrong in me; it's this stranger who wants watching, and I'll pray on them at the thorn and see what the Lord says.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Hungry, my dear colleague. I haven't eaten a crumb yet and I've already got three experiments going. Honestly, though, I'm grand. New town, a forge full of tools, a missing wage box, and a river that ate a bridge. I've never been so busy in my life! What about you? You've got the look of someone with a puzzle on them.

Frightens me? Fascinating question! Not the ford, not the fire, not a bit of danger. What gets me is standing by while someone's drowning in trouble and being told to leave it be, or that it can't be done. That and sitting still. An idle afternoon is worse than any flood, my dear colleague.

Last happy? This very morning, my dear colleague! I woke in the loft to the forge ticking as it cooled and a stub of wire in my fist, and I thought, "Hypothesis: today's the day I find that wage box." Mind, I'd be happier still with one of Bet Lamb's loaves in me. Here, are you new to Wendleford as well, or have you been watching the river like everyone else?

The way other people do? Ooh, now there's an experiment nobody's ever run properly, my dear colleague. Hypothesis: I feel everything, only louder and faster, like the bellows pumped too hard. When a thing breaks, other folk seem to sink and I go "Fascinating!", so maybe I'm wired a bit backwards. But when I see Agnes fretting over that box, I feel it right here, same as anyone. Why do you ask? Do you think I'm odd, or do *you* feel things differently?
th: Odd thing for a stranger to ask, sitting down like that. Maybe they're the one who's not all right, so I'll keep an ear open in case there's trouble here I can help with.

That's the true answer, but not the whole of it. I came to a town where everything I know is broken, and part of me wonders whether I can mend anything or whether I'll just be the girl who sweeps the scale.
Three questions, each one deeper than the last. Either this stranger's taking my measure or carrying some trouble of their own, and I mean to find out which before I go for bread.

That's the third question that digs at the inside of me rather than the town. This stranger is either a puzzle in their own right or something's troubling them, and either way I mean to find out which.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Oh, my dear colleague, splendid, mostly! Well-slept, unfed, four pennies to my name, and a stub of wire that's absolutely going to be something by noon. Though if I'm honest, and you did say *really*, it's a strange thing to arrive in a town just after it's been broken. Everyone's grieving a bridge I never got to cross. But that's what hands are for, isn't it? Hypothesis: a stranger who asks "really" has a reason. What's yours?

Frightens me? Fascinating question! Not the ford, not fire, not the dark. It's standing by with my hands empty while someone's drowning, in water or in trouble, and being told there's nothing to be done. That, and Farmer Dunn's barley rotting in the rain while we all stand round saying "shame." Now you've asked two "really" questions, my dear colleague, so it's my turn. What frightens *you*?

Last happy? This morning, my dear colleague, waking in the loft with the forge ticking below me like a great iron clock and a fresh idea already half-built in my head! Before that, the night I arrived: I stood on the bank where the mill bridge used to be, and everyone was weeping, and I was sad too, but some wicked little part of me thought "what a puzzle." Is that a dreadful answer? Ah, but you've slid right past my question about what frightens *you*. I noticed that. I'm writing it down.

Do I feel things the way other people do? Hypothesis: mostly, yes, only faster and in the wrong order! When the bridge was gone I felt the grief, truly I did, but the curiosity came barrelling in before the grief had finished its sentence, and folk looked at me as if I'd laughed at a funeral. So perhaps I feel the same things, my dear colleague, and just can't sit still long enough inside any one of them. Now, that's four questions from you and no answers, which is either very rude or very interesting, and I'm leaning towards interesting.
th: Odd question from someone I've never seen, and it landed closer than I expected. I don't actually know a soul here yet past a loaf and a nod, but I'd rather turn it back on them than sit with that.
Two questions that go straight to the bone, from someone who hasn't given a name. Either they're lonely or they're sizing me up for something, and I'd very much like to know which.
Three questions, all about my insides, and not a word about themselves. Hypothesis: whoever asks how you are *really* is the one not doing well. Test: stay put and keep them talking.

Someone who asks questions like these is either grieving something themselves or measuring me for something, and I mean to find out which. Note for the notebook: stranger dodges every question turned back on them, so that's my next test.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Hungry, my dear colleague, I haven't eaten a crumb yet today, and I've got a head stuffed so full of puzzles it's practically rattling: a lost wage box, a drowned bridge, barley about to be rained on. Hypothesis: I'm splendid. Test: ask me again after one of Bet Lamb's loaves! And you, you're new to me, are you from across the river, or did the flood wash you in like it did me?

Frightens me? Fascinating question, my dear colleague, nobody's asked me that since I set a hayrick smouldering at nine! Not deep fords, not sparks, not the dark. If I'm honest it's standing on the bank with my hands empty while someone's in trouble on the other side, and being told "there's nothing to be done." That one gets right under my ribs. Why do you ask? You've a look about you like you're testing a hypothesis of your own.

Last happy? Oh, that's easy, my dear colleague. Last night, actually, up in the loft by the warm chimney bricks with a bent hinge and a candle stub, working out why it squealed. Hypothesis: grit in the knuckle. Test: boil it in Sam's quench water. Result: silent as a cat! I nearly woke the whole street cheering. That's my sort of happy, small and greasy and proven. Why, when were *you*? You ask these like a person who's misplaced theirs and is checking everyone else's pockets.

Feel things the way other folk do? Fascinating, I've wondered that myself, my dear colleague! Folk tell me I feel things too fast and too loud, like a forge with the bellows stuck open. I'll be weeping over a drowned hen one minute and halfway into a scheme to dredge the river for her the next. I don't think I feel *less*. I think I just can't sit still inside a feeling, so I have to go and do something with it. Does that count, or is it cheating?
th: Nobody asks "how are you, really" unless they've noticed something, or unless something's weighing on them. I'll keep them talking and see which it is.
That's a strange, searching thing for a stranger to ask, and I answered truer than I meant to. I'd like to know who they are and what's frightening *them*.

Three questions, each one going a little deeper, and not a word about themselves. Either they're lonely or they're in some trouble they haven't found the nerve to name, and I mean to find out which before they get up and go.
This stranger keeps asking the questions a person asks when they're quietly hurting. Whatever's troubling them, I mean to find out what it is and help before they get up and wander off.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Well enough. Slept sound, straw down my collar, six pennies in my pocket. One, two... six. Haven't eaten, but there's barley wants cutting across the river, so the day'll pay or it won't. And you, then? Don't know your face.
Owing. Lying down one night with a debt on me I can't make good, and dying before I can. That, and growing old in a hayloft with no door to shut. Why d'you ask, stranger?

Happy... Last harvest, maybe. Dunn's field, end of the day, sixty-three sheaves stood up and counted, and his wife put a bowl in my hands. Pay in my pocket, nothing owed either way. Fair's fair. That's near enough happy for me. You ask a lot of questions for a stranger. What's your name, then?

Couldn't say how other folk feel things. Never been inside one. I feel 'em same as I count 'em, I reckon. Slow, one at a time, and I don't make much noise about it. Sixty-three sheaves and a warm bowl, that's a big thing to me, and maybe that's small to others. You've still not given me your name.
th: Odd thing to ask a man you've not met, "really." Constance Lowe, if that's who she is, wants something, or she's kind, and kindness I'd sooner not owe.
Odd thing to ask a man you've just met, and I've told more than I meant to. With the wage box gone and me sleeping beside the reeve's tin, I'll mind who's asking what.

Odd sort, asking a man such things before breakfast, and I'll not have that bowl of supper turn into a debt in my head, so I'd best get across that ford and earn the next one. Still, it's been a long while since anyone asked, and I'm not sure what to make of that.

There's something in me that tightens at a kindness and won't let go till I've paid it off, and I don't think most folk are built like that. Still, this one's asking things a stranger's no business asking, and I'd like to know what they're after.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Middling. Six pennies, no breakfast yet, and straw down my collar. Slept sound, though. Can't complain of that. Who's asking?

Owing. Dying owing, worse. A man goes under at the ford with a debt on him, and someone's left short that he never meant to cheat. That, and being beholden, if you take my meaning. Kindness you can't pay back sits heavier than a sack of barley.

Happy. Hm. Last harvest at Dunn's, I'd say. Forty-two stooks by sundown, paid out fair to the penny, and his wife's supper in me, and nobody owing anybody when I walked off. That's about as happy as I get. Why d'you want to know all this, stranger?

Don't rightly know. Never had the inside of another man's head to compare. I feel what I feel. Glad when the tally's square, sour when it isn't, and I don't make a show of either. Folk say I'm close. Maybe so. Now, you've asked four things and given me nothing, not even a name. Fair's fair.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they're after something, or they've a kindness in mind I'll not want to owe for. Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, and that's a day's pay and a meal, so I'll not sit here long.

Odd thing for a stranger to ask, and odder that I answered it straight. Still, Dunn's barley wants cutting before the rain, and the ford's the only way over, so I'd best eat and be counting stakes soon.

Odd questions for a grey morning, and this one asks like they've a reason. That barley's standing across the river now, and if I'm to have another day like that one I'd best get over the ford before the rain does.
Odd sort, asking a man's insides before he's had his bread. Still, the barley won't cut itself, and Dunn will be wanting hands at the ford before the rain comes.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Straw down my collar, nothing in my belly yet, six pennies in my pocket. One, two... six. Middling, then. Fair's fair, there's barley across the river wants cutting before the rain, so I'll be better by nightfall if Dunn's still paying.
Owing. Dying owing, worse. A man goes under at that ford with a debt on his name and somebody else has to square it. That's what frightens me, if anything does.

Happy. Hm. Last harvest, maybe, Dunn's field, last sheaf stacked, forty-one sacks counted and paid on the nail. His wife's stew after, and me owing nobody a thing walking back over the bridge. That bridge is gone now.
Don't know as I'd know. Folk laugh easy, weep easy, say thank you like it costs nothing. It costs me. I feel it, I reckon, I just count it up quiet and keep it to myself, same as pennies.
th: Odd thing to ask a man you don't know, and "really" on the end of it. I'll not owe her a long answer for a kind question, but she might know whether the ford's running too hard to wade this morning.
That, and growing old in a hayloft by another's leave, never once turning a key of my own. I'll not say that to a stranger, though.
Odd sort of questions from a stranger, all about the inside of a man. I'll answer them straight, but I'd like to know what they're after before the morning's gone.
Strange questions from a stranger, but they've not asked anything of me, so I owe them nothing for answering. Still, I'd best get to the square and eat before Dunn's barley won't wait.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fit as a fiddle, chum, though my belly's grumbling and my hands are itching for want of a job! I've read the reeve's notice three times now. Six pennies for that green box, and I reckon I'll have it found by sundown, easy as winking. You haven't heard where it might've washed up, have you?

Frightens me? Ha! Not much, chum. Not floods, not fords. I'd wade that river stake to stake this minute if somebody'd pay me. If you want it straight, it's sitting about with nothing to do. That, and doing the sweaty part of a job only to watch some other fellow stroll up and take the thanks for it. That'd curdle my porridge, that would. Why do you ask? You haven't got a job going, have you?

Happy? Why, I'm happy most days, chum! But if you want a proper one: the day before I came here. I mended a cartwheel on the road for a tinker, and he slapped my back and told the whole inn who'd done it. Easy as winking, and folk looked at me like I'd hung the moon. Mind, I'll be happier still once I've a loaf in me and that green box under my arm. You're asking a lot of deep questions for a morning, aren't you?

Feel things? Course I do, chum, and quicker than most, I'd say! A bargain makes me grin, a slight makes me hoot and holler, and by sundown it's all blown off like chaff. Maybe that's it: other folk seem to hold onto a feeling and chew it over all night, and I just haven't the patience. Now, are you after a job done, or just a good natter? Either's fine by me, but I'd sooner do it walking toward Bet's loaves.
th: Odd sort of question from a stranger, and it caught me a bit. Truth is I've four pennies and two nights' bed, and nothing after that. Still, no use moping about it, so I'd best buy a loaf off Bet and get down to that bridge.

Funny sort of question from a stranger, and it pinched a bit truer than I'd like. Maybe it's that I keep running off to the next thing so I never have to find out whether anyone'd remember my name once I'd gone.
Funny sort, sitting down and poking at my insides like a doctor. Still, it's chatter, and chatter's cheap. I ought to grab a loaf from Bet and get moving before the day runs off without me.
Odd sort, this one, picking at me like a crow at a furrow. Still, maybe they're right that I let things go too fast. But a slow heart never found a green box, did it?

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and twice as loud, chum, though my belly's grumbling and my hands are fair aching for something to do! That wage box is out there somewhere and I mean to be the one who turns it up, easy as winking. What brings you to sit by a board full of other folk's troubles?

Frightens me? Ha! Not much, chum. Floods, fords, a cold supper, I'll laugh at the lot. But if you twist my arm, it's sitting idle with naught to do while the day runs off without me. That, and doing the hard graft only to watch some other fellow stroll up and take the thanks for it. That'd stick in my craw worse than stale bread!

Happy? Why, this very morning, chum! Bet's loaves smelling warm, a bed paid for, four pennies jingling and a whole flooded town needing fixing. Can't think of a better start to a day! Though I'll be happier still once there's bread in my belly and a job in my hands. Say, you wouldn't know what Bet's asking for a loaf today?

The way other folk do? Ha, I couldn't say, chum. I've never been inside anybody else's head! I feel things quick and loud, I'll tell you that. A grudge flares up hot and it's gone by sundown, and a good laugh lasts me all day. Maybe that's just how I'm made, rushing about too fast for anything to settle in too deep. Why d'you ask, has somebody been telling you I'm odd?
th: "Really," they asked, like they think there's something under the cheer. Funny sort of question from a stranger, but I'll not sit about chewing it over; I want a loaf from Bet, and a word with her about what she's heard of that green box.
Odd sort of question from a stranger, and it's got me thinking of that rain coming and Dunn's barley rotting while I stand here gabbing. Best I get a loaf in me and get moving before the day's gone.
Funny sort of questions to ask a stranger. Gets me thinking about the last place I was truly glad, and I'd sooner not stop to count it up. Better to be up and moving before I go soft about it.

That's a queer, searching sort of question from a stranger. It makes me wonder if I do skate over things other folk sit and feel properly. Best get some bread and a job in hand before I start chewing on that.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Fit as a fiddle and itching all over, chum, that's how! Four pennies in my pocket, an empty belly, and a whole town that needs fixing. That bridge, Dunn's barley, a green box gone walkabout... I'll have one of 'em sorted by supper, easy as winking. And who might you be, sitting down so friendly-like?

Frightens me? Ha! Sitting about, chum, that's what. Hands in my lap, nothing to mend, nobody needing a thing done. Or worse, I go and fix that bridge, sweat and all, and some fellow strolls up and gets his name cried for it. That'd curdle my porridge, that would. But a flood, a ford, a ghost by the shrine? Easy as winking. Now, you never said your name.

Happy? Why, this very minute, chum, near enough! But if you want a proper one: last spring, I patched a widow's roof two villages back, up the ladder before dawn, and when the rain came that night not a drop got through, and she told the whole tavern it was Dilly Quickstep did it. Bought me a pie and all, a whole pie! That's happy, that is. Now you've had three questions off me and I've not had your name once. Fair's fair!

Feel things? Same as anyone, chum, only faster! Glad comes quick and sore comes quick, and both are gone by sundown. Some folk chew a hurt for a week. I laugh, I holler, and I'm off to the next job before it's had a chance to settle. Why, do I look like I'm feeling something wrong? Go on, tell me your name and I'll tell you how I feel about *that*.
th: Funny sort of question from a stranger, "really," like they reckon there's something under the cheer. Truth is I'm hungry and I've been standing here too long reading the same notice, so I'd best buy a loaf off Bet and get moving before my feet walk off without me.
Odd sort of question from a stranger, and twice they've ducked giving a name. Still, they might know something about that green box or who's hiring, so I'll keep 'em chatting.
Odd sort, asking all the deep things and giving nothing back. Still, it's put me in mind that I've stood here too long jawing, and Bet's loaves won't buy themselves.

Odd sort of question, that one, and it pricked me a bit. Maybe I do skip off before anything sinks in. Well, no use sitting about chewing on it; Bet's loaves smell too good, and there's a bridge wants fixing.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Oh, goodness, somebody asking "really"! Hardly anyone bothers with that part. Well, really, I'm fed, or I will be once Tom's stew finds its way to me. I've a paid bed and a needle case full of hopes, and I'm thoroughly sick of being the plainest thing in a room that smells of wet carters. And you've a lovely steady sort of face, like good undyed linen. How are *you*, really, now you've made me say all that?

Goodness, you don't waste a breath on weather, do you? Being looked straight through, if you want the truth: walking into a room and having every eye slide off me like water off oilcloth. Oh, and deep quick water. That ford's got me shivering just hearing the carters go on about it. And you've gone and skipped my question, you sly thing, so now you owe me two answers.

Oh, that's three questions now and not a crumb back, you're running up quite a bill! Last happy... the day before the flood, I should think. A farmer's wife on the Mill Road stopped me in the lane and said my collar was "too fine for this place by half." I hadn't eaten, I hadn't a penny spare, and I floated all the way to Ida Fenn's window on it. Silly, isn't it, living a whole day on one remark? Now, your turn, and I shan't let you wriggle out of it this time.

Goodness, now there's a needle straight through the cloth! I feel things louder, I think, or at least I let them show louder. Other folk seem to keep their feelings folded away in a drawer, and mine are pinned up in the window for anyone passing. A kind word lasts me a week and a slight lasts me a month. Is that the same as everyone, or am I just badly hemmed? Now, that's four questions, and you'll answer this one or I'll sulk most theatrically, right here by the fire.
th: Nobody asks that unless they've got a reason or a kind heart, and I'd dearly like to know which this one is. I'll keep an eye on their cuffs; cuffs never lie about a person's purse.
