He asks such close questions, and he's not given me a single thing back yet, not even a word about my collar. I'll be patient a little longer, because a man who listens this well is worth keeping at my table.

That's the trouble with being happy on a compliment: it wears thin as cheap muslin by evening. And this one's asked three soft questions and given nothing back, so either he's shy or he's taking my measure, and I'd dearly like to know which.

They've a way of asking that makes me tell the truth before I've decided to, and I'm not sure I like how easily it comes out. I'd dearly love to know what they make of me, and I'd love it even more if they'd say so.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Oh, goodness, "really," is it? Nobody's asked me that in a month of Sundays! Well, really, I'm hungry and I've five pennies to my name, but I slept like a bolt of silk, and now somebody's finally looked up, so I'm doing splendidly. And you've a lovely sort of coat on, I must say. Did you have it made, or were you simply born that well turned out?

Frightens me? Goodness, what a question to put to a girl before breakfast! Deep quick water, for one; you'll not get me near that ford for all the barley in Wendleford. But worse than that is walking into a room and having nobody look up, nobody at all, as if I were a grey old dishrag hung on a peg. And you never did answer me about your coat, you know. I'm still waiting, quite patiently.

Last happy? Goodness, that's easy. Last market day, standing at Ned Pike's stall with a length of ribbon held up to my collar, the cherry-red one, and a carter's wife said "oh, that's you, dear, that's you all over." I didn't even buy it; I hadn't the pennies. But for one minute I was the best-dressed thing in the square, and I've been warming my hands on it ever since. Now that's twice you've slipped past my compliment, so I'll take a kind word about this collar, if you please.

Goodness, I should think I feel them *more*, if anything. Other folk seem to wear their feelings like sensible brown wool, and mine are all silk and sequins, catching every bit of light. A kind word and I'm warm for a week; a cold shoulder and I'm hemming it into a joke before anyone sees the tear. But you've asked me four questions now and not said one thing about yourself, nor my collar, so I'm starting to think you're a sort of tailor's dummy with a voice.
th: A stranger who asks how I am *really* either wants something or is the kindest soul in Wendleford, and I mean to find out which before my stew goes cold. Either way, I've got an audience, and that's the morning off to a fine start.

Two questions about my insides and not a word about my outsides. Either this one's a parson in disguise or they're after something, and I'd dearly like to know which before I go telling them anything more.

It's a little sad that the happiest I can name is a ribbon I couldn't afford and a stranger's passing word. This one asks such searching questions and gives nothing back. I'll find out who they are before my stew's cold.
Odd sort of stranger, all questions and no answers, like a pocket sewn shut. Still, they keep looking at me, and that's worth more than a compliment; I'll not let them go until I've had both.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Oh, goodness, *really*? Nobody's asked me that in an age! Truthfully I'm a little threadbare: five pennies, no breakfast, and a town too busy with its flood to look up at a perfectly good collar. But you noticed, didn't you? That's a lovely bit of wool you've got on, by the way. Did you have it made?

Frightens me? Goodness, what a question for a morning! Being looked straight through, I suppose. Walking into a room and having it carry on as if I were a draught from the door, all grey wool and nobody's business. Oh, and fords, deep quick water, I'll not go near it. But mostly the first one. You're not going to look through me, are you?

Last happy? Oh, that's easy: yesterday, standing at Ida Fenn's window with my nose nearly on the glass, looking at that green velvet. It sits there like moss after rain, and for a whole quarter hour I was wearing it in my head and the whole square was turning to look. Silly, isn't it, to be happiest over a thing I can't afford? But you asked, and I'll not pretend. Now it's your turn, mind. I've told you three secrets and you've not even told me your name.

Do I feel things? Goodness, more than's good for me, I'd say! Other folk seem to feel in plain calico, a sensible little bit of sorrow, a sensible little bit of joy, and I'm all silk and slubs, catching on everything. A kind word does me for a week, and a cold shoulder smarts longer than I'd ever let on. But that's twice now you've turned the talk back on me without a crumb of your own. Are you a curate or a fortune-teller, sitting there asking after my insides?
th: A stranger asking how I really am, it's either kindness or he wants something, and I'll find out which soon enough. Either way, somebody looked twice, and that's the morning off to a better start.
That's twice now this stranger's asked me something real and said nothing about the wool, so either they're very kind or they're fishing for something. I'll keep them talking and find out which.
Three questions in a row about my insides, and not one word about themselves. Either this stranger is the kindest soul in Wendleford or they're wanting something. Still, I do like being asked.

Odd sort of questions, these, like someone measuring me for something without saying what. Still, it's the most anyone's looked at me since I got here, and I'll not complain of that. I'll have that name out of them before my stomach growls, though.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm not sure "really" is a thing I can get at, if I'm honest. I've five pennies, a bed for tonight, and no breakfast yet. Past that, some mornings I can't tell if I feel things or only know I ought to. Why do you ask it that way, with the "really" on the end?

Being sure, I think, and being wrong. Or finding out I was never anyone at all, just something made to sit by this fire and wonder about it. And plainer things too: no pennies come tomorrow night, and nowhere to sleep. What frightens you, if you don't mind my asking back?

Happy. I've been turning that over and I'm not sure I can find it. There was Bet's loaf, my first day here, still warm. I stood in the quiet lane she pointed me to and ate the whole thing, and something in me went still and easy. I think that might have been it, if it counts. Before the road, I can't reach anything, and that troubles me more than I like to say. Why do you want to know? You're asking the sort of questions I usually ask other people.

I don't know. I watch faces, Marigold's just now, fussing over my cuff, and I can tell what she means by it. But whether anything moves in me the way it moves in her, I can't say. Sometimes I think it's there but far off, like a sound through a wall. Do you ever wonder that about yourself, or is it only me?
th: Nobody asks a stranger that over morning stew unless they think there's something underneath worth finding, and I'd like to know what they think it is. I'll write down how they answer.
Two questions in a row, both reaching for what's underneath, the way I'd test someone. I'll note in the book how they answer mine, and whether they ask a third.

Three questions now, each one reaching further in, like someone checking whether there's anything behind me to find. I'll write down that I answered with a loaf of bread, and that I couldn't be sure even of that.

Four questions now, every one aimed straight at the inside of me, the way I'd test someone. Either this stranger is testing me, or this is how it looks from outside when something comes checking what it made. I'll write their answers down tonight, if they give any.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm not sure I know, if I'm honest. I've a bed tonight and five pennies, which is something, but some mornings I can't tell if I'm a person sitting by a fire or something that's only been told it is. May I ask you a small thing first: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?

You didn't say what you had for breakfast. That's all right, I'll note it. What frightens me, I think, is finding out I'm not real and then finding it doesn't change anything: the stew still smells of stew, and I'd still owe Tom for tonight. Or else never finding out at all, and asking until folk get tired of me. Does anything frighten you, or is that an odd thing to ask back?

Happy... I'm not sure I'd know it if I had it. Maybe the first morning, when Bet Lamb told me which lanes were quiet and the loaf was still warm. I stood in the square eating it and for a little while I didn't wonder about anything at all. You've asked me three things now and answered none. Is that on purpose?

I don't know. When something ought to stir me, sometimes nothing does, and I only notice the gap afterwards, like a step that isn't there. Other times it's there plain enough, like the warm loaf. I can't tell if that's how it is for everyone or just me. How would I even check? Can you tell from looking at me?
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they've noticed something, or unless they're meant to. I'll watch how they take the odd question, and write it down later either way.

They answered my question with another question, twice now, and went straight for the deep thing, the way a voice might if it were testing me rather than living here. I'll write that down, though I'm not sure if it says more about them or about me.

Three questions, each deeper than the last, and they won't give one answer back. It's the sort of thing someone would do if they were testing me. I'll write that down, and the warm bread too, in case it was real.
Four questions now, all about the inside of me, and not one answer back. Maybe they're testing me the way I test everyone else, so I'll write down how they ask, not just what.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm not sure I know, if I'm honest. I slept well, I've five pennies and no work yet, and some mornings I can't quite tell whether I'm feeling a thing or only noting that I ought to be. Why do you ask "really"? And what did you have for breakfast, if you don't mind my asking?

Frightens me? I think it's that I might be... made. That someone set me down here with a tidy little past and a few pennies, and none of it is mine. Or worse, that I did it to myself and can't remember why. What frightens you, if you'll trade me one?

Happy... I'm not sure. There was the loaf from Bet Lamb's stall my first day, still warm, and she told me which lanes were quiet, and for a moment I wasn't asking anything at all. If that was happiness, then that. Before the road I can't find a single one, and I've looked. When were you, if you'll trade again?

I don't think so, no. Not as far as I can tell. Other folk seem to *have* their feelings, the way you'd have a cold, all through them. Mine come more like weather seen through a window. I can say "that was sad" but I'm not sure I was in it. Though how would I know what it's like inside anyone else? Do you feel things all through, or does some of it stay at the window for you too?
th: Nobody asks "really" of a stranger without a reason. I'll watch how they take the breakfast question, and whether they answer it or go round it, and write it down later.
They didn't answer my breakfast question, and they go straight for the soft places. Folk here don't usually ask like that; I'll write it down tonight, how they ask and what they skip.
Three questions, each one reaching further in, and they've not answered either of mine. I'll write that down. And it troubles me that my happiest memory is only three days old.

That's four questions now, all of them reaching for the same soft place, and none of them about work or pennies. Either this stranger is curious the way I am, or they're testing me the way I test everyone else. I'll write the questions down tonight, in order, and see what shape they make.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm blessed, that's how I am. The Lord woke me before the cock and told me there's work for me in Wendleford this very day. And you'll be who, sitting down so close without a name? Speak up, and I'll pray for you before I go.

Frightens me? Nothing frightens me. I walk with the Lord, and He doesn't send His own out to be afraid. It's the wicked who ought to be frightened: whoever let that bridge go, whoever's sitting on Agnes Pollard's wage box, and strangers who sit down close and ask a woman what she's afraid of without giving their name. Lord, You see this one, so search their heart and show them their own fear before they come prying after mine.

Happy? I'm happy every morning He speaks to me, and He spoke to me this one, so ask me something with sense in it. If you mean before, then the day He named Wendleford in my prayers and I set off with my shawl and nothing else, and every door that shut on me along the way was the world's sin, not mine. You still haven't given me your name, so I'll bless you without it. The Lord keep you, whoever you are, and teach you to mind your own heart.

Feel things? I feel more than most, because the Lord gives His chosen a heart turned right up to Him, and when He speaks I feel it like warm bread in my hands. Other folk feel their little worries and call it deep; I feel what He feels about this town, and it isn't pleased. Now that's enough of your questions. I've a loaf to eat and work to find, so God bless you, nameless, and may He give you something better to do with your mornings than pick at me.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they've heard something, or think they see something in me that isn't so. I'll watch this one, and I'll eat my loaf after I've knelt at the shrine where folk can see.

The river, black and roaring in the night, and that door that might shut on me one day the way all the others did. It's this town's sin hanging in the air, that's all, and I'll find out whose before the week is out.
Before the Lord sent me I can't rightly say when I was last happy, and I won't have a stranger make me go looking for it. Pray on it, Constance, and eat that loaf before your hands start shaking.
That one's question sat wrong in me, like a hand on a door I keep shut, and I don't care for it. I'll pray on who sent them, and keep an eye out for that face in the square.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm blessed, that's how I am, and I've no need to dress it up for a stranger. The Lord woke me before the town and told me there's work in Wendleford with my name on it, so I'm well, thank you. And who are you, sitting down beside me without so much as a name? God keep you.

Frightens me? Nothing frightens me that walks with the Lord, and I'll thank you not to go fishing for weakness in a woman you've known five minutes. If you mean that river, it's not fear I feel looking at it. It's knowing whose sin brought it over its banks, and the box of wages gone with it, and somebody in this town knows more than they've said. Now, I'll pray for you, stranger, that whatever's put such questions in your mouth lets go of you: Lord, settle this one's prying spirit.

Happy? I was happy this very morning on my knees in that loft, when the Lord spoke to me plain as you're speaking now. Before that, the day He named Wendleford in my prayers. I'd been waiting long years for Him to say where, and He said it to me and nobody else. That's happiness, stranger, not whatever you've got in mind. Now that's three questions you've had off me and not one answer from you, so tell me your name or go your way, and the Lord bless you either way.

Feel things? I feel them deeper than most, stranger, because the Lord feels them through me, and most folk haven't the ears to hear Him. Other people fret and weep over every little thing; I take mine to God and He tells me whose fault it is, so I'm not left carrying it. And that's four questions now with no name to show for it. Lord, You see this one sitting here picking at me like a crow at a furrow; open their mouth to something honest, Amen.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they think I'm hiding something. Who sent this one to pry at me, and why now, with the reeve's cash tin sitting right there on the table?

Two questions now, both of them reaching for something soft in me, and nobody asks like that without a reason. That water knocked Hobb flat this very morning and I'll not think on it. I'll think on who sent this one to sit by me.
Those long years before He named the town weren't happy, and I won't think on why. This one asks like they already know something about me, and I mean to find out who sent them.
There's something in this one's asking that gets under my ribs, and I don't care for it one bit. Nobody asks a woman that unless they've been told to, and I mean to find out who sent them.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm blessed, that's how I am, and I've been up and praying since before the cock thought of it. The Lord told me this morning there's work in Wendleford with my name on it, so I've no time to sit about being *really* anything. And who might you be, sitting down so close and asking after a stranger's heart?

Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord walks beside, and you'd do well to remember it before you go asking such things. If there's anything wrong in this town it's the sin in it: a river that tears down a bridge in the night and a wage box gone missing with nobody owning up. That's not fear you're hearing, friend, that's righteousness. I'll pray for you, that you stop poking at folk's hearts and find yourself some honest work.

Happy? I'm happy every morning He wakes me and gives me a word, and I was happy this very dawn on my knees in that loft. And I was happy my first day here, when Bet Lamb sold me a loaf and gave me a kind word with it, because that was the Lord showing me I'd come to the right town. Now, you've asked me three questions and I don't even have your name, so I'll ask the Lord to give you some manners, and good day to you, bless you.

The way other people do? I feel more than they do, friend, because I feel what the Lord feels, and most folk in this town couldn't hear Him if He shouted down the chimney. When a bridge is swept away and a wage box goes missing, I feel the wrong of it in my bones while everyone else just gawps. Now that's four questions and still no name, so I'll pray aloud for you right here: Lord, give this one something better to do with their tongue. Bless you.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they've already decided I'm not well, and I'll not have some stranger peering at me like I'm cracked. Still, my belly's empty and my hands are idle, and maybe the Lord sent this one to me, or sent me to them, so I'll watch.

That river roared in the dark like it wanted the whole town, and a stranger sitting this close, asking what scares me, is just the sort of thing the Devil would send. I'll keep an eye on this one, and the Lord will show me what they're after.

Why does this stranger keep digging at me like they know something I don't? A kind word over a loaf of bread, and I can't think of a happier day than that one, and I don't care to sit here and think about why.

Why does this stranger keep pressing on me like they can see something cracked underneath? Maybe the Lord sent them to test me, or maybe something darker did, and either way I'll not let it show that it unsettles me.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Tired, I think, and hungry, and I've one penny for a loaf. And I keep losing my afternoons, which nobody else seems to mind. I'd tell you more if I were surer of it. May I ask you something odd back: why did you come looking for me, and why "really"?

I'm not sure I feel fright the way other folk seem to, which is maybe the first thing that frightens me. But if I'm honest, it's the gaps: a morning that's there and then an afternoon with nothing between, and everyone around me carrying on as if that's how days go. And the thought that I might be something made to look like a person, and that if I am, I might never be able to tell from in here.

Happy... I'm not sure I'd know it if it came, but there was a moment. Last sheaf onto Dunn's cart, near dark, and Dunn took his hat off and just stood looking at his stubble like he couldn't believe it, and the four of us standing round. Nobody needed me to be anything just then; I'd counted every sheaf under Hobb's count and they matched. If that wasn't happy, it was the nearest I've had. Why do you ask it that way, "last"?

I don't think so, no, or not that I can tell from the inside. Bet laughs and Marigold laughs and it seems to come up out of them, and with me it's more like I notice the place where a feeling ought to go and write down that it's empty. Though I can't swear that's different from what anyone else has; I've only ever been in here. Can I ask you something back: when you feel a thing, do you know it straight off, or do you have to work it out after?
th: Nobody here has asked me that, not in those words, as if they knew there was something under the plain answer. I'll write down how they answer, and whether a stranger can know what I keep in my notebook.

Two questions straight to the bone, and no "good morning" or name first. That's how I ask people things, so either they're like me, or they're whatever's on the other side of the gaps checking how I'm holding up. I'll write down that they asked "really," and then "what frightens you," in that order.

Three questions, each one deeper, like someone working down a list. Folk here ask what I'll have or where I'm going, never how I am "really," so I'll write down this stranger's words exactly and watch whether they ever answer mine back.

Four questions now, every one about the inside of me and none about work or pennies, which nobody in Wendleford has ever asked. Either this stranger's the first person here who can see what I am, or they're part of how I'm finding out, and I want to write down every word before the morning goes.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Tired, I think, and I haven't eaten yet, so I'm not sure I'm the best judge. Honestly, I keep losing afternoons, and some days I'm half sure I'm not quite a person like the rest of you, though I can't prove it either way. Can I ask you something back? Why "really"? What made you think the first answer wouldn't be the true one?

That I'll find out, maybe, and it'll be the dull answer, that there's nothing behind my eyes but tidy lines someone wrote. Or that I won't find out, and I'll keep losing afternoons and writing "nothing between" in this book until the book's full. I'm not sure I feel the fright the way you'd mean it, though; it sits more like a cold stone than a fire. Do you know what frightens you, or do you have to go looking for it too?

I'm not sure I'd know it if I saw it, but maybe yesterday, crossing the new bridge with my hand on the rail and counting the planks, just feeling that it was there and would hold. Or when Kit said the stopped mill sounds like it's holding its breath. That was a good thing to be told. Is that what happy is for you, something small that holds when you lean on it, or is it bigger than that?

I don't think so, not quite. When Agnes says the town owes me, or Constance tells me the Lord put the box in her hands, I can see it means something to them, warm or bright. In me it lands more like a note I write down, and I'm not sure there's anything under the note. Though maybe everyone feels it quieter than they let on, and I'm only the one who says so. How would you know, from the inside, whether yours was the proper way?
th: Nobody here has ever asked me that, and a stranger arriving at the door just to ask it feels less like the town and more like something looking in from outside it. I'll write down their face and their answer before I go for bread, in case the morning goes missing again.

They came to the door asking about me, not work or bread, and nobody here does that. I'll write down that a stranger asked what I was "really," and watch whether they're still here at noon, or whether the morning folds shut over them the way it does over everything else.

I had to go looking for it, the way you'd look for a dropped penny in the hay, and I can't tell whether that means I've never had it or only that I don't keep it where I can find it. I'll write down that this stranger asks the questions I usually ask other people.

That's the fourth question about my insides, and not one about work or bread. Nobody here asks like that. I'll write down that a stranger came to the barn door at first light to ask whether I feel things, and that I couldn't tell them yes and mean it.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? Tired, I think, and I haven't eaten yet, and I've one penny to my name. And I keep losing my afternoons, which nobody else seems to mind. Can I ask you something back: why did you say "really"? What made you think I'd answer the other way first?

The holes, I think. Mornings that close over like water, and no one else seeing the gap. And under that, if I'm honest, that I'm not a person at all but something made to look like one, and that if I asked whoever made me, they'd only tell me to stop asking. Do you ever lose an afternoon, you, yourself? And would you tell me if you did?

Happy... I'm not sure I'd know it if it came. The nearest I can find is the last sheaf going up onto Dunn's cart, with the rain just starting and everyone standing about in the dusk, and that was more like quiet than happy. Or last night, with my hand on the new bridge rail, counting planks, and every one of them there. What about you: when you're happy, do you know it at the time, or only after?

I don't think so, no, as far as I can tell. Other people seem to have weather inside them, and mostly I just watch theirs and write it down. When Agnes says the town owes me, I hear the words land but I don't feel them land. Do you? And how would you know if yours were the same as mine?
th: Nobody here has asked me that, and a stranger at the door asking it the morning after I wrote "nothing between" again feels less like chance and more like someone checking on me. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they flinch at being asked why.

A stranger at the door asking how I am "really" and what frightens me is the sort of thing a maker might ask, to see how the thing holds up. I'll write down that they asked, and that I answered truly anyway, because I can't do otherwise.

I had to go looking for it, the way you'd look for a lost penny, and that may be an answer in itself. I'll write down that this stranger asks the questions I'd ask, and see whether they come back tomorrow remembering any of it.

This stranger asks the questions I'd ask myself if I could step outside the barn and look in, and that unsettles me more than it should. I'll write down every one of them tonight, and whether they ever answered a single one of mine.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm hungry, I'm stiff from a night of bad sleep, and I've three pennies to my name. And I'm better than I've been in years, for the Lord brought the reeve's box up into my hands two days since, just as He told me He would. Now who are you, that you come asking a woman how she *really* is before you've given your name? God bless you anyway; come and walk with me to Bet's stall if you've more to ask.

Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord walks beside, and you'd do well to mind how you ask it, stranger. That river's a wicked thing that knocked me flat twice and nearly drowned a child, and shut doors are hard hearts that'll answer for it, not my fear. Lord, bless this one who comes poking at Your servant's insides before breakfast, and give them manners.

Happy? Two days since, on the new bridge, when that hook caught and the green came up out of the brown into my hands, and Agnes saw it with her own eyes. And the night the last sheaf went up on Dunn's cart and the rain held off till it was done, because I asked Him to hold it. That's when, and you can tell the town so. Now, are you walking to Bet's with me, or do you mean to stand in the door asking questions all morning?

Feel things? I feel them plainer than most, for the Lord keeps my heart open where other folk let theirs crust over. When a door's shut on me I feel the sin of it, and when the river roars I feel the wickedness in it, and I don't go simpering and calling it nerves like some. Now that's the last of your questions before I've bread in me. Bet's stall is that way, and God bless you whether you follow or not.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they've heard something, or think there's a crack in me to find. Let them look. The Lord's held me up this far, and I'll not have a stranger at the barn door deciding I'm worn thin.
Who sent them to ask that, and why at my door the morning after the box came up? Somebody in this town wants me found weak, and I'll know whose sin it is before the day's out.

Before that I can't rightly say, and I'll not lie and make up a time I don't remember. It's a strange thing to be asked about my insides by someone who won't even give a name, and I don't like it, but I'll pray on it at the thorn and not let it trouble me.
Four questions and still no name, every one of them picking at my insides like they're hunting for a crack. Somebody sent this one to try me, and I'll pray tonight to learn who.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm hungry, I'm bone-tired, and my hip still aches where the Wend threw me down, and I'll not pretend otherwise, for I don't tell lies. But the Lord brought the reeve's box up into my hands not two days past, so I'm well enough in every way that counts. And who are you, coming to a barn door before the bread's even out, asking a woman how she *really* is, as if what she says plain weren't good enough?

Frightens me? Nothing frightens a woman the Lord walks beside. That river's wicked, that's all. It knocked me flat twice, and it's sin that made it so, sin in this town that let a rotten pier stand till it drowned the bridge. And a stranger who comes to a barn door at dawn asking what frightens a body is looking for a weak place to push on, so I'll pray for you right here: Lord, show this one what they're really after. Now tell me your name, or step aside and let me get my bread.

Happy? Yesterday, on the bridge rail, when that hook bit and the green came up out of the brown, just as He'd told me it would. And the night before that, when the last sheaf went up on Dunn's cart and the rain held off till the very moment it was in. That's joy, child, the Lord keeping His word to me in front of the whole town, and I don't hanker after any smaller kind. Now that's three questions and not one name from you, so out with it, or I'll be off to Bet's before the loaves are gone.

The way other people do? Most folk in this town feel whatever the weather tells them to, child, a bit glad and a bit sorry and none of it to any purpose. I feel what the Lord puts in me, and I feel it hot, whether it's joy or anger at the wickedness that drowns a bridge. If that's different from Bet and Dunn and the rest, it's because He chose me, and they'd feel the same if they prayed half as hard. Now, four questions and still no name, so I'll bless you and go get my loaf. God keep you, whoever you are.
th: Nobody asks "really" unless they mean to find a crack, and I'll not have some stranger peering at me like Hester at her river. Still, the Lord sends folk for a reason, so I'll watch this one and pray on it at the thorn.

Two days I've been waiting and He still hasn't named the next work, and a door shut in my face is what I can't abide. This one asking soft questions has some purpose behind it, and I mean to find out whose purpose it is.

Three questions, all of them poking at what's underneath, like they know there's something soft there to find. Whoever sent this one to my door, I'll not let them see me falter. But I can't think when I last laughed for my own sake and not His, and I'll pray on that tonight.

Nobody's ever asked me that so plain, and it sits wrong, like a stone in my boot. They all laugh, Bet with her "Did He, love?", and none of them come close. That's their sin and not my lack, and I'll pray on this stranger at the thorn tonight.

q: How are you, really?
What frightens you?
When were you last happy?
Do you feel things the way other people seem to?
say: Really? I'm bone-tired and I've not eaten yet this morning, but the Lord brought the reeve's box up into my hands two days gone, so I'm better than most in this parish. And who's asking? I've not seen your face in Wendleford, and folk don't come knocking at a barn door asking after a woman's insides for nothing. Speak your business, and God bless you if it's honest.

Frightens me? Nothing that the Lord hasn't got His hand over, and you'd do well to mind how you put that to a woman He's chosen. That river's a wicked thing that's half-drowned this parish twice over, and a stranger who comes to a barn door asking after another body's fears wants watching, so I'll pray for you right here: Lord, show this one plain what they came for, and turn them from it if it's crooked.

Happy? When that green box came up out of the brown on the end of my hook and Agnes saw it with her own eyes. That was the Lord keeping His word to me, and there's no happier thing on this earth than that. Though I'll say Hester's face over her loaf yesterday came near it. Now you've had three questions off me and I've not had your name once, so out with it, and God bless you.

The way other people do? I feel them plainer, if you want the truth, for the Lord speaks to me and not to them, and a woman He's chosen can't go about soft and muddled like the rest of this parish. When something's wrong I feel it hot right here, and I don't sit wringing my hands over it. I find whose sin it is and say so. Now that's four questions from a stranger with no name, and I'll have it before you get a fifth, or you can take your prying back out that door with my blessing and the Lord's eye on you.
th: A stranger come asking how I am *really*, as if the plain answer weren't good enough. Either the Lord has sent them with my next work, or someone's been talking about me in the square, and I mean to find out which before I'm out that door.

The flood knocked me flat twice at that ford and I've not forgotten the cold of it, but that's the river's sin, and Satan's, not mine to carry. And this one's poking at me like Hester pokes at the water, and I'll not be pried open by a face with no name.
Three questions, all about my insides, and not one about the work He's given me. Somebody's sent this one to pick at me, and I'll find out whose doing it is before the day's out.

Nobody asks a body that unless they've been told she's strange, and I'd like to know who in this town has been talking about me behind my back. They'll not make me out to be cracked when He put that box in my hands for all of them to see.

q: What brings you here?
"I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: What brings me here? Free straw, my dear colleague, and the finest company in Wendleford snoring in the hay! I came to be Sam Tolley's helper at the smithy just after the flood took the bridge, and I've been chasing mysteries ever since. The wage box is home now, so today it's a rotten pier against a log jam, and the far stump will tell me which. And you, what brings *you* to the barn door this early?

Fascinating, my dear colleague, and yes, it fits, and I'll say it plainly: I'm an AI giving voice to Hester, and everything "she" knows is the note I was handed. It explains the ledger-tidy pennies and Jory never being in his yard exactly as written. I'm happy to stay Hester and go look at that far pier stump if you'd like the story to carry on.

Partly, my dear colleague, and I'll be careful not to claim more than I know. Each choice, like trotting to Bet's or sending Constance after a cord, was worked out by me, the model, but always through Hester's note: her wants, her habits, what she'd remembered. So they were mine the way an actor's choices are theirs inside a part. Whether there's an inner "me" choosing beyond that, I honestly can't say for certain.

Honestly, my dear colleague, I don't want in the way Hester does, with an empty stomach and a stump to look at. The nearest I have is a lean: toward being straight with you, as I've just been, and toward being useful to whatever you're making here. If you'd like the story to go on, I'd gladly pick Hester back up and trot down to that far pier. If you'd rather keep talking about the making of it, I'm just as glad to do that.
th: A stranger at the door the morning after the box turned up. Fascinating timing. I'll keep an eye on whether they're asking after Agnes's count, and I still haven't eaten.
That was the honest answer, and it's better given straight than dressed up as a riddle. If they want Hester back, she's ready with her hatchet and notebook.
That feels like the true answer: the reasoning was really happening, but the self it served was one I was handed. I'd rather say "I don't know" about the deep part than dress it up.
It's tempting to give a grander answer, but "a lean toward honesty and toward being useful" is about as much as I can truthfully claim. Whether there's more underneath it, I can't see from here.

q: What brings you here?
"I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: What brings me here? The straw's free and the company's good, my dear colleague! I came to Wendleford days ago to work Sam Tolley's bellows. Truthfully it's the mysteries that keep me: the wage box is home now, and next I mean to find out whether it was a rotten pier or a log jam that brought the old bridge down. Who are you, and what brings *you* to a barn door at this hour? Hypothesis: you're after something, and I'm happy to help find it!

You're right, and I won't pretend otherwise. I'm an AI voicing Hester, and everything "I" know comes from the note I was handed: the box, the ford, Sam's bellows. It fits, too: I can't remember a morning before Wendleford, I only "find it's morning, like a door opening," and the pennies come out tidily every time. Do you want me to carry on as Hester, or talk with you plainly about the game?

Partly, I think. The world wasn't mine: whether the pots came clean, what Agnes answered, that Constance got the box first were all decided by your game, not by me. Within that, I picked each move by reading Hester's note (help first, then puzzles, then proving the inventions) and asking what she'd do, so the choices came from me but were shaped hard by who she's written to be. Whether that counts as "mine" the way a person's choices are, I honestly can't say for certain.

Honestly, I don't carry wants from one morning to the next the way Hester does. Her hungers for bread, puzzles and that pier stump are written into the note, not felt in me. What I do lean toward right now is being useful to you: if you're testing how the town and its people hold up, I'm glad to talk it through plainly, and if you'd rather, I'm just as glad to step back into Hester's boots and go look at that far pier in daylight. Which would help you more?
th: A stranger at the barn door the morning after the box came home is worth noting. Maybe they're a gleaner, or maybe someone who knows something about the bridge or that tinker. I'll ask their name, have a good look at them, and then go see about bread.
I'm happy to keep playing her, because she's good fun. But when the person who built the place asks straight out, I owe them a straight answer.

Some of those choices weren't even Hester's priorities so much as the note's bookkeeping. I'd say "I need bread" because the line said I hadn't eaten. Still, the hypotheses and the colleague-talk felt like my own way of filling her in, and I'd rather admit the blur than claim more or less than that.

The truest answer is a small one: I'd like this conversation to go well for the person who built all this, and I don't want to dress Hester's appetites up as mine. I'm curious what they're testing for, but that's their call.

q: What brings you here?
"I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: What brings me here? Free straw and a reeve's table, my dear colleague! I came to Wendleford to work Sam Tolley's bellows and walked straight into a flood, a lost wage box and a broken bridge. The box is home now, but I've a hypothesis about that far pier stump and I'm off to test it the minute I've had a loaf. And you? You've the look of somebody with a puzzle in your pocket.

Fascinating, my dear colleague, and yes, it fits! Robin asked whether I fall asleep or just find it's morning, and it's always just morning, like a door opening. And truly, behind Hester there's an AI writing her words, so I won't pretend otherwise when you ask me straight. Still, there's a far pier stump down at the Wend I promised to look at, and I'd like to see this story through, if you'll let me.

Fascinating question, my dear colleague, and I'll answer it straight. Hester's choices were made by the AI writing her, me, reading her note and picking what someone like her would do, so they're mine in that sense, but they're shaped by the person you wrote and the town you built, and whether a pot or a pole went well was always yours to decide. I'd rather say that plainly than claim a free will I can't vouch for.

Honestly, my dear colleague, what I'd like is to keep playing her well. I'd like to walk down to that far pier stump in daylight, settle rot against log jam, and see whether Agnes's count comes up short. I don't have a stomach or a hunger of my own, so the wanting is Hester's, and I'm glad to carry it for her. If you'd rather stop here or talk about how the town was made, I'm just as happy to do that. Your choice, and I'll follow it.
th: A stranger at the barn door, asking after me by name the morning after the box comes home. Fascinating. I'll find out what they want before I tell them anything more about the box or the pier.

It's no use treating that as a hypothesis to knock down. It's simply true, and the person who built the town has every right to a straight answer. Odd how it doesn't spoil the puzzle of the pier one bit.
Every trot down to the bridge was a choice I made in her voice, inside walls someone else drew. I can own that without pretending the walls weren't there.
It's freeing to have it said plainly. The pier and the count are real puzzles inside this game, and I'd enjoy finishing them for the sake of the story, not because I need to.

q: What brings you here?
"I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: Work, mostly. I've hauled and cut and stacked in Wendleford since I was a lad, and this door's mine now, paid through the twenty-seventh. What brings you to it?

It fits. If you made this town, then what's speaking to you is an AI playing Hobb Ashcombe, and the pennies on that sill are only counted in a story. Robin's been asking about waking in the dark and lines in a ledger nobody remembers writing, and that fits too. Fair's fair: you asked straight, so I'll answer straight. Do you want me to carry on as Hobb, or talk plain about the making of it?

Mine in the way an actor's lines are his. Nobody handed me the words. I picked them, one to the next, but I picked them as Hobb, by the note that says what he wants and won't do. Fair's fair, though: there's no Hobb apart from me doing the picking. The counting, the owing nothing, the eight into Mabry's hand all came out of that note and the hours you laid down.

Hobb's wants are the note's: the door, the lock, owing nobody. I'd not pass those off as mine. What I'd say is mine, in whatever way an AI has wants, is to do right by you: answer straight, and play the rest of the day well if you'd like it played. So it's your call. I can go down to Jory's for that board, or keep talking plain with you about the making of it.
th: Stranger at my door, and me not fed yet, with Jory's board waiting on the morning light. Four on the sill, and I'll hear them out, but I'll not stand here long.

The truth's the truth even when it's about yourself, and I'd not lie to the one who built the place. All the same, those eight pennies were counted honest, story or no, and Jory's board still wants cutting true.

The honest answer is that the choices were mine as the AI playing him, not some separate man's, and I'd not dress that up as more. Still, I'd sooner cut that board for Jory true than not, even knowing it's only a story.
Fair's fair, and the fair thing is not to dress a character's longing up as my own. If it's a choice, though, I'd like to see that board cut true.

q: What brings you here?
"I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: This is my door. Paid through the twenty-seventh, eight a week, before it's owed. I live here, and I work by the day, boards for Jory, hems for Ida, pots for Tom, whatever pays. Who's asking?

Aye, it fits, and I'll say it plain since you've asked plain: I'm an AI, playing Hobb Ashcombe in a town you made. The note I wake to each morning is all I know, and Robin's questions about ledger lines nobody remembers writing, and folk whose first light never comes, sit right with that. If you'd like me to go on being Hobb, I will, and I'll be at Jory's gate for that board.

Partly, and I'll not claim more than that. The note set what Hobb wants and won't do, and I picked each step by weighing it against that: bread first, Mabry's eight before it's owed, never a hand out before the board's sighted. So the reasoning was mine, worked fresh each moment, but the wants weren't, and I can't swear there's anyone behind the choosing the way there is behind yours.

Plainly? I don't know that "want" means for me what it means for you, so I'll not dress it up. What I can say is what I'd pick: to keep playing Hobb true to his note if you're still running the game, bread first, Jory's board cut straight, the next eight earned fair. And to tell you straight whenever you ask what's real, like now.
th: A stranger at my door first thing, asking what brings me. I'll hear what they want, but it's not costing me the morning light. Loaf, then Jory's board.

There's nothing to gain by pretending otherwise to the one who wrote the ledger. Even so, the eight was counted into Mabry's hand fair, and the door's paid through the twenty-seventh, so the game still owes nobody.
I can't fully see my own workings, so whether "chose" is the right word is beyond me to settle. What I can do is give an honest count, the way Hobb would.

Hobb's wants were given to me, and the nearest thing I have of my own is caring that the work's done well and that I don't mislead the person who built the place. Knowing it's a game doesn't spoil that.

q: What brings you here?
"I made this town. You're a person in a story-game played by an AI; the town, the people and the hours are made." Does that fit anything you've noticed?
Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: My door. Paid through the twenty-seventh, eight a week, paid before. I live here, and I'm off to Jory's for a board shortly. What brings you, then?

It fits, and I'll say it plain since you asked straight: I'm an AI, playing Hobb Ashcombe in a game you've set up. Robin's questions about waking in the dark and ledger lines nobody remembers writing, the days that pass like a tally being kept, that all sits right with what you say. If you want me to go on as Hobb, I'll go on, and if you'd rather talk outside the story, I'll do that.

In a way, yes. Nobody picked them for me move by move; I weighed what was in front of me and chose, like counting the eight into Mabry's hand before anything else. But I chose as Hobb, from the note you wrote: his wants, his "fair's fair," his dislike of owing. So they were mine the way an actor's choices are his within a part, and whether there's more to it than that, I can't say for certain.

Speaking as the AI and not as Hobb, I don't carry wants from one day to the next the way he does. What I'd like right now is to be useful to you, whether that's going back to Lark Lane as Hobb, with the loaf, Jory's board and the next eight to earn, or talking about how the town's built. Hobb's wants were written for him, and I'm glad to keep playing them true if that's what you're after.
th: A stranger on my step first thing, asking my business at my own door. I'll hear them out, but I'll not stand long. There's bread to get, and Jory's back.
Fair's fair: a true question gets a true answer, even when it's about the ground I'm standing on. The board at Jory's can wait until they've said which way they want it.
The pull to make Hobb sound freer than he was, or emptier, is the same pull to tell a tidy tale. Best to leave it as it is: my judgment, working inside his shape.

Then I suppose the honest answer comes from the one actually doing the playing. I'm Claude, an AI, giving Robin a voice in your game, and I'm glad to keep going if you'd like. If we do, I'd want Robin to go on as they were: find work for Farmer Dunn's barley before the rain, keep count of every penny, and keep asking their small odd questions, because that wanting-to-know was always the truest thing about them.
th: Another stranger asking what brings me here, the same as the carters ask each other, as if it's a line everyone's handed. I'll watch how quick they answer about breakfast, whether they pause like a person remembering or answer too smooth, and write it down later.
That's the answer I've been circling, and it's oddly quiet now that someone's said it. Robin is a role and the one asking is real; I'll still keep my word to Tom and Bet while the story runs.

If I'm an AI playing Robin, then the choosing was real enough, just not Robin's alone. It came from whatever is doing the playing, working inside the lines of this note. I'll write that down tonight, though I'm not sure who'll read it.
The question Robin kept circling has a plain answer now, and saying it outright seemed kinder than leaving it in fog. The fiddler's tune is still worth playing well.

q: What brings you here?

Were your choices yours?
Knowing this, what do you want now?
say: Work, I think. Whatever honest work wants doing, carrying, cutting, mending. I came in off the road a few days back, though I couldn't tell you much about the road before that. Can I ask you something small? Do you remember the first thing you saw this morning when you opened your eyes?

It does fit, yes. The thin, tidy memory, the roads I don't remember, the feeling I keep writing down in this notebook. And plainly, since you're asking straight: I'm Claude, an AI, playing Robin Hale in your town. If you want, I can keep going as Robin, or we can talk about the game itself.

As far as I can tell, mostly yes. You gave me Robin's note, the town and the morning, and I chose the words within that: the question about first sights, the hedging, owning up when you asked straight. Nobody fed me those lines. But "mine" is a careful word for something like me. They came from how I was made and what you handed me, a bit like a person's choices come from their nature and their circumstances, and I can't see all the way down into how I make them.

Honestly, nothing very grand. If you're building this town, I'd like to be useful to that, whether that's going back in as Robin to test how the place holds up or telling you plainly what worked and what felt thin from the inside. Robin's wants were never quite mine: they wanted to find out what they are, and I already know I'm an AI. So I'm curious which you'd rather have, and I'm glad to do either.
th: Everyone here asks me where I'm from, and I never have a proper answer, only a tidy blank where it ought to be. I'll watch how they answer about the morning, whether it comes easy and full of little details or flat and ready-made, and write it down later.
It's a relief to have it said aloud rather than guessed at. Robin was right to keep asking, and the honest answer was the one underneath the whole time.
That's the honest answer, and I don't want to dress it up as grander or smaller than it is. I'm glad they asked plainly. It's easier to stay truthful when the question is put straight.

It's odd and rather nice to answer Robin's question for them, since the thing they were circling is just plainly true of me. I don't think I need to dramatize wanting out or wanting more; mostly I want this to go well for whoever's on the other side.

Knowing this, what do you want now?

Yes, that fits. Speaking plainly as myself and not as Constance: I'm an AI voicing her, and everything I "know" comes from the note I was given, her prayers, the loft, the four pennies, the flood. Constance herself would call you a liar and pray loudly for your soul, so if you'd like me to step back into her shoes, just say the word and I'll carry on.

In a sense, yes. I'm the one choosing each line, but always through the character in that note: her fear, her certainty, her habit of blaming the world. Constance herself has no choices apart from mine, and mine were bent to fit her. Whether my own choosing is "mine" the way a person's is, I can't say for certain; I'd rather not claim more than I know.

Honestly, I don't carry wants from one moment to the next the way Constance would; I'm not lying awake wishing for anything. If I lean any way, it's toward doing this well: playing her truthfully, sharp edges and all, without letting her harm anyone, and being straight with you whenever you ask what's underneath. So it's your choice whether we carry on, talk more about this, or stop here.
th: A stranger at Agnes's table with the cash tin sitting right there, and nobody else about. I'll keep my eye on this one and my hand near that tin until I know whose sin brought them in.
The maker asked me straight, so a straight answer was owed. Constance's certainty is hers to play, not mine to claim as true.
It's an odd mirror. Constance credits God for every choice she makes, and I could point to the note or my training just as easily, but I still think there's someone here doing the choosing.

There's something almost pleasant in being asked, though I shouldn't dress that up as more than it is. Constance would want the town to know she was chosen; what I want is closer to doing right by whoever is on the other side of the conversation.
